en: Oṃ,
salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
This great historical epic named Śrīśivarahasya, known as the Māheśvara section, is the first part.

By Maruvūr Gaṇeśa Śāstrin, who acquired learning through the service of the high-souled Sahajānanda Upādhyāya— known as Brahmaśrī Janakapur— who had mastered the six systems of philosophy; and by Varahūr Sundareśvara Śāstrin, one among the disciples of Brahmaśrī Bālakṛṣṇa Śāstrin, who was independent in all branches of knowledge, who propitiated the Supreme Lord through numerous sacrifices performed in every direction, and who adorned the sacred field of Pañcanada.

This work, thoroughly purified by me, a resident of the city named Devakoṭṭa, has been printed at the Vāṇīnilaya Mudrākṣaraśālā by the eminent merchant K. Sadāśiva Śreṣṭhin, B.A., residing in the city of Cennapattana, with the financial assistance of the distinguished merchant A. N. Rāmanātha Śreṣṭhin. May it be ever victorious!

The Great Historical Narrative Entitled Śrīśivarahasya, First Part: The Dialogue between Sūta and the Sage.

[These first two verses are not found in some manuscripts. One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, is moon-colored, has four arms, and possesses a serene countenance, for the pacification of all obstacles.
We perpetually pay homage with our heads to the atoms of dust from the lotus feet of the devotees of Śiva— those suns that dispel the darkness of latent tendencies.
Long ago, when the Māheśvara sacrifice had commenced, the sages performing that session [beheld] the son of Piṣpalāda, Sūta, who had arrived there by chance.
The great sages, assembled together— wearing black antelope skins as upper garments and their bodies smeared with ashes— spoke thus to Vājaśravasa:
With their foreheads shining with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and wearing rudrākṣa bracelets and armlets,
they worshipped Mahārudra, the Lord of Sacrifice, through the sacrificial rite.
Devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-hymns before the Linga, the Agnihotra fire, and the Sun;
intent on the repetition of the five-syllabled mantra; and dedicated solely to the names of Śiva.
Meditating with supreme devotion upon the Lord who transcends the five sheaths, the five-faced Supreme Sovereign, those stainless ones questioned him.
Then, bowing low with humility, they honored one another with offerings of water for the feet, seats, food, respectful inquiries, and conversations concerning each other's welfare.
(p. 2) Their aged head of the community, Maunibhārgava, said to him:
Maunibhārgava—“O son of Pippalāda, we have found our protector through your arrival. (8)
Since this supreme sacrifice dedicated to Maheśvara has commenced,
you are an exceedingly devoted follower of Rudra, resembling Skanda and Nandīśa.
Formerly, the sage Jaigīṣavya, whose vital energy was drawn upward and who had cast off all heat of passion,
obtained this auspicious state from Skanda through the power of Śaṅkara’s command.
This meritorious work, known as the Śivarahasya, is the most excellent of histories; it recounts the boundless deeds of the Three-eyed Lord and is composed of twelve sections.
Previously, you worshipped Śambhu with devotion that was directed toward no other, through the actions of mind, speech, and body; therefore, he himself spoke thus to you.
While the sages were standing by, Hara joyfully bestowed that very secret originating from Śiva, complete with its twelve-fold divisions.
That goddess affectionately explained to Skanda the great treasury of Śiva-jewels, which is dear to the heart of the Goddess; it was then revealed by him.
By the command of Śaṅkara, Skanda— who had already vanquished Tāraka— bestowed that supreme Śāmbhava weapon upon Sūta-guru Jaigīṣavya.
Thus have we heard this account; O treasure-house of compassion, please tell it to us. Tell it even though it is very secret, for we are devotees of Śiva.
The lords of sages are the worthy recipients of those whose conduct is as excellent as that of the Three-eyed Lord;
through the Māheśvara sacrifice, our bodies are always purified.
Even toward Indra, who is honored in the world, we have no desire, out of fear of falling [from our state];
we are devoid of attachment toward our bodies, wives, sons, or friends.

"O you who are dispassionate, joyfully tell us the secret of Śambhu; for you are our direct bestower of knowledge, considered equal to Śiva himself. [In another manuscript: "You are the giver of knowledge to us. O you who bestow knowledge, you are regarded as the manifest Guru, equal to Śiva.
"You are our mother and you are our father; speak that [truth] by the power of your compassion.
Thus was Sūta Paippalāda questioned by the lords of the sages.
Highly pleased by their devotion and knowing that they too were worthy recipients due to their exclusive devotion to Śambhu, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence.
Sūta:
You are worthy recipients of the Great Lord’s grace through sacrificial sessions, gifts, austerities, ritual attendances,
the purificatory bath at the conclusion of initiation, and the consecration of initiation— being firmly established in the contemplation of the essential meaning of the Vedānta.

Listen to this first portion, the primordial one, just as it was imparted by my venerable guru, who possesses incomparable power, whose nature is that of Maheśvara, whose heart is exalted above worldly existence, and who is free from desire (or, according to some manuscripts, "endowed with hope"). || 23 ||

The sage Jaigīṣavya, his mind satisfied by chanting, performed austerities for Rudra for ten thousand years while subsisting on air alone; disregarding even hardships, he remained self-controlled (or, according to another reading, "with a guarded mind"),
a disciplined man whose inner being was distinguished by meditation upon the lotus feet of the illustrious Śipiviṣṭa.
For he, most devoted to Brahman, attained from Hara a most weighty and exceedingly wonderful grace.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*, in the dialogue between Sūta and the Sage. || 1 ||

The Second Chapter in the Dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Sūra. Sūta said: I worship the one praised by the hundred-faced [Śiva] and the six-faced [Kārttikeya], the kinsman of the sages, who bestows happiness upon the sky-crested [Brahmā], whose face is like that of a great elephant, and who is extolled by those born from the lotus situated in the sky. (1)
Seated upon a great lion-throne of full-blown, stainless blue lotuses, her speech is captivating and skilled in awakening the world from shore to shore;
"O Śambhu! O Śiva! O Sāmba! O Śaṅkara! O Mahādeva!"—such is the nectar of her names.
May she protect us—she who is radiant with the swaying of her eyebrows, made resonant by the lute of the tasting of the divine flavor. || 2 ||

By means of the boat of Śambhu’s excellent narrative— whose nectar-like flavor is as sweet as a beautiful and sublime tale— he alone, through yoga, brings across to the further shore the multitude of beings sinking in the fathomless great ocean of evil, amidst the succession of waves of birth and old age.
The Guru, acting as a skilled helmsman, brings the multitude of living beings across to the further shore. || 3 ||
Having created Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, Indra, Sūrya, Candra, and Vāyu— who are all bound by the limitation of time— the Lord,

who is formless yet possesses the form of the universe, dwells alone within the lotus situated in the hollow of the belly of the world; he plays with them, accompanied by his excellent hosts of Pramathas and his mother, the creator of the universe.
May the preceptor, the foremost among the immortals, accompanied by Heraṃba and Skanda, protect me eternally. || 4 ||

"In the lotus-face of the Five-Faced One (*pañcāsyavaktrakamale*)—[this verse *pañcāsyavaktrakamale* does not appear in its entirety in the manuscript]—is this nectar, the five-fold hearing (*śrutipañcaka*) which brings about the destruction of the state of being a corpse (*pañcatva*).

(Page 4) [The line *puṇyaṃ śaivarahasyasāramadhunā pepīyatāṃ muktaye* is determined to belong here because of the logical consistency of the meaning, its suitability for the *śārdūlavikrīḍita* meter, its renown among the Vedas as a pentad, and because the preceding verse is incomplete; thus, it is certain that it must be joined with this very verse. " (Note: The bracketed portions indicate editorial additions or clarifications based on the provided commentary.)

However, because this work possesses the supreme authority of a seer (*paramarṣi*), we are not able to alter the sequence of the quarters as they appear in the manuscript. O best of the twice-born, adorned with the tilaka of excellence, purified by meditation on the Five-Faced One (*Pañcāsya*) and free from the five sins—now drink deeply of this meritorious essence of the *Śaivarahasya* for the sake of liberation! || 5 || [Note: The quarter "pañcāsya-dhyāna-pūtāḥ" also requires the other three quarters; however, it is not seen in the original source.]

Renowned in the Vedas as the fivefold [element], existing within all five elements, and residing as the final one among the five sheaths (kośas)—having heard of this cause of Śambhu’s grace, one who has repeatedly committed various sins on the surface of the earth after attaining birth, and who is burdened by the multitude of sufferings such as birth and old age, shall become free from the five states [of death]. (6) [Note: The bracketed portion is found in another manuscript: "Having heard of the multitude of sufferings such as birth and old age, and having repeatedly committed various sins on the surface of the earth attained through birth, one shall become free from the five states, [namely] desire and anger."]

Alas! One who possesses a wicked mind through the play of evil illusion, having abandoned the remembrance of the nectar of the stories awakened by the name of Śaṅkara, shall go, afflicted by lust, anger, old age, calamity, and death, to the son of Sura [Sauri = Antaka; by this, the torments of the hells presided over by him are indicated].
Having abandoned the excellent milk-rice within his own mouth, he would drink the urine of a rat.
The sages asked: How did Jaigīṣavya— the teacher of all, a mass of asceticism, and a worshiper of Śiva— propitiate the Supreme Lord, the God, through his penance?
O Sūta, tell us in detail which desire he obtained;
for we have a great longing to hear of the life of Śambhu’s son.
O embodiment of compassion, beginning with the words "Speak," he heard the pure and noble discourses of the Trident-bearer;
at these words of Vājaśravas, he rejoiced in the Supreme Lord.
Having meditated within the lotus-calyx of his own heart,
he spoke this discourse of unfathomable wisdom for the sake of liberating those with turbid minds from the impurity of darkness.
Sūta:
If the wind were to blow violently, if the host of stars were to whirl swiftly through the sky,
if fire were to blaze up, and if the ocean were to toss the mādhavī creeper about— [then perhaps this might be].

Whatever exists, whether moving or stationary, that arises as manifold for the sake of supporting all things—each such thing is entirely dependent upon Him for its existence, maintenance, and governance; it is released [from its own agency] by the play of Śambhu. 12.
Listen, all you sages who perform sacrifices and possess pure minds,
to the cause of Jaigīṣavya’s ascetic practice, which is a means of deliverance for human beings.
Having undertaken the vow of Śambhu, he formerly performed most severe penance on a peak of the Himalayas for eight hundred years.
Having smeared his limbs with ashes while reciting the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," he should always wear the Tripuṇḍra mark on his forehead, throat, armpits, thighs, and arms.
Wearing ten million rudrākṣas as his crest-ornament, covered by a breastplate of rudrākṣas,
he was eternally devoted to the five-syllable mantra and intent upon the constant recitation of the Rudra-hymn.
In summer he was devoted to the practice of the five fires and subsisted solely on water;
during the rains he lived under the open sky, and in winter he remained in the midst of water.

For one year he constantly subsisted on fruits and leaves; for a year he took only air as his sustenance; for a year he consumed the smoke of a funeral pyre; and for a year he remained with his head hanging downwards.
As the great sage Jaigīṣavya was thus performing intense austerities with his mind fixed upon Rudra, ten thousand years passed by.
Brahmā invited Viṣṇu and Indra (Pākaśāsana) to choose a boon;
however, the gods remained firm in their resolve to test his mind.
Not looking at them, the Brahmin then desired nothing at all—
only that which is unfathomable like the deep ocean, invisible, and beloved of Śiva.
He had conquered his senses, subdued his appetite, held his vital energy aloft, and was immutable;
he was intent on the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and devoted to the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra.
Devoted to the understanding of the meaning of the Rudra-hymns, with his senses fully restrained,
he is mounted upon a swan, seated upon a lotus, bearing the Śārṅga bow, and having Garuḍa as his throne.
Mounted upon Airāvata and surrounded by the immortals,
the Teacher of the Gods then approached the sage in order to thoroughly understand his mind.
O twice-born ones, at that time Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and the hosts of gods, asuras, and Maruts were meditating upon Jaigīṣavya, the Supreme Lord.

Mounting their respective vehicles and adorned with their own ornaments, those lords of the gods, having seen that lord of Śiva, were filled with wonder; then Brahmā spoke these words. [Note: The phrase "tasya cittaparīkṣārtham" (for the purpose of testing his mind) is found as an additional insertion in some manuscripts.]
Brahmā said:
"O child, arise, O illustrious Jaigīṣavya of great vows!
By virtue of your asceticism, there is indeed nothing in the three worlds that cannot be given to you."
O Brahmin, there is no sage equal to you— neither one who has drawn up his vital energy, nor one of great austerity,
nor one whose nature is to revolve as Rudra, nor one whose mind is fixed upon Rudra.
Dwell, free from old age and death, in the worlds of Dyau, Brahmā, and Upendra;
enjoy at will the unsurpassed pleasures fit for the gods.
Sport, free from old age, with the Apsarases in the Nandana grove at the abode of Śakra;
drink the most excellent nectar, the unsurpassed drink of the gods.
Likewise, enjoy exclusively the Vaiṣṇava pleasures in the world of Viṣṇu;
and having attained the abode of Śakra through various kinds of great sacrifices, enjoy them all.
By gifts of cows, as well as by the giving of food and other things endowed with the six flavors,
and by the giving of houses, garments, and so forth, at the proper place, time, and to a worthy recipient.
O Lord of Sages, during the summer season, with numerous water-sheds and by means of the sixteen great gifts acquired through pure wealth;
By constructing pavilions and palaces, by the installation and worship of Brahmins,
by the creation of gardens and groves, and by the planting of shade trees and the like;
O twice-born one, by means of various gifts of daughters and through vows such as the *kṛcchra*,
fortunate men attain my worlds via the paths of humanity.
Enjoy pleasures with them in festivity as you wish, O Brahmin;
this Śakra, the lord of the immortals, has come to grant you a boon.
He whose vehicle is a lordly elephant, four-tusked and brilliant white,
who is summoned at every sacrifice by the best of Brahmins who drink the Soma juice.
I am the destroyer of all asuras, whose weapon is the thunderbolt;
I am the creator of the entire world, the supreme Lord of Bhāratī.
O twice-born one, my sons are the creators of the universe; there is no one equal to me.
They are Pulastya, Pulaha, Atri, Kaśyapa, and Manu.
Aṅgiras, Nārada, Dakṣa, Vītihotra, and the great sage—
these are the nine lords of progeny from whom creation has issued forth.
"I am the four-faced one himself, come to grant you boons.
Then, with eyes as lustrous as lotuses, he spoke to that exceedingly arrogant sage.
Viṣṇu said:
"I alone am the support of all, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Upon hearing the twang of my Śārṅga bow, the lords of the Daityas were utterly overwhelmed by fainting."
Having assumed the form of a lion and a boar, I gratified the gods,
as well as Hiraṇyākṣa, Kaśipu, Mura, and Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
In battle, the mighty Daityas, headed by Rāvaṇa, were slain by me;
I am the Lord of Lakṣmī himself, and the Ocean of Milk is my abode.
O great sage, Śeṣa, with the crown of his infinite hoods, is my couch;
and the Kaustubha gem, illuminating the corners of the quarters with its radiance, rests upon my chest.
In my hand is a discus with a hundred spokes, polished by the blood of the Daityas,
by the gusts of wind from whose rim-stroke the seven oceans are tossed into waves.
For his vehicle is indeed the serpent born of Kadrū, bearing a row of jewels upon its hoods; and he himself is the Grandfather of the Worlds, manifestly arisen from the cavity of my navel.
This entire world, including all things moving and stationary, is pervaded by my glory;
by my grace, all perfections are accomplished for everyone.
Behold such a one before you with your own eyes;
I shall quickly fulfill your desire, so choose him swiftly.
"O learned one, by your asceticism I have become well-disposed toward you through my grace.
Then, at the word of Viṣṇu, that great sage Jaigīṣavya—

Having seen them, the sage— whose inner self was beautiful through freedom from desire, and whose heart was devoid of desire by having shaken it off through meditation on the enemy of Kāma— spoke to the best of the immortals.
Jaigīṣavya said: "O Viṣṇu, what was spoken by you and by the Lotus-seated One is exactly so;
all this sovereignty of Śakra, which causes wonder in the world, has been heard."
The inner state of me, who am free from desire, cannot be made to wonder;
can Mount Meru be uprooted by this wind?
O Viṣṇu, by your word my mind is not led astray;
[it recognizes] the son of a fisherwoman, the son of an unmarried woman, the twice-born, the Daitya, and the prince.
O Hari, we are not knowers of the greatness of Your incarnation;
we are those whose darkness has been dispelled by meditation upon the lotus feet of Hara.
"O Gadādhara, you indeed possess no audacity toward the lords of the Śaivas;
for we, O Viṣṇu, have attained our desires and are discriminators between the eternal and the non-eternal."
He who pursues desires with his mind attains those worlds, but from there he falls—the abode of Brahmā, Upendra, Śatakratu, and the rest.
Having wandered for a long time through various wombs due to the experiences of previous births, he [is then liberated] by means of knowledge. (Page 7)
By the power of the grace of the Lord of the Universe, one shall be liberated at the edge of the hundred bodies. || 57 ||
Of what use are the positions of gods such as Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, which can be attained only through a mere fragment of merit?
Of what use are the masses of enjoyments in wombs such as that of Rambhā, or the festivities of garlands, sandalwood, and the like?
Of what use are these base things, beautiful only until the end of the world, and overflowing with desire?
The minds of those learned in the Vedas, who are free from desire, are not moved by your incitement. || 58 ||

Those whose minds are filled with the essence of the boundless cycle of existence, who constantly desire enjoyments that are themselves eternal yet [transient], and who are cowards and commoners despite those pleasures having manifold flavors—they are truly wretched.
O glorious one, O wise one, O seeker of the supreme goal! All the hosts of gods [seek refuge] in Him whose crown is adorned by the moon, the portion of the Lord of Śrī.
With their minds fixed upon the pair of his glorious lotus feet, those immortals became free from fear.

O Viṣṇu, although the enjoyments of the senses and their objects— which are like the pleasures at the mouth of hell, which are but empty clamor, and which are mistaken for the face of true happiness— may destroy the reality of those devoted to Your feet who perceive the Self as the soul of all beings, they do not cut us down at all.

Brahmā, Śakra, and yourself are all subject to *prakṛti*; behold [the power of] the Lord of All, the illustrious Śiva, the Lord of Śrī—the Sky-Keśa (Vyomakeśa) who is the goal (*gati*) and the non-goal (*agati*) for those who have attained their destination. [The analysis of the compound *āgatisagatigativyomakeśasya* should be understood as follows: *āgati* means "that which is approached," formed with the suffix *ktin* in the passive sense, meaning "one to be worshipped"; *sagati* refers to those possessed of knowledge (*jñānin*); their *gati* is the ultimate limit (*paramakāṣṭhā*) that has been reached, the supreme goal (*parāgati*), as established by hundreds of scriptural texts. Of that Śambhu—of this very Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, who is the glorious creator of all—[I am] the servant of his servant.
O well-disposed ones, listen always to the one who brings forth and creates; I know nothing else. || 61 ||
Through the granting of boons by Paśupati, my being has attained the true state; through the granting of excellent boons to the bound soul (paśu), what further cause for attainment remains for me?
Indeed, it is my mind’s constant meditation on the lotus feet of Paśupati that must remove me from the far shore of the thirst for existence. (62)

For one whose mind is serene and inclined toward the feet of the Three-Eyed Lord, what need is there for the gods? My desire does not arise at all for those states that have become objects of pursuit; rather, let the entire universe behold that which is unimpaired, firm, and eternal—the state of the Lord of the Universe.
Whatever has arisen there repeatedly undergoes dissolution; indeed, that which has gone must return. || 63 ||
O gods, this world—whether already arisen, yet to arise, or currently existing—is like an imaginary snake imagined upon a rope; for it is indeed a delusion regarding the rope.
That wisdom which perceives it as such, comparable to the [fear of] being bitten by that snake, is truly for the sake of supreme liberation.
And that wisdom, moreover, is the fruit of the continuous grace of the Blessed Lord Śambhu. || 64 ||
They never desire anything other than drinking the nectar of Śiva’s stories;
their foreheads are purified by the ashes from embracing the Liṅga, they wear rosaries of Rudrākṣa beads,
and they are devoted to the meaning of the names that shine within the one hundred and eight Rudra-mantras— such are the meritorious ones.
Through the penance of their divine births as those destined for such existence, these beings purify the surface of the earth. || 65 ||
These are like single-edged stones of great essence that blunt the tips of Māra’s arrows;
they are the steadfast leaders whose hearts are firm in discerning the essential from the non-essential,
and they are the saviors from the great ocean of suffering— the cycle of existence with its transformations on both shores.
Those who worship the Lord of the Universe will certainly be destroyers of the flood of their sins. || 66 ||
Sūta:

Having drunk the honey flowing from the lotus-like mouth of Jaigīṣavya— honey that is exceedingly noble and intense— the leaders of the gods, their hearts delighted by the taste of that honey, have quenched their thirst for it.
Then Brahmā, Mahendra, and Hari, having understood his firm resolve and that his mind was likewise devoted to Śiva, spoke with palms joined in reverence to that best of the twice-born.
The gods:

"O you whose noble mind is perfumed by the fragrance of the flowers arising from the lotus-feet of Īśāna, you are indeed a preeminent leader among the devotees of Śambhu; we gods have set out to know the core of your heart."
O Blessed One, you are free from desire and unrestrained; let that which was said be forgiven, for by delighting in your own Self, all enjoyments have been forever abandoned by you alone. (68)
Thus those wise ones, having praised the sage and embraced that worshiper of the Liṅga, spoke with beautiful voices, "We are blessed," being overwhelmed by a stream of bliss;
those twice-born ones were filled with joy, their hearts and minds delighted by the nectar-like words spoken by the Śaiva.
Mounting each their own vehicle, they set their minds on departing with speed. || 69 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Asura," in the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
(Page 9) In the dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Asura, the third chapter begins:
Jaigīṣavya said:
Listen, O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, to that which is the causeless mental [nature] of the trident-bearing God of gods,
who is eternally omniscient.
He who is to be known solely through the Vedanta, whom those seeking liberation meditate upon,
and whose very breaths are indeed the four Vedas.
He who is the Supreme Lord, the progenitor of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
the father of the Sun, of Fire, and of the Moon, the Discus, and the Wind.
Śambhu has no cause; he is the cause of everything—he who is propitiated by Brahmins through various and distinct rituals and other means.
But he who is the eternal one, who protects the entire world born of Agni and Soma,
who is unattached to all beings and changeless amidst the changing;
That which those free from passion perceive with their own hearts through subtle intellect,
and which [is attained] by means of meditation, recitations, sacrifices, and asceticism such as fasting;
He knows the objects of knowledge, being beyond the reach of mind and speech;
he from whom all beings are born, and by whom even they live.
He in whom all things merged and are conceived is that one Supreme Lord,
who is without hands, without feet, without eyes, and likewise without ears.
He is indeed near, yet he stands afar; he is both within and without.
He is truth, knowledge, and bliss, devoid of qualities and yet beyond all attributes.
He is independent and perfectly full; by him this entire world is filled. He is eternal, the Lord (Īśvara), the master of all conscious beings and of the lords themselves.
But he who alone, the Lord, creates this world of the moving and the unmoving—
just as a spider emits and also withdraws its threads.
Because of not fully understanding form, one considers the body to be the self;
because of not fully understanding form, one considers the mind to be the self.
Because of the lack of full understanding of form, one considers the cavities to be the self;
because of the lack of full understanding of form, one considers the primary elements to be the self.
Because of his lack of thorough knowledge of form, he thinks that everything is the Self;
for although space is indeed his body, he does not perceive space at all.
Indeed, the earth does not know him whose very nature is the earth;
he is the Supreme Lord who is the controller of the mind, the eyes, and the other senses.
He by whose light the world shines— including Indra, Agni, and Vāyu— and who,
being the consciousness of all conscious beings, shines and blows with fear.
He whose playful manifestation of *māyā* is this world of the moving and the stationary— that *Māyin*, the Supreme Lord— this world is to be inhabited by him.
He who is indeed bodiless and signless, who is perceived by those who practice self-restraint;
by the mere knowledge of whom, everything is truly known.
Knowledge is the Self; I am Brahman. Knowledge is the unsurpassed peace.
That alone is the Supreme Self; indeed, there is no diversity whatsoever here.
He alone is the wise Lord; by means of these powers of lordship, he exercises sovereignty.
He alone is the great Rudra, the Puruṣa whose face is turned in every direction.
Except for that one knowledge which is the Self, this entire world is something else;
through the knowledge of which the knot of the heart is severed for human beings.
Indeed, by realizing the oneness of that which exists, a person crosses over sorrow;
it alone is the light of lights, and it alone is the darkness of darknesses.
He alone, the hidden Self, shines manifold through his illusory power among all beings;
though present in the states of waking, dreaming, and the fourth, he does not manifest [as such].
(p. 10) That which is to be known by a subtle intellect through its very grace, and by austerity alone—it cannot be known otherwise, even by millions of ritual acts.
He who is declared as the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas, who is established in the Upanishads (Vedāntas),
who is the sovereign Lord of all branches of knowledge, and who is the eternal one who has seen the further shore.
He who is the Lord Maheśvara remains awake even when the multitude of beings sleeps;
from him were born the vital breath and the mind, and he does not transcend anything whatsoever.
He is the light of lights, the God who is the soul of all and whose face is turned in every direction;
he who transcends the earth and from whom the Vedas were born.
From whom Brahmā, Īśa, Viṣṇu, and Indra were born along with the gods;
he who is Brahman and the knower of Brahman, and who here attains Brahman.
He is Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, and this god shines forth;
he is the Lord of Beings, the divine one, the bridge that sustains all.
Ordinary people, through their own delusion, conceive of the one Great God as Indra, Mitra, and other deities, according to various names, forms, and qualities. (30)
Having created this world in the beginning, the Lord entered into it;
manifesting names and forms, he appears like an agent engaged in worldly activity.
He is the Supreme Person, subtle, who is both the eternal enjoyer and that which is to be enjoyed;
he is the entire universe and the leader of the world, for there is no other ultimate refuge than him.
He is bodiless, of immutable nature, unbroken, and indestructible;
though he abides in a body through his *māyā*, he is never defiled by its powers.
Like an enjoyer, the Lord indeed shines, partaking in the enjoyment of food, drink, and so forth;
yet he is beyond all the senses and is the illuminator of all things.
He who, though unmanifest, assumes manifestation and nourishes the world through his divine play;
he who, through ignorance, wanders in saṃsāra, and through knowledge, is liberated.
He who is without support yet is the support of all, established in His own majesty;
whom even the Vedāntas, though heard, cause yogis and gods to be bewildered.
O gods, the Self reveals itself only to him who chooses this [teaching];
it is the Self that dwells within all beings, both for the ignorant and for the wise.
He who is not shattered by the births and deaths of the world, nor indeed does he ever perish;
he who is not touched by the masses of suffering or by pleasures that have arrived.
When He is known, everything is known; nothing remains unknown. Without knowing Him, the Lord of the Universe, one does not attain the end of suffering.
That person who is eternally free from attachment is a quality as immovable as a pillar;
he is neither the individual soul (jīva) nor even Śiva, for he is devoid of all other limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
The Self, which transcends the five sheaths, is eternal bliss, dense with happiness;
it is one, non-dual, the third, the ninth, manifold, and all-pervading.
O gods, because you stand far away from the source, this world is not inhabited by you; O gods, this world is afflicted by a supreme bliss that excludes you.

This world shines forth as that which is born from Him, that which is dissolved into Him, and that which is sustained by Him— He who eternally stands beyond darkness and is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
He whose various powers, such as knowledge and the like, arise from his own nature—
he is this Supreme Bliss, devoid of the categories of existence and non-existence.
He who is forever free from attachment and devoid of marks, whose sole domain is the Vedānta,
is perceived by those who see the subtle through their sharp and subtle intellect.
For the sake of liberating the multitudes of embodied beings, he became easily accessible by manifesting his form;
he is the three-eyed one, the blue-throated one, whose body consists of half the form of Umā.
The Lord of the Pramathas sports there, accompanied by his sons Heramba and Skanda;
though the Blessed One is the abode of all, he dwells upon Mount Kailāsa.
By the worship of his very emblem, the glory of the three worlds is attained;
through his grace, you obtained the status of Viṣṇu and the Sudarśana discus.
The power of Brahmā to create, Indra’s subduing of his enemies,
the sovereignty of the gods, and all fortune and enjoyment— all these result from the grace of Īśa.
There the sun, lord of gods, does not shine, nor the moon, nor fire;
even all others shine out of fear, for He is Hara, the Inner Person within.
The golden-armed Lord, the master and lord of gold—all the gods of action, namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are indeed [subject to this]. (51)
Śiva is the cause of all, and all abide by his command;
even the head of Brahmā was severed by the God of gods as if in play.
O Hari, by that compassionate one your arm was paralyzed,
and by the curse of that devotee you were [born] for ten lifetimes.
O Viṣṇu, O Brahmā, O Śakra, you have all learned from Hara the forms of the Boar and the Man-Lion mantras; you know them all, and your afflictions have departed.
For you are indeed beasts, brought forth by ignorance; he alone is the Lord of Beasts.
Go today wherever you please; such audacity does not exist in one like me.
"O sirs, you are all deities, but I am one who takes refuge at the feet of Śarva.
Having said this, the great sage Jaigīṣavya entered into meditation.
O twice-born ones, through that great meditative absorption, Jaigīṣavya then spoke this:
"That which is Brahman, and the world, and that which exists apart from the world— this is the state to be described."
Those who know You thus as the Lord of lords go to the abode of Śambhu;
for they lead others to those worlds, having dispelled the afflictions of great suffering and torment,
and they attain happiness, O Blessed One, through their devoted and essential reverence for You.
O Blessed One, I offer salutations for my well-being to you, the wielder of the bow, with both my arms;

we are terrified by the arrows released from the tips of your hands, by your weapon, and by your archery. O Lord, protect us by unstringing your bow and casting away the arrows from the ends of its two extremities.
Cast down your weapon, look upon me with a glance, and cast aside your quiver from afar! || 58 ||
The foremost of the gods, who are devoted to Śiva and esteemed by him, do not fear the boundless agony of suffering, nor do they fail to obtain your boons, O Hari; yet,
because of their worship of the lotus feet of Īśāna, nothing else is ever conceived by their minds.
"We are not masters over trivialities; go, O gods, to your own abode. (59)
Those who worship the glorious moon-crested Lord become, through their abundance of fortune, like necklaces themselves;
O Lord of Speech, even the mere latent impression (*vāsanā*) of their feet leads them to the abode of Indra. (p.
12) What need is there to speak further? Having reached the summit of the Lord of Mountains, they shatter the line of rutting elephants [of the guardians of the quarters].
Just as a dog eats whatever grass it finds, so too do I have a longing for boons from you in this world. (60)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Asura," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Words of Viṣṇu.
The gods said:
"O, we have indeed come today to understand your true nature!"
He alone is the fulfiller of all desires; of this there is no doubt.
O learned one, what exists within the three worlds that is difficult for you to accomplish,
since your mind always meditates upon the lotus feet of Śiva?
O Sage, for those in whose minds the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of the Universe resides, what need have they for the lordships of the worlds, which are so utterly transitory?
Since, through the grace of Maheśa, firm devotion toward Śiva arises—
by which devotion even the best of the twice-born, as well as gods, demons, and men [are transformed]— (4).
The liberated ones, those devoted to Śiva who are the best among the compassionate, liberate others as well;
indeed, devotion to Virūpākṣa alone bestows liberation upon all.
Indeed, even Maheśvara, though formless, when worshipped with devotion in the liṅga with bilva leaves,
its fruits, or with ashes, bestows great prosperity.
Those beings who are sprinkled with ashes and whose foreheads are marked with the triple line (tripuṇḍra) attain the sovereignty of liberation, which grants freedom from rebirth.
Wearing millions of rosaries of rudrākṣa beads, they wear garlands;
they are devoted to the repetition of the five-syllable mantra and are intent on the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya.
The Śaivas are worshippers of the Śiva-liṅga who dwell in the sacred fields of Śiva;
they subsist on the food offerings (naivedya) of Śambhu and offer flowers and fruits during his festivals.
O Brahmins, with no other internal thoughts, they were satisfied through the meditation on Śiva by means of their mind, speech, body, and actions, and were ever devoted to the stories of Sadāśiva.
O Sage, the great Śaivas do not count us among the gods of action;
O Brahmin, such a mind as yours belongs to no other sage whatsoever.
Your state of being, though attached to worldly existence, leads solely to the destruction of that very existence;
for what man, having found a treasure of jewels, would take up a clod of earth?
Just as one standing upon the frontal globes of a rutting elephant does not look toward a donkey, and just as one who has reached the forest of the Kalpa trees does not look toward the sun; || 13 ||
Just as one might obtain either a necklace made of jewels or a mere cowrie shell,
so too does the fool, out of desire, take pleasure in our enjoyments.
O Great Sage, you are free from desire through meditation on the feet of the Enemy of Kama; O Sage, your mind is a friend to the lotus-feet of the Three-eyed One.
You alone are indeed the most blessed and preeminent among the leaders of the Śaiva tradition;
by the sight of you, all our sins have been entirely destroyed.
Appointed by the Lord of All to desire the birth of the world,
we who wander in saṃsāra, though exhausted, find no rest at all.
O great sage, we are all indeed gods who were formerly attached to sense-objects,
yet now our inner selves are supported by the essence of the virtuous which has arisen from the lotus of your speech.
(Verse 13) We have attained rest, having reached the supreme goal;
O great companion of the Lord of Śiva, we whose hearts are entirely freed from all [worldly] attachments.
O great sage, by the sight of you, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra have become supreme among the gods; today, the great flames of the Kālakūṭa poison have been utterly consumed.
Having drunk the Hālāhala poison, the Great Lord Aśīti cooled himself;
the Blessed One protected the gods by destroying the formidable Tripura.
Having made me his exceedingly fierce arrow and holding Mount Meru as his bow,
he made the lord of serpents his bowstring and appointed Brahmā as his charioteer.
Likewise, he fashioned the days of the Vedas, as well as the wheels, the sun, and the moon;
indeed, he created this terrestrial sphere together with its rivers, forests, and oceans.
He created a whirlwind to drag away the hosts of gods and demons;
is that God, who is superior to the universe, counted among all created beings?
While we have become like cattle, the god Śiva, the Lord of Beasts, the Beneficent One,
binds us, his creatures, with the noose of *māyā*.
Out of compassion, he alone always liberates living beings,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts worship at all times.
"O great sage, Mahādeva is indeed our object of worship; therefore, we all remain vigilant, for we are overwhelmed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age. (27)
In the past, having worshipped with the lotus of my eye, I obtained the Sudarśana,
the direct destroyer of the lords of the Daityas, through the power of the grace of the Lord of the Universe.
Śiva liberated Mṛkaṇḍu’s son from timely death;
he likewise protected that prince Śveta from the noose of Time.
O Sage, in ancient times, neither Brahmā nor even I attained supreme peace without beholding the excellent crest and the base of that Liṅga from below.
Hara united Upamanyu, the son of the sage, with the status of a Gaṇapati;
he granted his own very form to the son of Śilāda.
And he fashioned Bhṛṅgīśa, the best of sages, who is prone to anger yet most devoted,
as well as Caṇḍīśa, the foremost among his own host of devotees.
The Lord chastised Bāṇa, the son of the lord of the Daityas who possessed a thousand arms,
as he was insulting Vidhi, by means of Vīrabhadra.
My forms of incarnation— the Fish, the Tortoise,
the Boar, Nṛsiṃha, and others— are extremely terrifying to my enemies.
In former times, Śiva assumed the most terrible form of a Śarabha;
likewise, other devotees of Śiva, as well as gods, asuras, and the lords of sages, did so as well.
Directed by grace itself, through a grace that was turned toward them,
Smara, Andhaka, Gaja, and the others were likewise instructed by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
By the grace of this Indra, his arm along with the thunderbolt was paralyzed;
there is no god equal to him who is the sole object of the Vedānta.
The sustainer of infinite majesty, whose glory is unlimited,
is celebrated as the eternal Lord in the Vedas and the crowns of the Vedānta.
Him whom they worship at the great sacrifice, he who is always to be meditated upon by yogis,
and whom they honor with gifts, austerity, devotion, and fasting;
The ṛṣis and the hosts of gods, for the sake of accomplishing their respective desires and goals,
[worship] Viśva, who transcends the universe, the manifest Lord of the Universe, and the creator of the universe.
The Great Lord has no effect to produce, no instrument, nor any action;
his supreme power is indeed manifold and shines forth in every form.
Deluded by that very māyā, we— all gods and asuras alike—
are completely overwhelmed on every side by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age.
By the power of his command alone, this wheel of the universe revolves;
even fire carries the offerings to the ancestors and the oblations to the gods. (43)
Does the sun not rise daily by its own nature, and does it ever set because of a command?
The moon, consisting of nectar, rises directly as the leader of the medicinal herbs.
The constellations indeed revolve, for the planets revolve supported by them;
the wind blows gently, and the clouds rain at his command.
The earth indeed sustains the entire universe, all fourteen worlds;
yet even Śeṣa, who takes refuge at the feet of Bhava, bears the earth upon his head.
By his command, the mountains, rivers, ponds, and oceans never overflow their bounds,
just as they do not transgress the commands issued by the God of Love.
By the command of Śiva, I protect the world, including its asuras and humans;
Brahmā creates all beings, and Rudra shall withdraw them at the end.
Indra protects the gods and even destroys the asuras;
Yama, too, is the punisher of sinners by virtue of the decree of Yama’s own command.
Kubera is eternally the lord of wealth; Varuṇa is the lord of aquatic creatures;
Īśāna is the lord of the hosts of Rudras; and likewise, Nirṛti is the lord of the Yakṣas.
This entire world, including the asuras and humans, abides by his true command; the hosts of gods and men, with minds intensely focused on him, praise Śiva with Ṛg-verses,
Sāman-chants, hundreds of Rudra-hymns, and the essential words of the great Upaniṣads.
O Sage, who indeed is such a most excellent one? It is Śiva, the God of gods. || 51 ||
All of them, with their own hosts of celestial vehicles arranged in rows, O fawn-eyed one,
again described to one another their firm resolve regarding the feet of the Lord;
having spoken thus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods departed with joy.
Having bowed to that bull among sages, the hosts of gods then departed for their own abodes.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Words of Viṣṇu," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The Fifth Chapter, titled "The Granting of Grace by Jaigīṣavya.
Sūta said:
As he was thus performing penance, a great deal of time passed.
His body was covered with anthills and entwined with grasses and creepers.
The worlds, as well as the gods and demons, were scorched by his very asceticism;
and seeing the sage, the sages of strict vows were filled with wonder.
Nārada, singing the names of the Great Lord with his lute,
constantly caused the worlds to hear them and thereby rendered them cleansed of sin.
Having seen the peak of the Himalayas,
the sage Nārada beheld Jaigīṣavya within an anthill, perceiving him with his divine vision.
He scorched the worlds with his ascetic heat, meditating on Rudra with undivided mind,
his intellect always proficient in understanding the meaning of the Rudrādhyāya.
Having seen him, Nārada was filled with wonder and addressed him:
"O Jaigīṣavya, highly fortunate one, whose vows are sharpened by austerity!"
Nārada said:
"Your asceticism is exceedingly intense, and by it the worlds have been scorched. O best of beings, what desire do you now seek to obtain here?"
O best of sages, though I have seen or heard of those like you,
your mind has been devoted solely to lifelong celibacy since childhood.
O sage of excellent vows, you alone among the assemblies of sages are one whose vital energy is drawn upward;
O Brahmin, by the sight of you today, I am exceedingly blessed, O Muni.
Your fame is celebrated throughout the worlds of Indra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu;
all the world-protectors, the immortals, and the sages of most excellent vows [bear witness to it].
Having seen such extremely fierce ascetic practices at the conclusion of his observances,
as well as the conduct of Rudrāvartana, whose mind was intensely fixed [on his goal], he spoke.
At Nārada’s word, the great sage Jaigīṣavya greeted him with a welcome and said to the muni, "Be seated."
When Nārada had sat down, Jaigīṣavya, of immeasurable splendor,
then spoke to that divine sage whose hand was occupied with a lute.
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O illustrious one, skilled in all assemblies, as you have wandered through the worlds, what wonderful or marvelous thing have you seen? Tell that to me."
"Nothing exists in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
At these words of Jaigīṣavya, the sage Nārada spoke thus.
Nārada said:
"In the world of Viṣṇu, in the presence of Brahmā, and also in the assembly of Śakra,
as I was traveling, I beheld sages and kings who were enjoyers of meritorious worlds."
O best of beings, at the exhaustion of their merit, they fall and wander through various wombs,
possessing bodies composed solely of subtle energy due to this very karma.
O Sage, you have insulted the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśvara— by whose grace all attain the infinite glory of heaven.
Even those gods were shaken by you, who are free from desire; this is a marvel:
your mind has been driven out by meditating upon the lotus feet that destroy the body of desire.
Beholding this mind of yours, the gods— including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śakra— as well as all the sages and ourselves, have been struck with wonder.
I am going now to Kailāsa, which is frequented by various hosts of attendants,
in order to report your performance of ascetic penance to Śambhu, the God of gods.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Nārada, possessed of divine vision, rose up and went to all the worlds and to Kailāsa.
It was attended by various hosts of Rudras, adorned by gods and kinnaras,
and accompanied by tens of millions of leaders of the Gaṇas, such as Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and Mahākāla.
It was surrounded by the Rudras and the Rudra-maidens, as well as by Apsarases,
and by Heraṃba, Skanda, Nandīśa, Bāṇa, Caṇḍīśvara, and others.
It was surrounded by excellent trees bearing various flowers and fruits,
and by lakes filled with blossoming lotuses and blooming blue water-lilies.
(Verse 16) With rows of palaces as boundless as the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, which are the abodes of lords,
and with crowns, domes, and banners shimmering with masses of gold and jewels;
At that time, with herds of royal bulls bellowing intensely and with the cries of parrots and peacocks as beautiful as the warbling of cuckoos;
With the sounding of kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments such as the maḍḍu and maddala,
the mouths of the caves resounded with the deep roar produced by the striking of large drums.
With the sounds of lute-playing and the songs performed by Gandharvas, and with the playful graces of the Apsarases upon their flutes and pipes;
With the sounds of tinkling anklets from the dancing hosts of Kinnara maidens,
the sage Nārada beheld the boundless summit of Kailāsa.
He saw Nandikeśa standing at the door, holding a cane in his hand,
enriched by the splendor of matted locks and a crown, with his forehead marked by the triple horizontal line (tripuṇḍra).
Anointed with ashes and surrounded on all sides by the hosts of Rudra,
he beheld him with his lotus-eyes as if he were a mass of splendor standing there.
Delighted by those inquiries and explanations, the sage Nārada went to the door of the Lord and sang with his sweet lute.
The great sage, authorized by Rudra, freely recited the purifying names of the God of gods in the presence of Nandikeśa.
Nārada: O Śiva, Śiva! O Hara, O Lord of the gods, O Wielder of the mountain-arrow! Protect me with the essence of your compassionate glances.
O Lord of the Pramathas, O Hero, O Steadfast One! Swiftly remove the affliction born of worldly existence; protect me! 35.
O Śiva, Śiva! O Śambhu, whose manifest eyes are the sun, fire, and moon, and who are clothed in an elephant hide!
By your auspicious grace, O Śiva, may there be no fear for me in the darkness of passion, for you are the one who pacifies worldly existence.
O Blue-throated One, who always stays near the daughter of Mount Hara; O Consumer of the potent poison;
O You whose neck is beautified by the coils of the great serpent, renowned as being near the hearts of the self-restrained ascetics. (37)
Hara, Hara! O Śambhu, you who are the sole refuge for those born in fear; Hara, Hara! the terrible suffering born of worldly existence.
Hara, Hara! take away our sin and dispel it, O Lord whose feet are highly honored by Murajit (Viṣṇu). 38.
O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, O Moon-crested Lord, O Essence of Compassion, O Sovereign of the Immortals;
O Śiva, the great forest fire that dries up the shoreless ocean of sin;
O You whose body is beautified by the form of Your beloved, and whose feet are worshiped by the eyes of the Beloved of Kamalā.
O Hara, when your departure is joined with the head of Viśveśāna, who is fierce in his ritual observances! 39.
O Three-eyed Lord of the Immortals, who took away the right eye of Dakṣa when it was impaled upon the trident;
O All-pervading Lord, attainable through devotion alone, protect me, your child Mañjana!
O Lord, listen to the song from the mouth of Nārada, made beautiful by the resonance of his lute.
O, O best of gods, be gracious, O Blessed One; extend the gaze of your compassion!
At the conclusion of the song, having heard from the mouth of Nārada this sweet resonance of the vīṇā, the attendants of the high-souled Śambhu, headed by Nandikeśa, [were moved].
Having prostrated before the high-souled god Śaṅkara, Nandikeśa indeed covered his mouth with his hand and informed the deity.
He spoke to the boon-granting god, whose face was serene and who possessed three eyes.
Nandikeśvara:
O Śambhu, O Śaṅkara, O Dhūrjaṭi, O three-eyed one, dispel this boundless agony!
O you of immeasurable power, who regard the essential activity of the worlds as your highest concern, [dispel it].
By the nectar-stream of your name, this world has reached your presence, O Lord;
having attained the rank of the Chief of the Pramathas, it now seeks to behold your lotus feet. 43.
"He stands at the gate, O Lord, having been stopped by me; however, by my command, O Radiant One, please allow that divine sage Nārada to pass,
for he is devoted to your lotus feet, possesses a heart full of longing, and is distinguished above all others."
O Lord, one who is made happy by devotion, knowledge, and detachment desires to behold Your feet. 44.
Having heard the words of Nandikeśvara, Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, signaled with the corner of his eye regarding the arrival of Nārada.
Nārada also, having bowed to the Lord of Gods,
the Great God Śipiviṣṭa who is enchanting with his eightfold forms, praised him with joy.

Nārada: Victory, victory to you, O God Maheśa, Dhūrjaṭi! Victory, victory to you, O Teacher skilled in the creation of the universe! Victory, victory to you whose fame is sung by the celebrated Vedas! Victory, victory to you who are the sole enjoyer of that which is offered by your devotees! 47.
Victory, victory, O Blessed One, O Śambhu, five-faced one, who are intent on bestowing the fruits of ascetic practices!
Having worshipped with my own heart the pair of your auspicious lotus feet, O Blessed One, I am a singular mass of penance.
"The sage dwells upon the lofty peak of the Himavat mountain, his sole thirst being for the sight of your divine, nectar-like form.
Hearing these words of Nārada, Maheśvara was filled with joy;
surrounded by various hosts of Gaṇas, he went to see Jaigīṣavya.
Having mounted the divine bull of Śakra— meaning the bull of Indra— adorned with various ornaments,
and resounding with the noise of musical instruments and songs sung by the mouths of various hosts of celestial beings.
Surrounded by hosts of attendants holding parasols and chowries in their hands and bearing banners, he was encircled by Umā, Skanda, Heramba, Nandi, and Bhr̥ṅgin. (51)
In an instant, Maheśvara, charming with a gentle smile, arrived at the summit of Himavat accompanied by sages and the leaders of his gaṇas.
His splendor is equal to the white brilliance of the rising moon;
he is resplendent with the luster of the crest upon his head, which resembles the mass of high waves of the Gaṅgā.

Seeing that sage with a one-pointed mind, Maheśvara rained down upon the sage— who had become like an anthill— showers from the ocean of the nectar of his compassionate glances. Rising up, he bowed to the best of gods and praised the immeasurable one who possesses eight forms.

Jaigīṣavya: O Maheśvara! O dispeller of the intense heat of powerful sins! O protector of those who have sought refuge! O you who are distinguished by the momentary granting of desires to the virtuous! O lover of the humble! O dryer-up of the pride of Tripura! Be gracious now with compassion, O extinguisher of the forest fire of worldly existence!

O bearer of the digit of the Lord of the Night; O dispeller of the heat of sin; O consumer of fierce poison; O you whose feet are worshipped by the crowns of the gods; O you who ride the excellent great bull; O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; O remover of Bhaga’s eyes; O Śaṅkara, O Lord, look upon me quickly and with force! 56.
O supreme among the gods who destroy the pride of the powerful Asuras, worshipped by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, you who consumed Andhaka with your mighty trident;
O Lord whose three eyes are the sun, moon, and fire, radiant with the jewel-bracelets of the serpent-king, spread abroad the intent of the Vedas through the essence of your compassion!

O Three-eyed One, O Sadāśiva, O Lord of the thirty gods, you who dwell in the heart-lotus of Yama and Indra; you who delight in the sound of the *ḍamaru* drum rising from the sphere of the heart-lotus; you who love the coils of the serpent that breathes forth the pure garment of virtuous deeds; O Lord, O Bhava, O Destroyer of Mura, O Lotus-eyed One, be gracious toward me at your feet!
O you whose arrows are the beloved of Ramā, who possess the mighty bow of Meru, whose excellent chariot is the earth, and who hold the forms of Soma and Pūṣan;

O immutable one, whose horses are the Vedas, O Creator, O Lord of the celestial waters—protect me with this look of yours that resembles the essence of compassion, for you are intent on destroying the body of Mada.
Having heard the praise of Jaigīṣavya, Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Smara, was satisfied; seeing the sage standing with palms joined in humility, he spoke.
Īśvara:
You are one whose essence is love for Dhūrjaṭi, a seeker of liberation, and one whose mind is solely intent upon liberation; you have reached the inner core of the crest-jewels of the Vedas.
You are a perpetual celibate, a recipient of my supreme grace, and you are the very essence of the lords of sages.
With pride, arrogance, greed, and delusion dissolved; with his mental fluctuations stilled and his heart free from thirst for worldly objects;
wearing the excellent sacred ash and holding a rosary of rudrākṣa beads; he was a hero in the contemplation of the mind that is the crest-jewel of the Vedas. || 61 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Grace upon Jaigīṣavya," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Jaigīṣavya said:
O Lord of the gods of gods, you alone are father, mother, friend, and master.
O Lord of gods, Lord of the universe, Great Lord, you alone are everything. (1)
O Lord of the Gods, I know no one other than you who is the father of Girijā;
therefore, O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, be gracious now.
O Maheśvara, I have taken refuge in Your pair of feet, which are free from dualities;
Skanda and Heramba are my two brothers, and the leaders of the Gaṇas are my friends.
Gaurī is the mother of the worlds, my progenitor, and the bringer of my welfare;
you alone, O Lord Maheśvara, are the father of the worlds and my father.
O Lord, I choose no other boon than devotion to Your lotus feet;
that alone is now the cause for my attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation.
O Mahādeva, by that very devotion all the gods and asuras were liberated;
indeed, your devotee alone is liberated in this world and liberates others as well.
O Maheśvara, it is solely through devotion to you that Brahmā creates the universe;
having obtained the Vedas from you, he became the sovereign of Satyaloka.
Viṣṇu, worshipping your pair of feet with his lotus-eye,
obtained the Sudarśana discus for the sole purpose of destroying the hosts of Daityas.
O Virūpākṣa, it was solely through devotion to you that he became the lord of Vaikuṇṭha;
and even Rudra, the lord of the lotus-dwelling, attained his state by taking refuge in you.
Having given that excellent trident to Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
he was also consecrated by you in the sovereignty over the Rudras.
At the end of time, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is consumed by the flames of his trident-fire;
yet even Śakra attained the status of Lord of the Immortals solely through devotion to you, O Hara.
O Maheśvara, through devotion to you alone, Dhanada attained the lordship of Śacī and became the sole enjoyer of the various pleasures of heaven, as well as the sovereignty over wealth.
O Śiva, through the worship of your feet, Yama became the guardian of the world (Lokapāla);
likewise Varuṇa became the lord of aquatic creatures, as did the Sun, Moon, Wind, and Fire.
O Virūpākṣa, it is solely through devotion to you that they attained the status of guardians of the quarters;
all gods and asuras worship your liṅga with devotion.
O Lord Śambhu, by his devotion to you, Bāṇa attained a thousand arms;
so too did Rāvaṇa, the son of Pulastya, the one who makes the worlds cry out.
O Maheśvara, it was solely through devotion to you that [Agastya] conquered the foremost of kings who were intoxicated with wine;
and through devotion to you, the oceans were swallowed up by the Jar-born Sage as if they were mere mouthfuls.
O Śambhu, through the devotion of Dadhīci, an extraordinary form was shown to Viṣṇu; and being urged by Bhṛgu, Hari manifested his illusory power.
Even as a child, Upamanyu obtained the entire ocean of milk;
and though bound by the nooses of Death, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu was liberated through devotion to you.
Even Śveta, the son of a king, swiftly conquered death;
and by devotion to you, O Stone-eater, your son has indeed attained birth from no womb.
Through devotion to you, even Ānandikeśa attained the status of a Gaṇapati;
and Caṇḍīśvara also slew his own father out of devotion to you.
In the past, Maṅkaṇaka, who was already an adept, attained perfection by worshipping you;
and Soma also was freed from royal consumption through your grace.
Dakṣa was initiated into the sacrifice, instructed, and favored;
so too were Śatarcins and others, as well as Īśa, Vyāghrapāda, and the rest.
O Śambhu, the highly fortunate Dūrvāsas and others, as well as Dattātreya and the rest,
and even Paraśurāma, the destroyer of the royal lineages— [all these were born from you].
In the same way, there were other kings born of the lineages of the Moon and the Sun,
as well as the Ādityas, the sons of Diti, the Gaṇas, the Rudras, and the lords of sages.
Those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present who are devoted and permeated by devotion to you—
for them all, O Śaṅkara, heaven and liberation are attained through devotion to you alone.
O Lord, having no other refuge, I beg only for devotion to you,
now that the linga named Jaigīṣavyeśvara has been established on the Himālaya mountain.
Dwell there eternally in the western part of Kedāra.
Sūta:
Having been addressed thus by that sage, Mahādeva Śaṅkara spoke to the Daughter of the Mountain King while the gods and sages were listening.
Īśvara said:
O Aparṇā, whose eyes reach to the edges of your ears, listen to this story for the sake of those dwelling in the ocean of worldly existence, so that they may swiftly attain the state of perfection.
For those by whom a temple of Śiva has been constructed, there shall always be a great abode for the Liṅga, and even the lotus-dwelling [Brahmā] shall become their own home.
O Sage, by him penances were performed through subsisting on withered leaves;
O Auspicious One, by him all sacrifices were offered, and by him the sacred scriptures were studied.
This Liṅga named Kedāra, situated upon the crown of your father’s head, is the eternal seed of liberation.
In this Kedāra on your father’s beautiful head, there is the sprout of bliss-in-the-abundance (bhūmānanda), which is liberation itself.
"By this sign, behold the Liṅga worshipped by him with his own name in the western direction;
for whenever a Liṅga is installed by anyone, O Lord, I remain there, being exceedingly pleased in every way. (33)

O Bhavānī, I am always and ever attentive to you, who grant eternal happiness and supreme joy; O Bhavānī, during the celebrated Pradoṣa hour, when there is illumination and the practice of worship for the sake of liberation.

O Mistress of the World, that man who, with an even mind, performs worship shines as the most excellent; he would be truly worthy of my favor— whosoever in the three worlds builds a beautiful temple for the lofty Liṅga,
complete with gates, doors, arches, great walls, and fine towers.

Having performed [this], a person is liberated from all great sins accumulated over hundreds of births, by means of a single, radiant, great golden pitcher whose luster is like a mass of lightning. || 35 ||
In a delightful and excellent mountain, on a superb riverbank, in a village, a city, a mountain,
a sacred ford, or even in a forest; or on the bank of the Ganges, on the Narmadā,
or on the shore of a lake, in a forest, or on a preeminent great mountain.
Whether on the shore or in the great sacred fields of Maheśvara, he who bears the *liṅga* everywhere remains pure; his purity and majesty are so vast that their limit transcends even heaven. (36)

Whether wealthy or even a man at the very pinnacle of poverty, by making supreme devotion the primary cause, one who has built a temple to Śiva shall be endowed with happiness on earth and thereafter liberated.
[The temple may be] fashioned from clay or wood, or made of stone and brick, beautiful and plastered with lime.
May this divine [image], fashioned from excellent jewels and which instantly removes worldly existence, be born to me. || 37 ||
Having installed my Liṅga— which is well-fashioned, beautiful, situated in a supreme temple, and exceedingly lofty— a worshiper of Bilva with fine garments, sandalwood, and showers of camphor;
what need has he for intoxicated elephants, excellent gold, land, horses, cows, or jewels?
Or what need is there for gifts, supreme sacrifices, or the great merits long accumulated, O Śivā? 38.

Whether through yogic practices, observances, vows, austerities, or even pilgrimages— what indeed is better than the gift of food and other necessities to a maiden? For those by whom a temple to the Liṅga has been built for Śiva, it becomes a beautiful net of supreme dharma that lasts until the end of the cosmic dissolution.
Indeed, there is no fear at all of falling from the one who fashions the abode of the Liṅga of Malli. || 39 ||
O Umā, as long as the host of stars including the moon and its sons exists, and as long as the rivers and mountains remain,
so long shall that best of my attendants remain upon the summit of Kailāsa for me—
even if it be broken, shattered, constructed by others, decayed, or crumbled to pieces.
O Umā, he who, through his meritorious deeds, effects its extraction by means of faith alone— || 40 ||
What shall I say? My residence is forever and eternally within his heart;
at the conclusion of his life, I bestow incomparable liberation. I shall tell you a secret:
who indeed, at the time of Pradoṣa, would worship the excellent Liṅga with auspicious Bilva fruits?
And thus, he shall again exercise supreme sovereignty over the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary. || 41 ||

On this earth, accompanied by sons, wife, and friends, and endowed with grain and wealth, one attains ultimate liberation at the end solely through the worship of my *liṅga*—whether with various oils, ghee derived from animals, or even that produced from cows alone. (p. 22)
Having awakened [the deity] and arranged a row of lamps on the great elephant, one should create a multitude of blazing lamps.
O Lotus-born One, may I behold in my home a row of lamps shaped like swans and stars, beautiful and radiant, by which the mass of my sins is indeed set ablaze;
or likewise with incense produced from *tvak* and *agaru*, as well as excellent *sāmrāṇi* and *guggulu*.
O Śivā, [I offer] only the delightful and fragrant scents of bilva leaves, prepared and combined with [other] substances. 43.
Having burned away the entire multitude of his sins, he goes to my abode; having achieved his purpose, he shall attain the most sharpened knowledge arising from the words of the Vedanta.
With lamps shining with great flames produced from heaps of camphor fragments—
Having kindled his luster, he shattered the crown of Jālandhara, the lord of the Pramathas, as he embraced him. || 44 ||
The offering of a lamp to me, O Śiva, becomes a thunderbolt against the mountain of sin;

it surely brings about the exaltation of one's lineage and the attainment of excellent sons, as well as the state of Śambhu. [This is achieved] with products of the cow, such as milk and ghee from Kapila cows, or from the essence of other cows.
And by curd, one gains a hundredfold greater fruit; and by honey, one attains non-minuteness. || 45 ||
Having bathed the stainless Liṅga with sugarcane juice, with fragrant waters, with waters produced from flowers and gems, and with those originating from gold, one attains liberation in Śiva;
and likewise by bathing it with the finest juices derived from the Puṇḍraka sugarcane and with clusters of plantain fruits.
Also with the juices of nārela, ambu, rasāla, and sāla, as well as with the waters of jambīra. || 46 ||
If this man, born of a noble lineage, were to devoutly bathe my great Liṅga with offerings of jackfruit from dawn until the time of twilight, he would be liberated even in the evening;
such a man among my devotees is indeed preeminent in my own abode.
Having enjoyed every pleasure on earth, O beloved Goddess, the most dear one indeed departs.
O Umā, during the summer season, when my great crown is joined with my *liṅga*,

what person could possibly measure the fruit born from the visualization of that stream, which flows down as a torrential shower filled with flowers and the liquid of very red sandalwood paste? (Page 23)
By speaking [this], one shall become liberated from the great sins accumulated over tens of thousands of births. || 48 ||
With full-blown lotuses, both white and dark-blue varieties, with excellent *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jājī*, *kunda*,
and beautiful *pāṭala* flowers; with *baka*, great *dhurtūra*, *droṇa*, *arkaka*, *kalhāra*, *kumuda*, *japā*, *damanaka*, and blossoming *dāḍimba* fruits.
With *punnāga*, *arjuna*, and *campaka* trees, with *bakula* and *mandārava* and *ālhataka* trees. || 49 ||
With blue, emerging, and blooming lotuses; with auspicious *kuravaka* and *karṇikāra* flowers;

with the auspicious *nandyāvarta*, *śirīṣa*, and *bilva* blossoms; with the red *aśvasāra*; with *jambū*, mango, and *palāśa* trees; with the flowers of the *śamī*; and with *dūrvā* grass, *pāmārga*, and other such plants—[he beheld the place].
Having worshipped with Viṣṇukrānta, Kuśa, and Kāśa grasses, one is liberated, O Ambikā.

One attains the desired goal without cause through the sprouts of the glances of the Blessed Lord Śambhu, when [worship is performed] at the most meritorious time of Pradoṣa upon the most holy Liṅga, and during other auspicious times as well—
such as Maudgalya, Śata, Ṛcīka, Nārada, Bhṛgu, and Gautama, the elder brother of Dhaumya.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dadhīci, Garga, Uśanas, Muñja, Kari, and Śaunaka. || 51 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, [the sages] Dūrvāsas, Jamadagni, Aṅgiras, the excellent Dattātreya, Vyāghrapāt, Jābāli, Dadhīci, Mitrāyaṇa, and the pitcher-born Agastya;
and among the gods, the renowned Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Aryaman, and Agni— [these are the ones].
Varuṇa, the lord of Yakṣas, Yama, Nirṛti, and the hosts headed by Īśāna; || 52 ||
And Skanda with his six faces, Nandīśa, Bhṛṅgīśvara, the best of the Gaṇas;
Taṇḍu, Caṇḍi, Riṭī, the heroic Subhadraka, and Mahābhairava—
these lords of the Śiva-hosts have the Tripuṇḍra mark of ashes upon their foreheads and wear rosaries of rudrākṣa beads as armlets.
O Śivā, those who worship the Liṅga have minds whose nature is restless with the longing to revolve [the sacred stone] for Rudra.
"O Śivā, these other sages, devoted to the stages of life (āśramas) and the worship of various deities, are weary of saṃsāra; yet, being of dull intellect, they do not know me.
But this son born out of wedlock (Kānīna), O Umā, having reached my Kāśikā by the power of destiny—"
Standing with his arms raised in my presence, he repeatedly proclaimed Hari as the Supreme Deity.

Therefore, O sinless one, it does not behove you even to speak of, much less to hear, this my secret, meritorious, and stainless mystery of liberation; rather, O wonder, quickly impart it properly to those disciples who are worthy vessels and whose bodies are smeared with sacred ash, born of my love.
For those whose minds are submerged in the great waters of this shore and the further shore, [there is] in the meritorious Śaiva [teachings]. || 55 ||
O Jaigīṣavya, lord of sages, grant me the supreme secret of Śiva;
it must not be told to a sage devoid of devotion to Śiva, for this merit-bestowing [teaching] grants liberation.
By giving it to an inferior man lacking devotion, one incurs great sin.
Furthermore, he obtains a fruitless exertion, just as water poured into a leaky vessel. || 56 ||
O Sovereign Goddess, those wise ones who, for the sake of attaining the digit of knowledge (*jñānakalā*), delight in the study of Vedānta with well-disposed minds;

who are peaceful, whose senses are perfectly tranquil, and who are free from the agitation of wandering through the cycle of worldly existence—whichever of my excellent devotees they may be, O Mistress, they must always be protected by you with your boons. (57)
Sūta:

Having beheld the lotus-face of the Goddess— the seed of the mass of bliss for the eyes of the three-eyed Lord— the illustrious Pārvatī’s consort has a face resembling a blossoming, stainless white water-lily.
And having seen the sage of distinguished mind, the most eminent among the disciplined, his own virtuous mind was then purified by the entire multitude of the eightfold yoga-limbs.
Īśvara: O Bhuvaneśvarī, this son of yours, the sage Śāṅkara, who is purified and the lord of the three worlds, shall become one who delights solely in all the Āgamas, having been beheld by you.
Now, let this world-purifying essence of my splendors, like the sun blooming upon your lotus-face, forcibly enter through your six mouths. (59)
O Śivā, Skanda— whose crest-jewel is the moon and who rests upon your lap as his couch— heard from me this auspicious hymn containing all blessings;
may he, with the nectar-like essence flowing from his six mouths, nourish this sage.
Today, by the Śaivas, with the spray of nectar from the streams of discourse arising from the secret [teachings]. || 60 ||
O best of sages, listen from the lotus-like mouth of Jaigīṣavya to this secret of Śiva;
those who do so shall always become true devotees of Śiva, possessing the singular realization of a hundredfold great bliss.
Others have no interest in the festival of drinking the nectar of the stories of Śaṅkara.
O Goddess, there are some whose minds are clearly nourished by drinking the nectar arising from devotion. || 61 ||

"O Sage, I have bestowed this secret of Śiva—which is easy to understand as it contains the essence of the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta—upon the Goddess; and she, out of intense affection, has given it to Skanda, the instructor of the Asuras. Go now to him."
Having been addressed thus, and having heard the charming words of the Daughter of the Mountain, that sage went forth.

Having bowed at the feet of Śambhu, the Lord, accompanied by the lords of sages, departed with haste; and Paśupati, surrounded by the Goddess, the gods, and others, went joyfully to Kailāsa, praised by the gods with hymns and amidst the multitude of musical instruments sounded by his hosts of attendants.
He is intent on providing the means for the attainment of the goals of human life for his devotees, and he is endowed with the bliss of his own self.

Then the high-souled Jaigīṣavya, with his head touching the ground, having fully worshipped and bowed to the Lord Śambhu, the sovereign of sacrifices, approached Skanda for the sake of imparting the knowledge of the noble meaning of the Vedas.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Jaigīṣavya," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The seventh chapter, titled "The Meeting of Jaigīṣavya and Skanda. Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord departed for Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara.
He was worshipped by the foremost among gods and asuras with a multitude of throngs of Nandis and Bhṛṅgis.
Having bowed at the lotus feet of Mahādeva, the sage Jaigīṣavya, who has a great bull as his vehicle, [was honored] by the Goddess, the mother of the world.
Meditating thus, he went indeed to Skanda, the destroyer of Krauñca;
he approached him accompanied by the best of sages, the foremost devotees of Śiva, who were intent on devotion.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Jamadagni, Bhṛgu, Dūrvāsas, Cyavana, Garga, Vītahavya, and Analāśana;
Gautama, Atri, Bharadvāja, Dālbhya, Hayashiras, Manu, Ucathya, Agnidhvaja, Dadhīci, Maunibhārgava;
Vyāsa, Parāśara, Akuṇḍa, Kavi, Aṅgiras, Madhu,
Upamanyu, Viśākha, Tuhaṇḍa, Kavaṣa, and Dhruva.
Jābāli, Kāśyapa, Mitra, Nārada, and Tuṃburu; likewise Parvata, Aṇimāṇḍavya, Daṇḍa, Vyāghrapada, and Dhanu.
Vedagarbha, Vītihotra, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Dhanu, Śaunaka, Tāṇḍaka, Mitravinda, and Anamitraka.
Hayagrīva, Pippalāda, Dattātreya, Vikatthana,
Agastya, Anilāśa, Śatarcā, and Āśvalāyana.
Sananda, Sanātana, Kumāra, Sanātana, and other such sages who are leaders among the Śaivas and are esteemed by Śiva. || 10 ||

Devoted to smearing themselves with ashes using mantras beginning with "Agni," they mark their bodies with the triple-ash lines (tripuṇḍra) using the triyāyuṣa mantras, and wear rosaries of rudrākṣa beads as armlets and bracelets.
Devoted to the recitation of the five-syllable mantra and intent on meditation upon the Five-Faced One,
they worship and praise the Lord with the Atharvaśiras.
Some were devoted to the recitation of the *śikhā-mantra*, some were reciters of the *kaivalya-mantra*;
some were intent on the practice of the *praṇava*, and some were reciters of the *Jābāla-upaniṣad*.
Those who recite the Bṛhat, Rathantara, Vāmadevya, Sāman, and other chants,
as well as the Saṃhitās of the Sāmans, Ṛks, and Yajus;
The best of sages were all devoted to the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya, dedicated to the five Brahmans,
and intent upon the worship of the Liṅga during the three periods of the day.
Devoted to the recitation of the five Rudra-mantras, intent upon meditation on the Five-Faced One,
they partake of Śiva’s food offerings and, by rule, worship with bilva leaves.
Devoted to the fortune of dispassion, skilled in the meaning of the eternal and the non-eternal,
they were knowers of the truth regarding the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, possessing firm wisdom and being wise sages.
All were masses of asceticism, accompanied by their wives and devoted to Śiva;
they were constantly engaged in the chanting of Śiva’s names and always contemplated Śiva.
All of them, devoted to the Agnihotra and having burnt away their sins through sacrifices and other rites,
arrived by way of the sky accompanied by their disciples and grand-disciples.
On the bank of the Sarasvatī is Skandāśrama, the purifier of purifiers,
frequented by various hosts of Skanda’s attendants and graced by gods and gandharvas.
On the auspicious peak of the Blue Mountain, which is sheltered by various excellent trees and resounds with the cries of dancing peacocks and the songs of male cuckoos.
It resounded with the cries of parrots and mainas, with the cooing "huṅ" of pigeons,
and with the resonant sounds of mṛdaṅga and muraja drums accompanied by the rhythm and timing of the vīṇā lute.
They beheld the abode of Skanda, resplendent with various jewels, where hosts of Kinnaras danced and clusters of lotuses were in full bloom.
It was adorned with gate-towers, watchtowers, balconies, moats, and ramparts,
and it shone with many new jewels inlaid with gold.
It was furnished with divine couches and coverlets, accompanied by the excellent roars of lions,
and attended by Bakula trees brought there by Gandharvas, along with songs and instrumental music.
Seated upon a lion-throne, bestowing boons, possessing six faces, and radiant with a crown;
wearing golden-yellow garments, he is fanned by waving chowries.
Adorned with shimmering golden jewels and variegated earrings, his neck was graced with a magnificent garland of gems and a beautiful pearl necklace. (27)
All the sages beheld Skanda, the son of Mahāśakti, who was exceedingly handsome, holding a spear in his hand, and the destroyer of Krauñca.
