Having prostrated before the imperishable Skanda, the sages, Jaigīṣavya and the others,
sat comfortably upon seats assigned and occupied by him.
Touching the sky, moving with the speed of the wind, and having shaken off the entire multitude of his sins like ashes, he—
resembling the autumnal sky and possessing the luster of the full moon— beheld the one who has the splendor of the Mountain’s daughter.

He realized that Jaigīṣavya— who was situated in the midst of the ocean of great bliss arising from gazing upon the lotus-face of [Śiva]— had come into his own presence, having been sent by the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva);
and seeing him as a worthy recipient for awakening the meaning of the knots of the heart of Maheśvara’s friend.
Joyful and with a nourished body, he [addressed] the sage who possessed the awakening of the most excellent speech.

The six-faced god, Kārttikeya, his body clearly bristling with horripilation from contact with the limbs of Jaigīṣavya, gazed upon that best of Śiva’s devotees— the lord of sages whose body and inner self were whitened by sacred ash— and was delighted; for he saw that the great sage was free from passion regarding both the choice of a bride for Menā’s son and the bearing of worldly burdens.
Skanda:
Due to the agitation caused by your arrival, the series of my delusions has vanished. Long ago, Śiva spoke that which is named the *Śivaraha-syadharma*;
just as the ocean is filled by rivers, so too does my mind overflow with the nectar-ocean of Śiva’s stories. Nevertheless, you are the cause of my awakening.
You too have arrived here, sent by the enemy of Tripura, having acquired the fruits of matured penance through the accumulation of immeasurable merit;
for the compassion of Maheśa toward you is even greater than toward other sages, and there is no one else in the worlds who worships the Liṅga of the Lord of the Pramathas.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Meeting of Jaigīṣavya and Skanda," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Vision of Skanda. Sūta said:
Delighted by the sight of the six-faced god (Kārttikeya), they sat down near him.
Then those lords of the Śaivas, who are the objects of the compassion of the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti), were filled with joy.
With palms joined in reverence, all the sages, led by Jaigīṣavya, spoke:
The sages said: O Skanda, son of the Destroyer of Tripura, abode of happiness! (2)
O best of mountains, you who crushed Krauñca and tore asunder Śūra and the others;
you who are the ocean of the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, endowed with power, and the bestower of all goals.
O Youth, who resemble Māra, who are affectionate toward those who have taken refuge in you, whose couch is the lap of Śiva, and who dwell within the hearts of all beings! 4.
O Lord, who is served by many supreme hosts headed by Vīrabāhu, and who protects the armies of the lord of the gods and others, whose vehicle is the peacock! 5.
He who investigates the essence and non-essence of the great sayings (mahāvākya) beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava),
and who dispels the mass of darkness of doubt within the lotus-heart of his devotees.
O You whose fierce prowess is like the fiercely blazing sun rising with the dawn of knowledge,
those whose misfortunes have been destroyed by the sight of Your pair of lotus feet [attain liberation].
Through the ascetic power of Jaigīṣavya, Maheśvara was seen by us;
commanded by him, we all set out with Jaigīṣavya at our head.
May those who are bees for the nectar flowing from the lotus of your speech protect [the world] by drinking the nectar called the *Śivarahasya*, which destroys worldly existence.
Driven by the weight of their merit, they have come with intense longing into your presence—
these sages who are now scorched, standing in the midst of the forest fire of worldly existence.
"Be gracious to us quickly with a cool glance that is like a spray of nectar.
Having heard these words of the sages, Skanda, the son of Hara, [responded].
With a serene mind, the son of Hara spoke to those followers of Śambhu.
Skanda said:
"O sages, headed by Jaigīṣavya, you are the most excellent in being;
you are all endowed with the singular state of worldly existence and are devotees of Maheśvara."
Merely by the sight of you,
O Sage, my lotus-like mind has blossomed and is gladdened by meditation upon hearing of your ascetic practices.
O best of beings, even Jaigīṣavya’s devotion toward Mahādeva arose;
by Śiva’s command, the great sage Jaigīṣavya arrived.
Together with you followers of Śambhu, this has indeed been known by me through my very heart;
for you are worthy recipients, being worshippers at the feet of the Three-eyed Lord.
I shall speak that secret which, though it should be concealed, resides within the heart of Śiva;
this ancient mystery was heard by me long ago while seated upon the lap of Śiva.
Endowed with twelve parts, this was shown by the God to the Goddess;
it is meritorious, a destroyer of sins, and situated at the head of all the Vedas. (17)
And Bhava himself recounted to Bhavānī this narrative which destroys worldly existence,
which is the meaning of the Praṇava of the Upaniṣads, and which shatters great sins.
O you who have Jaigīṣavya as your leader, listen to this auspicious [teaching] according to the ultimate truth; it is the very essence of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (19)
For once one has heard this jewel of a narrative concerning Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self,
no other story will please the ear, just as one finds no pleasure in ordinary tales.

By means of narratives concerning the creation, preservation, and dissolution [of the world], those based on the histories of kings, and those consisting of the laborious exposition of the duties of the castes and stages of life; (21)
What is the use of discourses on the appearance of phenomena, when one has tasted the essence of Śambhu’s teachings?
Is he not like one standing in the middle of a blind well, completely enveloped by darkness? 22.
O Sage, one might likewise fill others with other stories, but what is the use of those already chewed up, which have been told previously in the Purāṇas? (23)
O best of sages, how do the stories of the gods— who themselves are subject to birth and death—
enable those beset by birth, death, and old age to cross over?
O Brahmins, the Śaivas who abide in the *Śivarahasya* tell the story of the glorious Mṛtyuñjaya, which renders the worlds free from death.
Standing in the midst of the ocean of nectar, would one ever drink the water of a well?
Just as one who has heard the resonant sound of a lute would regard the cawing of a crow as nothing but noise.
Just as one who has reached a mine of jewels might look toward a fragment of glass, or as a wild boar that feeds on filth might resemble a rutting elephant; so it is with this [person]. (27)
O best of the twice-born, how can a monkey be like the king of beasts?
Likewise, how can others be attached to other stories, having abandoned the essence of the story of Śiva?
O Sage, just as Śiva, the Great God, is praised by all the Vedāntas,
so too is this supreme history named the Śivarahasya.
And this Śivakaṇṭhamaṇi is the liberator of even those who have been liberated from sin;
it was proclaimed by the God to the Goddess of old upon the peak of Kailāsa.
The supreme goddess Ambikā spoke to the god Virūpākṣa.

The Goddess said: O Śambhu, Lord of the Universe, Bharga, Three-eyed One, Destroyer of the Cities, Death of Death, Dispeller of Darkness, O You whose brow is the moon, Eye on the Forehead, Slayer of Smara, Swallower of Poison, protect the gods and the twice-born!
Tell me your secret, by which the three worlds have been liberated; tell me now, what is the most exalted conclusion at the summit of the Vedas?
O Ocean of Compassion, if you are a vessel for the downpour of my spray-like words, then make this excellent vessel of my hearing fulfilled.
O Destroyer of the Cities, for the sake of removing the suffering of the world, place your entire life-story within my ears; have mercy on me! 33.
O Śaṅkara, Lord of the Pramathas, Supreme over the universe, though it be most secret,
place that [state] within me so that it remains firm for a long time and takes deep root in You;
for by Your grace, my inner self has been fully revealed.
She is endowed with all states of devotion toward your lotus feet.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Kāmaprabhañjana spoke to the Great Goddess seated upon his lap, regarding that which had previously been situated on her lap.
I have heard the secret of that ocean of stories;
I shall now relate it for the destruction of worldly existence and for the increase of devotion to Bhava.
Īśvara said:

O Daughter of the Mountain King, there exists nothing in the three worlds that cannot be given to you; for you, the Mother of the Universe, have been granted half of my own body, and by you, the Formless One has been made to possess form.
O Goddess, you protect the universe and likewise consume it; you are the entire power (śakti), while I am the possessor of power (śaktimat).
Though I am said by the Vedas to be devoid of senses, I have entered this body because of you. (37)
I am without hands or feet, yet my power is undiminished; I see without eyes and hear without ears.
I perceive all this; though existing together with them, the gods do not know me.
While things decay, I am undecaying, unborn, ancient, forever devoid of a body, and eternally unattached;
for the Vedas and the words of the Vedānta, O Mother, have always been directed toward me by the mind as one whose nature is withdrawn from worldly existence. (39)

How is it that these wretched ones—beings with the forms and gestures of monkeys, always possessed of lust, greed, and envy—shout while holding bowls and other vessels; are they gods, asuras, or perhaps brahmins? (40)
But you alone, O Skanda, Nandin, and the other leaders, have attained [this state], being uniquely thirsting for my supreme power;
for you have reached Maheśa, whose singular form is attainable through true being (bhāva), yet who is difficult to reach even by the words of the eternal Vedas and Vedāntas.
O Goddess, you know my primordial beginning, which is eternally pure, awakened, and of the nature of consciousness and bliss;
the foremost among the lords of yogis and the gods behold me as three-eyed, with the lord of poison around my neck, together with Ambā. 42.
"O Īśānī, for the sake of the liberation of the world, I shall today create a body and at the end restrain desire.
O Śivā, the common folk shall not know this story of mine, my manifest form which is difficult even for the gods and others to attain. (43)
Listen to this secret that is an ornament for the ears, the ultimate essence of the Vedas beyond their reach; though it is clearly hidden, it dwells within the heart.
This secret of Śiva’s mystery (Śivarahasya) does not take root in one who is under the sway of non-Śaiva traditions, just as a tree planted in a desert land never flourishes. 44.
May He—who is the sun causing the blossoming of the red lotus-pond renowned as the lake of the true Śambhu; who bestows singular satisfaction upon the devotees of Śiva;
who is the wind that scatters the clouds of sin by dispelling the mass of darkness within the heart—always dry up the mire of desire born of the path of evil. (45)

O Daughter of the Mountain, let the wise always partake of this auspicious nectar of Śravaṇa, which is the very essence of the Vedas and is beloved by those who worship Śiva; for it is clear that the minds of base people do not partake of this.
O Beloved, this nectar is certainly like honey, and as with honey, it is dear only to those who possess the tongue of a bee.
They possess an excellence of flavor and disposition, and they are the ones who dry up the ocean of worldly existence.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Vision of Skanda," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Chapter Nine, titled "The Dialogue between Skanda, Śiva, and the Gaṇas.
Sūta said:
Thus, by the command of the Lord of the Assembly (Sadasaspati), they arrived properly.
Emerging from the pure and vast mouth of Skanda, they take refuge in Śiva.
Then Nārada went to the gods and the daughters of the serpent-king to hear stories that were difficult to endure for those on the wrong path and unpleasant to the ears of the lords of heaven.
The stories concerning the accounts of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the worlds were told on earth to Viṣṇu,
to Brahmā, to the guardians of the quarters, and to the lord of the immortals.
And he told the lords that which was born from the grace of Jaigīṣavya;
having heard this from Maheśvara, those gods were filled with agitation in their minds.
Their eyes were eager to hear the discourse as they gathered together with Nārada;
meanwhile, the unwearied Lord of Lakṣmī was mounted upon the son of Vinatā.
Then Brahmā, resembling a white cloud and mounted upon a swan, arrived;
and the Lord of the Gods (Indra), mounted upon an elephant, approached as the lord of Bhāratī.
Then the gods, adorned with various ornaments, mounted their respective vehicles and departed with joy; they reached the assembly of the slayer of Tāraka.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra sang [this].
The gods said:
O Lord whose lotus feet are worshipped by the multitudes of those who rejoice in Skanda,
O Sovereign of the immortals who possess the nature of Śiva, we wish to hear auspicious words from your mouth.
The sages, along with Jaigīṣavya, respectfully began to listen to the stories contained within the Śivarahaṃsya, which are the very essence of all auspicious things belonging to Śambhu.
Therefore, propagate those auspicious [teachings] which ward off the torment of sin;
then, filled with joy by the words of the gods and the lords of sages, [he did so].
Having prostrated before the Lord, who shatters the mountain of obstacles, he spoke;
then, having meditated upon Jaigīṣavya residing within the lotus of his own heart, he gazed upon him.
With his face like a full-blown lotus, the Lord of the Assembly spoke forcefully to the Śaivas, the Indras, the Anamarendras, and the officiating priests present in the hall.
He spoke to those whose foreheads were marked with the triple ash-line (tripuṇḍra), who wore rudrākṣa beads as armlets and bracelets,
and whose minds were intent upon the lotus feet of Śiva.
Skanda said:
"O Jaigīṣavya, you alone are a devotee of Bhava; listen, together with these sages and the gods, to the Śivarahasya."
"O Goddess, that which dries up the heat of sin has been told by the God.
While they were thus conversing, [the Lord], whose cheeks were as red as vermilion, spoke.
With the great face of the lordly elephant and the dispeller of hosts of obstacles,
he then reached the hermitage of Skanda, attended by a multitude of his own attendants.
Then, mounting his excellent celestial chariot, he departed from Mount Kailāsa,
accompanied by Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Bāṇa, Caṇḍīśvara, and others.
Tuhuṇḍa, Huṇḍa, Sānanda, Mahānanda, Bhairava, Tunda,
Kālāgnirudra, and those others who are the best among the Gaṇapas.
Somanandi and others, the leaders of the Gaṇas sent by Maheśa, who bestow boons upon tens of millions of attendants, have arrived. (19)

(Verse on page 32: With their heads adorned by matted locks shining with the crescent moon as a crest, their foreheads resplendent with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and wearing rudrākṣa beads as armlets and bracelets;
With the faces of the quarters resounded by the *huṃ* sounds arising from the blast of the great *ḍamaru*,
he saw them and rose up suddenly along with the sages, gods, and asuras.
Having bowed to the one who has descended as an elephant, having offered a grand seat and water for the feet,
and having worshipped him with sweetmeats, cakes, dūrvā grass, perfumes, unbroken rice, and other offerings;
The enemy of Tāraka embraced Nandīśvara and the other lords of the Gaṇas with a firm heart and affection; they, in turn, honored him with highly precious offerings.
The lords of sages and the hosts of celestial guardians sat down all around Skanda,
gazing with palms joined in reverence at the six-faced one of excellent countenance.
Nandikeśa and the others spoke to Skanda, the destroyer of Krauñca.
Nandikeśvara: By Śiva, who was pleased by the asceticism of Jaigīṣavya,
[we have been made] longing to hear the discourse that flows from the nectar of your speech.
The Lord of Umā has sent us to your presence;
formerly, while seated upon the lap of Umā, you heard his enchanting words.
This secret of Śiva, which destroys sins, has been told to Śivā;
endowed with twelve parts, it directly grants liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
In the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, and Āgamas as well, animal sacrifices— which bestow the cycle of worldly existence— have been proclaimed by the sages.
The Lord of Umā spoke the singular discourse on the duties of a husband, which bestows liberation;
these stories, arising from the essence of the Vedas and Vedānta, are the destroyers of sin.
He recounted that secret,
which is equal to the Vedas, the essence of the Jābāla Upaniṣad, spoken directly from the mouth of Hara, to that Goddess.
Nor do we have a place of residence even in the vicinity of that spot;
we are stationed outside the seven walls, at the front of the gate-tower.
Today, you have heard that supreme [teaching] while seated on the lap of the Goddess;
now tell it to us, for that which was proclaimed by the God is not to be kept secret.
There, on Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara, the lords of serpents were propitiated with joy by Aparṇā as a consequence of her union with Hara, the lord of Indra.
O Jaigīṣavya, both the lords of the gods and the lords of the sages have been sent by Śambhu to you, the object of Śambhu’s affection, because of your ascetic penance.
Placing Jaigīṣavya at our head, O ocean of compassion, please speak to us of that which is like a treasure-trove of excellent jewels, the singular refuge for those devoted to the Śivadharma.
Upon hearing these words from Itthandīśa, the son of the daughter of the mountain lord experienced incomparable joy, like the ocean at the rising of the moon. (37)
Gladdening with his speech all the lords of the Gaṇas, the sovereigns of the immortals,
the lords of sages, Gajendramukha, and the great sage Jaigīṣavya.
Having bowed down to his elder brother, Maheśa, and Ambikā as well,
the six-faced one then praised Gajānana with a hymn.
Having joined his palms in reverence, together with the lords of the Gaṇas, the gods, and the brahmins.

Skanda said: O gods, worship the one born of Maheśa, who has the splendor of Indra, whose lotus-like face is blooming like the white foam on the ocean of milk, who is clothed in the skin of an elephant blinded by rut, whose son is Puṣkara, who is radiant with the tilaka-mark of three lines, who shines with the frontal globes of an elephant-faced being, and who is the King of Obstacles bowed down to by all.

I bow to the gracious one who removes the affliction of obstacles, whose head is adorned with a jar filled with vermilion and dūrvā grass, whose cheeks are draped with a multitude of chowries, and who has made a lotus bud his ear-ornament. (41)

I bow to Vighnarāja, the excellent son of Paśupati, who wears a garland of bees and birds attracted by the mass of fragrance from the streams of ichor flowing from his temples; who has drums bound around his ears; who is the essence of the Vedas; and who wears the serpent as a sacred thread. 42.
I bow to Gaṇapati, the cause of supreme knowledge, who holds a goad, an axe, a tusk, and a lotus; who has attained the essence of the stream of love within the elephant-faced one;
who holds a fruit, a cluster of grapes, and molasses; who is fond of a multitude of sweetmeats; and who is the boon-bestowing son of Paśupati—I bow to you, O Lord with the face of a serpent-king.

I bow with words in both prose and verse to the primordial one, who has the face of the lord of elephants, who is praised by the hosts of the Vedas, who is worshipped by the sages, and who is lauded by Ākha, Vāha, Maja, Śauri, and Sureśa.
Sūta said:

Having thus praised the elephant-faced one, the six-faced Lord (Kārttikeya), dwelling within the belly of the pot-bellied god (Gaṇeśa), then spoke to those Pramatha chiefs, the lords of the gods, and the Brahmins.
With the permission of his elder brother and of Śiva and Pārvatī, Skanda expounded that doctrine to Jaigīṣavya, the best of sages, who was distinguished and equal to Śiva himself.
Skanda said:
The hosts of fine spray from the ocean of Īśāna are Brahmā, Indra, and Nārāyaṇa;
those creations born of his son are set in motion by the movement of the winds beginning with Śakti.
These kings and others are born from his sons; what fruit is gained by talk of them?
For here, these emanations are indeed false, consisting as they do of the great elements and so forth.

The dharma established here through the conduct of this illusory world— consisting of the essential core of deliberations on the boundaries and limits of the castes and stages of life— is merely the labor of those [worldly people].
But for the wise, does the arising of true knowledge ever occur through the chewing of what has already been chewed?
That which they declare to be the supreme Dharma, the one Śiva who is to be realized through austerity. 48.
O Jaigīṣavya and the hosts of Brahmins, you who are the attendants of Śaṅkara;

O Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the lords of the gods, along with the hosts of sages—before the illustrious Gaṇeśa, I shall speak with great reverence of the boundless deeds of Śiva and Śivā on Mount Kailāsa. (Page 34)
The abode of the glorious Maheśa is unattainable for those of very dull intellect, yet it is accessible even to those of keen intellect. 49.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Skanda and Śiva’s Gaṇas," in the first part of the glorious *Śivarahasya*.
In the dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Skanda, the tenth chapter.
Skanda said:
"The glory of the lotus-feet of Śiva [surpasses] the glory of the Lord of Lakṣmī (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā."
That auspicious goddess brings forth Indra, Candra, and the other gods.
And [he saw] Duṇḍi and Nandikeśa, as well as the sage Bhṛṅgiriṭi,
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dadhīci, Dūrvāsas, and Jāmadagnya.

Victory, victory to the Lord of Auspiciousness, most beautiful and most auspicious among all that is most auspicious! Victory, victory to the one skilled in the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe! O most beautiful friend, clad in excellent animal skins, praised by the multitude of sages; O destroyer of the sacrifice censured by others; O delighter of the divine hosts, slayer of the cities of the demons; O dryer of worldly existence, consumer of poison; O refuge for the young calves of the sages trembling with fear of Śamana (Yama); O Lord of the Dawn, mine of compassion, savior of the people; O one stationed upon the sun, cause of the gods; O dryer of Māra, whose feet nourish the multitudes of the Vedas and the three qualities!
Be a refuge, be a refuge, be a refuge through your compassion! || 3 ||

O You who transcend the words of the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*; O You whose mind is like the interior of space; O Cause of the protection of those established in wisdom; O Destroyer of the abode that withers Māra; O Bestower of boons; O You with pure, burning eyes; O You who transcend the reach of thought; O You who travel upon the bull as Your vehicle; O Destroyer of worldly existence; O You who are the refuge of the hosts of gods and Brahmins; O You who sport in the forest of the ancestors (*Śmaśāna*); O You who transcend the cavity of the small form (*Hṛdaya*); O You who recline upon the excellent mountain (*Śeṣa*); O You who stand amidst the rays of the sun and moon; O Slayer of Mura; O Wielder of the arrow; O Destroyer of the cities; O Supreme Steed of the Vedas.

O wielder of the deer-marked bow, whose excellent quivering bow was fashioned by the Lord of Serpents; O you who are skilled in protecting the divine warriors headed by the one armed with the thunderbolt—be a refuge, be a refuge, be a refuge through your compassion! 4.

O Lord who has humbled the Fire, Wind, Sun, Indra, Brahmā, Varuṇa, and Yama; O Protector of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings; O You whose beautiful and supreme deeds begin with the creation of all things; O You who remove the suffering of the multitude of devotees who bow before You; O You who possess incomparable compassion born from worshipping Him whose vehicle is the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa); O You whose eyes resemble blooming lotuses and who grant the chariot that carries You; O You adorned by the lotus-like head of Brahmā; O Blessed One, who can dry up the power of the Wind, Fire, Śiva, and Viṣṇu—surely even the movement of a blade of grass is not possible for You when You have already performed such great deeds.
O You whose conduct is praised by the crest of all the scriptures, be my refuge, be my refuge, be my refuge through Your compassion!

O Lord, whose pure and beautiful neck is like a cloud, its stainless whiteness arising from the splendor produced by the poison born of churning the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa; O protector of Hari, who swiftly swallowed the poison that arose there; O one resembling a rain-cloud, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the pure lotus-eyes of the slayer of Madhu; O you who satisfied the mind of the sage born from a jar (Agastya) by drinking the ocean in a single mouthful; O supreme ornament of ascetics, wearing serpents as bracelets; O Lord, remover of misfortune, who has purified the world with the drops from the pure and graceful crescent moon upon your head.
Be a refuge, be a refuge, be a refuge through your compassion! || 6 ||

O You whose mouth is satiated by the consumption of oblations offered in the fire facing Makha; O You whose greatness transcends the lotus-like assembly of the gods who have risen up after eating the sacrificial offerings; O You who, out of incomparable wrath caused by being deprived of worship, raised a roar from Your host of attendants and threatened the gods while consuming them; O Son of Vidhi (Brahmā), O You who were disciplined [by him], O Destroyer of the End of Sins, O Slayer of the Elephant (Gajāsura); O Lord of the Mountain (Himalaya), O You upon whom the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) lies as Your couch, O You who wear the garland formed from the hair on the head of Vidhi; O You who destroyed the lotus-face of the son of Bhaga and Daivata (the Sun and Moon) according to the will of Valabhid (Indra)—be my refuge, be my refuge, be my refuge through Your compassion! 7.

O Lord, whose matted locks and tresses are beautified by the sky-like waistband produced from splitting the rut of the lord of deer; who dwells upon the banyan tree as the protector of the armies of the Vedas and Agamas; who, as the leader of the gods, shattered the potsherds of the creation of the entire universe; who drew the bow of Hara and consumed the city of Tripura; O Blessed One, whose clever form brings about the stability of all things; O ocean of existence that becomes bitter [to the ignorant] yet carries the clouds of the world's emergence through Your arrival; O Destroyer of Tripura, who pacified Antaka (Death) and Andhaka; O All-pervading Lord who has pacified all suffering—be my refuge, be my refuge, be my refuge out of compassion! 8.

O you whose necklaces are made of gems that feed on wind; O Madhusūdana, who consumes poison; O destroyer of the abode of Yama’s younger brother; O you whose heart and face are beautiful with virtues superior to those of the best of the sons of the daughter of the sand-eater (the Ocean); O you praised by the best of sages; O you whose face resounds like the roar of the hosts of Gaṇas; O you who have made the moonlight your eye; O you whose lotus-feet are the source of joy for the multitude of lily-pools that are the leaders of the gods and the lords of stars; O you who grant delight to the son of the elephant-faced one (Ganeśa).

O You whose lotus-feet rest upon the slopes of the crown of the gods, which is adorned with a net of rays from nails as smooth and crimson as the young moon’s crest and resembling the buds of blue lotuses—be my refuge, be my refuge, be my refuge through Your compassion! 9.

O You whose name is the essence of the sweet, languid joy arising from the contact with the parrot-beaks of all cosmic eggs; O You who provide the delight of the songs sung by the sage Jamadagni; O You who effect the destruction of all the hosts of elephants born from the golden lotus; O Destroyer of Yama; O You whose stainless head is adorned by the crescent moon; O You who are softly adorned; O You who wear the Lord of Serpents as an earring; O Destroyer of Brahmā; O You whose beautiful eyes are like the crest of a peacock; O You whose tongue is formed by the submarine fire; O You who grant awakening to the one whose vehicle is the peacock; O You who are the crown of the circle of the Vedas; O Punisher of the Cities!

O wielder of the bow that shattered the pride of Indra; O you who provide protection to the assembly of sages; O you with the axe that split [the mountains]; O you who are devoted to the dance upon the waves made resonant by the deep, gurgling sounds of the *tāla* and *maddala* drums played by Taṇḍu, Nandin, Gaṇapati, and Caṇḍika; O you whose auspicious *liṅga* sports upon the banks of the waters brought forth by Jahnu—be my refuge, be my refuge, be my refuge through your compassion! 10.
Thus, with eight verses, Skanda praised Hara, who dwells within his own heart and possesses eight forms;
then, having bowed, he began to praise the Mother of the Worlds.
With most noble and profound verses, he [praised] his own mother, the heart-pleasing Maheśvarī,
the enemy of Tāraka, who was seated on the left lap of the God.
Skanda said: I bow to and praise the Blessed Māyā, who takes refuge in Maheśa, who is intent upon beholding the worlds, and whose form is established through the creation of grace for the universe.

I shall always honor with body and speech the Goddess who is authorized by Śiva, who is eloquent with grace, and who is capable of bestowing the great imperial sovereignty over Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the hosts of Maruts. (13)
She who surpasses all the hosts [of stars] with her broad stream of light, like the moon, jasmine, the trunk of a rutting elephant, and the bimba fruit;
she whose stainless splendor is like a dark cloud, a blue lotus, and a sapphire; she who has the lion-king, the excellent mountain, and the tortoise as her supports. 14.
By their faces, teeth, gait, lips, hair, eyes, hips, and breasts, the daughters of the nāgas, yakṣas, gods, and humans were surpassed by the dust of his lotus-like feet. (15)
I worship Ambā, the lotus-eyed one, who alone satisfies the entire assembly of gods;
the Annapūrṇā of the Lord of Kāśī, praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the beloved of Bharga, peaceful, with an inner self that is tranquil, and the beautiful destroyer of the serpents that are the masses of sins of those who take refuge in her.
I bow to the beloved queen of the Lord, the most excellent among the best, who is eternally established in consciousness.

She was being fanned with fly-whisks resembling white lotuses, held by attendants stationed upon lotus pedestals; she was accompanied by her moon-faced husband’s wife who held a parasol; she sat upon a lion-throne with shoulders like a mass of white clouds; and her gaze was filled with the joy born of love for him whose vehicle is the elephant-faced one and the peacock.
The Goddess [crushed] Raktabīja, Turagāri, Dhūmraja, Cāmarāri, Varaśumbha, Niśumbha, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Varabhaṇḍaja, and Muṇḍa, as if they were lotuses upon the battlefield.

May she, whose feet are praised by the heroes of the celestial groves, protect us for our ultimate welfare—she who [is reached] by means of the streams of showers of excellent arrows discharged from the drawn bow. 19.
Sūta said: As Skanda, whose mind was pure, was thus offering praise,
the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, appeared mounted upon his bull.
Blue-throated and three-eyed, adorned with the coils of a serpent,
he is illuminated by a mass of rays shining with the brilliance of ten million suns.
The mass of darkness at the face of the quarters was warded off by the moon-like crest-jewel,
while his garments were tossed upward by the wind arising from the rows of waving chowries.
The moon, whose rays were shielded from the rising sun by the shade of his parasol,
arrived accompanied by Umā and surrounded by hosts of attendants.
There was a continuous downpour of showers of excellent flowers released by the hands of the gods and asuras;
and the wind, delighted by the fragrance of that [downpour], was filled with joy through its connection with the binding of those scents.
His body was radiant with a garland of the fragrance of blooming lotuses,
and his neck was encircled by shimmering strings of jewels, pearls, and other ornaments.
Adorned with many excellent ruby bracelets fashioned from the jewels on his hoods,
Śiva approached, mounted upon his bull which resembled a moving mountain.
Praised with continuous songs by sages, kinnaras, and gandharvas,
Skanda then rose from his lion-throne upon seeing the God.
He prostrated before Maheśvara along with the lords of sages, the lords of the Gaṇas, the lords of the gods, Gaṇapa, and the sage Jaigīṣavya.
Seeing Skanda with his hosts, the sages, and the gods bowing down,
as well as the elephant-faced one, the lord of sages, and Jaigīṣavya, the ocean of compassion [acted].
Śaṅkara gazed upon them with a vision overflowing with compassion; having firmly embraced his two sons and smelled the crown of their heads, he looked at them with his mother.
The Lord spoke to Skanda in the presence of all the gods.
Īśvara:
My child, I am pleased with this praise of yours, along with your mother—she who is blessed and worthy of honor;
may Skanda, who is exceedingly dear to me, come to you.
O Bhōja, you have heard from my mouth this essence of the Lord,
the Śaiva work known as the *Śivarahaśya*, which is based on the excellent narrative of liberation.
And among the hosts of gods and sages of purified soul,
Jaigīṣavya— my devotee who has conquered his senses— is placed at the forefront.
May there be no misfortune nor any obstacle for you in the essence of this story, since your elder brother, the remover of obstacles, stands present before you today. (34)
Having spoken thus and looking at the Great Goddess, Hara smiled.
For one who has wandered through various births as stationary and moving beings, human birth is attained;
within human birth, the state of being a Brahmin; then the mastery of the Vedas and the practice of right conduct;
thereafter, hundreds of activities such as sacrifices and works of public utility performed with mastery; and finally, the state of being a Śāmbhava.
With a mind that does not cling to signs, he indeed becomes signless and happy, liberated. || 36 ||

Foolish people, whose nature is pleasure and pain arising from the cycles of the three *guṇas* rooted in the karma produced by the web of hundreds of scriptural injunctions, abandon reflection upon and investigation of the playful union of the mind with the bliss born of the god of love. (37)

Having entered the mouth of hell and reached the world of Indra, and having attained the mortal world within the realm of existence, they undergo birth once again due to the remnants of their karma, and even attain a most terrible state of mind. (38)
O Umā, what is the use of all the Vedas, or the collections of Purāṇas intent on mutual disparagement,
or the glorification of the Bharata war, or the minor dharmas and the like? For in them, there are only essence-less stories devoid of the propagation of the narrative of Īśāna.
What fruit is there in this poetic narrative of Rāma, which results only in intense suffering? (39)
Sūta: With palms joined in reverence, the Goddess spoke to the eternal Śambhu—
the Great Lord (Maheśa), the support of the universe, the supportless, the Supreme Sovereign (Maheśvara).
The Goddess said:
"O Hara, for those who have become the recipients of your grace, no inauspiciousness exists;
from me they have heard the essence of the meaning of the Vedas, the secret doctrine of Śiva. (41)
This Skanda, who has destroyed his enemies, is disciplined and free from envy;
O Lord, let him hear the secret that was spoken by you to the sages.
O Maheśvara, among the hosts of gods on earth and the lords of the Gaṇas,
let your grace be bestowed today, for the sage has been made ready to listen.
The wise Jaigīṣavya, your devotee whose mind is fixed on no other,
having then heard the words of the Goddess, [placed] his excellent lotus-hand [upon her].
Śaṃkara placed [his hand] upon the head of Jaigīṣavya and Skanda;
through the touch of Śaṃkara and Śrīkara, Jaigīṣavya and Kumāra [became perfected].
With their hearts and faces blossoming with joy, they both bowed at the lotus feet of Śiva;
Skanda, meanwhile, touching those lotus feet of Śiva with both his hands, sang aloud.
With joy and devotion, he consecrated him with his own mantra using the nectar flowing from his lotus-like eyes; he considered nothing else at all.
Then Mahādeva said to Skanda, "There is a moment for Jaigīṣavya."
Īśvara said:
O Śivā, he indeed brings satisfaction to the lords of sages, for he is especially dear to them and is gazed upon by a multitude of streams of compassion.
Just as the moon, marked with the young deer, is gratified by the multitude of its digits, may this Jaigīṣavyaka likewise be satisfied by my glance. 48.

Having propitiated all the immortals, the lords of sages, the lords of the Gaṇas, Skanda, and the Munis, Maheśvara, the creator of the worlds, departed while being praised by the hosts of sages and gods along with Gaurī. || 49 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya, in the dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Skanda. || 10 ||
(Chapter 39) The eleventh chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Twelve Parts" in the Dialogue between Skanda and Jaigīṣavya.
Sūta said:
[He who was] overflowing with the bliss of the abundance of joy born from the vision of Śiva...
Having beheld the sage Śaṅkara in such a state, Prāhaśūra’s enemy spoke thus.
Skanda said:
O Jaigīṣavya, listen today to this supreme narration of a secret,
a story told by the Lord to the Goddess within the secret Śaiva tradition.
I shall declare that to you in brief; listen together with the sages, and first of all, I shall relate it along with the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the gods.
Having paid homage to the immeasurable Mahādeva, the source of bliss (Śambhu),
to the Goddess, to the elephant-faced god, and to the stainless Śaiva teachers;
O best of sages, he was first known by the name Jaigīṣavya, a portion of Maheśa; through the grace of Maheśa, his meeting with Him took place.
O best of beings, there was a gathering of the hosts of gods, the divine assemblies, and the sages; and the Lord was propitiated by me with this excellent hymn of praise.
Therein is the wonderful description of Kailāsa belonging to the illustrious Maheśvara, as well as the dialogue between the Goddess and Maheśa on that best of mountains, prompted by curiosity.
There, on that best of mountains, was the wondrous life-story of Śiva and Śivā,
as well as the worship of the Lord of Kailāsa and its performance by Maheśa.
O best of Brahmins, [I shall describe] the arrangement of the gates and walls, the designation of the stations for the Gaṇas,
and those for me, my Goddess, and the high-souled Gaṇeśa.
The chapter on the Thousand Liṅgas, the performance of penance at Kailāsa,
the propitiation of the Lord by him, and likewise his dwelling upon his head.
The consecration of Kailāsa was performed by Śambhu with the mountains;
and there was the inquiry of the gods regarding the manifestation of the Goddess, O deities.
In this [Purāṇa] dedicated to Maheśa, the exposition of the meaning of knowledge, the worship of the signs of the Self, and various discourses were indeed proclaimed by Śiva, the Great Lord.
O best of sages, this has been narrated by the one named Bhava in its second part, consisting of one thousand sections according to the count of the directions, as proclaimed by Hara.
The penance performed by the Goddess, her arrival at Maṇidvīpa,
and a description of the Kalpavāṭī grove and the beautiful Nīpa forest on the island.
The description of the great palace of wish-fulfilling gems and of Śrīpura;
from there, the embodied one’s journey to Kailāsa with Kāmeśa.
O Sage, the Goddess Kāmeśvarī resides there eternally;
it is the arrival of Himācala and the destination of the Goddess herself.
In this second [chapter] named Bhava, the greatness of Dūrvāsas and his performance of penance have indeed been described by Śaṅkara.
O lords of sages, Śaṅkara is described by three thousand and a half verses; Hari is the third portion mentioned by the Lord.
In that [chapter], at the request of the sage,
Vyāsa proclaimed the performance of penance by Gāyatrī and the supreme arrival of the Goddess.
The dispatching of the hosts, as well as the greatness of the Lord of Tīrthas,
the majesty of Śrīśaila, and the visualization of mental worship.
O Śaṅkara, there is the dialogue between Janaka and Yājñavalkya,
and the most wonderful dialogue between Padmāvatī and Ratnanidhi.
In its northern half is the portion belonging to the Jewel-Treasury of Worship,
as well as to Śiva, the God of gods, Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident.
The account of the realm of Yama, as well as the vision of Śiva and Śivā,
their conversation, and the greatness of wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
The description of the attainment of boons by the Gaṅgā and the Narmadā, as well as the Māheśvara vow and the description of the illustrious Maheśvara. (24)
The description of the worship of Śiva and so forth, as well as the narrative of Śiva’s attendants (ḍuṇḍis),
is indeed proclaimed with a count of thirty-three thousand verses.
The fourth is indeed known as Śiva; it is declared to be a direct portion of Śiva himself.
It contains the exposition of the Bṛhajjābāla-dharma and other teachings for the group of ten.
The greatness of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, the greatness of worshipping the Śiva-liṅga,
and the greatness of feeding those devoted to Śiva and followers of Śiva.
The description of residing in a sacred field of Śiva, the worship with bilva leaves,
and the proclamation of the power of that worship are celebrated in this section.
The auspicious number four thousand has been declared by the God of gods;
herein, it has indeed been stated by Śiva that one-fifth of this belongs to the name Bharga.
Therein is proclaimed the majesty of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas,
as well as the instruction of Vāmadeva and the exposition of the established tenets of the Śruti.
The majesty of Gaṅgāsāgara and of Puṣkara at Prabhāsa,
the power of Haridvāra, and the merit of worshipping at the root of the Bilva tree.
The greatness of the trident-bearing God of gods, consisting in the recitation of his thousand names, has been specifically described by the God of gods himself. (32)
O best of sages, six thousand [verses] have been recounted here concerning Śivā;
then, the sixth part of Śaṅkara follows, numbering ten according to the sequence of the directions.
In that [work], Śrī Maheśa spoke of the description of Rudra,
as well as of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and of those who wear sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
The greatness of the devotees of Śambhu has indeed been recounted in detail;
this sixth part, consisting of the dialogue between Nidāgha and Ṛbhu, is an expansion of knowledge.
Indeed, the seventh [chapter] here is called "Ugra" by Śaṅkara;
it contains the dialogue between the God and the Goddess and the proclamation of the Thousand Names.
The praise of Avimukta, the performance of ascetic penance with a hundred ṛks, the recitation of the names known as the "One Hundred and Eight," or else the Mahimnaḥ-stotra of Hari; || 37 ||
O best of beings, there is the narration known as the *Puṣpadantamahimā*,
the account of Kāṭakoṭara, and likewise the majesty of the sacred fields (*kṣetra*).
Also, the greatness of Śrīśaila, Aruṇādri, and Vṛddhācala,
as well as that of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakailāsa, has been told in detail.
The wonderful glory of Śrī [Śrīraṅgam] at Puṇḍarīkapura and Kāñcī,
as well as the praise of Kumbhaghona and Madhyārjuna.
It was narrated here by Śiva in fourteen thousand verses;
indeed, the eighth great portion, Bhīma, has been told here in detail.
O Lord of Sages, O Sage, the description of the greatness of the Liṅgas in the netherworld (Pātālaloka) was told by Dignāga and by a thousand others.
The greatness of Śrī Hāṭakeśa, the performance of penance by Śeṣa here, and the favor shown to him by Maheśa for the purpose of bearing the burden of the earth. 43.
The ninth [chapter] is Sadāśivāṃśa;
therein is the narrative of Śambhu, wherein the Thousand Names, the most excellent, were spoken by Śiva to Mahādevī.
In the Kali age, the proclamation of the Mahāśaiva dharmas, which bestows liberation through the authority of Śaiva conduct, is highly extolled.
Today, my recitation shall be exactly one thousand times, equal to the number of faces of the six-faced one;
here, the tenth is the portion of Īśvara, consisting of the recitation of the ten dharmas.
The worship of the bilva tree, the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, the great excellence of the five-syllabled mantra,
as well as the worship of the Śiva-liṅga and the glorification of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads.
The greatness of the tenth [chapter] consists of the worship of Śiva-bhaktas in the sacred field of Śiva by the Śāmbhavas,
as well as the recollection of the names of Śiva.
O Brahmin, in that [kalpa], the eleventh portion was proclaimed by Śambhu as Mahādeva, according to the enumeration of Śaṅkara’s names (or, according to another reading: "the sequence of Śaṅkara").
The sequence of the worship of Śiva, enumerated according to the order of the eyes of Manu, and the glorification of the fruits of the consecrations among the flowers; [this is the content].
There is likewise the glorification of the ten types of devotion and their worship;
the number of sages is according to the text, and the Lord here is the twelfth by name.
The recitation of the thousand names of Śiva is proclaimed therein;
the grace of Śaṅkara is also of the nature of my own favor.
This greatness of the narrative of the Śivaratnākara, which brings satisfaction to the sages,
has indeed been proclaimed by the illustrious Śiva in a thousand chapters.
The secret approved by Śiva was told to the Goddess by the God:
"There is no god equal to Sadāśiva even in the three worlds."
Likewise, O best of sages, there exists nothing else equal to the Śivarahasya; this is a great treasury of jewels containing the very essence of Śaivism. 55.
This is meritorious and purifying, resting upon a narrative whose essence is devotion;
it is devoid of the descriptions of worldly toil and its attendant dharmas.

O great sage, this [work] is free from the weariness of discourses concerning the distinctions of caste and stage of life; it is a treasury of the duties prescribed for those who have transcended the stages of life (atyāśrama).
The Śaiva discourses, which are nectar-like, filled with supreme bliss,
and spoken by the Lord to the Goddess, exceed one hundred thousand in number.
O lords of sages, this incomparable and most excellent of historical narratives, a jewel of stories from the essence of Śiva, should be heard by devotees; it is their very soul.
Just as the Great Lord’s affection for Skanda, Gajāsana, and Gaurī is supreme,
so too is this auspicious secret within the Śivarahasya to be kept strictly hidden.
"O Sage, you must not give this nor speak of it to them at first;
otherwise, O Brahmin, curse my feet, lest your head fall off this very day!"
This essence of the entire Vedānta, which illuminates devotion to Śiva,
should be given to a devoted Brahmin or to a son who possesses intense longing for it.
O Sage, this must be told to you, who are free from egoistic mind, who possess self-discipline, who are a devotee of Śiva, and who are endowed with devotion to the excellence of Śambhu.

It is said as a truth that this [instruction] is for one who has resided for a year, who is devoted, and who dwells at the end [of the practice], and for one whose vessel is the contemplation of the Three-Eyed One; it is not for anyone else.

Skanda said: The Teacher of the worlds joyfully spoke to the Mother of the three worlds, [who is] the remover of the suffering and pain of the threefold afflictions from the hearts of the beings of the three worlds.

This sun of the jewels of the *Śivarahasya* repeatedly dries up this worldly existence (*bhava*), which consists of the states of arising and dissolution pertaining to both the insentient and the sentient. (65)
O Lord, speak of that very [state] which dries up the fire of worldly existence for you,
which possesses the brilliance of the manifest lunar light emerging from the mouth of Rāhu,
and which is comparable to the whiteness celebrated as it spreads across the faces of the quarters.
Even the wise, who consume the sacrificial offerings in the mouth of the fire, consider nectar to be supreme.
Having shaken off [their worldly bonds], those who go to the world of the gods recite the stories of Śambhu:
"O Lord of the protectorless, O Lord of the Pramathas, I am your servant;
O Lord of the heart of the daughter of the best of mountains, [I seek] your lotus feet."
Spread forth a state of devotion toward you that transcends the path of all desires.
Now, he who possesses the chariot of forbearance, whose bow is his noble hand,
whose bow is the golden mountain, and who is the Lord of the entire universe—
he alone is the treasure-trove of happiness and prosperity, the abode of boundless merit.
He alone is truly virtuous who always performs sacrifice and studies the Veda. || 68 ||
He, who had made the gift of fertile land at the excellent ocean’s edge— wherein the essence of Dharma abounded through the power acquired by his accumulation of gifts—
and who listened with even greater devotion for half a moment to the teaching of the *Śivarahasya*, [attained the highest state].
He alone was the leader of the assembly, a worshiper of the pair of Śiva’s lotus feet.
By means of the processes for the creation, destruction, and protection of gods, asuras, and all that is moving and unmoving;
by means of the arising of the sufferings of battle at the onset of the nine cycles of ten-thousand-year ages;
and by means of the various castes, dharmas, and stages of life (āśramas) whose sole essence is labor.
Through discourses on this [subject], that which is perishable here does not become the crest-jewel of the Vedas.
What grain is obtained here from repeatedly threshing the mountain of husks?
Likewise, without the story of Śiva, the mind of a living being does not attain peace.
The *Dvādaśastotra* is like a great island in the vast ocean of the secret bliss of the devotees of Śiva.
These indeed were the portions ordained by Śaṅkara; I shall now state their names.
(Verse 43) Māheśa is the first; after him, indeed, is Bhava; the fourth is Hara; then Śiva, Bharga, Śaṅkara, Ugra, Bhīma, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Mahādeveśa—these are the names in sequence.
By means of these texts, which are difficult to master due to their weighty crowns of verses and which transcend the essence of the Vedānta—
Śiva [is praised] by means of these words, which are sweet with the playful charm of beautiful speech, through a multitude of chapters.

And with thousands and hundreds of eyes, each having the form of a thousand rays, Śaṅkara—[according to another reading: *diglokāmarabṛndavedartubhiḥ*]—is equal in number to the quarters, the worlds, the gods, Brahmā, the Vedas, the seasons, and the world-elephants; Śaṅkara, whose sequence of eyes is like a pure blue lotus from my mouth.
The sequence of his eyes, consisting of the sequence of the Munis, was told by Śiva to the Goddess.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Twelve Parts," in the first section of the Śrī Śivarahasya, within the dialogue between Skanda and Jaigīṣavya. || 11 ||
The twelfth chapter, titled "Description of Kailāsa.
Sūta said:
That which was spoken by Skanda of immeasurable splendor to Jaigīṣavya—
Of the boundless palaces of Kailāsa, of its gate-towers, and of the mountain itself.
The measurement of the assemblies of lingas and the construction of the ālayas were directly fashioned by Śiva himself with his mind alone, possessing incomparable splendor.
Skanda said:
"Jaigīṣavya, listen today to the description of the supreme abode of Kailāsa;
listen to the mountain with its peaks, the excellent residence of Śambhu."
Even for the omnipresent god Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, that which is called Mahākailāsa has been described by those who know the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva. || 4 ||
O Sage, this is Kailāsa, the southern hermitage of the chief attendant of Īśāna;
and this lofty Meru is the abode of the lords of the immortals.
Having entered sixteen [yojanas] below and being renowned for extending thirty-two [yojanas] above,
the bull, consisting of pillars, shines in the vicinity of the great Kailāsa.
Fifty thousand yojanas to the east of Kailāsa stands Mount Meru, the abode of various hosts of gods and asuras.
Resembling a blazing fire and like a mountain of the finest gold,
know Meru— the abode of the gods— to have a height of a thousand yojanas.
O Yogin, Kailāsa, the supporter of the earth, is said to be sixty-six [lakṣas] in height from its single base, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas.
There are seven hundred boundary mountains serving as the crossbars for the ramparts,
and within the intervals between those ramparts lie the seven continents together with the oceans.
The great mountain Kailāsa measures seven oceans in extent; it is fanned by the pure waves of the ocean of nectar and spans ten million yojanas.
It shines exceedingly from the king, measuring fifty lakhs [of yojanas];
its height extends from the base of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) up to the end of the seven worlds.
The great expanse of ground was made of silver, possessing a luster equal to ten million moons;
neither fire, nor moon, nor sun on earth possesses a splendor like yours.
The fourteen great worlds themselves are its height,
and it stands in the midst of the ocean of nectar like a mass of foam.
Neither Śiva, nor Viṣṇu, nor Brahmā, nor the deities headed by Mahendra;
neither the Suparṇas, nor the serpents, nor the Yakṣas, nor the Gandharvas, nor the sons of Diti [are able to do so].
O twice-born one, they are not even able to look upon it, much less go there directly;
for their vision is struck down by its splendors, like the deer of Śiva.
By his splendor, the sun, moon, wind, and fire were repelled; likewise, the breezes from the waves of the ocean of nectar and those that touch Mount Kailāsa were overcome. (17)
They purify all the worlds, including Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, and the other gods;
indeed, even in thought, neither gods nor asuras can go there.
The great mountain Kailāsa cannot be described even by the words of the Vedas; who is capable of speaking even an atom of the majesty of a mere fraction of that fraction? 19.
Śeṣa, though possessing a thousand faces and a thousand eyes, cannot even look upon it;
how much less so can those wretched and miserable humans, gods, and asuras?
A hundred principal kulaparvatas stood like ramparts;
some, with their great and lofty peaks, stood like gate-towers (gopuras).
In the intervals between those are oceans shaped like iron bars;
beyond even that is the supreme inner chamber of Śambhu, consisting of seven walls.
Those mountains serve as its ramparts; listen to them, O best of the twice-born:
Kumuda, Pāriyātra, and Maināka are situated in the eastern direction.
O bull among yogis, Dardara, Malaya, and Vindhya are in the west;
Udayācala, Astācala, and Muñja are situated in the northern direction.
Nīla and Dakṣiṇakailāsa, as well as Himavat situated to the south—
all of them, having plunged into the oceans, pervaded every direction.
The islands and oceans are their enclosures, as are the seven ranges of mountains;
in the spaces between them dwell the denizens of heaven.
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Nāgas, Yakṣas,
Suparṇas, Kinnaras, meritorious Puruṣas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas.
The sages and the hosts of Gaṇas, those on various stages and those on the single stage,
as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others, are forms of Rudra who possess lordship.
The lords of the Pramathas dwell there, having taken refuge in that excellent rampart of the ocean of milk, and even further on the shore of the ocean of sweet water.
Beyond that, the jeweled wall extends for ten thousand yojanas;
by the streams of light from those jewels, the three worlds are adorned.
There stands a mountain of jewels, the best of ruby peaks, rising a hundred yojanas high, with a luster like the eyes of a rutting cuckoo.
Within that [city] is a rampart made of moonstones, which is obscured by the spreading rays of the multitude of rays emitted from the garland of flames.
O twice-born one, it is fifty thousand yojanas in length;
from the moon, it is endowed with streams of nectar flowing forth.
The grounds there were colored by the streams of the essence of his splendor;
he was the supreme bull, pervading with streams of great frost-like essence.
Therein dwells a mountain of diamonds measuring ten thousand [yojanas];
within it is a rampart made of pure sapphire jewels.
He too was fifty years of age by measure, possessing the luster of a deep blue lotus; he was the singular, steadfast ground for the stream of beauty inherent within that very blueness.
There stands a preeminent mountain, a mass of sapphire stones,
possessing a luster like a streak of lightning clinging to a dark blue cloud.
It is ten thousand [yojanas] in width and likewise in circumference;
within it, there is a wall made of the finest emeralds.
The grounds there are indeed green, shining with the luster of the light of those supreme jewels;
and there stands a coral mountain, twenty thousand [yojanas] in height.
The Lord of Mountains, lovely with a splendor as radiant as a pure bimba fruit, stands there;
and within that space, there is also a rampart fashioned from gomeda gems.
O Brahmin, there stands a lofty mountain measuring thirty thousand [yojanas], beautiful with a honey-colored luster, possessing the brilliance of kuruvinda gems.
With a thousand peaks numbering in the hundreds of thousands, it was likewise;
within its interior, there was also a rampart adorned with stones of emerald.
It is forty thousand yojanas in height;
its grounds there are equal in measure to the masses of its stainless-colored peaks.
There too, the best of mountains was strewn with hundreds of pearl-jewels,
possessing a pure luster like the large eyes of a mouse-eating cat.
In the space between them, however, was the splendor measuring twenty thousand [yojanas];
and that splendor caused all the quarters of the sky to become entirely golden on every side.
There, the grounds— expanding with the essence of clear streams from many lapis lazuli threads— shine forth, bestowing wonder upon those who are already amazed.
There stands an excellent mountain, its surface endowed with the luster of the nine gems;
in some places it has the appearance of waves as clear and green as emeralds.
In some places it resembles coral, in others it has the hue of evening clouds;
in some places its luster is like that of the clear facets and bases of precious diamonds.
In some places, the quarters of the sky were illuminated by the luster arising from strings of lapis lazuli;
in others, it resembled the color of the eyes of a mad cuckoo or a kuruṇṭaka flower.
In some places it was crimson, reddened by the rising passion of rubies;
and in others, resembling the sky through the deep blue of sapphires that grasped the very grass.
In some places it possesses a luster equal to a stream of honey from a *gomeda* stone,
endowed with a smooth and pure brilliance that surpasses the splendor of pearls.
With all the horizons reflected upon its edges of perfectly clear crystal,
it resembled a rainbow in some places due to the mass of rays consisting of various colors.
Therein is an excellent pavilion, variegated with various colorful designs,
enchanting with pillars and pedestals made of ruby gems.
Taking the forms of lions, tigers, śarabhas, elephants, swans, and parrots,
he was filled with wonder as he was painted with various designs such as snakes, trunks, and lotuses.
It was resplendent with a singular height of blue sapphire fashioned from individual gems,
and adorned with thousands of pillars made of the nine jewels arranged in rows.
Its walls were smooth and beautiful, rising from the footstool-like base up to the parapet;
its floor was entirely adorned with a surface resembling that of a clear mirror.
There, the sun and moon do not shine, nor do fire, the stars, or lightning, compared to the radiance of that pillar which possesses the splendor of a hundred moons.
There, all lights were eclipsed; there was neither night nor day anywhere.
Thus, pavilions provided with a hundred thousand pillars were constructed there.
O Sage, it was surrounded by ten thousand lofty jewel palaces with gate-towers at their extremities, and was endowed with pillars and pot-shaped capitals numbering in the thousands and lakhs.
The dimensions of the gate-towers (gopuras) cannot even be conceived by the mind;
their forms are fashioned from jewels, representing the various incarnations of Rudra and other deities.
The forms of the God of gods, as well as those of the Goddess together with her vehicle,
and those of Skanda, Heraṃba, and Nandin, extend upward as far as the end of the seven worlds.
With divine gate-towers (gopura) at their extremities, measuring one hundred thousand in width and length;
then the Liṅgodbhava [shrine], and beyond that the Vṛṣavāha [shrine] on its side.
In one place he was encircled by Sindhu bark and accompanied by Amba and his sons; in another place he was joined by Skanda and Heraṃba, surrounded by hosts upon hosts of Gaṇas.
In some places he has a body half-formed with Umā, engaged in the grand gestures of dance;
in other places, his left and right limbs manifest Janārdana and Vidhi respectively.
In one place he has the form of marrying a goddess; elsewhere his appearance is that of wandering for alms;
and here in the city, he has a trident fixed in his hand and a deer in his other hand.
The destroyer of the demon Andhaka, assuming the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
bestows knowledge upon the sages and is distinguished by the Gesture of Consciousness (cinmudrā).
Tatpuruṣa, Vāmadeva, and the others, known as Īśāna and Aghora—
all of them wear the crescent moon upon their crowns and are beautifully adorned with matted locks.
Indeed, the forms of Śaṅkara were richly adorned with jewel ornaments,
while the guardians of the quarters held them, their splendors shining like various passion-colored gems.
Created by the Supreme Lord and variegated by the divine play of Śiva,
these bulls have the luster of crystal at their extremities and possess dark-blue eyes.
All of them were adorned with great horns, single crests, bells, and jeweled ornaments; they possessed great diamond-like peaks and rose high above the city gates.
The walls were adorned with royal bulls fashioned from precious gems,
along with millions of terraces and the construction of gate-towers.
With great jewel-crested pitchers atop their gate-towers that eclipsed the stars,
their banners fluttered and shook as they were tossed by the wind.
There, the inner sanctum of Śambhu is radiant, adorned with the nine gems;
therein stands a jeweled pedestal arising from moonstone and crystal.
The great Liṅga is of massive form, adorned with the hoods of jewel-encrusted serpents,
and embellished with garlands of blossoming flowers grown in a forest of great gems.
It was worshipped with many bilva and campaka flowers inlaid with gold by Śambhu and the Great Goddess out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds.
It was worshipped at the three junctions of the day, especially during the evening twilights;
at that time, it was illuminated by the radiance emanating from the jewels situated there.
There, the hosts of the high-souled Śambhu play musical instruments:
the kāhalī, mṛdaṅga, āpāra, maḍḍuka, ḍiṇḍima, and jarjhara drums.
Conchs, maddalas, bherīs, niḥsāṇas, paṭahas, ānakas,
gomukhas, svastis, pātālas, flutes, and lutes resounded with their music.
Indeed, thousands of Rudra-maidens perform dance there,
charming with their gestures and expressions, and accompanied by sweet and elegant speech.
The streams of intoxication from youth [were evident] through the tinkling of anklets on her feet;
the pure luster of her cheeks was enhanced by the shimmering jeweled earrings.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant with the intense scent of the singular aroma of incense;
there Śaṅkara dwelt with Ambā, while his hosts were driven away by Nandin.
Beholding that great Liṅga, which had been well-worshipped with jewels and struck by the clinking of the nails arising from the lotus-like hands of the daughters of Rudra;
He was constantly listening to the singing of the Gandharvas arising from the mouths of the lute-strings, accompanied by his mother.

Śiva, Śiva, Śiva, O Śambhu, O Moon-crested one of pure soul! Remove, remove my heavy burden; gladden the devotees of Śambhu! Grant me supreme liberation; may there never again be worldly existence for me. Having sought refuge in You, the savior from the ocean of birth and becoming—83.

O Goddess, while thus bathing the Gaṇas with the nectar-essence of the name of Śaṅkara, look at Śaṅkara as he forcibly [drinks] that which issues from the lotus-face of Śivā, like bees hovering around a lotus. (84)
Īśvara:
O Śivā, this stainless Liṅga of the Lord of Kailāsa, having been seen even once and worshipped, has begun to make even my heart instantly moist with the essence of nectar.
Having spoken thus and looking at her, the Blessed One, Śiva himself, said:
"And the sight of the abode of the Liṅga is easily attained even through immeasurable merits. (85)
Neither the gods nor the asuras, nor the Pramathas, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or Īśvara see it;
only Maheśvara, together with Girijā, beholds his own liṅga with great reverence,
its single crest adorned by the jewel shimmering on the hood of the serpent’s coil.
Deprived of the power of passion produced by the movement of the moon's rays.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Kailāseśvara during Pradoṣa," Śrī Sūta said:
Mahādeva, the eternal one, [is present] at the Kailāseśvara Liṅga.
Even Śaṅkara, who is himself worthy of all worship, personally performed the *varivasyā*—which means worship—in this [work]. || 1 ||
The Sages said:
How did that Lord Agajapati, who is worthy of worship by all, perform the worship of the Linga of the Lord of Kailāsa? Tell us.
Sūta said:
In this very manner, Śaṅkara was questioned in the past by Jaigīṣavya;
formerly, the Lord of the celestial army spoke to him as he stood bowed in humility.
Skanda said:
Well asked by you, O Brahmin; I shall now relate that to you—the life-story of the God of gods, which destroys the sins of those who hear it.
O twice-born ones, that righteous-souled one is all-pervading and exists in every form; for the worship of the Liṅga bestows liberation upon all.
The Lord Īśvara, the husband of Ambikā, acts himself for the sake of enlightening all, [showing] that which bestows enjoyment and that which bestows liberation. (pṛ0 48) || 6 ||
Maheśvara must rescue those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
this is the task that must be performed by the gods and asuras, as well as by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the hosts of Maruts.
Then Śiva, in order to demonstrate that worship alone is the supreme good, [appeared] before the gods, the lords of sages, the leaders of the Gaṇas, and the twice-born followers of Śaṅkara.
Indeed, Mahādeva himself performs worship of the Liṅga before the Goddess;
listen now to how that worship of the Liṅga was performed by Śiva for the sake of the Goddess.
O lords of sages, at dawn, at midday, at noon, and at twilight,
Sadāśiva is accompanied by Nandikeśa and the other Gaṇapas, as well as the Rudrāṇīs.
O Śambhu, listen to me as I describe the arrangement of the worship of the Lord of Kailāsa’s liṅga, performed by Śambhu through his ritual service.

Śiva [was honored] with streams of nectar rising from vessels filled with the seven oceans, and with all the necessary offerings brought by his attendants, which were beyond the reach of mental imagination.
To demonstrate both worldly enjoyment and liberation to all through worship,
Śambhu performs the adoration of the Lord of Kailāsa.
Jaigīṣavya said: Tell me the manner of worshipping Him, for my ears are uplifted by the desire to hear it—
especially from these best of sages, the gods, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Skanda said: Listen, you shall hear how the worship of the Lord of Kailāsa was performed by Maheśa, the God of gods—a practice that bestows liberation. 15.
O Brahmin, listen with a one-pointed mind along with these gods and earthly priests; even by hearing it, this bestows liberation upon all devotees.
Śaṅkara himself related to the Goddess, who was questioning him, the worship of Ambikā’s Lord by the hosts of Gaṇas led by Nandikeśa, as performed by the God.
I shall speak of that in brief; listen, for it is the destroyer of sins.
Having bathed on the jeweled bank of the Kailāsa-Gaṅgā, Lord Śambhu, together with the Goddess and the foremost of his excellent Gaṇas headed by Nandīśa, smeared his body with ashes; then,
remaining in his own temple of the Liṅga, he sat down upon a throne inlaid with clusters of gems.
The best of the wise indeed honors him who is the remainder, the giver of all desires, and who is equal toward the equal and the unequal. || 18 ||

Having fashioned the triple-tilaka mark upon his forehead, wearing the crescent moon upon his crest, with a necklace and armlets of pure rudrākṣa beads around his neck, and possessing the five faces and five syllables;
he wears a garland of rows of lotus-like eyes, slightly raised and glancing upward.
Seeking victory over all living beings, Śiva repeatedly offers himself here with his bull.
There, in the presence of the five-faced Īśāna, who is the bestower of the five boons, stands the most wonderful Liṅga of Īśvara known as Pañcavaktraśvara (p.
49). From the pure mouths of that [Liṅga], five rivers have issued forth with the weight of their cascading waters.
Their sole magnificent palatial abodes were the great liṅgas situated on the banks of the rivers of Mount Kailāsa. || 20 ||
In the east stands the Ratnāccha-gaṅgā, originating from the most auspicious source; indeed, the Deva-gaṅgā is situated to the west.
Beyond that lies the Kailāsa-gaṅgā, provided with jeweled stairs.
There, to the south, is the exceedingly fierce Śuddha-gaṅgā, joined by multitudes of lotus clusters.
In its midst flows the Brahma-Gaṅgā, with water like crystal; those who have reached the five elements find their end in the five elements. || 21 ||
These supreme, meritorious rivers, known as Kūlaṅkaṣā, which issue forth from the five faces of the Maṇiliṅga pavilion, possess exceedingly pure and cool waters;
they are filled with throngs of great liṅgas situated within the divine and boundless abode of Śiva.
On the banks, there were magnificent pavilions constructed with jewels, which seemed as if they had descended from the ocean of nectar.

With various groves of bilva trees and boundless forest-born trees crowded with blossoming flowers; with the cries of birds and *vakula* trees along the banks; with red-leaved *hallaka* trees; and with flocks of ruddy geese (*kokas*), large turtles, great fish, and flocks of cranes (*bakas*).
With small young cakravākas and kuraras, and with auspicious, noble sārasa cranes; || 23 ||
In a beautiful pavilion on its bank, fashioned with great gems, upon a splendid lion-throne, the Lord of Hara sat with the Goddess, Nandin, and Gaṇeśvara; gazing at the rivers and waterfalls,
Śaṅkara honored the Pañcamukheśvara Liṅga with the side-glances of his eyes full of sweetness.
Then Ādīśvara [drank] those meritorious rivers arising from the pure lotus of his mouth. || 24 ||
Īśvara:
[I salute] Him who is as white as the snowy mountain, as bright as the foam of cow’s milk,
whose body is smeared with ashes, and whose eyes are like the rows of flames from the fire that consumed the body of Anaṅga.
I salute the western face of Sthāṇu, whose feet are worshipped by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the hosts of Maruts; from which arises the sound of the Ṛgveda, which is complete and free from all blemish.
Fair-complexioned, smeared with saffron paste, adorned with a beautiful tilaka, and with cheeks that are slightly pale;
with eyes sparkling as they cast glances from the corners accompanied by the movement of the brows, and with ear-lotuses slipping down;
with lips as glossy as the bimba fruit and smiling, He is graced by dark tresses of hair.
I salute the northern face of Hara, which is the source of the knowledge of the Yajurveda.
His splendor is red, rivaling the brilliance of molten gold blazing like the morning sun and lightning;
his beautiful copper-red lips produce the Sāmaveda with their deep resonance;
and he is bound by serpents within a mass of tawny matted locks that shimmer with the luster of the half-moon.
I bow to the eastern face of the Wielder of the Trident, which is saluted by the Siddhas, gods, and lords of the Asuras. || 27 ||

Resembling the luster of a dark cloud, black bumblebee, or collyrium; with tawny eyes turned upward; with the tips of his fangs protruding from the jewels on the heads of serpents adorning his ears; with skull-halves and shells threaded upon snakes scattered up to his crest; The Lord of the World, who is the source of all worlds, was worshipped by the gods led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as he stood there like a mountain peak. || 17 || Then, having bowed down to that Lord of the World, the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, spoke these words to him. || 18 || "O Lord of the World, you are the creator of the worlds, yet you do not create them yourself. You are the protector of the worlds, yet you do not protect them yourself. You are the destroyer of the worlds, yet you do not destroy them yourself. You are the witness of the worlds, yet you do not witness them yourself. You are the enjoyer of the worlds, yet you do not enjoy them yourself. You are the one who ordains the worlds, yet you do not ordain them yourself. You are the one who conceals the worlds, yet you do not conceal them yourself. You are the one who reveals the worlds, yet you do not reveal them yourself. You are the one who impels the worlds, yet you do not impel them yourself. You are the one who sustains the worlds, yet you do not sustain them yourself. You are the one who destroys the worlds, yet you do not destroy them yourself. You are the one who nourishes the worlds, yet you do not nourish them yourself. You are the one who grants the fruits of the worlds, yet you do not grant them yourself. You are the one who bestows the fruits of the worlds, yet you do not bestow them yourself. You are the one who takes away the fruits of the worlds, yet you do not take them away yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to arise, yet you do not cause them to arise yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to perish, yet you do not cause them to perish yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to increase, yet you do not cause them to increase yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to diminish, yet you do not cause them to diminish yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to manifest, yet you do not cause them to manifest yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to disappear, yet you do not cause them to disappear yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to endure, yet you do not cause them to endure yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to cease, yet you do not cause them to cease yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to be experienced, yet you do not cause them to be experienced yourself. You are the one who causes the fruits of the worlds to be known, yet you do not cause them to be known yourself. I bow to the southern face of the Lord, from which the arising of the Atharva Veda flows.

This supreme, imperishable reality, described as both manifest and unmanifest, which abounds in the quality of pure sattva, is the ultimate principle beyond that; it is to be meditated upon constantly by yogis.
It is the source of all mantras beginning with Oṃ, and is the highest, subtler than the subtle.
One should meditate upon the fifth face of the Lord, which pervades the sky and consists of light.
Those men who constantly recite these five names of Maheśvara at dawn go to the abode of Śiva in radiant celestial chariots; they sport eternally before Śiva in the company of Śaṅkara’s attendants.
Having spoken thus, he then departed from the bank of the celestial river, his bright jeweled sandals shimmering with necklaces swaying as they were shaken by the lords of serpents;
he went toward the beautiful abode of the Lord of Kailāsa, the sole seat of the essence of great bliss.
Having seen the excellent Liṅga at the time of Pradoṣa and having worshipped it with a multitude of offerings, || 31 ||

Śrī Viśveśvara— [this half-verse is found as an addition]: Hara, the fierce one, dear to the enemy of Ugra’s son (Viṣṇu), Śaṅkara, Śrīkaṇṭha, the self-sovereign destroyer of the mountain of impurity (Kāla), free from attachment, the auspicious one,
with a face as radiant as a full-blown, deep-red lotus, spoke to Bhavānī.
"Behold," [he said], "the singular burden of worship consisting of the manifestation of my own majesty, exercised with force. (32)

Īśvara: With millions of jars— filled with milk from the ocean, surpassing the whiteness of fresh clouds, resembling the moon rising on a festival day, and made of crystal— I have reached the limit of number.
With these drops, as beautiful as the essence of the finest cream of milk, I sprinkle my *liṅga* named Kailāseśvara, O Śaṅkarī, which removes birth, old age, and disease.
O Śivā, O Umā, when that milk born from the ocean was brought to me by the heroes, the lords of the Gaṇas,
I was pleased at the time of Pradoṣa; with a stream of pure and virtuous conduct,
I instantly remove all hardships for those who are devoted and bestow upon them a mass of merit.
Therefore, O Girijā, I worship him who is the excellent worshiper of the Tsiñca-liṅga. || 34 ||
Having offered that thickened mass of curd-fragments, produced from the ocean of curds,

which possesses the luster of a rising circle of kettledrums, into his own supreme liṅga at the time of evening well-known for milking cows— which shatters the multitude of sins— O Indra among elephants! [May he grant his grace.]
This very worship is my duty at all times, even by all the gods.
