I worship that Linga upon the crown of the foremost among the upholders of the earth,
with abundant streams of clarified butter shining from lofty, stainless jeweled jars at night;
it is held by my countless hosts, who have brought it from the ocean of their own clarified butter.
There, the quarters of the sky were made fragrant, rendered beautiful by the essence of the dark scent of clarified butter.
I sprinkle the Kailāsa-liṅga with the essence of honey, a sweet nectar gathered from the ocean of honey in jeweled jars; it is a radiant light, thick with the finest clarified butter,
beautiful with the luster of the finest gems rising from within, and possessing the glow of gomedaka stones.
O daughter of the best of mountains, I sprinkle this honey of most sweet essence within the womb.
O Ambika, look with joy upon the streams of sugar falling from the top of my linga;
resembling the lofty peaks of mountains, like the essence of towering summits,
as beautiful as the peak of the Himalayas, and pure white.
Having given that [gift], it is equal to the stream of moonbeams shimmering upon the crown of my linga. || 38 ||
(Verse 52) O Daughter of the Mountain, my heart is daily flooded with joy as I behold the charming streams there, originating from the blue Nāreḷa;
they are crowded with vast millions of currents, augmented by hundreds of thousands of excellent jars and other vessels.
The honey-born [river] flows by the name of Devagaṅgā with the waters used for sprinkling that great Liṅga. || 39 ||
All of them— Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, Indra, and Varuṇa— surrounded by blissful devotion, having recognized and experienced this sacred ford as the sole fruit of the succession of all holy places,
constantly and intensely serve it, O Daughter of the Mountain, in order to conquer saṃsāra once again.
The gods dwell within her, beautiful amidst the breaking of the waves of the flood of high obstacles.

O Daughter of the Mountain, this excellent mountain Saptacchada, abounding in fruit, has been fashioned by me from the very essence of Meru; and through its bark, stripped of its outer rind, you have attained a birth that is indeed the fruit of worshipping the Linga of the Moon-crested Lord. (41)

O Umā, with these well-fashioned vessels made from the heartwood of lofty *sāla*, *surasa*, and *rasāla* trees—whose interiors resemble molten streams of gold—I perform the sprinkling of that Liṅga; this bestows upon men even the station of the Lord of the Pramathas.
O Ambikā, I sprinkle you with jars containing the fragrance of the *likuca* fruit, which resembles the breasts of women, and filled with vast, intense, and great essences;
you whose unique and true ornament is the *liṅga* shining upon the crest of the Kailāsa mountain.
This is the Linga, [to be worshipped] with waters stirred by boundless fragrances and with scented waters. || 43 ||
O Goddess, this crest of the Liṅga is especially distinguished by the great waves of the ocean of sugarcane juice;
O Daughter of the Mountain, it has been made beautiful by a thousand jars pouring forth streams of nectar for its sprinkling. 44.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the head of Śiva is clearly covered by the heaps of his pure, unblemished skulls— skulls born from the forest,
which have become fragrant with the faces of the quarters through the mass of exceedingly yellow luster flowing forth from the essence of the streams of honey within them.
I behold [it], O you of renowned vision, now that the meritorious evening has appeared before me.

My preeminent Gaṇas are utterly exhausted by the jars filled with the essence of musk, camphor, saffron, and great *mahāpāṭīra*, joined with water stirred by the spray of moonbeams and perfumed with the fragrance of excellent *pāṭala* flowers, during my meritorious evening twilight. (Page 53)
O Daughter of the Mountain, when you took up the marriage procession of the pot that was sweet, pure, and deep blue! 46.
With thousands of conch shells adorned with jewels, with streams from cow-horns and the like, with oceans of flowing milk, clarified butter, honey, and even oils;
and with the rubbing of auspicious unguents made from the finest fragrant pastes smeared upon them—
With bilva leaves, soft, pithy, and fine grasses, and even with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 47 ||
O Śivā, [I worship you] with hundreds and thousands of great streams arising from the finest golden jars, with arghya waters produced from the tips of kuśa grass fashioned with gems and gold,
and with the most sweet waters of the womb contained in jars, prepared as the eightfold arghya.
Having sprinkled all [the quarters] with the great nectar of moonlight, jasmine, and the excellent fragrance of pāṭala flowers. || 48 ||

At the time of evening twilight, by me— with water-pots resembling clouds rising in form, with the manifestation of the threefold music, with incenses, and even with showers of honey-offerings (*madhuparka*) exceeding the great honey produced from *madhūka* flowers— [I worshipped] the autumnal moon of the sky.
With clusters of blossoms that are friendly toward light, they are rare for those in darkness.

These four Vedas, out of affection for the stream of the most renowned mass of my glory, have become like four silver mountains— mistaken for heaps of silver by those [clouds] who, having offered their essence to the crown of the beautiful Liṅga which is as lovely as a digit of the moon, have been rendered white.
In the process of sprinkling the water of the sweet, pure, and stainless [nectar], [the tree] acted through its branches and tips in succession. || 50 ||

O Śivā, by praising the Rudras, they remain here as my very personified forms, bringing me satisfaction; with their hands placed upon the foremost lotuses, they have become the very embodiment of my trust.
It was enveloped by the scents of musk—the essence of the deer of thick fragrance—and by the perfumes of camphor and moon-fragrance;
it was encircled by the lord of serpents, and in its splendor it equaled ten million moons and suns.

O son of the Sovereign of the Lineage, behold with discipline this Linga, which has been anointed by those whose faces fill the quarters of the sky with the resonant fragrance of blooming flowers—fragrance that restrains the self and bestows the bliss of one’s own state, shining as a singular light. 53.
O Gaurī, I am exceedingly delighted by the fragrant yakṣa-paste, whose scent is unattainable even by the gods;
and by putting on spotless, fine golden silk garments, which are variegated with jewel-encrusted borders of shimmering gems. (54)
O Daughter of the Mountain King, I behold my Śiva-liṅga adorned with fragrant perfumes and garments;
O Umā, the sphere of the cosmic egg is not equal in splendor to the sphere of my liṅga, which bears the finest jewels.
When the moon-crested Lord, adorned with the crescent and the jewel on his forehead, gazes upon the daughter of the mountain, neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu is capable of such a feat;
even the Lord of Yakṣas has his eyes averted today. Tell me, who else could endure it, having beheld her with an equal heart?

Behold here Vāmadeva, who brings an end to suffering through his vision, whose crown is exquisitely adorned by a collection of the finest jewels, and who fulfills the desires of all people; he is the embodiment of true desire. 57.
His face is adorned with thousands of hood-jewels from which pearls hang down;
it is endowed with a luster drawn from the multitude of gems upon his radiant chest;
and his forehead shines with a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and is graced by a bright, sparkling tilaka.
O Daughter of the Mountain, behold my stainless linga upon my crown.

May that [Lord] protect me, whose splendor surpasses the brilliant luster of the rubies in the crowns of the thousand-faced and hundred-hooded pre-eminent serpents encircling his own body, and whose primordial white parasol surpasses the radiance of the garments fashioned from the sheen of their hoods.
May they always place [the moon] upon my auspicious head, just as it rests upon the crest of my linga.

This [liṅga], equal in measure to the excellent liṅga named Viśveśvara, which bestows the bliss of supreme joy— this which is so dear to me— I worship with complete devotion, for it destroys the entire heap of sins of all people and grants a multitude of all desired objects.
Behold that very Liṅga of Malli, adorned with rows of rays from various jewels, which resembles the petals of a lotus;
at this auspicious time of Pradoṣa, I am joyful, for I stand within the majesty of that Liṅga’s inner sanctum together with you.

With garlands of blossomed white lotuses and jewel-lotuses, with thousands of wreaths made from fresh blue water-lilies, with divine fragrances possessing a honey-like sweetness, and with white and red garlands of mandāra flowers; || 62 ||
This [darkness] of mine has been dispelled by the clusters of jasmine flowers with sweet fragrance blooming at the close of day,
and by the clusters of mallikā flowers shimmering with the sweet scent of spring buds—
[dispelled] by that which rivals the radiance of the manifest orb of the moon.
It was accompanied by a pure garland of droṇa-flowers and joined with a maiden from a noble family. || 63 ||

O Śivā, behold with the corners of your eyes— resembling the luster of blossoming *mañjarī* flowers— the Lord who stands upon His trembling, excellent throne, His manifest *liṅga* upon His head, amidst the weight of shimmering, boundless garlands born of the *kadaṃba*, *vana*, and *nīpa* trees.
O Ambikā, at the time of dusk, that is the fruit born of [your] eyes.
O Bhavānī, having worshipped with those pure bilva fruits, jewels, and lotuses, as well as with punnāga, nāgakesara, campaka, and dūrvā grass;
with blue lotuses, damanaka, karavīra, jāti, droṇa, arka, kāśa, javaka, and gold—[you shall attain your desire].
O Ambika, behold [the Lord] worshipped with great joy by excellent *puṇḍarīka*, *vakuḷa*, *dhava*, *karṇikāra*, *mālūra*, and *kunda* flowers;
by bees blinded by the intense fragrance arising from the abundant blossoms of lotuses and pure *mallikā* jasmines;
and by hovering bees emerging from the flowers of the blooming trees.
This excellent Liṅga, adorned with a crest of Bilva leaves at the time of Pradoṣa, shines exceedingly today with the Dhuttūra flower, surpassing even the moon situated upon its crown.

The paths to heaven were made to blossom by the networks of spreading incense smoke arising from agaru trees, which caused the quarters of the sky to expand with abundant fragrance, while the winds, stirred into agitation, cast down vast streams [of scent] as if opening the celestial way.
In a golden jeweled vessel, by the rays of the gems in the *dākṣya* [righteousness] of the child— who reflects the mass of light from the beloved sun upon the rising lotus—
my mind, transcending the path of desire, acts as a garland of beautiful forms (*suligamālā*).
With the luster of a very pale moon, and with the brilliance of snow, frost, and jasmine flowers.
With rows of great lamps fashioned from excellent pieces of fine cloth like the moon’s crescent, and with clusters of brilliant lamps featuring wicks soaked in pure cow-ghee,
they zealously dispelled the mass of darkness in the courtyards of the houses.
With ornaments that were exceedingly beautiful and renowned for their resemblance to lotuses and swans. || 69 ||
O Queen of the Mountain King, behold the radiance of my beautiful crown, which possesses the luster of a lattice of pearls as playful as a cluster of stars;
it has perfumed the various directions with the fragrant scents of the great mountain of diverse foods.
O Auspicious One, with streams of savory soup made from ghee and heaps of ageless, sweet-smelling rice.

O Śaṅkarī, [I worship] with vegetables as large as mountains crushed with honey, with milk-rice, curd-rice, and excellent jaggery resembling the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya), offered as an oblation; and with coconuts, *likuca* fruits, fine *kapittha* fruits, *mātuliṅga*, plantains, and *surasāla* fruits. (71)
May there be joy for me from the mountain-born offering of dates, fragrant ripe jujubes, pomegranates, oranges, *kaṅkola*, myrobalans, *surādāna* fruits, *rājādana*, and *jātī* fruits,
along with stalks of sugarcane.
With betel leaves made fragrant by khadira and cloves, and combined with nutmeg and cardamom; || 72 ||

O Girijā, at that very time of dusk, I offer an oblation consisting of betel leaves that are as radiant as the rising mountain king, sweetened with betel nuts filled with pearl powder and scented with camphor.
With songs as sweet as a continuous stream of nectar, charming and beautiful with the resonance of the lute.

O Lord of Lords, O Śambhu, Śaṅkara, Dhūrjaṭi, Three-eyed One, Hara, destroyer of Kāla and Andhaka! May the nectar of my name, joyfully offered by the Rudrāṇīs, be yours; O Lord, Sovereign of the Pramathas, you whose form is the Liṅga of Greatness, protect us! Protect us!
O Śivā, [I bow] to her who is adorned with jewels and accompanied by the sounds of drums and the blasts from conchs.
It was sweetened by the rising sounds of the *kāhala* drums and the resonant blasts of the *maḍḍu* and *ḍiṇḍima* drums.
I am pleased by the sounds of drum-beating, by the passionate deep breaths of my foremost Gaṇas,
by the rhythms produced by fingers resting on the holes of flutes, and by well-played cymbals;
I am gratified at the celebrated hour of evening by those who are devoted to bathing that Liṅga.
O Daughter of the Mountain, I was not aware of anything else, not even the activities of the three worlds.

In this arena, O blessed one, millions of Rudrāṇīs and their attendants dance before the Liṅga to the beat of great maddala drums, which are as restless as the breaking of lofty waves; they move in time with the rhythm that matches the resonance of lutes and flutes, accompanied by the tinkling sound of their anklets.
O Śambhu, O Śaṃkara, O Sāmba, protect us, O Śiva; grant us your grace swiftly! || 77 ||
(Verse 57) Thus, these fortunate women, sweet with their playful charms,
possessing faces that rival the brilliance of a full moon through their gestures and expressions,
with breasts resembling the uplifted frontal globes of elephants and the tinkling sound of their girdles—
With the sounds produced by the striking of their lotus-feet against the ground, they create the roar of lightning.
With the radiant trunk of Gaṇeśa serving as its handle, bearing the imperial sovereignty over various worlds as its distinct markings, strung with the well-rounded pearls of the moon,
and extended by the rows of bright, visible pearls of the great host of stars—
O daughter of the lord of mountains, millions of immeasurable parasols were held by the Gaṇas.

O Śivā, today [behold Him] being served by the entire multitude of Gaṇas with the waving of chowries from their hands— raised as they move their limbs in longing born of delighting in others— and by the shaking of my own linga-temple.
With a victorious chowrie made of coral-staffed Malaya breezes— blown by the winds from the slopes of Mount Malaya, held in the hand of the enemy of the best of mountains (the Elephant),
and consisting of clusters of the trembling hair-tufts of yak-cows.
O Umā, my *suliṅga* was then conquered by him with great devotion, and I became happy.
With the tails of forest peacocks held in the hands of joyful women serving as millions of fans,
and with the rays of green moonstones adorning my jeweled pavilion fashioned from emeralds—
O Girijā, today [the world] was illuminated by those renowned splendors, just as it was then. || 82 ||

The banners, reaching to the foremost of the excellent lords of the quarters, shone with various choice jewels set in the raised hands of the hosts of attendants, hanging from the tips of the arrows, and gleaming with clusters of fresh gems.
O Girijā, through the process of approaching the Liṅga and by bowing with devotion to that Liṅga, I contemplate my own Self as being "He," enveloped in a stream of bliss; indeed,
the entire multitude of people who rise up before me is nowhere different from Me.
Moreover, O Śivā, this entire world is merely the web of mental constructs born from my own mind.
O Umā, all things dissolve into me alone; I am the one and non-dual, eternally not manifold—thus do the Vedas forcefully proclaim that which is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
O Umā, those yogins who know my stainless bliss as distinct from other blisses [the reading is *anyānandamume*], [they truly know me].
Neither the Vedas, nor the ascetics, nor the hosts of gods and asuras, nor even the Viśvedevas born from the lotus [know Him]. || 85 ||
O Umā, this world is knowledge and the knowable; there is no knower, nor any state of existence.
I am the Infinite (Bhūman), the abode of bliss for the great; I am neither short, nor minute, nor even stable.
O Umā, this [world] is but a small portion of my own self-bliss; though in the linga, I am without a linga.
And I am unattached to the states of origination, persistence, and dissolution, which are as remote as space and the like. || 86 ||
"Thus, in the ultimate sense, I abide in the three worlds as one who transcends the universe; yet, O Daughter of the Mountain King, my secret heart has been shown to you by me.
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord, the master of the three worlds, though possessing a universal form—
Having seen the Liṅga on his head worshipped with countless bilva flowers, [he was amazed].
Beholding that elephant-faced one, he— whose sole ground was the serenity of supreme bliss,
who resided in the excellent pavilion atop the crest of Mount Kailāsa in the presence of that Liṅga,
whose great roar was like the thundering of the shattering of the cosmic egg, and whose head of Brahmā was dancing in his fierce *tāṇḍava*— began to dance.
His cheeks were adorned with earrings fashioned by Kuṇḍalīśa, and his feet moved to the rhythm arising from the sound of the drum *taṇḍumaḍḍu*.

For that stage was adorned by the sounds of the *ḍiṇḍima* drums played by Nandi and Bhṛṅgi, as well as by the sounds of conchs blown by the king of serpents and the sounds of trumpets produced by the six faces [of Śiva]. (89)
The clusters of stars, brushed against by the mass of matted locks, fall down;
the world-elephants vomit blood from their mouths;
and the universe, as if in the flurry of a cosmic dance, is shaken with ease.
The leaders of the monkeys, the gods, and the sages had their limbs trembling with fear. || 90 ||

[He] whose chest is adorned with a great garland of blooming lotuses and severed heads, [and who is resounded] by the sounds of the eight-faced one, the well-sung *Sāman* chants, the fierce and most violent drumbeats, the roaring of foam, the *maddala* and *mahāḍamaru* drums, and the roar of the eight tusks. (p. 59)
With the great serpent coiled upon his crown, its head shimmering as his hand was moved in graceful play.
Pārvatī beheld him dancing, his beauty bathed in jewels that colored her eyes; his matted locks, resembling the rays of the rising sun, acted as a sovereign fillet for his empire,
while the waves of the Gaṅgā rose from the shimmering blue sapphire-lotuses swaying there.
The dance-exhibition arising from the thick nectar of the near and far shores is beautiful upon the serpent’s hood.
Accompanied by Umā and the hosts of Rudra, they beheld Him standing upon the summit of Kailāsa, dancing amidst a stage of excellent jewels within which the entire web of worlds was bowed down;
His bracelets were shimmering with sound, and His anklets were tinkling as He moved His feet.
Resounding with the tinkling sound of small bells and encircled by a girdle of crystal gems.
He is auspicious, with wood-boring insects making their sound, with anklets of precious gems on his feet, and with the resonance of lotus-like forefeet arising from the *caṭat-caṭat* sound. 94.
He was honored by gods, asuras, and kinnaras rising from the three worlds at the sound of the great music arising from the triple symphony (tauryatrika);
he was adorned with a gentle smile and a dress that enchanted all, and he whitened the quarters of the sky with the splendor of the moon’s light.

At twilight, Umā beheld with a gaze consisting of the essence of the sentiment of compassion that blue-and-red Śiva— the cause of the origin of the universe, the bestower of desired boons, dancing with a circle of satisfied [deities] (or, according to another reading, with a face)— who possesses eight forms and removes all suffering.
Beholding that daughter of Agni, Mahādeva, as if smiling,
dispelled the hardships of the world through the delightful worship of the Lord of Kailāsa along with Kailāsa itself; then, with a gracious countenance, he spoke to Umā.
Saying "Look at me," Śiva, whose crest is the charming moon, [spoke] from the tree of Sadāśiva.
Īśvara said: This stainless Kailāseśvara Liṅga bestows liberation and is eternal; its root is submerged in the netherworld (Pātāla), and it has been worshipped by me repeatedly.

(Verse 98) Even though his stainless crown is directed upward, neither the scriptures, nor the gods and others, nor even by the sages, by you, or by me, do they truly know him; for who indeed could be his worshiper?

Devoid of the words "worship," "worshipper," and "object of worship," I alone am that Śiva; yet that excellent Liṅga, Sadāśiva, shines eternally upon my preeminent mountain, O Ambikā. (In another manuscript, the reading is: "Even so, that excellent Liṅga, Sadāśiva, shines..."). If it were as in that version, the line "devoid of the words 'worship,' 'worshipper,' and 'object of worship,' I alone am that Śiva" would remain incomplete. On my king of mountains, O Śivā, stands that bestower of boons, the embodiment of Sadāśiva.
To behold Him, sages, gods, and demons—unwavering in this world—perform austerities even today. (The reading *harāja-viṣṇavaḥ* is also found. || 99 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Sadāśiva, it is indeed a marvel that even you have spoken thus; 'It is not known even by you.
O Lord, tell me this secret: why is it so, even for you, despite your performance of the worship of the Liṅga? (100)
Having heard these charming words of Girijā, Śaṅkara laughed and spoke to Ambikā: "I am the Creator who brings forth the world, its Protector who sustains it exceedingly, and its Guardian;
Śiva, the bearer of the cool-rayed moon, who brings happiness with speech as cooling as sandalwood."
Then the Lord of Beings, his face like a beautiful, full-blown lotus, spoke to the Goddess.
Īśvara said:

O Īśvarī, neither by action, nor by meditations, nor by recitations, nor by austerity, nor by various sacrifices, nor by vows, gifts, and observances, does one attain Me—what indeed can be attained without the worship of My feet? (102)
Therefore, with constant joy, I worship this most excellent Liṅga, which grants the desires of the worlds;
it is my conviction that this task is for the sake of instructing [others] toward liberation and bestowing all goals—this is for my delight. (103)
I meditate upon that supreme reality, which is to be attained through the Upanishads and reached by the syllable Om;
it is truth, auspiciousness, knowledge, and bliss, perfectly intelligible, free from dualities, non-dual, and infinite in form. 104.
I meditate in my heart upon that One which is stable, eternal, and imperishable, wherein this entire universe did not exist prior to creation, and from which it has again emerged. 105.

Since there is nothing else whatsoever beyond or inferior to it—[the reading is "since there is nothing more subtle" (yasmādaṇīyaḥ)]—there is indeed nothing by which this entire universe, as it is perceived, is filled; I realize that all this, beginning with the gods, is that very [Brahman]. 106.
Having spoken thus to Girijā, Śiva— the most auspicious one— meditated upon Bhava, remaining as motionless as a pillar, his body undisturbed like an ocean without waves;
and the Goddess too rejoiced, her limbs filled with the weight of joy, as did those Gaṇas.

O best of sages, having heard this truth regarding his excellent worship, I declare clearly that even at the end they shall attain great liberation; such is the domain of those who dwell there. (Note: This additional verse is seen in some manuscripts. 107.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Pradoṣa Worship of Kailāseśvara," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The Fourteenth Chapter, titled "Description of the Enclosure Wall of Kailāsa.
The hosts of sages and gods said: "O Kumāra, who resembles the god of love, born from the limbs of the enemy of Māra!"
My sins have been destroyed by meditating upon the lotus feet of Umā’s Beloved. || 1 ||
O great hero, enemy of the immortals, after the demon Tāraka was slain,
I heard from you in its entirety the method of worshiping the Lord of Kailāsa.
Those whose minds are delighted by the auspicious stories emerging from your mouth have become cleansed of all sins; they are the fortunate ones, the purifiers of purifiers.
Furthermore, O son of the enemy of Tripura, whose splendor is incomparable, make their minds rise toward the waves of the ocean of Śiva’s stories.
Sūta said:
Thus entreated then by the gods, the sages, and the lords of the Gaṇas,
Kumāra spoke to those blessed ones, with Jaigīṣavya standing before him.
The enemy of the mountain (Śiva), whose face was as lovely as the radiance of the full moon, whose eyes were like blossoming blue lotuses,
whose nose had the beauty of a fresh campaka bud, and whose lips possessed the luster of rubies, spoke to the brahmin.
Skanda said: O all you sages, Parṇādās,
now listen quickly as we approach and hear the majesty of Aparṇā’s husband.
O you whose vehicle is Suparṇa and others, I shall describe the life-story of the one who dwells within the ocean— a nectar for the ears.
On the region of Mahākailāsa, measuring five crores [of yojanas],
the residence of the Gaṇas was established within a mountain rampart.
The gate-towers at the eastern entrance and the others measured nine lakhs [of yojanas],
composed of the essence of blue mountain stone and inhabited by various hosts of Rudras.
It was beautifully adorned with ten million deities, including friezes and pedestals,
and with its great, lofty peaks, it seemed as if it were scraping the very sky.
(Verse 12) It appeared as if latticed with windows consisting of ten thousand panels,
and was surrounded by bulls that shone like stone and possessed auspicious forms.
There was the abode of Nandīśvara, resplendent with gold and silver,
endowed with various palace floors and adorned with groves and gardens.
It was provided with a thousand pillars, adorned with banners and shining water-jars,
spread with curtains and latticed windows, and furnished with an excellent lion-throne.
There stood Nandikeśāna, his hand radiant with a golden cane,
beautifully adorned with a crown shining with the luster of the nine gems.
His face is equal to the abode of the moon, he is crowned with the shining crescent moon,
possesses four arms and noble limbs, and his forehead is radiant with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and a plowshare.
His body was smeared with ashes, his head was adorned with matted locks, and he wore red earrings;
he shone with hundreds of rudrākṣa rosaries interspersed with pearls.
Having offered prayers to the Lord of Su-Yaśā, his inner heart purified by meditation,
[he was attended] by the lords of the Gaṇas, the lords of the Munis, the lords of the Suras, Nārada, and others.
The high-souled one was attended by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as by Rudras, Nāgas, and Siddhas, just as Indra is attended by the Maruts.
There is the abode of Maheśa, adorned with the nine precious gems, where Nandikeśāna is served and surrounded by the Pramathas.
There, the inner sanctum of Śambhu was constructed of crystal stones, endowed with golden walls and adorned with various bulls.
There exists a single, enchanting Liṅga named Nandīśvara;
by its mere sight and touch, it destroys the entire multitude of sins.
With incense, lamps, offerings, and so forth, with constant foods to be chewed and eaten,
with garlands of pure lotuses, and with thousands of blue water-lilies;
With bilva, campaka, punnāga, bakula, dhurtūra, and pāṭala flowers, with a thousand bilva leaves, and with the sprinkling of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 24 ||
He was worshipping Maheśāna, Nandikeśa, and Śilādaja with incense of *sāmrāṇya* and *garu*, and with lamps made from pieces of camphor.
O Sage, listen with respect as I today recount that hymn of praise which he recited with vigilance three times a day while lauding Īśāna.
Nandikeśvara said:
O Lord whose stainless crown is graced by a crescent moon, whose supreme body resembles the luster of a kunda flower;
O one worshiped by the eyes of the Beloved of Indirā, who dwells within the deep lotus of my mind! 27.
Skanda said: While that linga was being praised in this manner, Suyashanatha, situated atop the palace on the eastern rampart, stood there surrounded by ten million attendants.
Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa are the mountains to the east of the rampart;
there, at a distance of five hundred thousand [yojanas], is the southeastern gate-tower (āgneyagopura).
There stands the abode of Maheśa and the high-souled lord of the Gaṇas, surrounded by peaks as majestic as bulls, which are the very embodiments of Rudra’s incarnations.
There, Śambhu, known by the name Sukeśeśvara, exists in the form of a liṅga;
he is worshipped by Gaṇapendra and surrounded by a hundred thousand attendants (gaṇas).
The Liṅga praised by Sukeśa is known by the name Sukeśeśvara;
it is likewise worshipped throughout the three worlds with auspicious bilva leaves.
Sukeśa:
O Śambhu, who transcends the sky of the five sheaths; O Vyomakeśa, the swan of the essence of all qualities;
O Maheśa, dweller in the city of Kāśī; protect me, O Śaṅkara, O Maheśa with beautiful hair! (33)
Nīla and Mandara are the mountains on the southern wall;
there also is the gateway of Śambhu, surrounded by various hosts of Rudras.
It was ten lakhs in measure, towering high above the sky,
scraping the path of the gods, and possessed of a thousand floors.
There, the temple of Caṇḍīśvara shines, adorned with the playful manifestations of Rudra’s incarnations and with pillars shaped like bulls, and embellished with refined gold.
It was joined with a thousand pillars, its archways covered with pearls,
fashioned from beautiful blue gems, and resplendent with hundreds of enclosures.
It was adorned with new ornaments and provided with stairs that reached the shining peaks of the palace; it was covered with jewels and graced by groves.
There, he sat upon a lion-throne, wearing matted locks as yellow as lightning.
He bore the crescent moon, the lord of the night, upon his head; he was adorned with ashes, his forehead shone with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and he was graced with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads.
Clad in costly garments and adorned with various jewels,
he meditated with closed eyes upon the divine lotus feet of Śambhu.

[Why go] to that place whose feet are served by perfected beings, those seeking perfection, throngs of sages, and Yama; and which is attended by the lords of the Gaṇas and frequented by the hosts of Rudras? (41)
Therein was the abode of Īśvara, the destroyer of Madana,
provided with ramparts and gate-towers, and fashioned from the nine precious gems.
The Caṇḍikeśeśvara Liṅga is the destroyer of fierce sins;
by the light of that Liṅga, all the suns and moons shine in the heavens.
This Caṇḍikeśa worships that great Liṅga three times a day with bilva fruits,
mandāra flowers, mallikās, and karavīras.
One should worship Śaṅkara with karṇikāra, apāmārga, and mālatī flowers, along with incense, lamps, offerings, and the like, accompanied by dances and the clapping of hands. || 45 ||
With palms joined in reverence, Caṇḍikeśvara praises Mahādeva with hymns of praise.
Caṇḍikeśvara:

O Caṇḍīśa, wielder of the broken axe, whose crest is the crescent moon, whose crown is the cosmic egg, Lord of the bow that is the mountain; you who wear a noble garland of skulls fallen from the pierced [demon], Lord of the earring-wearers, Great Lord of the fierce tāṇḍava dance, wielder of the trident-staff! 47.
Śrī Skanda said:
Having thus offered praise with devotion to the Moon-crested Lord of the three worlds, the Master of Caṇḍī,
and having bowed at the lotus-feet of Maheśvara, he always brings happiness to the lotus of his heart by constantly meditating upon Him.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Enclosure Wall of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Chapter Fifteen, titled "Description of the Mountain Wall," Skanda said:
To the southwest is the gateway of Śambhu, measuring five hundred thousand [yojanas].
It is adorned with the deeds of the Rudras as well as with its mountain peaks.
There Bāṇa worships Mahādeva, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of attendants,
adorned with lakes of the nine gems, and seated within a magnificent palace.
Then he constructed that temple, fashioned from jewels and adorned with a thousand pillars;
there, in the abode of Bāṇeśvara, he fashioned a linga.
It was provided with pavilions and gate-towers, and [worshipped] three times a day with bilva sprouts.
Bāṇa said:
O Lord of Bāṇa, Śambhu, you who hold the arrow of Hari in your hand, protect me, O Gaṅgādhara, Moon-crested One!
O Lord of the Universe, Bharga, Destroyer of Madana, Death of Death, O pervasive Śaṅkara, worshipful to the Lord of the Gaṇas, [protect] me today. (4)
O Śambhu, you who are skilled in destroying the sacrifices [of those] unskilled in initiation, provide for my welfare this very day!
O Maheśāna, whose singular abode is most excellent like the moon-faced lion; O Lord, be gracious, be gracious, be gracious! 5.
Skanda said: Thus did that Bāṇa, the lord of the Gaṇas, praise Śiva, the Lord of Bāṇa,
while stationed within an excellent palace at the southwestern gate.
The Astādri and Pāriyātra mountains form the western wall;
there itself is the gateway of Śambhu, measuring one million ten thousand yojanas.
It was fashioned with decorative bands, divine cow-pens, pillars, and finials at the corners, featuring the playful sports of the incarnations of Rudra and surrounded by bulls.
It was constructed with a thousand pillars and featured variegated altars;
with its golden and jeweled pitchers, it was more beautiful than Mount Kailāsa.
Therein is a preeminent palace, adorned with a thousand pillars,
inlaid with gems and rubies, and surrounded by divine lion-thrones.
Abounding in incense, lamps, and the like, and provided with various kinds of food and edibles—
therein stood Bhṛṅgin, possessed of great splendor, his body smeared with ashes.
His forehead shone with three sectarian marks, his wrists were adorned with bracelets of gems and rubies,
and he bore matted tawny locks bound by a crest of the crescent moon.
Seated upon his lion-throne, bestowing boons, he was surrounded by Gandharvas and the leaders of the Gaṇas,
as well as by Varuṇa and the other guardians of the quarters, by Garuḍas, and by hosts of Apsaras.
Residing in a palace of jewels, he was attended by ten million [deities],
as were Vāsuki, Śaṅkhapāla, Kambala, and Aśvatara.
Śeṣa, Takṣaka, the lords of the Daityas, and likewise kings,
attend upon Bhṛṅgiriṭi, whose impurities have been destroyed by meditation on Śiva.
Therein is a palatial inner chamber with excellent walls and gate-towers;
having worshipped that liṅga known as Bhṛṅgīśvara, he praises it with devotion.
With the five nectars, the juices of fruits, and even the water of the five products of the cow;
with sandalwood, flower garlands, bilva, mandāra, and campaka flowers.
With incenses, lamps, as well as flowers, food offerings, and mouth-fresheners; || 18 ||
Bhṛṅgī said:
O Lord Bhṛṅgīśa, may my mind become a bee at the lotus-feet of your hymn, delighting in it with ever-fresh joy day after day.
May it attain complete devotion to your lotus-feet, and may Māyā, O Īśa, depart along with all your [worldly] conduct that leads to sin.

O Śrī Śaṅkara, O remover of disease, O Lord, O you whose form is the universe, O Sovereign superior to the universe, O you who hold the young fawn upon your hand—[the reading "karaṭaṃka-kuraṅga-bāla" is also found]—O Lord of gods, with divine armlets and serpents, wearing garlands of mandāra, kunda, fresh campaka, and bilva, protect me! 20.
Skanda said: Thus he constantly praises Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
surrounded by hundreds of lakhs of attendants equal to himself.
To the northwest is the gateway of Śambhu, measuring five hundred thousand [yojanas],
endowed with the playful manifestations of Rudra’s incarnations and adorned with jeweled altars.
There stood the divine palace of that great-souled one, strewn with hundreds of jewel-pitchers, its banners fluttering in the wind, and adorned with a bull.
Seated upon a golden throne supported by a thousand pillars,
R̥ṣiṭi remains there, all the darkness of his heart having been dispelled by meditation on Śiva.
Smeared with ashes, marked with the triple-tilaka, adorned with ornaments of jewels,
his crown resplendent with the crescent moon as its crest, and fanned by the wind.
It is attended by hosts of two hundred thousand Gaṇapas and throngs of Rudras;
there is the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) of Śambhu, the Great Lord known as Riṭīśa.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara—who is endowed with walls and gate-towers—with fragrant incense, charming lamps, and *jātī*, *mallikā*, *mandāra*, and *bilva* flowers, [he should proceed]. (27)
With palms joined in reverence and his heart permeated by devotion,
Iṭīśa praised the Lord who resides within the liṅga during the three periods of the day, his body bristling with horripilation.
R̥ṭi said:

O Lord of the Universe, O Destroyer of Madana, O Universal Form, O Beloved of Gaurī, O Delight of the hoods of the serpent-king of the gods, O Bearer of the Gaṅgā, O Enemy of the Destroyer (Śiva), O Sovereign Lord of the Pramathas, O Moon-adorned Forehead, protect me today with Your thought! 29.
Skanda said:
Thus did Ariṭi praise the Lord of Ariṭa with devotion, his heart filled with joy;
thereafter, the principal mountain ranges were situated within the northern enclosure wall.
There is the mountain named Dundubhi, then Mandara, and then Raivata;
there also stands the gateway of Śambhu, extending ten lakhs of yojanas upward.
It was provided with a thousand floors, adorned with friezes and railings,
and featured fluttering banners shimmering atop its jeweled peaks.
There stands a preeminent palace, its floors paved with rubies, filled with the playful manifestations of Rudra’s incarnations and even with bulls.
Adorned with a thousand golden pillars and lined with rows of forest trees, it was furnished with golden lion-thrones and graced by the fragrance of incense.
Illuminated by the luster of jewels, it surpasses the expanse of the sky;
there resides Kālāgnirudra, attended by the lords of the Yakṣas. (Note: *tamoguṇam* is an alternative reading.)
His limbs were encircled by ashes and rudrākṣa beads, and he was adorned with ornaments of pearls and rubies;
his face shone with the brilliance of a crescent moon rising from his crown as a source of nectar.
Charming with the forehead region adorned by the three lines of the *tripuṇḍra*,
holding a trident in his hand, granting boons, and seated upon a golden lion-throne.
And by Kubera, by the gods, and even by the five hundred thousand attendants who bore weapons, nooses, and great tridents, yet were free from anger.
Therein was the temple of Maheśa and of Kālarudreśvara,
provided with walls and gate-towers, and surrounded by hundreds of incense burners and lamps.
Having worshipped with offerings of food, sandalwood, and bilva, mandāra, and lotus flowers, he praises the god who wields the Pināka bow with supreme devotion.
Kālāgnirudra said:
O Tryambaka, O Sadāśiva, O destroyer of Tripura, O ender of Time! [An alternative reading is: "O slayer of the enemies of the gods such as Kāla and Andhaka, O Hari, O you whose bow is the mountain.
O you whose hands are joined with the excellent trident and noose, O you whose bow is the mountain!
O Lord whose face is born of grace, who possesses the manifest splendor of the fierce sun, who wears the crescent moon as a crest, and who is the master of the nectar of truth—protect me! 41.
Thus, with a joyful soul, Kālarudra praised Maheśvara;
he was situated in the northeast corner of his enclosure wall.
Vīrabhadra always remains there, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Gaṇas;
beyond that indeed is Kailāsa, where there is an excellent gateway.
O Sage, it measured five hundred thousand [yojanas], was provided with a railing and a terrace, was inlaid with gold and jewels, and was adorned with water-pots.
Adorned with the bulls that are the incarnations of Rudra, that place was enchanting;
there, in an excellent palace constructed with a pavilion of a thousand pillars, [he dwelt].
Seated upon a divine golden lion-throne studded with gold and jewels,
he was accompanied by Īśāna, the Rudras, and hundreds of thousands of Gaṇas.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and marked by the triple-tilaka,
he was adorned with armlets of royal gems and wore necklaces of jewels and rudrākṣa beads.
With matted locks adorned by a crescent moon rising from a crown of nectar-like luster,
Bhairava indeed holds a trident in his hand and is the supreme worshiper of Sadāśiva.
Therein is one divine mansion belonging to Śambhu and Vīrabhadreśvara,
adorned with the nine gems and possessing excellent ramparts and gate-towers.
That linga, which perfumes the circle of the quarters with the fragrance of incense and is resplendent with the luster of jewels,
he indeed worships with bilva, mandāra, and campaka flowers.
With lamps, offerings, incense, sandalwood, unbroken grains, and other such items,
he joyfully praises that supreme Liṅga of the Lord three times a day.
Vīrabhadra said:

O Kṣayadvīra, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, O Lord who is the refuge for those devoid of hope—being thus satisfied, you alone are the auspicious one; you alone are the welfare of this world. Quickly liberate me today, both for the virtuous and the wicked.
Thus Vīrabhadra, the leader of the Gaṇas, constantly praises Sadāśiva;
this indeed is the mountain-enclosure of Śambhu, which is the refuge of the auspicious Gaṇas.

(Verse on page 67) Measuring ten lakhs [in extent], with a width like a bar (parigha), it is endowed with millions of gate-towers (gopura)— [an alternative reading is "endowed with gate-towers and watchtowers"]— and is adorned with beautiful pavilions (maṇḍapa).
It was provided with thousands of millions of pillars and water-pots,
and featured lofty royal gateways topped with bulls as crest-ornaments, along with beautiful temples for the Liṅga.
I have described to you this abode of the Lord, which sets the circle of the quarters ablaze with its radiance, is surrounded by mountains, and is vast and long in extent.
Thus were the inner [enclosures] laid out, with excellent ramparts and gate-towers,
occupied by the lords of a thousand Pramathas who dwell within the seven oceans.
Having meditated upon this object of meditation, fashioned from mountains, islands, rivers, and forests, the assembly of Brahmins becomes one with Śiva.
Skanda said:
Neither Hara, Vidhi, nor Hari are within the ramparts; nor are the Gaṇas, nor the wind, nor the moon, nor the mass of the sun’s rays, nor the three fires, nor the gods.
There, the one Maheśvara dwells at his own will with Ambā in joy;
even the Vedas would not be able to describe that, so what need is there to mention anyone else? 58.
The arrows were the autumnal chariot-parts, the charioteer was the vehicle, and that excellent bow with its string was the warrior; the enemy host was the chariot itself.
Hari, Brahmā, and the Vedas were the earth, the sun and moon, the ocean, the king of mountains, and the lord of serpents respectively; thus, O glorious Maheśa, you destroyed the city of Tripura.
The Lord Niśvāsa alone dwells together with Ambā and Bhava;
his are the innate powers (*śakti*) consisting of boundless and manifold creations.
O twice-born ones, those hosts are the supreme states of devotion toward him who is a mass of bliss.
Appointed to the positions of Brahmā, Indra, and the Maruts, they remained devoted to the worship of Maheśa.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Mountain Rampart," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Five Brahma Walls.
Jaigīṣavya said:
O Śikhivāha, salutations to you, O great lord, grandson of the Mountain!
O assembly of beautiful-faced ones, you whose eyes are like twelve blue lotuses!
O leader of heaven, kinsman of Maināka, born from fire,
you who remove the life-breath of the wicked Daityas who were silenced by grief!
O Destroyer of Tāraka and Krauñca, speak again in detail;
for I am not satiated by the abundance of the cascading streams of the nectar of your oral discourse.
Furthermore, how many walls, beautiful with gate-towers and watchtowers,
belong to Kailāsa, the incomparable abode of Maheśa?
Sūta said: Thus urged by Jaigīṣavya, Nanditaman-dāra, his lotus-like face fully blossomed, [addressed] the gods, the Gaṇas, and the sages.
Having bowed to the Goddess, his own mother, he spoke to the Lord of the Pramathas.
Skanda said:
Listen, O best among the knowers of Brahman—[according to another reading, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others"]—and you sages, the foremost of the Gaṇas—[according to another reading, "rich in asceticism"].
O highly wise Jaigīṣavya, listen to these pure stories.
The stories of Śambhu, whose manifestations are manifold, are pure vessels for the ear;
the Milky Ocean is its great moat, and it stands as its rampart within.
Resplendent with waves and the rays of the risen moon,
its lofty silver peak was marked by the emblem of a great bull.
The quarters of the sky were illuminated by the radiance of the multitude of jewels from its various gate-towers,
while the forms of the Lord of Gods were rendered exceedingly beautiful with crystals.
It was beautified by clusters of gate-towers and was exceedingly splendid;
to the east of that deity was a charming region situated to the east.
The gateway was as beautiful as a palace, adorned with coral figurines upon its pillars,
and flocks of female pigeons emerged from the crystal-clear balconies fashioned of jewels.
There, upon an excellent lion-throne variegated with the nine gems,
he sat surrounded by hosts of gods whose hands shone with the splendor of tridents.
With matted hair bearing the moon and sun, with eyes made pure by sacred ash,
and with their foreheads shining with the triple-line mark (tripuṇḍra), their faces and eyes gleamed.
With necks graced by rudrākṣa rosaries concealed within jewels,
and with necks resembling lotuses radiant with the rising luster of clouds.
With streams of water moving from the breaths of those who subsist on air, they were enchanting;
and with the roar of great ḍamaru drums, they terrified the entire expanse of the quarters.

Accompanied by hosts of attendants with lion-like physiques, whose bracelets, armlets, and anklets were fashioned from the jewels of their hoods, and who made the tinkling of their jingling anklets and bangles resound.
Their hips were adorned with black stripes from the lotus-skin garments they wore, and they were clad in the skins of great elephants, possessing a luster like the rising morning sun.
He was surrounded by tens of millions of preeminent leaders of the Gaṇas, who resembled lordly elephants, whose arms were as thick as elephant trunks, and who were free from anger toward serpents.
To the east, that excellent city, possessing the splendor of the moon and jasmine, shone forth, guarded by the best of warriors bearing arrows, swords, and bows.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, bearing the luster of the king of kings,
smeared with ashes, marked with the triple-tilaka, four-armed, and noble-minded.
Having worshipped that great *liṅga* of Tatpuruṣa with ritual service— [the Lord] who has three eyes, a blue throat, and the brilliance of ten thousand rising suns—
O best of Brahmins, the worshipper of Śiva honors that linga,
which is a mansion of jewels, with bilva leaves while praising it with focused attention.
(p. 69) Tatpuruṣa:

[He is] delightful with a clear umbrella, surpassing silver in luster, pleased by songs and melodies, free from desire in his own will, covered by the great serpent of his own ocean, and possessing a body as pure as crystal.
I bow to Him who is beyond destruction, whose body is pure and stainless, who is unborn and undecaying,
whose left side is shaded by the clusters of peacock feathers, whose mind is intoxicated with joy, and who desires the destruction of His enemies.
O Maheśa, who always wears serpents as armlets; O destroyer of Kāśī’s forest of worldly existence;
O enemy of Tripura; O annihilator of Yama; be gracious! Destroy this fear immediately today.
Skanda:
Thus does the person (Puruṣa) constantly praise the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara)—[an alternative reading is "the Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord"]—the Lord of Puruṣas (Puruṣeśvara).
Therein resides the Chief Lord of the Gaṇas, protecting the eastern quarter.
O Brahmin, a wall made of black iron, surrounded by the salt ocean,
shines resplendent on the south, adorned with gate-towers.
There, resounding with the gurgling wind from the waves of the salt ocean,
stands a great [serpent] whose abode is the jewels on the hoods of his many massive coils.
Seated upon a throne within the palace, his face contorted with a frown,
he shattered the circle of his enemies with the strokes of his most fiercely drawn bow.
His crest was adorned with a circle of matted locks shining like the orb of the moon;
his face was beautified by fangs like a lightning flash across a dark cloud.
Beautiful with unguents illuminated by the luster of his dark-blue, stainless body,
he was like the interior of a water-laden, unrestrained cloud made radiant by a brilliant flash of lightning.
Marked with a beautiful tilaka of similar purity, adorned with ornaments and unguents, bearing a bow and weapons, he was likewise surrounded on all sides by hosts of attendants.
With excellent arms resembling the Prasannakara [moon], fierce with their prowess, adorned with supreme bows, and making sounds like the shattering of the cosmic egg; || 33 ||
Aghora, with a terrible countenance, has cast [his gaze] toward the southern direction;
his locks of hair are adorned for the fierce shattering of the dense darkness of ignorance caused by Caṇḍa.
Having worshipped the great liṅga Aghoreśa, he praises it with devotion.
Aghora:

[I bow to] Him who is the conqueror of the cities in battle, who delights in destroying the afflictions of the world, whose lotus-feet shine with the lustration performed by the crowns of the kings of gods and asuras, and who is ever intent on shattering the distress of the universe.
O my heart, serpent-like lover of the daughter of Jahnu, worship Dhūrjaṭi, the giver of sovereign empire even in this very life through the path of existence, and of union through sacrifice. 35.

I bow to the one who wears a golden girdle, who is skilled in rending the mass of sins, and who possesses a sky-clad garment that is a deceptive mountain of words approaching nearby, yet is intent on dancing. (Page 70) 36.
Skanda:
There is also a wall made of topaz in the west,
the intermediate quarters of which are illuminated by the radiance of topaz gems.
With many forms of Rudra engaged in play, fashioned from that supreme jewel, and with similar bulls stationed at the front of the gateways; (38)
There stands a holy mansion, resplendent with various jewels and adorned with gate-towers shaped like mountains, beautiful with their shining domes.
Equipped with a railing and a plinth, surrounded by excellent lion-thrones,
Sadyojāta sits comfortably, adorned with the essence of refined salt.
His body was as enchanting as the radiant moon born in former times;
he wore the moon as a crest-ornament formed by his silvery-brown, pure matted locks.
His forehead-eye was as radiant as the fire at the end of an eon, presided over by the Lord of Stars (the Moon),
and he was adorned with the most fierce and supreme orb of the sun.
Beautiful with a neck-ornament resembling a blue lotus,
his throat was adorned with many garlands made of topaz.
His hips were adorned with a tiger-skin and a beautiful girdle of gems;
he was accompanied by many such leaders of the Gaṇas, as numerous as the sons of Ahimanyu.
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, he is attended by Pāśin;
his excellent abode is a magnificent palace situated in the midst of the great ocean of curd-cream.
And it was frequented by hosts of Mahodaṇḍas and terrifying Ḍimbhas,
as well as by Pāśis, in that western direction where [the enemies] had been cast down.
He praised the Sadyojāteśvara Liṅga, worshipping it with devotion. (47)

Sadyojāta: He who roars with the mass of matted locks born from the insects of the sandalwood tree, and whose mass of hair on the banks of the river is made into a canopy by the high-flying, spreading rays of the sun.

Roam upon the banks of my mind, which has become a vast expanse clothed in the elephant-hide garments spread across the slopes of artificial cow-hides fashioned from horses, and where the trees of the forest are the skulls of the earth’s lords. 48.
He who bears the moon as his crest-ornament, who is a mine of jewels consisting of a multitude of excellent qualities,
who has burnt the fish-bannered god of love with the fire from the eye blazing on his forehead,
and who is marked by the sandalwood paste upon the slopes of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King—
I worship Śaṅkara, the Lord who always grants fearlessness to those who worship him. || 49 ||
Skanda— thus Sadyojāta always praises the Liṅga of Maheśvara;
to the north of that is a rampart fashioned from Gomedha gems.
It was covered by an ocean of clarified butter, and there it was surrounded by winds arising from its waves and by auspicious gate-towers constructed from the finest jewels.
(Verse 71) That assembly hall of his was indeed joined by bulls whose forms were emerging as incarnations of Vararudra,
and it was beautified by their splendors.
There he beheld the mighty-armed Vāmadeva, the three-eyed one, seated upon palatial mansions with boundless peaks and adorned with many pillars.
Seated comfortably upon a lion-throne, white with the smearing of ashes,
his form resembling an emerald and his matted locks like flashes of lightning.
He whose excellent forehead is marked with three lines of ash, who holds a sword and a shield,
who is auspicious, whose face is serene, who has a blue throat, and who bears the crescent of the shining moon.
It was served by green-faced Gaṇapas and winds,
which were as swift as the wind and beautiful with the fragrance of emerging marataka flowers.
They bore the triple-crested mark and the half-moon, their heads crowned with masses of matted hair;
they held arrows and bows, and were adorned with hallakas and ornaments.
It was attended on all sides by heroes with gleaming tridents in their stainless hands, who were expert players of the vallakī lute, the muraja drum, and the large mṛdaṅga drum. || 58 ||
Vāmadeva, born of the Sāman chants, with his waist girdled by a deerskin,
a serpent wound around his neck, and eyes as pure as those of the king of beasts.
Kubera protects the northern quarter, which is surrounded by the lords of the Yakṣas;
having fully worshipped the Vāmadeveśvara Liṅga, he praised the Lord.

Vāmadeva: O Lord, how many are there who, having cast off from their minds all deceit and harshness— which are like spittle spat out— stand intent solely upon Brahman while reciting hymns of praise to you?

O Abode upon the jewel-throne worshipped in Vaikuṇṭha, O Śrīkaṇṭha, You who shine upon the necks of [the gods] Nīla, Jyeṣṭha, and Kaniṣṭha, and who destroyed the leprosy [of Atri]; abide within my heart as the most excellent one. 61.

I worship the Lord, who is the moon to the blue lotus of Śrī, praised by the Sāman hymn named Vāmadeva, the abode of the limit of all virtues, the protector and destroyer of the world, whose desire for bliss arises from Śambhu, and who has burnt away Kāma with the side-glances of his own eyes.
Skanda:
While Vāmadeva, his mind serene, was thus praising Mahādeva,
Hīrakasaudhaka stood upon the summit of that mountain in the meantime.
With bodies originating from the incarnations of Rudra and even from bulls, he wears great necklaces of serpent-kings and possesses the brilliance of the midday sun. (64)
His body is adorned with the ashes that serve as a crown for the Lord of Night;
he is clothed in the skin of a lordly elephant, and his limbs are decorated with strings of diamonds.
In the intermediate space, the captivating sky is guarded by hosts of Rudras,
who carry quivers, wear armor, and bear daggers and other weapons.
By the grace of Vyomakeśa, Īśāna became the protector of the virtuous;
having worshipped the great liṅga Īśāneśa, he praised it with devotion.

Īśāna: [He who is] dear to the sound of the *rathantara* chant; whose arrow is the hand of the chariot and its parts; who transcends the path of the mind's desires; and who possesses the excellent bracelet of the Lord of Chariots.
I worship the one whose matted locks are formed by the daughter of Jahnu following the path of Bhagīratha—the beloved of the chariot of the gods (Agni), who destroys boundless sins. (Verse 68)

May the God manifest in my heart, resonant with the neighing of His own horses in the goblet, the tinkling of the anklets of Vāyu’s beloved wife on her feet, and the abundant trumpeting at the boundary of the waist. 69.

May that Lord—who has made the mass of the Vedas his own mount, who has accepted the enemy of Śambara as his body, and who has turned the enemies of the Dānavas into weapons—always shine within my heart. (70)
Skanda said: Thus does Īśāna, surrounded by his hosts, praise at all times—
the inner chambers, the enclosures, and the excellent ramparts and gate-towers.
In the great abode of Kailāsa,
this supreme enclosure of jewels fashioned from gems was indeed constructed by the five Brahmās.
O Brahmin, by hearing that [account] of Maheśa at that time, there is the destruction of sins.
The manifestation of Śiva is manifold; the activity of Śiva is manifold;
manifold is that Māyā of the wielder of the trident, the Great Illusionist.

May the two who are the conquerors of Hara— the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, whose left arm is the earth, and the one born from the right eye— grant you the destruction of the cycle of births, karmic actions, and worldly destinies, by means of even a hundredth part of a minute fraction of a tiny portion of their power.
In one kalpa, the Creator (Brahmā), Śiva, and Viṣṇu act as the guarantors; in another, Brahmā is the instrument; and in yet another, even Rudra is the instrument.
Yet, the maintenance and destruction of the world are not brought about by the qualities of the material nature (prakṛti) acting as instruments.
And by the grace of Śambhu, the fathers and sons will honor one another.
Even his conduct, which transcends the range of mind, speech, and sight—these are the celebrated and far-reaching divine plays (*līlā*) of Śiva.
This Śambhu is independent; though devoid of a multitude of qualities (*guṇa*), he is yet possessed of qualities.
By his own power, the Lord of the Mountains today performs wonders in this world.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Enclosure of the Five Brahmas," in the first part of the glorious *Śivarahasya*.
Chapter Seventeen, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Palace.
Skanda said:
Within that [palace] as well, there is a rampart made of moonstone (candrakānta-śilā).
He was situated upon the summit of the great peak of the mountain of refined gold.
O best of Brahmins, it was five hundred thousand [yojanas] in length and height,
and its circumference was likewise, O lord of sages, radiant with brilliant splendor.
With a pinnacle of pure golden jars, it possesses the radiant luster of glittering jewels and gems;
its footstool shines with the surging waves of the waters of the ocean of nectar.
It has four great gates on all sides, topped with excellent gopura-towers; it shines with ten thousand moons and its interior is surpassed by its own dazzling brilliance.
Beautiful with the reflections within the great orb of the world’s wheel,
even the directions were whitened by the streams of his lovely luster.
It is pure, with water released by the rays of the rising moon, resembling foam from the upward laughter of dancing waves of nectar. || 6 ||
This supreme mountain is the very essence of the entirety of Mount Kailāsa;
indeed, it is the white trees that exist in the world which serve as its description through their whiteness.
O best of the twice-born, because of their extreme whiteness, they are incomparable;
upon the great crest of that rampart, they are fashioned from crystal stones.
The bulls had blue eyes, were adorned with horns on their tails,
possessed tongues shimmering like kuruvinda gems, and were radiant with the fullness of their humps.
With rows of shimmering fly-whisks suspended from the tips of their ears,
some, filled with bliss, gaze at one another with their eyes.
Some, solely intent on enjoying the fragrant hindquarters,
were adorned with rows of tusks that shone with the brilliance of emerging diamonds.
Some had the corners of their eyes copper-red like the great stones of a celestial water-wheel,
and they possessed pendulous testicles fashioned from coral and gems.
Those who have conquered the quarters of the sky rejoice in the sounds of their dense armor;
thus they stand there, situated upon the excellent ramparts of the great palace.
There was a grove of *kalpa* trees there, covered with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
its crests in full bloom with various leaf-buds and blossoms.
There, the ground was encircled by a basin of jewels and possessed a radiant altar of loveliness,
while a gentle, pure breeze arose, fragrant with the scent of those flowers.
It was exceedingly gratifying to the sense of smell, pervaded by cool sprays,
and surrounded by many seasons headed by spring.
There, that great family of Kalpaka trees bestows an abundance of desires;
it is surrounded by Mandāra, Pārijāta, Santāna, and Candana trees.
Producing joy for the eyes and warding off the three types of suffering, that enchanting place is the very essence of the great ocean of Kailāsa. 18.
Resembling an emerald, with a luster equal to the shade of a clear umbrella,
its breeze was made fragrant by the intense, humming scent arising from those flowers.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, as well as the sages, the Gaṇas, and the deities,
their hearts satisfied and filled with joy, no longer even desire the Nandana grove.
"Indeed, even a hundredth part of a hundredth part of that happiness does not exist there.
Thus they converse with one another; how then can that forest be reached?
"O twice-born one, without the grace of the illustrious Maheśa alone,
we have no access there"— thus they spoke, their hearts filled with wonder.
There, they shine with rows of stairways made of great, blossoming jewels,
and are completely filled with water as clear as pure crystal.
They were adorned with earrings resembling golden, soft, and swaying lotus stalks,
and beautified by jewel-lotuses, white water-lilies, and night-blooming lilies.
They were covered by thousands of petals of blossoming jewel-lotuses and endowed with excellent green emerald canopies spread above.
The gentle breezes were like pearls from the dark-blue waves shimmering upon its surface,
and they were colored by the mass of pollen from its lotuses.
O Śaṅkara, even the extensive groves of blue water-lilies there spread their fragrance through the quarters of the sky with the sweet scent of those clusters.
Resplendent with boundless blue lotuses, they are entwined and fixed by the intensely beautiful filaments of many buds fashioned from sapphire.
Covered with the petals and filaments of blooming white water-lilies,
they possessed leaves as steady as the movement of cranes upon the surface of the lake.
With its rising, beautiful white lotuses, it has rendered the mass of nectar pale;
here, they remain like the pure autumnal sky with its stainless lotus-petals.
At its edge, that lake was then surrounded by thousands of palaces with pinnacles possessing the luster of gems and rubies shining with jewels.
It was resplendent with rows of pillars made of various excellent jewels from boundless oceans,
and featured coral maidens upon pillars covered by networks of coral creepers.
With its eaves adorned by radiant finials reaching the windows,
it fixed the quarters of the sky with the luster of shining jeweled pitchers.
Resplendent like the rising light of a thousand suns and shining with the form of filaments,
there was in one place a lion-throne variegated with the nine gems.
In some places there were beautiful couches with feet made of jewels and bases adorned with coral,
their surfaces fashioned from crystal stones and spread with fine coverings.
They also had floors made of emeralds and spotless floors of kuruvinda gems,
enchanting with great pedestals fashioned from sapphire jewels.
The couches were enchanting and beautiful, adorned with canopies of pearls, featuring hanging chains of jewels, and graced with decorative pillows. || 37 ||
There, the great seats shine with the splendor of topazes, agates, and lapis lazuli surfaces, endowed with a radiance like that of flashing lightning.
In some places, the hosts fall down violently, mistaking the high for the low; in elevated regions, they are always prone to the delusion that it is low ground.
There was the delusion of water upon dry land and the delusion of dry land within the water;
it resounded with the cries of parrots and mynas as various jewels fell like leaves.
It was resplendent with rows of parrots and mynas situated within jeweled cages,
and with play-peacocks whose plumage hung from the balconies.
There, all the flocks of birds cried out: "O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, protect us!
The pure wind is made fragrant by the great scent of the incense smoke."
The moon and sun were constantly eclipsed by the radiance of the jewels;
the excellent water-pots rising from the palaces situated in the midst of the lakes shone forth.
The quarters of the sky were illuminated by the intense luster produced by jeweled pillars,
which were adorned with vast, pure pearls fashioned from gold and fine cloth.
Resplendent with rows of lattices, railings,
and canopies, he rests upon an excellent, lofty lion-throne set with diamonds in its center.
There, Mahādeva [delighted] the Goddess with diversions, beds, and seats,
and with the high sprays from the showers of water poured from large jars at the edge of the lake.

(p. 75) Sometimes, standing there in the midst [of the water], he was fanned by the Goddess with a fly-whisk in her hand, amidst the spray from the mass of falling streams rising with the scent of the riverbank.
The illustrious Maheśāna was served [by his attendants], and at one place Śiva remained seated upon a throne;
there, Maheśvara engaged in various kinds of sports with the Goddess.
Delighted by the various activities of the Goddess, which were performed out of a desire to please the Three-eyed Lord, the God remained there in those excellent palaces.
O Śambhu, O Brāhmaṇa, listen as I describe some of them there today:
in the forest, on the banks of lakes, at the tops of palaces, and at the city gates.
Then Mahādeva Śaṅkara sported with Bhavānī;
the Lord gazed upon the mountain, while the Goddess was with her host of female companions.
He showed him various wonders upon that Mount Kailāsa.

With *sāla*, *tāla*, *kṛtamāla*, and *tamāla* trees; with *āmalaka*, *avakula*, *arjuna*, and *pāṭala*; with *phānasa*, *likuca*, *bāhlīka*, and *nīpa*; and with *dāḍima*, *surasāla*, and *rasāla* trees. || 53 ||
With the fruit-laden *jambū*, *nimba*, and *kadamba* trees; with *takkola*, *hintālaka*, *aṅkola*, *sarala*, *aśoka*, *tilaka*, *tindūka*, and *mālūraka*;
with *punnāga*, *nāga*, *nāga-sarjarasika*, *cāmpeya*, and *mādhūka* trees.
[It was filled] with *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *tintriṇī*, *bhūnimba*, *jāla*, and *dhava* trees. || 54 ||

With *vaṭa*, *kuṭaja*, and *kuraṇṭa* trees; with *karṇikāra*, *aśvamāra*, *khara*, *badara*, and *palāśa*; with *lodhra* and excellent *candana*; with *kuravaka*, *śuka-tuṇḍa*, *śiṃśupā*, *ceṅgudi*, *likuca*, blossoming *bhaṇḍa*, *ketaka*, and *sinduvāra* flowers. || 55 ||
With *kedāra*, *kovidāra*, *devadāru*, and *kapittha* trees;
with *tagara*, *agaru*, *kṛṣṇābhra*, and tall *nīpaka* and *kamraka* trees. || 56 ||

With pairs of *mandāra* trees, *pārijāta*, *vakaja*, and *arka*; with *saptacchada*, *pūgī*, *nāra*, *kharjūra*, and *kuṭaja*; with *nāraṅga*, *jāti* trees, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *kandala*, those born of sages (*munibhava*), *rājādana*, and *barbara*—
With *śālmali* trees, excellent *śigruka* trees, those born of honey, and fine *mātuluṅga* fruits as well. || 57 ||
With *bhūtāvāsa*, *harītakī*, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), those produced from the *śamī* tree,

*kindara*, *prācīnāmalaka*, *karañjaka*, *kakubha*, fragrant *jambu* fruits, *bandhūka*, those born of *ciribilva*, *taraga*, and trees arising from black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāgaru*)— [Please provide the second half of the verse for a complete translation.]
And with *cāmpeya* trees, flowering *śirīṣa* trees, and other hundreds of branches. || 58 ||
By the clusters of *vallī* creepers— fragrant with *mallī*, *mālatī*, and *jātī* flowers, awakened at evening,
opened by the moon and the spray of dew, exceedingly white, and like garlands of true moonlight;
and by the breezes carrying the mass of fragrance from the pollen of *kadamba* blossoms— (pṛ0 76) [the forest was adorned].
With blooming *tilaka* trees, with blossoming *tamāla* flowers, and with shining filaments. || 59 ||
With ponds whose mouths are spread wide by moonbeams, with swaying *saptacchada* trees,
and with saffron-dyed flowers sweet with their radiant red luster and emerging filaments;
with excellent clusters of grapevines, both dark and white, and mines of the essence of sugarcane.
The betel-vine creepers were rendered sweet by their bodies being treated with the juice of the areca-nut tree.

With clusters of Mandāra trees more beautiful than the lovely, with blossoming Dāḍima flowers and Bakas and Karṇikāras; with Campakas possessing a splendor that appears golden, and with blooming Pāṭalas, Kadambas, and Jāravṛkṣas. || 61 ||

O Ambika, behold today this mountain of gold, most enchanting with its clusters of trees, its peaks bearing the weight of blossoming flowers—of *kiṃśuka* trees with the hue of parrot-beaks, excellent *śalmali*, *punnāga*, *nāga*, and *vanīpa*. (62)
O Bhavānī, your body, expanded by the creepers, shines forth forcefully like a multitude of millions of rising moons.
Surrounded by full-blown white lotuses, night-lilies, beautiful blue lotuses,
and reddish lotuses and water-lilies, with steps made of fine gems on all sides,
Śaṅkara took the form of a great liṅga at the base of a pure bilva tree on its bank.
The goddess Sarasvatī indeed praises the Lord of Mountains even more highly than the hosts of gods and Rudras.
Satiated by drinking the nectar of that stream of meditation, the cakravākas seemed as if absorbed in their own singular essence;
likewise, the swans, cranes, and rows of sārasa birds had their wings drenched by the moving waves upon the lakes.
Indeed, by my power, entities do not move about with their limbs moistened, as if they were in the ocean of existence.

The grounds, once as solid as the peaks of mountains, now shine brilliantly and are simultaneously mired in mud by the falling of fruits, the downpour of showers, the scattering of flower-pollen, the initial agitation and sight of the noble monkey host, and the flowing streams of ichor from the temples of elephants.
[The forest] resounded with the quiet cries of parrots, cranes, cuckoos, crows, owls, and ruddy geese;
it was filled with the sweet warbling of cakravāka birds perched upon the branches of the trees in the dense forest.
On the summit of that best of mountains, the interior of his palace resounds with the arrogant cries of peacocks dancing, with the trumpeting of elephants belonging to the host of Śiva,
with the calls of cranes on the mountain peaks, and with the sweet warbling of parrots and cuckoos.
The mountain ridges were hollowed by the hooves of wild asses and the horns of yaks and elephants;
it was filled with honey hanging from the droṇis where bees delighted in the pollen of trees, which was stirred by breezes dear to the gods and the world.
With branches lengthened and bent by the weight of the excellent blossoms of their fruit-clusters, resembling dark blue lotuses garlanded by swarms of bees,
and with the tips of their branches— well-formed and rich in sweet sap— reaching down, these golden trees shine like the peaks of the great mountain Meru.

Behold this [forest] on the king of mountains, where clusters of kola fruits are repeatedly covered by musta grass that resembles a mountain of refined gold; and where, due to the deep gurgling sounds from the nostrils of white-tusked elephants, there arises a great roar. 71.
This herd of elephants, with the ground covered by clusters of pearls and gems mixed with the profuse blood gushing from the frontal globes of the rising tuskers torn open by the lion’s claws,
flees in great terror at the roar of the lion, its own loud trumpeting now silenced.

Behold, O Girijā, the family of lordly serpents, their hoods raised above anthills, fleeing with eyes terrified by the circle of directions stirred by the wind; they have abandoned their young, who were born in fear from the roars of Hari, and run away like a herd of leaping does. 73.
Seated upon the great lion-throne in the jewel-palace of Mount Kailāsa, the Lord,
having drunk with his bee-like eyes the essence of honey dripping from the lotus-face of the Goddess, says to her, "O Umā, look at these signs!"
It was worshipped daily on the peak of Kailāsa with the tender sprouts of the bilva tree.
Behold, O Mother, [these trees] covered with the plumage of peacocks intoxicated by passion, fanned by the bushy tails of herds of yak-cows,
and constantly sprinkled with the milk of wild cows from that forest, whose ears are spread wide like palm-leaf fans.
These [trees] were honored by the falling of bilva leaves, which served as coverings for the bodies of deer and lordly elephants that had been crushed by the friction [of the chariot].
Skanda said:

O Goddess Gaurī, now that you have assumed the form of a Bhilla, the Lord Śauri bears a peacock feather, a bow, a serpent, and a wicked bowstring; and the Mountain (Himavat) assumes the state of your playful bow.
O Lord of the Universe, O Supreme over all! The Vedas are Your horses, and Brahmā is the creator of destiny;
through the comprehension of Your divine play, the destruction, manifestation, and maintenance of all worlds occur. (77)

O Three-eyed One, who removes the initiation of Manmatha, Tripura, Dakṣa, and others through Your glance; who are far removed from the senses and the like, yet grant the wisdom of the Great Lord of Monks who has renounced all;
whose gaze favors the act of eating out of compassion, and who dwell within the very core of the chest—[salutations to You]. (78)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kailāsa Palace," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The Eighteenth Chapter, titled "Description of the Summit of Kailāsa.
Skanda said:
Indeed, Śaṅkara, tormented by the heat, [resided] in the great palace shaped like a diamond.
He was seated upon an excellent jeweled lion-throne on the shore of the Goddess’s lake.
At that time, his great body was anointed with the liquid of excellent moon-fragrant sandalwood,
and the tips of his flames were perfumed by the thick smoke of great agallochum.
Maheśvara then ate the food from the sky, consisting of supreme great delight contained in a jewel vessel; even more than that, he ate the fruit of the kalpa tree provided by the Goddess.
Upon seeing fruits placed in vessels made of many jewels and inlaid with excellent gems, the Lord of Gods, who feeds upon nectar, is sometimes satisfied.
Beholding the jewel-mirror, he saw his own reflection therein;
on the surface of the queen’s forehead was a tilaka fashioned from jewels.
Śiva, whose self is exceedingly joyful and who is a mass of eternal bliss, imagines himself as sandalwood paste,
camphor, and musk smeared upon the Malaya mountain.
Having anointed the Goddess, the Lord, filled with great joy, out of excessive delight,
took pleasure in the fragrance of the jasmine flowers in the Goddess’s braided hair, which brought him the bliss of his own senses.
With flower garlands abundant with the fragrance of *kalpaka* trees and with ornaments,
he abandoned his matted locks for an excellent crown fashioned of jewels.
Greatly delighted, Maheśvara holds the pair of moons;
with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, he adorns himself and Umā.
Having abandoned the great jewel of Kākodara, which surpassed the radiance of gems,
he wore a magnificent necklace of nine jewels with pearls suspended from it.
Śaṅkara indeed impales his own throat upon the neck of the Goddess;
there, the blue-throated, odd-eyed Lord sports with the Goddess.
O best of the twice-born, as he dwelt there in this manner, hundreds of kalpas of Brahmā passed away— past, future, and present— all within that single period of time.
Who indeed is able to describe even half a moment of those sports of that god Kālātīta, who is ever victorious over death? 13.

In houses where showers fall like rain and which resound with the beating of conchs and drums, Śiva is delighted by his Mother with waters fragrant with sandalwood, ushīra, and jasmine, and scented with the aroma of fine *pāṭala* flowers;
yet his body is scorched by the rays of the sun and the fire rising from his forehead. (Page 79)
And she sits upon a lion-throne, adorned with rays of jewels playfully shimmering.
By the swaying of great swings of jewels set within diamond chambers;

by the masses of white brilliance from the gems stirred up by the rising, expansive wind; by the delicate radiance of shimmering silken garments; and by the splendors resembling the peaks of mountains in full bloom—
He gazes upon the world with his eyes like plantain trees, he who is an ocean of the waves of nectar. || 15 ||
Īśvara said:

O Ambikā, behold the lands of Maṇidvīpa; that ground bestows upon you boundless joy, O Great Goddess, for its great winds, cooled by the waves of the ocean of nectar, produce the very root of supreme bliss.
O Daughter of the Mountain, because of the radiance of your body which resembles an emerald, even this preeminent mountain, though composed entirely of gold,
shines with a green luster, filled with deer, birds, creepers, and trees.
O Ambikā, beholding [your reflection] in the mirror, he is surpassed even by the fortune of possessing a form like yours. || 17 ||
The King of Mountains is ever graced by the mass of moonlight resting upon his crest, by his own splendor, by peacocks dancing on the tips of his boundless peaks, by the cries of male cuckoos,
and by the deer, ruru antelopes, cranes, and yaks with their uplifted tails.
