With multitudes of rhinoceroses, herds of buffaloes, and flocks of leaping deer; || 18 ||
Those golden deer roam about, moving upon the tips of green jewel-grass, their bodies adorned with falling drops of water;
they resemble silver pigeons with feet of precious gems, seeking grains of food while following behind their beloveds with the jingling sounds from their own necks.
With the great pearls produced from their own mouths, those swans— whose pure bodies are stainless and whose brilliance fills the quarters as they shake their wings—
sport forcefully in the abundant water amidst blossoming red lotuses.
Like those standing as neutral witnesses, the flocks of ruddy geese maintain silence when Śivā [appears].
Even the gentle breeze here today brings me joy, as it intoxicates me with the fragrance of the pollen of musk-flowers, which are now scattered by my fear.
Even musk deer run most swiftly out of desire for the scent, yet they do not perceive it even when it resides upon their own bodies, like fools;
O Umā, even so, the sages and gods do not recognize me, though I abide within their very forms.
In the same way, even the deer on Mount Kailāsa of mine are of deluded minds.
With the ridges of its excellent mountain peaks turned tawny by the mass of exceedingly soft *ketaka* pollen, who that dwells here would not worship you?
Even the gods in heaven surely laugh [at such hesitation].
Resembling emeralds, with parrots for their ruby-like gems and their faces as gomedaka stones, fashioned with the jewels of the gods and possessing the luster of gold, diamonds, and sapphires—
O Lord Śiva, O Śiva, protect us as we dwell upon the crest of the mountain!
O Lord of the Pramathas, remove this suffering with a glance of supreme compassion.
"O Hara, O Lord of Hari, O Lord of the Universe,
O you who are compassionate toward the helpless, O Destroyer of the Cities, look upon us today!"—
thus do the poets of resonance always [sing], like the Ganges flowing from the peak of Śikhari.
They resemble precious gems of coral, with flickering luster and red eyes. || 25 ||
Look, O Daughter of the Mountain! The sprouts born from the celestial *surasāla* tree torment parrots at their feeding with the warbling of male cuckoos;
bees fall profusely into the mouths of parrots, and this foolish parrot is utterly deluded by the mistaken belief that they are *jambū* fruits. (26)

O Mother, just as these bees are agitated by the thirst for merit and the suffering of worldly existence due to their pleasure in the pollen while hovering around the buds of the *palāśa* tree, so too are those possessed by sense-objects. 27.
On a beryl throne swaying with chains suspended from a tree, Śiva sits;
likewise, Ambikā rests upon a throne shimmering with the lovely red hue of a *puṣpaka* flower.
Thus do the two beautiful Śivas sport at will in the forest by means of swinging on a cradle.
Then they were surrounded by goddesses holding beautiful clusters of chowries and served by them. || 28 ||
With their limbs anointed with the essence of the finest śrīcandana sandalwood, the two sported with the fragrances of breezes raised by excellent mountain trees;
the Goddess offers him the finest seeds, resembling jewels, emerging from pomegranate fruits split open by her nails and mouth. (29)

Seeing the Great Lord’s smile as his own lotus-hand served as a cover for the parrot’s beak, the parrot too, beholding the lotus-face of Śaṅkara and bowing to the Goddess, addressed her with words in the speech of a child. (Page 81) [Verse 30]

"O Lord of the embodied, O Śaṅkara, O All-pervading One, O you who have the crescent moon as your crest-jewel! Command me, O Śambhu, so that I may utter your name, 'Viśveśa,' in order to eat this ripened, succulent plantain fruit. At these words of his, the Lord laughed.

With her own lotus-like hands, she [worships] the pair of lotus-feet of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), who reclines upon a couch in a palace constructed of sapphire gems, which is as lovely as the radiance of the moon streaming over the bed.
On the stage, Mother repeatedly plays the lute, chanting the name of Śaṅkara.
Before the Lord and before the Goddess, upon floors of spotless palaces arisen from jewels,
the Rudrāṇīs— whose breasts are covered by their fresh youth— sport in hallīsaka dances;
with hands that bend down toward clusters of jasmine blossoms, they wear tinkling anklets that ring out as they move.
Dwelling upon the crest of Mount Kailāsa, they sing most sweetly and dance.
O Lord of All, O Supreme Over All, O Friend of the Wretched, protect me, O Lord Śambhu, with a gaze moistened by compassion!
Protect me, be gracious, O Mother of the Worlds, whose gait triumphs over the intoxicated swan-king and the elephant! 34.
Even while remaining there upon the summit of the mountain, which surpasses the boundless luster of their own crests as far as the seven worlds,
the gods bow down out of fear to those two, the moon and the sun, who have ceased their movement.

O people, behold that mountain of gold, whose footstool is washed by the waves of the ocean of nectar through the boundless dispensation of Maheśvara’s compassion, and which is scraped by its own limitless peaks! 36.
There, by taking refuge in Maheśa, the Gandharvas, hosts of Maruts, throngs of sages, and the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Suras would always shine, day and night, like rivers.
Indeed, the wind does not blow forcefully there, for both the sun and the moon are afraid;
nor is fire seen, as the dry grass and clusters of kīcaka bamboos are licked by its own flames.
"There is only one Rudra"—so says the Śruti; there is no other besides him.
In that sacred tradition, he is always the one whose hand is held by the Goddess, while the rest are but bound souls (paśus) wandering right there.
Beholding the multitude of liṅgas and the mountain abounding in clusters of blossoming trees, [he remains there].
There, Śaṅkara always wanders at will upon the courtyard marked by the gateways of the shoreless ocean. || 39 ||
(Verse 82) There indeed exist millions of Gaṇas and Rudrāṇīs, skilled in guarding that excellent enclosure alone; they move about in its vicinity, and neither other Gaṇas nor gods do so.
Not even the wind, nor the rays of the sun, can cause it to tremble.
The beautiful hands of Soma do not prevail at all. || 40 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Summit of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of Kailāsa.
Skanda said:
Within that [palace] is a rampart fashioned from lapis lazuli gems.
With bulls that were the crest-jewels of kings, adorned with lapis lazuli gems.
With all its mountain ridges traversed by the crossing of his bowstring,
it stood as if drunk by the brilliance of that light, shining like refined silver.
There, it was adorned with divine flower-groves and possessed multitudes of various jewels, including precious blue gomedas, rubies, and corals.
Adorned with kuruvinda gems, emeralds, and pearls,
it stood like a pond filled with blue lotuses and water-lilies.
With young shoots, clusters of blossoms, buds, and fully opened flowers, and with various fashioned jewels possessing a luster like that of Indra’s bow (the rainbow), [it was adorned]. || 5 ||
With the rays of his hands licked by the whetstone-like luster of the expansive, clear, and shimmering jewels,
there was no such forest anywhere in all the worlds, including heaven and earth.
It was the very essence of all beauty, lovely with its charming breeze,
and filled with the wind rising from the pollen of blossoming golden campaka flowers.
By even the touch of its wind, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara become truly fulfilled; at that time, the gods are most blessed indeed.
With forms resembling emeralds, bearing those beautiful flowers hanging from the *kekī* birds, it possesses a delightful fragrance from the pollen of the scent of those blossoming flowers.
It was thick with the fragrance of trumpet-flowers, covered with clusters of blue lotuses,
and beautiful with fresh patches of grass cropped by wandering deer.
The earth shines as if covered with young grass by means of its great emerald stones,
where bees sing in response to the fanning of the tails of free-roaming yak-cows.
The sky shines like gold with golden *karṇikāra* flowers,
joined by *kāśa* and *mandāra* blossoms that resemble masses of white clouds.
With auspicious red, clear, and lustrous maṇi-mandāraka flowers and buds,
the breeze was rendered pleasant by its coolness and its fragrance, which was made harmonious by the scent of those blossoms.
It was terrifying with the unrestrained, gurgling roar of *tamāla* and *sāla* trees,
and adorned with blossoming clusters of flowers arising from the creepers of *āragvadha*.
With clusters beautiful with petals as bright and clear as a parrot's beak, and with blossoms and buds born of the flowering punnāga tree; || 15 ||
The sky, resembling a scattering of stars, shines even more intensely like pearls due to the blossoming devadāru flowers and the clusters of kadamba blossoms hanging down.
It was enchanting with the copper-red clusters of *śephālī* flowers, with the dense foliage of the dwarf mango trees, and with the fragrant blossoms of the *kurava*, jasmine, and *vakula* trees. (17)
With *allaka* and *sallaka* trees as clear and bright as the rays of the rising moon, and with flowers produced from the abundant *bhallātaka* and *pāribhadra* trees; || 18 ||
The breeze was made fragrant by clusters of *tāla* and *pippalī*,
while the quarters of the sky were filled with the intense scent of *madhuka* flowers.
The earth shines with falling flowers like stars fallen from the sky,
appearing like lofty virtuous men rendered fruitless through the exhaustion of their merit.
It was bent down by the weight of fruit at the base of its luxuriant jackfruit trees,
and it also shone with *liṅkuca* fruits that had the beautiful form of golden balls.
It was also filled with clusters of ripening *śalāṭu* fruits rising from the fragrance of blossoms,
and with tall *mātuluṅga* trees possessing thick, low-hanging, and massive branches.
It was surrounded by *rasagarbha* and *rasāla* trees, and by fruits produced from *kamra* and *kāmra* trees, as well as by *jambuka* and *ārañjaka* trees which resembled great sapphire gems.
With blossoming flowers from bending pomegranate trees and their bursting fruits, as well as with *aṅkola*, *śirīṣa*, and the shining clusters of *arjuna* trees; || 24 ||
It was fragrant with the exquisite scent of the aroma of ripe bilva fruits,
and likewise filled with the falling clusters of kapittha, āmalaka, and other such fruits.
It was adorned with the lofty branches of orange trees dyed in their own color,
and possessed branches bent down by the weight of the fruits of pomegranate, āmrātaka, and date palms.
It was crowded with intoxicated troops of monkeys eager for the taste of the juice of nutmegs,
and its breezes were gladdened by the fragrance arising from lovely groves of palm trees.
It shines like a sapphire with its clear, beautiful yellow plantain leaves;
it is endowed with lovely *saptacchada* trees and clusters of *nārikela* fruits.
With trees whose heads were bent by the weight of white and black fruits and shaken by the wind, and which bore clusters of betel nuts shining with the luster of the rising sun within them; (29)
With rows of silver *kuṭaja* trees in full bloom with clusters of blossoms,
as well as *vaṭaja* trees, it stood like a gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*).
It was radiant with the exceedingly clear white filaments of the young sun,
and with *nīpa* trees, noble *jāti* jasmine, and tall *aśoka* trees that destroy all sorrow.
[The place was filled] with birds dwelling under the canopy of the tree of perfect enlightenment that had awakened at dawn,
and with *vakula*, *dhava*, and *kelī* trees, beautiful with the fragrance of *kesara*.
With *takkola*, *aṅkola*, and white, fragrant *badarī* and *dhava* trees,
the wind was filled with the sweet scent of fragrant, clustered *jambū* fruits.
It was filled with the filaments of saffron trees resembling the body of Kandarpa,
thick with the fragrance of tagara, and joined by mountains of black agallochum.
It stood like a cluster of Lodhra, Avadhraja, Bheruṇḍa, Kāṇḍa, and Tāṇḍava blossoms,
appearing as if it were an ascetic performing penance, adorned with a mass of matted locks.
With its *khadira* and *badara* trees, it was as if adorned with coral by their fruits;
its great branches of *kovidāra* rent asunder the vessel of the sky.
In the forest, the breeze was as charming as the fragrance of *bhallāta*, *liṅgita*, *sanmallī*, and *suma* flowers; it resembled the sound of a lute produced by the friction of bamboo reeds.
It was filled with sallakī trees whose branches were entwined with mallī creepers,
and it possessed blossoming bhallaka trees whose branches performed a dance of joy (hṛllīlā) as they swayed.
Fragrant with its own scent, that celestial chariot, curved in form and beautiful like a tree,
drew the planets moving within the sphere of the sky along with it.
That great forest of jewels was like a vast tree with branches extending for a *nalva*, its full-blown flowers being clusters of stars resembling a boat floating upon the water.
It was filled with sandalwood trees that brought joy to the eyes and possessed a most fragrant breeze; its great branches were swaying, with garlands hanging down from them.

(Verse 42) It is adorned with clusters of *guñjā* flowers and swarms of bees, beautiful with swaying creepers that bestow nectar; it is surrounded by a new garden and possesses an abundance of cascading streams of jewel-like luster.
There, the water ripples like royal crystal and precious pearl;
the breeze carries a shower of cool, clear spray from the fragrances of the forest.
There a lake shines forth, beautiful with a mass of pollen rising from lotuses fragrant with scent, and lovely with blue water-lilies.
It was connected by jeweled staircases and possessed swaying, reddish porticos;
its center was radiant with the brilliance of the finials atop the turrets of the palace.
It had waves more beautiful than gold, with surfaces as pure as coral;
it was supported by a thousand pillars and provided with seats and rafters.
There stood a chariot with a bull made of silver and coral, its banners fluttering,
adorned with a brightly shining altar of great jewels.
Seated upon that excellent lion-throne together with the Goddess, the Bull-bannered Lord dwells there, surrounded by a stream of diamonds that eclipses the luster of the sun.
Smelling that enchanting fragrance of the blossoming flowers in the forest, and hearing the cries of the cranes as flocks of swans moved about, Hara [wandered]. (49)
Beholding the lotus-face of the Goddess, Śaṅkara passes his time;
there likewise are millions of Rudras, their hands shining with stainless tridents.
They guard the rampart on the outside, but not within;
that rampart, that forest, and that beautiful lotus pond. (51)
Those Rudras, by the command of the God of gods, the moon-crested one, [acted]. || 52 ||
Īśvara:
By the mountain torrents flowing from the peaks of the Lord of Mountains— green, yellow, blue, and crimson,
with a tumultuous roar like a rushing stream, and having cast out all worldly conventions;
This mountain, possessing the brilliant luster of intense rut flowing from the temples of its lordly elephants,
is adorned with white *tilaka* marks of *tamāla* trees and with yellow *tilaka* marks of red chalk (*gairika*).
It is graced by the excellent celestial bards of the lords of mountains and by noble elephants that have returned from their tasks.

O daughter of the limbs of the best of mountains, this king of mountains shines forth with hosts of trees possessing blazing splendor, as enchanting as great *iṅguda* fruits; therefore, take refuge in me. 54.
There, in the center of a jeweled altar fashioned at the foot of that bilva tree, upon the stainless pericarp of a jewel-lotus, the Lord—
his arms embraced by the daughter of the mountain king— beheld the Goddess amidst the excellent lingas formed of moonstones.

Śaṅkara repeatedly worships Hari and the Moon— the two whose splendors rival the light of the young sun— with dūrvā grass possessing a beauty far exceeding the luster of emeralds, and with the finest leaves of the bilva tree, as fresh as the rising dawn.
And with fruits filled with juice, such as pure jambū and nāraṅga; || 56 ||

Having offered into the hands of the Daughter of the Mountain fruits produced from the finest pomegranates, radiant with bursting luster, and ripe *kapittha*, plantain, and *rasāla* fruits, they hold them as being superior to red lotuses. (57)
The Lord of Gods, the refuge of all, whose greatness is celebrated by the peaks of the Vedas;
the elephant-headed one, who is like a manifest Varuṇa for awakening those who bow before him;
he whose formidable cavernous mouth is the agent in the act of shattering the fiercely blazing cosmic egg.
He is the supreme dancer, delighted by the joy of shattering the fierce [demon] Khaṇḍapramada. || 58 ||
His feet are served by Mukunda, Brahmā, Indra, and the ornaments of the immortals,
as well as by the hosts of Gaṇeśas beginning with Caṇḍīśa, and by the foremost of the gods and the leaders of the Tuhaṇḍa and other gaṇas.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Chapter Twenty, titled "Description of the Sacred Field," from the Dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī:
Skanda said—
In that interval, moreover, there is a rampart extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
The brilliance of the moon was eclipsed by the great stream of the essence of diamonds. || 1 ||
By the splendor of Mount Kailāsa, by the steady radiance of his intellect, and also by the moonbeams reflected in the great waves of the ocean of nectar; || 2 ||
The multitude of directions was illuminated by the expansive digits of the moon, unrestrained as it rested upon the crown of Maheśa, [shining] from the tips of the peaks of its ramparts.
O twice-born ones, the moon, the sun, the planets, the stars, the lightning,
and even fire were eclipsed by their splendors as they stood at the summit of that excellent gateway.
Constructed from emeralds, with blue eyes and possessing tusks,
its bright front gateway was five hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure.
It rose up from the depths of the seven netherworlds, fashioned of diamond,
and was adorned by rows of pigeon-shaped turrets, shining with hosts of gods.
On that upper surface, amidst the playful manifestations of Rudra, with jars and even bulls, the Lord took his seat upon a divine lion-throne beside the Goddess.
In a palace-jewel with gateways like the finest mountains of Kailāsa, seated upon a throne fashioned from many divine gems,
Paśupati spoke for a very long time to Umā, as she recounted the entire world of the gods and other beings.
Īśvara:

O Daughter of the Mountain, listen! Even if Hari, Indra, Brahmā, and the Lord of Serpents were to count the number of divine liṅgas situated upon the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, they would be like the multitude of dust-motes among the stars in the sky, or like the raindrops produced by a downpour. (Page 86)
O Girijā, O Śaṅkarī, this very family of Liṅgas is worshipped with garlands of Mandāra flowers,
fresh tender leaves of the Bilva tree, and sprouts of Dūrvā grass at the most auspicious time of evening, O Śivā, when all hosts of sins have been dispelled.
This task, illuminated by the light of jewels, must be accomplished by me, even against all the gods and asuras.
This circle of the mountain Kailāsa is a radiant mass of matted locks,
where the great *kākodara* snakes are mistaken for the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā;
it is adorned with heaps of Mandāra tree blossoms, great bilva fruits, jasmine flowers, and more.
Behold indeed that which resides within the center of the shining interior of a fine jar from the treasury of jewels.
At the base of the *bilva* trees,
its crown is constantly encircled by pure, cool-wind-sustaining hosts of monkeys who delight in gems, sandalwood, and intensely cooling camphor, and who seek to inhale the fragrance.
I, an ocean of compassion, am to be served by both worlds through the collection of my own lingas.

The great Īśvara-liṅga was consecrated on all its limbs with the mass of rays from his own crest-moon as if with floods of Gaṅgā water, with warbling cuckoos as if with excellent twice-born (brāhmaṇas), and with great mantras such as the Mahārudra, using those petals.
Behold my [body], honored by the very winds that have been shattered and fallen from their course. || 13 ||
On this supreme ground, by the winds rising from the fierce plumage of the peacocks due to intense heat, this circle of peacocks performs a most violent *tāṇḍava* dance;
and in the forest, it reaches the state of beautiful female dancers, enchanting with their warbling cries.
Having reached this place, which is indeed renowned for its manifold flavors through the multitudes of meritorious deeds, one truly seems to sing aloud.
In this bilva grove, where the broad branches are covered with fresh reddish leaves and provide deep shade, herds of yaks have taken refuge at the roots out of sheer fear of falling;
there, the leaves are agitated by the contact with the wings of flocks of birds swooping down.
And with their bushy tails, like rows of chowries, they fan the Lingas of Uma.

Be content, O Śivā, daughter of the mountain; beyond this, there exists no other supreme means for the worship of my Liṅga that bestows eternal liberation. What is the use of sacrifices, the performance of all vows and the like, or what is the use of multitudes of gifts and recitations?
What does this extend? It is liberation, for that indeed belongs to those whose nature is suffering. 16.
O Śivā, [behold] the mountain whose lofty peaks are graced by ruby and pure diamond ornaments resembling the rising young sun and moon,
and which cause wonder to arise in the hosts of gods dwelling in those various worlds.
It shines with a splendor exceeding the great luster produced by various suns and moons. || 17 ||
On the peak at the foot of the slopes of Mount Kailāsa, where truth abounds, the hosts of world-guardians (Lokapālas) who gaze upon the worlds have taken up their positions there for Śiva;
these include Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, the foremost of the immortals, and these seven sages along with the planets.
And these masses of stars, the offspring of Ścuttāna, shine exceedingly brightly. || 18 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, behold now how they constantly circumambulate Meru,
amidst the sounds of the triple symphony resounding from the central courtyards of those various gate-towers,
and the blasts of kettledrums and conchs sounded during the worship of Śiva at their respective times.
O Sovereign of the Lord, even this Kailāsa possesses an inner resonance of great thundering.
Even by hundreds of clouds, he remains delighted, his face adorned solely by the sound [of the Dharma].
O Umā, today the young lions dwelling within the caves of the mountain ranges, along with the elephants whose tusks have been shattered,
mock the blazing fire with the manes of their own tails and the peaks of the great mountains.
These hosts of enemies of horses hear the sound of the neighing of the horses that draw the chariot of the Sun;
their faces, ears, horns, and eyes are bent down, and they possess a single roar that eclipses all sounds arising from lightning.
O Mother, today behold the sun, resembling a rain-cloud due to the dust raised by the striking of the hooves of the donkeys;
even the sun, as if out of noble shame, has [hidden] its principal steeds behind the mountains.
Having violently shattered the mass of clouds with his hands, he proceeds toward the southern quarter, thinking, "I am victorious.
Before him stands this mountain of silver, my own abode, and beyond that shines the mountain of gold.
(Verse 24) Behold the network of worlds situated above my crest, while I stand upon the mountain below.

O Śivā, this Brahmā incessantly creates the entire world, Hari protects it, and Rudra destroys it perpetually, along with the hosts of gods, the guardians of the quarters, and the assembly of the best of deities;
yet this Viṣṇu, established in truth, beholds his abode, Vaikuṇṭha.
This city of Piśācaka is in the mountain range of Purīyama, and this is the city of Indra.
This is the well-ordered city of Saṃyaminī on the far shore of the Ocean of Milk;
this is Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, who removes the sins of the three worlds; and this is my city, Vārāṇasī, O Śivā, which is honored for its ten million Liṅgas that resemble mountains.
O Goddess Annapūrṇā, you have [worshipped] the excellent Liṅga known as Viśveśa-Maheśa. || 26 ||
Where the gods and demons dwell for the sake of liberation, having abandoned their undesirable envy;
because it was not abandoned even by me, they call it Avimukta (the Unreleased), and even the Vedas proclaim its power.
This is Gaṅgādvāra at the great crown of your father, and this is Kedāraka;
and this is that Pāṭalīnagara on the Gāyā, from which the Mānasa rivers flow. Here, for the liberation of men, the union of the Gaṅgā and the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) has been established.
And the Jāhnavī is always embraced by the best of rivers, the lord of streams, for those who have bathed in her. || 28 ||

O Girijā, here at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean is this Someśvara, who always makes fruitful the service of those who worship him, and removes the sins and mental anguish of his devotees. || 29 ||
This is Prayāga, the refuge of all flowing rivers, where even Gaṅgā, joined by the daughter of Ambuja (the Yamunā), resides;
O Goddess, for those who have bathed there, their dwelling is in heaven, and if they cast off their bodies there, they attain liberation.
O Bhavānī, that Gayā is the sacrificial altar of Brahmā, bestowing infinite merit and bringing joy to the ancestors;
behold today my own footprint right there, as well as those of the gods, the twice-born, and Viṣṇu.
Behold that most meritorious Naimiṣa forest and that Badarī, crowded with great sages;
together with Citrakūṭa and surrounded by hosts of gods, these seven cities here are the causes of liberation.
O Agajāmbikā, this collection of twelve Liṅgas is situated in those respective cities:
Oṃkāra, Ghusṛṇeśvara, and this Śrī Kāmanātha;
this excellent Mahākāla Maheśa, and Nāgeśvara, who has his sole refuge in the Veṇuvana forest. (Page 89) 33.
This is the Śarmadāna, joined by the Narmadā and surrounded by a multitude of liṅgas;
this Śoṇa flows toward the lord of rivers (the ocean), taking refuge in a multitude of liṅgas.
This is the holy Bāhunadī, this is the excellent Puṣkara, and this indeed is the holy Prabhāsa.
Born from the best of mountains, he is the stainless destroyer of Malla’s emblem and a thorn to the gods. || 34 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, this Śrī Rudra is the abode of ten million immortals; this Piṇḍāraka is dear to me, as is this excellent field born of the Kurus; and here indeed is the Vindhya range.
This is the crest of Śrī Śaila, the sole destroyer of the multitude of great sins produced by worldly existence.
And here is this well-established river Godāvarī, born from the mountain of Tryambaka. (Note: "O Blessed One, this is the people" is an alternative reading. 35.
And Kṛṣṇā also, the best of rivers, which flows into the ocean, is surrounded by lingas and bestows merit.
O Ambikā, that lord of sages born from a jar (Agastya), who was previously sent by me and who took away the Vindhya mountain, is situated at its edge;
furthermore, this Gokarṇa on the shore of the ocean is my own Liṅga.
O Ambikā, this Vindhya, the best of mountains, having become enraged at the golden mountain [Meru], obstructed the path of the gods;
yet, through your refuge, he has become a holy place that bestows great merit upon Pratiṣṭhānapura.
This city was sought after here by the Asura Kola while he was performing penance; it was conquered by you through his slaughter.
This Aruṇādri of renowned power, though it is the Vṛddhādri, is my desired abode. (39)
And here the mountain Goparvata shines; Kāñcī is joined with the Liṅga that adorns the world.
Because she has you as her refuge, she is most beautiful, and for the sake of worshipping you, she is served even by Hari.
O Great Goddess, behold this Śeṣācala, my daughter’s abode, shining to the north of that;
for this is the esteemed Kailāsa to the south, from which flows the Marudvṛdhā river.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the highly powerful Liṅga-maṇḍala on the banks of the Sahyāpagā is indeed renowned;
so too is the multitude of Liṅgas on the banks of the Kāverī, which has Śrīkaṇṭha and Ratnādri as its presiding deities.
O Bhavānī, Hari is there, and beyond that the one called Pañcāpageśa;
then this beautiful Kumbheśvara Liṅga, as well as Arjuna and Mayūraliṅga. (43)

O Ambikā, that which is celebrated as Śveteśvara to the north of that [place], which bestows liberation, is Viraja, free from sorrow; it is my pure lotus-heart, my very abode, where I dance together with you. (pṛ0 90) 44.
It has always been seen situated on the shore of the celebrated salt ocean, bestowing great merit;
it is the excellent forest named Veda, known as Abja, which is surrounded by lingas and called Kamalālaya.
O Goddess, beyond that is Śrīsundara and Viṣṇupura; furthermore, O Mother, on Gandhamādana, the best of mountains in that island, is my excellent Liṅga.
O Ambikā, Hari, though formerly cursed by the son of Bhṛgu and separated from his wife, nevertheless slew Rāvaṇa;
behold now that most meritorious and excellent Setu, which was worshipped by him alone. 47.
To the west of that, O Mother, is my most meritorious place known as Hālāsya and Varaveṇu;
right there the ocean meets the Copper Mountain (Tāmrācala), and behold, O Goddess, those [sacred sites] situated upon its shore.
The lofty and enchanting Lingas—the Mahendra mountain and the Malaya mountain—these excellent sacred fields of yours, O Goddess, have been seen by us with our eyes and heard with our ears. (49)
Behold how those who have been liberated from sin by even a single glance at this sacred field are able to shatter the peaks of the mountain of evil.
He is always declared in the Vedas to be the Lord of the fields (*kṣetra*); behold how, though pervading the entire world, He remains hidden from the wicked-minded among the learned.
Even disregarding the hardships here, He who is established with reverence within these fields—
I bestow that liberation upon him who is devoted to the elephant-headed Ganesha and who honors Rudrākṣa beads and sacred ash.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sacred Field," in the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī within the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī concerning the destiny of living beings, the twenty-first chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, O Śiva, who indeed are these hosts of gods that go [to their respective realms]?"
Who are these supreme men who have thus pierced the orb of the sun?
Who are those who have entered the abode of Soma and who have returned from there again?
Who are those resembling streaks of smoke, and who are those beautiful-faced women?
Who are those men who go forth joyfully in celestial palaces resembling the sun,
while others are being beaten with lashes of whips and iron mallets?
Women and children are led toward the southern direction by men with deformed limbs who strike them and drag them along while they are bound with nooses.
In the same way, O Great God, you are the one who sets in motion the wheel of the universe today;
you are the initiator and the terminator of the tasks of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Skanda:
Thus questioned by the Goddess at that time, Mahādeva Maheśvara spoke there to Girijā within that palace on Kailāsa.
Śaṅkara beheld the paths of the gods and the paths of the ancestors.
Īśvara:
O you whose face shines with a fully blossomed, deep-red lotus, and whose wide-open eyes gleam like full-blown blue lotuses— truly, even the ascetics [gaze upon] the orb of the rising sun.

O Śivā, those whose hearts are filled with the essence of reflecting upon the meaning of the Vedānta, having heard it from the mouth of their Guru, pierce through and enter the world arising from the blossoming lotuses of the mind.

O Girijā, those excellent ones who, through the intended meaning of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) such as "That Thou Art" (*tat tvam asi*), are devoted to the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), go to that world of Brahmā;
O Umā, once liberated, they certainly do not return from that world of Brahmā.
Those who follow the Karmamārga [should perform the rite] with the mantra beginning, "ye vai tvantimakālaśabdataḥ."

O Śivā, even those who have reached the path of the sun fall from there, distressed and diminished like a mass of lightning; yet, O Umā, having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa and entered the final stage of life,
they become established in the Vedānta under a guru.

From the words issuing from the lotus-face of the Supreme Lord, the best of the twice-born—those born from the lotus-seed—having attained this world, constantly worship Him for the sake of liberation. || 10 ||
These beings, who are ever in accordance with the sacred scriptures, are called "sacrificers";
they have now been brought here by the oblations offered in the Vedic fires and are being honored.
With splendors equal to a mass of lightning, they are being entreated from all sides, saying, "Come!"
By means of the showers of moonlight, they always proceed incessantly from that abode. || 11 ||

Those foremost of the twice-born were performers of the perpetual *agnihotra*, the *pūrṇamāsa* and *darśa* sacrifices, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, the animal sacrifices, the well-conducted four-monthly offerings, the *sautrāmaṇī* rites, and various collections of other rituals, as well as the *soma* sacrifices and the *kaṭhaka-agni-citi*.

O Daughter of the Mountain, that twice-born man who constantly performs sacrifices with the Ekāha, Ahīna, and Satra rites, and who maintains the sacred fires, goes to the realm of the Moon's rays even from the world of Aruṇaketu. (13)
Through the states resulting from the *kiṃpāka* sacrifice and through dharmas born of memory, there comes about an extreme ripening by means of well-performed actions and their results.
What essence is there here in water consumed by the *kiṃpāka* tree? I consider that, in its ultimate effect, it becomes nothing but *kiṃpāka* itself.
Those who, honoring the Lord of Sacrifices and the Sovereign of All through the Rājasūya, Naramedha, Sarvamedha, and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and who, O Bhavānī,
attain by their meritorious deeds the solar path that carries one beyond the sun through the performance of the Saptahotṛ ritual— [they do not go to the abode of Yama].
O Gaurī, he who considers sacrificial rites and charitable works alone to be dharma, being devoid of meditation upon and worship of my lotus feet,
goes at the end through smoke, night, and the periods of a month and half-month to the realm of the Moon.

Through the practice of austerity, faith, and yoga, those devoted to the various stages of life and social orders then attain liberation through dispassion, becoming intent upon the Vedānta taught by the renowned Guru;
likewise, they reach the Supreme Person, who is beyond the human and even the divine.
O men, for me who am going to the solar realm, there is indeed only manifold worship. || 17 ||

From the moon [he creates] the cloud, the mass of smoke, the wind, lightning, and rain among the hosts of medicinal herbs; and having become food, he is born as the person who is eaten, and becoming semen, they fall into the womb of women. 18.

O Goddess, those who are indeed sinful—such as dogs, Caṇḍālas, serpents, and those who dig into the earth—go to the wombs of animals; whereas those who are meritorious, such as Śūdras born from the arms or thighs of Brahmins, enter into meritorious or non-meritorious wombs.
Deluded by their sacrifices and charitable works, many others, whose minds are devoted to the worship and meditation of other deities,
think as children do— that there is no other higher good. O Mother, all these dharmas and these sacrifices are but fragile rafts for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.

O Śivā! O Śivā! You whose magnificent deeds are gladdened by the contemplation of the meaning of Vedānta; [attained] through initiations, austerities, vows, observances, penances, gifts, as well as through yogas, the recitation of the Vedas, studies, sacrifices, and works of public utility.
The student, the householder, and the forest-dweller should also always have reverence for the dharma prescribed therein. || 21 ||
Whatever fruit one obtains from the entire world, and even more excellent than that, is attained by reaching Kailāsa, my supreme abode, through profound meditation upon me. || 22 ||
(Verse 23) [The gods] have streams born from the moon at the mouth of the sacrifice, and likewise streams of clarified butter spread over the crest of fire;
their faces are marked with the sound *lakha-lakha*, and they are joined by the chariot of the lord of birds (Garuḍa) as well as by the rat-vehicle of Indra’s consort (Lakṣmī).

O you whose eyes are like the faces of pure lotuses, behold today as they approach, gazing toward the sky; led by Śikhivāha, accompanied by celestial chariots, and having drunk in [the sight] with their excellent golden vimānas.
Having joyfully drunk the soma juice with hosts of celestial nymphs, they dwell together with their own retinues born in the Nandana grove;
with their bodies moistened by excellent sandalwood paste, they dwell stationed within the finest of celestial palaces.
O Umā, those others who are merely performers of sacrifice, whose sole devotion is to ritual action,
and who have abandoned the singular devotion to the great gift of bestowing the other injunctions upon Śiva—
they indeed go to the world of the Moon, O Daughter of the Mountain, by way of the path beginning with smoke.
Having exhausted the entirety of the collection of actions consisting of coming and going—[an alternative reading says "consisting of provisions for the journey"]—they eventually fall. || 26 ||
O you who are beautiful with thighs like the stalks of plantain trees, whose backs are like those of frogs,

and who are covered by a thick hip resembling the swelling pitcher of an elephant; having drunk the nectar of your lips, which are as lovely as the bimba fruit, those with exceedingly plump limbs [dwell] among the Nandana groves.
O Ambikā, behold the sacrificers whose hearts are captivated by the sport of Your breasts.
This youthful circle of women, with fine ketaka flowers clinging to their abundant tresses,
their minds intoxicated by the drinking of their husband’s embrace, adorned with divine unguents and garments,
and radiant with the mass of light from all directions illuminated by various jewels— [is like the sky].
He always goes joyfully by means of celestial vehicles to the cremation ground where his husband was indeed consumed by fire.

Behold, those who have given cows, land, clothing, food, gold, base metals, silver, grain, earth, gems, and the Brahmins— those donors go to the assembly of the gods and Śakra, joyfully fanned by hosts of celestial chowries from their celestial chariots. (29)

By means of gifts to Brahmins, the planting of groves, and the construction of ponds, he refreshed travelers who were exhausted by the burden of fatigue from the harsh rays of the sun, with pleasant cool breezes and excellent service such as maidens, food, and drink. (30)
O Mother Śivā, behold today those who take rest for a moment in the halls; they go [to the highest state]. 31.
(p. 94) These heroic warriors, who cast off their dear lives through the showers of arrows discharged from the tips of excellent weapons,
quickly enter this radiant orb within the jewel of light, O Umā.
They indeed proceed, with all the horizons of space filled by the fame acquired through their wondrous valor. || 32 ||
Having enjoyed the pleasures of Indra’s world, which possesses the beauty of diamonds,

stars, and moons, O Goddess of the Immortals, they gradually fall; then, O lady of beautiful teeth, behold them entering the womb once more at the edge of the waters, on the shore, or among medicinal herbs, despite their former vast prosperity.
They do not cross so swiftly by means of well-performed sacrifices or even meritorious works of public utility.

Behold this multitude of sinners as they hasten toward the abode of Yama with cries of distress, their hands bound by the nooses of Yama’s messengers, their heads smeared with blood from being crushed by mallets.

They indeed remain in the mouth of Kāla, unable to endure [the heat]; situated upon heated frying pans at the mouth of Kumbhīpāka; in the auspicious [yet terrible] lake of impurities filled with worms and boundless;
and in the thick mire of salt-water that has no limit, their limbs covered with scars from wounds and their eyes constantly burning.
Behold, O Ambika, how they are tormented by crows and swarms of scorpions and stinging insects! 35.

These are the inhabitants of hell: those ever-attached to their bellies, who engage in sexual intercourse with the wives of others, who are joined with various sins, who are corrupters of elders and of Śiva’s devotees;
thieves, plunderers of travelers, those intent on the food of others, and those whose dwellings are defiled by wicked gambling.
The heretics were joined at their arms with great iron rings and heated discs. || 36 ||

Those whose foreheads lack the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), those who have abandoned the recitation of the Rudra-hymns, those who are averse to the means of worshipping the Liṅga and so forth, those who have abandoned the name of Śambhu,
those who are averse to wearing Rudrākṣa beads, and those who have abandoned the five-syllabled mantra— [these are the ones excluded].
Those whose minds are devoid of residence in my field and who are malicious toward my devotees; || 37 ||
Behold those who see me—Śiva, the Lord supreme over all, the foundation of the three worlds—as equal to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the hosts of Maruts; behold them indeed!
Those men who are devoid of worship during the Pradoṣa hour, or those who have abstained from eating what has been offered to me.

O Śivā, I believe that those who destroy the abodes of Śiva and pluck flowers from the groves of Śiva will, overwhelmed by suffering, fall into hell during the *kalpa* of their transgressions; for them, there is never any liberation. (Page 95)
Those who hate Śiva, who worship other [deities], and who are always intent on reviling me; || 39 ||

Those who wear Rudrākṣa ornaments and the beautiful triple-ash marks (tripuṇḍra) on their foreheads become like worms with mouths of fire, delighting in dwelling within the interior of Yama’s palace amidst the variegated wonders of hell.
Feasting on the nectar of the food offerings, they are devoted with reverence to the names "Śiva" and "Mahādeva."
O Śaṅkarī, those who are constantly intent on worshipping my liṅga, who have mastered the meaning of the Rudra-mantras,

and who take delight in the pure and excellent stories of Rudra— they are my attendants. Wearing the ash-mark (tripuṇḍra), the śivajā beads, and the rudrākṣa, they are like necklaces that serve as helmsmen for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.

O Girijā, those whose minds are solely intent on contemplating the Rudrādhyāya, who are devoted to the five-syllabled mantra, who are dedicated to the ritual bathing of Śiva with its mantras, and who are absorbed in the worship of the Liṅga—
they are my chosen ones, and this is their dwelling place. (42)

O Daughter of the Mountain, those followers of Śaṅkara— who possess the equipment for practicing the stream of conduct prescribed by the Vedas, who are free from obstacles, whose inner minds are devoid of interest in base conduct and inquiry,
and who have abandoned all regard for this worldly ocean that is harsh, substantial, and tasteless— [attain liberation].
They go forcefully to this abode of mine; no others today—I speak the truth.
O Girijā, these forms of Rudra on Mount Kailāsa, who have the crescent moon as their crest-jewel, who possess three eyes like blue lotuses, and who are ever blue-throated—
these attendants of Śiva always remain by my side; they are forever devoted to Śaṅkara.
Skanda—
Having heard all these destinies from Śaṅkara, the Supreme Goddess,
the Great Goddess, bowed down and spoke at the excellent gate of Kailāsa. (45)
The Goddess said: The Vedas declare that the essence of the essenceless is women, progeny, cattle, and gold. (p.
96) Being situated within the three qualities (*guṇas*), they are merely a source of attraction; having fallen under the sway of the qualities, no one remains devoted [to the Self]. 46.
Children, intent on worldly activity, desire the great web of suffering through the notion that it is the source of happiness;
just as fish in the water, perceiving food, are caught in great nets by fishermen.

How is it that those of wicked countenance, agitated by suffering, come to Your lotus feet—the very mine of liberation—just as children, through their singular play with the unreal, perceive You, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, as being real? 48.

Just as there might be news of a hare's horn, or as there might be turtle-milk in a desert, or as there might be water in a mirage—so too do people here in this world desire objects that pervade the universe; yet the mind is the root of these desires, and where the mind is not, these desires do not exist.

You are the Infinite, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the most auspicious one who bears the crescent moon; you are Hara, whose form is half-woman, whose majesty is immeasurable, and whose face is the abode of the moon.
You are the enemy of Kama’s body, yet your heart is unattached to desire; you are the one whose garment is the skin of a black antelope.
O Maheśa, having approached you, Śaṅkara, who bestows satisfaction upon the gods and their hosts, [we have attained our goal]. 50.

Those of deluded heart pray for sensual desires; their effort is in vain. O Lord, the Master of Lakṣmī, whose eyes and feet are ever gracious, you are eternally present as smoke-colored clouds; O Blessed One, you are forever Vyomakeśa (the one whose hair is the sky).
And Śaṅkara, the Lord of Umā, whose pair of lotus feet were worshipped by Dhaumya’s fire. || 51 ||
O Lord, grant me my desires; you are praised by the Vedas and by sages such as Gautama.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Destiny of Living Beings," in the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī within the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga.
Skanda said:
To the east of Kailāsa shines [a mountain] with the luster of refined gold.
Three hundred thousand yojanas from that point shines Meru, the abode of the gods.
At the tip of that bull-pillar, Dhruva and the others, all situated within the Kālacakra, revolve day and night in a clockwise direction.
By the command of the Destroyer of Smara, Dhruva, the Seven Sages, and King Triśaṅku likewise took their places upon the peaks of the mountain situated above that.
There is a vast, enchanting lake there named Mānasa, endowed with various trees and creepers, and frequented by beautiful birds and deer.
On the crest of its peak, it was radiant with blooming golden kahlāras and golden lotuses, belonging to the gods whose natures are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. (Verse 5)
And for all the guardians of the quarters, abodes for the Gandharvas were constructed;
Satyaloka belongs to Brahmā, and Vaikuṇṭha is the city of Viṣṇu.
O Sage, the three cities of Rudra are each one-third [of a yojana] in size, respectively;
they are shaped like gold and are adorned at their perimeters by mountain ranges.
The vast jewel-grove of Sāl trees upon the summit of that Mount Meru shines like a white water-lily, surrounded by the oceans at the earth's edge.
There stands the gateway of Śambhu, adorned with jewels and rubies;
sometimes Śrī Mahādeva himself sports there with the Goddess.
Indeed, that region of the mountain has been cursed by the God of gods:
"Whoever shall enter here shall become a wretched woman in form."
O best of beings, Meru resembles a pillar of bull-hide;
on that mountain, Śambhu dwells with the goddess Pārvatī, surrounded by the Rudras.
Once, seated upon a divine lion-throne surrounded by the goddess’s companions,
Śiva [spoke] to the hosts of gods in the sequence of the Purāṇas.
On the summit of Mount Meru is a magnificent great liṅga named Aurvīśa, enchanting,
with a great palace as its gateway and a royal golden altar.
There, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara indeed worship that Liṅga with bilva leaves and even with golden lotuses.
With incense, lamps, and captivating food offerings,
as well as through circumambulations, prostrations, and other such acts, those gods and demigods offer praise.
The gods—[behold] the abundance of the great *mandāra* flowers, as auspicious as the nectar of jasmine and *amanda* blossoms;
the great *gaṅgā*, shimmering with the play of high, restless waves; and the clusters of lotuses.

Today, having respectfully abandoned the suffering born of this great misery of saṃsāra, let us meditatively contemplate Śiva, whose lofty head is honored by the crescent moon that delights the nights. 16.
I bow to the Great Lord, whose crown is reddened by the pollen and nectar of red lotuses from clusters of kuruvinda gems;
whose lotus feet are worshipped by the assembly of Vṛndāvana; who granted boons to Sunda and Upasunda; and who is the primordial root of the universe.

O Lord, your glance— a stream of nectar flowing from the mountain of your head— is accompanied by the humming of bees above your crest and the cascading of your matted locks; like a mountain torrent, it flows down from you,
yet it does not instantly cast our feet— soiled by rising passion— from its heart-lotus.
They are blessed; may that Blessed One, with his hands joined in prayer, grant prosperity in every way. || 18 ||
Sūta: Thus do those gods, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, and sages free from all taint, praise Śiva as he stands upon the summit of Mount Meru.
(Verse 98) Indeed, Mahādeva is always present here on Kailāsa;
this Śaṅkara sports with the Goddess in a palace made of jewels.
Listen now to that account of his dwelling, which destroys all sins;
it contains the various and manifold sports of the Supreme Lord.
Together with the Goddess, by whom indeed can those best of gods be described? || 22 ||
The wives of the Rudras, with breasts swelling in fresh youth, resembling the splendor of the moon, their slender bodies adorned with the stainless luster of gems,
radiant with brilliance, and with garments, hair, and bracelets clinging to their breasts, are intent on the duty of service.
They shine upon the peaks of the silver mountain, their playful anklets jingling.

There, those streaks of lightning— resembling great white champaka flowers with rising clouds as their stalks and fine pearls as their blossoms, encircled by necklaces and bracelets of excellent gems in the form of stars—
shone upon Hara, the Maheśvara who is the support of the three worlds. And the Rudras [worshipped] Maheśvara...
Having abandoned weariness through incomparable and respectful service at each respective time, || 24 ||
With water-pots beautiful with jewels for the ritual bath, with offerings of garlands, perfumes, and incense, with lamps, fragrant fumigations for the hair, retinues, and the gift of couches;
with parasols, the fanning of yak-tail whisks, footstools, mirrors, and betel—
With lutes, fine garments, swords, and excellent elephants, they serve Śarva and Śivā. || 25 ||
Nine crores of Rudrāṇīs and ten crores of youthful Rudras, as well as Bhairavas and Digambaras, constantly attend him with their crores; likewise,
three crores of Yoginīs and crores of Ḍākinīs surround him on all sides.
Those whose faces possess the luster of the moon together with Rohiṇī serve Śambhu and Śivā.

On Mount Kailāsa, upon a throne resplendent with the nine jewels of power (*navaśaktiratna*), situated in the center of the Śrīcakra within the Bindu— a couch of four thrones (*catuṣpīṭhaka*) consisting of a pair of ten-million-fold moons and suns produced by the Great Reality (*mahātattva*)— which extends for a single crore [of verses].
We hold within our hearts, together with Girijā, that which consists of the five Brahmans.

The mountain, rendered increasingly white by the rays of the moon spreading forth like hands, appeared as if it were being washed by the rising waves of the ocean of dawn-nectar, using a boat fashioned from all kinds of gems. (p.
He, whose locks are like fragments of the moon, sports clearly with his mother.
His body was exceedingly white, surpassing the luster of the peaks of a great mountain of pure gold on the far side of a clear mountain;
his flapping ears were fanned by a multitude of beautiful whisks hanging from the slopes of his crowning tusks.

The Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, his forehead protected by his eye, mounts [the bull] and proceeds accompanied by the daughter of the King of Mountains— the bull who, with its own luster, seems to steal away the rising sun.

O Śiva, O Mahādeva, O Lord, always protect me— the Gaṇa named Sānanda, who moves beneath the hooves of the bull at the base of the Lord’s lotus feet, and whose own shoulders shine with excellent jeweled sandals— while he cries out, "Save me, O Lord!"
O Tārānātha, wearer of the crescent moon, you who rest upon the crest-jewel of the millions of Upaniṣads.

Beholding the rows of lingas situated upon the supreme peaks as white as the crown of Mount Kailāsa, the Three-eyed Lord, filled with great joy, repeatedly says to the daughter of the Mountain, "Look!"— He who is to be contemplated with an unwearied eye and mind.

O best of the twice-born, the renowned Lord of Chariots (Agni), having ascended the chariot of the Goddess— which has a lofty floor inlaid with gold and jewels, fashioned with lattices of gems, and features a pinnacle like the moon’s radiance— traverses the summit of the mountain by the will of the gods.
It was covered by a mass of radiance from millions of various jewels,
adorned with clusters of pure pearls, joined by rows upon rows of swan-kings, and provided with pearl canopies;
it was endowed with shimmering divine banners and yak-tail whisks, and furnished with boundless parasols.
Then Hara, having ascended a divine celestial chariot together with the daughter of the king of all mountains, [departed]. || 34 ||
On Mount Kailāsa, the Lord Śiva always gazes upon the rows of the nine crests; he indeed beholds all the gods and others, as well as those worlds beyond.
With his crest crowned by the surging waves of the celestial river Ganges extending to the very edge of the cosmic egg, Śiva shines forth.
The universe is variegated and endowed with boundless diversity; yet he alone is joined with that underlying continuity.
Īśvara:

O Girijā, behold the karma-born gods, who thirst for the multitude of enjoyments favored by the celestial trees, and who, possessing the waters of divine merit favored by those very trees, depart with great haste in excellent, magnificent celestial chariots. 36.
Illuminated by the expansive radiance of the jewels shimmering on the bracelets of celestial women,
and even by the fragrant breezes carrying the scent of garlands from the lovely groves of the divine gardens,
the inhabitants there subsist solely on the taste of the nectar of the pure moon.
Those gods, O Ambika, nourish themselves along with their multitudes of enjoyments and fortunes; behold! (37)

That lowest of men who looks upon me— accompanied by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the hosts of Maruts— as equal [to those] who dwell in an ocean of filth, amidst endless worms and pus in mouths dripping with saliva; and who,
while wearing armor on their limbs at the edge of a forest of raised weapons, are occupied with eating for the duration of an aeon.
He remains standing, though corrupted by the harsh words of his younger brother and struck with a whip. || 38 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, when [the Moon] is aspected by [malefics], one becomes a partaker of the fruits of fortune consisting of miserable enjoyments due to censuring me.
Behold the multitude of hell-beings, greatly afflicted, deprived of the sight of auspicious signs;
Yama swallows them like food, well-cooked by boiling in jars of oil. (39)
With excellent necklaces of rudrākṣa beads around their throats and great garlands upon their ears, their pillar-like arms were beautified by crowns and bracelets. || 40 ||

Those whose conduct is gladdened by the worship of the Liṅga at dusk and by the sight of the abode of the Liṅga go indeed to my supreme abode, Kailāsa; they alone, O Śivā, are considered by me to be true pearl necklaces.
In the abodes of the great Liṅgas situated upon the crest of Mount Kailāsa, those jeweled pitchers, rising up, produce in you the illusion of many suns and moons; likewise,
the Ganges and the moon from the matted locks on the crown of the stainless Liṅga here [produce a similar effect].
Today this mountain appears to me like a mountain peak resplendent with a blazing crest.
Behold, O Daughter of the Mountain, the multitude of great lingas upon the peak of the mountain, worshipped with shining fresh bilva leaves;
right there, they possess the luster of blooming blue lotuses by the rays of the moon resting upon their crests, which are joined with the excellent jewels of the Gangā’s water-born lotuses.

With the sweet sounds of conchs arising from the hollowed palms of the Gaṇas, and with the sounds of maddalas and ḍiṇḍimas, the Gaṇas stationed at the summit of Śiva’s liṅga shone forth; even my mountain was always filled with such resonance.
O Daughter of the Mountain King, even this Kailāsa, the crown upon my liṅga, has always been heated by that great Mandara mountain;
yet such [heat] was never produced by the multitudes of asuras and the hosts of sages who performed penance there. (p. 101)
O Śivā, even though my excellent attendants are lords among the devotees of Śiva, my compassion for him is supreme.
Having observed this speech of Ambā, Lord Śaṅkara, the abode of joy, spoke before the Goddess a description of the multitude of Kailāsa’s virtues;
"Ah, I shall joyfully describe my delightful abode there, even to you who have the face of a noble elephant."
Having indeed placed it before that wonderful and righteous Lord. || 46 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya, within the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "The Praise of Kailāsa Performed by Skanda," begins with Skanda saying:
"Listen, O Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, and you foremost of the Gaṇas, Jaigīṣavya!"
In that interval, there is a rampart constructed of go-meda gems. || 1 ||
O best of men, it was adorned with four gate-towers (gopuras) in the four directions;
the gate-towers in the four directions measured one hundred thousand [yojanas] in size.
Indeed, they were adorned with railings and plinths,
and with archways decorated by shining pots and the tips of banners, as well as by bulls possessing the luster of those jewels.
They were also endowed with divine assembly halls featuring crystal windows fashioned by the incarnations of Rudra, as well as lotus-filled ponds and elevated platforms.
With thousands and tens of thousands of pavilions arranged in rows, variegated with jewels and gold, and adorned with archways draped in pearls; || 5 ||
With lakes resembling oceans, adorned with jeweled staircases,
and with excellent pavilions at their edges beautified by thousands of pillars;
Even with lofty pavilions shining with central jewels in the midst of lakes,
within that enclosure wall, to the south of the gateway.
There, my divine abode is auspicious, inlaid with various jewels;
it is a palatial mansion with a hundred thousand pillars and peaks made of the finest nine gems.
It was illuminated by the luster of jewels emerging from its statues of carved women;
thereafter, it had its crest fashioned from radiant gems that dispelled masses of darkness.
It was adorned with various lattice windows, surpassing [all others] in the luster of the nine precious gems,
and featured peacocks and excellent cocks fashioned from emeralds.
It was adorned with the tops of pavilions and excellent palace archways,
with most beautiful ramparts and radiant rows of gate-towers.
It was filled with the pervasive, intense, and delightful fragrance of incense, featuring jeweled door-panels and golden bolts.
There, the entire horizon was suffused with the radiance of the light of jewel-lamps;
and there was a forest, fragrant with divine flowers, surpassing even the Caitraratha grove.
It was pervaded by the radiance of jeweled altars set within jeweled basins,
and it shone with clusters of vines from various divine trees that extended to its very limits.
There is a lake named Kaumāra there, filled with blossoming lotuses,
featuring rows of jeweled steps and gem-encrusted pavilions along its banks.
There, amidst toy deer, parrots, and śārika birds in jeweled cages,
was my excellent mansion situated within that palace.
There was a lion-throne fashioned from jewels, five yojanas in extent;
there I was served by nine hundred thousand heroes with uplifted weapons.
By heroic youths of lion-like build, with weapons raised, possessing arms like the trunks of elephants in rut, and endowed with spears; || 18 ||
At that time, I was served by Vīrabāhu and others, who held flowers, garments, and unguents in their hands, as well as parasols and chowries.
Clad in garments of great value and adorned with ornaments of the nine gems,
he is resplendent with a crown featuring six faces, and wears jeweled earrings and armlets.
His lotus-like feet have toes and soles shining with jeweled rings; his ankles, feet, and waist are adorned with tinkling anklets made of gems and rubies, and a girdle.
He was also attended by the army of Devalyā and by Indra and the other gods;
with six faces and twelve eyes, he praised the Lord.
Indeed, beholding the Lord Kaumāreśvara on Kailāsa,
he stood to the south within the great enclosure wall made of the essence of diamonds.
The quarters of the sky were overspread by the high blue archways and the expansive blue streams;
it shone uniquely with the splendor of the ground where Rudra’s incarnations sported.
The bull, the crest-jewel of kings, [was led] to Śambhu’s gateway at Kailāsa,
which was fashioned with a measurement of five hundred thousand [cubits] in its width and length.
To the south, at the edge of the gateway and within the enclosure wall of Śambhu,
lies that city of Kumāra, which today shines with various palatial mansions.
It was protected by my foremost hosts of Kaumāras and by me;
therein, situated in the middle of my city, is the gateway of Kaumāreśa.
Beautiful with ramparts and watchtowers radiant with the luster of the nine gems, its inner sanctum was so intensely brilliant that it seemed to set the quarters of the sky ablaze.
There, indeed, is my beloved liṅga of the trident-bearing God of gods, its crest licked by the flames rising from the jeweled pitcher, as they kiss the courtyard of the sky.
There, surrounded by my attendants, I worship that Liṅga three times a day with incense,
lamps, food offerings, and the sprinkling of the five nectars.
With the sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, conchs, and trumpets;
with sweet and unrestrained songs; and with the dances of young maidens.
He was enchanting with the three arts of music, dance, and song, which were made captivating by various gestures and expressions;
he shone with the three-lined sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) and the tilaka applied to his forehead, which resembled the crescent moon.
Adorned with ashes, rudrākṣa bracelets, and a string of gems,
he [was nourished] by the great nectars equal to the ambrosia flowing from his six lotus-like faces.
I praise Śambhu with the best of hymns; O best of men, listen to that praise! 34.

O Bhava, Great Lord, omnipresent one, protect me—you who are praised by the celestial realms, the foremost among those who have come [to you], and worshipped with the dūrvā grass of the Karkārya-āgama; you whose hands hold the sacrificial ladle fashioned from the cord of Mount Meru. 35.

O Trivikrama, whose stride traverses the worlds, even the base of Your foot is not within our reach; how then could a frog dwelling in a well hope for the means to cross the ocean? (p. 103) O Hara, [how much less so for us]? 36.
O You whose eyes are fashioned with a golden hue, who steal [the hearts of] women as far as their ears, who dwell within the great ocean;
O You whose scriptures have been extolled by Aparṇā, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the chariot of leaves! 37.
O Lord of the foremost serpents who serve as earrings upon Your ears, O excellent helmsman who carries us across the ocean of worldly existence,
O King of Kings whose stainless crown is adorned with a crescent moon shining like a swarm of bees around the fragrance of its kinsman!
Worshipped by the multitude of blue night-lotuses that have descended from the river of the world of the gods,
with a pair of eyes numbering as many as the tongues of serpents, and likewise adorned with ten pairs of breasts— the very ornament of his couch— is the Lord, who is like a celestial *mandāra* tree.
O Youthful One, O Śaṅkara, whose words are far beyond the reach of the mind; O You who possess a body as white as camphor and wear the lord of serpents;
O Unfailing Lord, destroyer of Māra and the cities of the enemy; O Sovereign of the Universe—by Your grace, this child is dear to You. 40.
Thus, with my six faces, I praise the Great Lord Kaumāreśa,
who resides in the city of Kumāra along with my ninety-six million attendants.
The gateway was fashioned with sapphires, and that enclosure wall was likewise constructed;
it was Kailāsa, belonging to Maheśa, guarded by the hands of his Śaktis with uplifted weapons.
O Brahmin, I always protect [them] by the command of the Moon-crested Lord.
It possessed gate-towers fashioned from blue sapphire with rows of rising kalaśas and a network of extended golden banners;
it had a magnificent wall of diamonds where herds of bulls roamed, and within its palatial mansions stood great lingas of precious gems.
O Brahmin, worshipping the crown of Bhagaṇeśa along with the foremost of the Gaṇas, I dwell upon Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Praise Offered by Skanda," in the first part of the *Śrī Śivarahasya*, concerning the description of Kailāsa.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of Gaṇeśa in the Description of Kailāsa," [begins with] Skanda:
On its western side, it is resplendent with emeralds and green gems.
The wall, with its jeweled gateways, measured five hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent.
It was provided with rows of windows fashioned from great emeralds,
and it was constructed to measure eighty-eight thousand yojanas.
In the western quarter, however, the directions shone with a luster resembling emeralds;
there stood a pavilion adorned with emeralds from the garuḍa-bird.
(On page 104) It was surrounded by cascades flowing clear as the rays of the rising moon,
and there it was filled with hundreds of magnificent lion-thrones made of pure crystal.
Abounding with incense, lamps, and other offerings, and covered with various beautiful flowers, he sat upon a well-spread seat within a pavilion inlaid with gems and rubies.

While he dwells there, the Great Lord of the Universe resides with his hosts, his feet worshipped by seven hundred thousand leaders of the Gaṇas, the great thunderbolt against the mountain of obstacles.
Adorned with many ornaments studded with various jewels, his forehead glistens with sindūra, and his face is like that of a great ocean.
Resplendent with a plow adorned by the moon shining from his ruby crown,
he delighted the heavens by the loud trumpeting of his massive trunk.
His face was shaded by clusters of pearls hanging from within his water-pot,
and the luster of his pair of ears was radiant with the gem-studded earrings upon them.
Beautiful with ivory and great jewels encircling its tusks,
it shone below with dangling pearl ornaments and jeweled filigree.
He shines in the midst of a jar marked with white ash and the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra),
beautified by the joy of his blossoming face adorned with a sindūra tilaka.
With bees flying away from the tips of his ears as they were fanned by pearls strung thereon,
and with the scent of rut flowing from the slopes of his temples that perfumed the very quarters of the sky;
His eyes opened by the bliss of meditating upon the lotus feet of Śiva;
his eyes opened by the joy of beholding the Gaṇas.
Possessing a body bound by great serpents and joined with a belly like a cooking pot,
his pure face was like a blooming lotus, and he was bowed to by the hosts of gods and asuras.
His excellent hands were occupied with sweets that shone like nooses and goads;
his arms, possessing the luster of an elephant's trunk, gleamed with jeweled armlets and bracelets. || 15 ||
Adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets set upon his feet, beautiful with divine unguents, and clothed in garments and necklaces of gems; || 16 ||
He is resplendent with glory on both sides, adorned by Siddhi and Buddhi,
and attended on his two flanks by those adorned with all manner of ornaments.
In that Kailāsa pavilion, the illustrious Lord Gaṇeśa was served by the lords of the Gaṇas, who held aloft umbrellas, staffs, jeweled fly-whisks, and fine fans.
With the winds from their waving chowries and the tips of their ears moving like chowries,
such were the leaders of the Gaṇas there, likewise bearing nooses and goads.
Possessing great strength and great enthusiasm, with excellent axes in their hands,
their foreheads were as red as vermilion and beautifully adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
There, those hosts of lords of the Gaṇas and guardians of the Gaṇas, possessing a strength measured at seven hundred thousand, protect that rampart and that gateway.
In that very place, by the command of the God of gods, the moon-crested Lord,
Gaṇeśa also remained constantly meditating as a worshiper of the Lord of Gaṇeśas.
Therein was his desired liṅga, surrounded by a rampart and gateways of excellent materials;
it was divine, inlaid with the nine gems, and its interior was adorned with pillars of precious stones.
That Liṅga, known as Gaṇeśvara, was likewise situated within a jeweled temple,
its upper cloth fluttering in the wind from the tips of the banners atop the rising domes.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five nectars from the lofty jars held in its own lotus-hands,
and having smeared it beautifully with sandalwood paste mixed with streams of nectar;
Adorned with the great crest-jewel and the gems of his crown,
he today worships [the Lord] with bilva, mandāra, and campaka flowers.
One should worship Īśa with dūrvā grass, lotuses, incense, beautiful lamps,
various kinds of food offerings, betel leaves, umbrellas, and chowries.
Accompanied by songs, dances, and the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, lutes, and kahalas,
and endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, he praises the god Maheśvara.
Gaṇeśa:
O Gaṇeśa, who transcend the three qualities (guṇas), whose head is the lord of the celestial spheres;
whose matted locks are darkened by the multitude of lightning flashes arising from a mass of roaring clouds. (29)
O Lord whose hair is the sky; O Blessed One, by whom all the Soma [offerings] are arranged through the hymns of the Ṛgveda and the Sāmans;
O You whose desire is the arrival of greatness upon the earth; O You whose throat possesses a luster as intense as the radiance of smoke.
O Śambhu, destroyer of the heroic Māra; O Hero, steadfast one, whose feet are the crest-jewel of the gods;
O annihilator of the terrible Asura Andhaka; O Death of Death; O Lord of the Imperishable, who removes the pride of Tripura and possesses a cruel inner nature! 31.
O Śambhu, you are the crown of the dense forest of the heart, the abundance of faultless happiness for all the worlds;
you who are far removed from the course of the three qualities (guṇas), whose feet are praised today by the revealed words of the Vedas. 32.
I worship Him who holds a deer in His hand, whose matted locks are like the Ganges, who has serpents as His necklace,

who dwells in the hearts of the self-controlled, whose body is like that of a youth, who is smeared with white ashes, who is the bodiless one (Ananga), and who destroys the elephant of passion (Madana).
Skanda—
thus does the lord of the hosts on Kailāsa, the leader of the Gaṇas, the master of the Gaṇas, and the foremost among the attendants of Sadāśiva, ever praise Śambhu.
By the command of the moon-crested Lord Śambhu, he, together with his own hosts of attendants, protected that gateway and even the jeweled rampart of Śambhu.
To the west is the excellent gate-tower made of emerald, shining with courtyards marked by the luster of the horns of the preeminent bull,
and possessing the finest jewel-palaces with the radiant glow of the best of emeralds.
It has a rampart-like body that is manifest, most excellent, and beautiful.
Relying on the strength of his own arms, accompanied by the excellent hosts born from the elephant-faced one, the leader of the Gaṇas proceeds, serving the lotus feet of Śiva. (37)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise Offered by Gaṇeśa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya, concerning the description of Kailāsa.
Chapter Twenty-five, titled "The Praise of the Bull," in the Description of Kailāsa:
Skanda said— Within Kailāsa, toward the east, there is a temple fashioned from topaz (puṣparāga).
The excellent wall and its gateways measure five hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Captivating with a brilliance exceeding that of hundreds of rising suns,
it was presided over by vṛṣabhas emerging from puṣparāga gems.
The wall was fashioned by the wielder of the trident with a mind measuring one hundred thousand [units],
and it was endowed with cornices and friezes depicting the deeds of the incarnations of Rudra.
The tips of the banners fluttered atop the frontal globes of the king’s excellent elephants,
and the splendor of the moon was eclipsed by the radiance of emerald jewels.
Right there was an unsurpassed pavilion with a great jewel-womb,
ten thousand pillars high, and enchanting in its loftiness.
Its sky was kissed by crevices fashioned like crest-jewels,
and it was adorned with coral figurines upon the pedestals of great altars made of various gems.
It was adorned with clear clusters of jewels and featured seats hung with garlands;
there, upon a divine lion-throne inlaid with collections of the nine precious gems.
Abounding in incense, lamps, and other offerings, adorned with strings of pearls, with canopies illuminating the circle of the directions, and joined by various hosts of Rudras; || 8 ||
[They were] sixty thousand in number,
free from anger, with foreheads shining with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and adorned with excellent rudrākṣa beads.
With their hands raised holding tridents, white, and equipped with spears, bows, and arrows;
with crescent moons bound upon the masses of their matted hair, they possessed a radiance like that of the moon.
The great bull, whose form is Dharma, is eternally served on all sides;
he has great feet that are the support of Dharma, and his broad hooves are the navel of the Yuga.
His feet are formed by the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), which possess the fierce colors of the twilight periods;
he possesses the singular sound of dharma, resonating with the tinkling of jeweled anklets.
He was one who shattered the teeth of the doctrines of Vedānta arising from the four Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (upavedas),
and who possessed the great bell of the two systems of Purāṇa, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā.
He whose throat resounds with the thunderous roar of the words of the established tenets and the final conclusions,
and whose neck is graced by a magnificent necklace and adorned with a large bell.
Kailāsa was like a moving mountain, adorned with two peaks, possessing a great luster that was exceedingly white and lofty, as if it were a mass of nectar. || 15 ||
Nandikeśvara stood in the presence of the God of gods, accompanied by five hundred thousand attendants whose bodies resembled camphor. (16)
His body was like the full orb of the rising moon, his back reached a height of a hundred thousand yojanas,
and he possessed a hump that was ten thousand yojanas high and circular.
Thirty thousand [beings] were in his mouth, two thousand in his eyes,
five thousand in his ears, and one thousand in his tusks.
From the openings of his nostrils issued five thousand clear serpents,
and his tongue, a full thousand yojanas in length, was licking the tips of its own ends.
With unblinking eyes, he gazed upon Maheśvara,
whose pearl necklaces hung from a couch made of clear gems spread across his own back.
The great mountain was tossed by the wind rising from the openings of his nostrils,
and the ocean shores were shaken by that wind, causing the waves to surge upward again and again.
The oceans and the rivers, torn by his moving hooves,
caused the earth to appear as if trembling, agitated by both mountains and seas.
He was resplendent with a crown shining with jewels at its peak,
and white chowries hung down from his ears, bright as the light of the moon.
It measured five million [yojanas] and was endowed with excellent hooves,
ten thousand in number, which possessed the luster of sapphire gems.
The multitude of mountains was rubbed by his hooves, the mountain caves resounded with his roar,
and his dewlap hung down for five thousand yojanas, appearing as clear as crystal.
Greatly terrified by the sound of "humpha" cries, he was surrounded on all sides by millions of herds of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu) dwelling in the depths of the three worlds.
He split the mountain peak, which was radiant with the light of the autumn moon,
even as he hung there with his testicles dangling for a hundred yojanas.
He was adorned by a trailing tail of hair thirty thousand yojanas long,
a magnificent mass of hair at the tip of his chowrie.
There stands the gateway of Śambhu, the lord of the bull, where the radiance of jewels rises up through lattices of pearls and rubies.
Having bathed the Lord’s beloved Liṅga, which is like a bull for the king of ramparts, with the milk produced from the udders of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), [he worshipped it]. 30.
With perfumes, bilva fruits, mandāra flowers, lotuses, incense, and lamps; with food offerings, milk-rice, cakes, betel-leaf, umbrellas, and chowries. || 31 ||
Adorned with ashes and rudrākṣa beads, marked on his forehead with the triple-crested sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra), and bearing the moon, he worships and praises Dharmeśa from his two horns.
Beholding this, his soul thrilled with joy, he offers praise, while the quarters of the horizon are pinned down by his sound.
Dharma—
O you who have received training from the side of Dakṣa, who bore upon your great bull the sight of the demon Bāṇa who held the earth in his eyes,
