whose belly contains the entire world, and who are distinct from the body of the son of the bird-vehicle (Garuḍa)! 34.

O Śambhu, neither the deer in the form of Viṣṇu nor Brahmā could perceive the root of Your feet, which extends beyond the surface of the earth’s sphere; thus, Brahmā and Viṣṇu dispute over the contact with Your feet and Your crown, respectively.
To Hari, he offered a horse with a Sindhu-horse as its girth, a bull, a great-limbed garment of hide, one with uplifted limbs,
one with the moon upon its head, a chariot-wheel, and one standing on the back of a great bull, whose heart was fixed on the eye.
Skanda:
Thus Dharma, assuming the form of a bull, praises Mahādeva;
that very Dharma, exceedingly radiant, carries the Lord of Gods. (37)
Surrounded by hosts of Gaṇas, he protects that excellent eastern gate of the enclosure at the command of that God of gods and the Destroyer of Smara.
On the glorious peak of Kailāsa, he is surrounded on all sides by the excellent Gaṇapas of Śiva, by those with elephant faces, by the Kumāras, by the Gaṇapas of the lordly bull, and by the Rudras;
yet even Viṣṇu, the lords of the entire universe, the hosts of gods, the multitudes of Vedas, and the best of sages are unable to fully comprehend him. (p. 108)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Bull," in the description of Kailāsa within the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
In the description of Kailāsa, the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description Introducing the Goddess," Skanda said:
To the north of that is a rampart adorned with lapis lazuli gems.
And with threads of infinite lapis lazuli, the quarters of that place were made yellow.
Therein was a lofty gate-tower, resplendent with lapis lazuli gems,
beautified by the life-story of Rudra inscribed from its base to its pinnacle.
It measured five hundred thousand [yojanas] and was made of excellent great beryl;
it was adorned with friezes, divine chambers, pigeon-cotes, and decorative moldings.
That army, brilliant with jeweled water-pots and numbering five hundred [thousand], consisted of nine hundred thousand hosts of Rudras, who bore uplifted weapons for Śambhu. (4)
With their foreheads shining with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), wearing crescent moons in their matted hair,
resembling intoxicated elephants, these youths wore polished earrings.
And they guard that excellent gateway and its surrounding wall;
for within it is a vast space adorned with various clusters of jewels.
The residence of the Goddess was magnificent, adorned with rows of palatial buildings,
and beautiful with thousands of pillars inlaid with precious rubies.
With great settings of diamond essence, with topaz, emerald, and sapphire, and with lapis lazuli, gomedaka, pearl, and coral; || 8 ||
[The palaces] were fashioned with topaz gems, joined with gomedaka-arches,
produced from excellent emeralds, and radiant with strings of pearl-jewels.
There is a certain wall there, composed of well-formed pillars of coral creepers, with expansive pedestals of kuruvinda gems, and adorned with moonstone slabs.
It was designed with a measurement of twenty thousand yojanas,
and it was provided with four gates, great gate-towers, and altars.
It was fashioned from jewels, diamonds, gomedas, and topazes;
it shone with jeweled peaks shaped like the rising sun. || 12 ||

Adorned with rows of peaks that were like playful lions due to their delight in sporting with goddesses (an alternative reading is *śṛṅgaiḥ*), and resembling the autumnal moon, they were colored by the finest crystal. || 13 ||
With distorted faces, lolling tongues, and necks adorned with flowing manes,
ten thousand [demons] were stationed there within the inner apartment of the Goddess.
And it was adorned all around with nine kinds of jewels for many yojanas;
it resembled the rising rays of the moon and was uniquely beautiful through various artistic crafts.
There, the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of the Goddess shines like ten million suns, resplendent with rows of light having the appearance of clusters of pearls and stars. || 16 ||
The illustrious Maheśvarī resides in the center of a great mansion made of the nine gems;
she is radiant with a surrounding lake abounding in the fragrance of lotuses.

Seated upon an excellent lion-throne fashioned from the central jewel of the celestial palace, her form is slightly swaying on a great couch of emeralds. (An alternative reading is "her body is swinging on a swing. || 18 ||
Sometimes that Great Goddess, served by hosts of Yoginīs graceful in their hallīsa dance, rests upon an excellent seat of coral.
Seated upon an excellent gem-studded throne resting on a choice pedestal of coral,
she dwells within a palace of rubies, adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Once, residing alone within a palace made of rubies, she played with a ball of sapphire and a ball of crystal, as if possessed by the spirit of playful curiosity.
(21) [Note: "līlākutukabhūtāccha" is an alternative reading.]
And because of the slaying of those two, O twice-born one, the sun and the moon constantly rise and set as they move upward and downward. (22)
To the accompaniment of the *karatāla* rhythm, she moved through the lattices of the magnificent jeweled pavilion atop that excellent mansion, wandering amidst the openwork of the palace floor.
It possesses the wonderful splendor of palaces expanded by the rays of the moon,
and it has as its excellent refuge noble jeweled mansions surrounded by flower gardens.
Sometimes the auspicious Bestower of Boons resides in the midst of the Prince’s quarters;
sometimes she stays upon a couch of flowers within a house of rubies.
Holding jeweled pipes in her hands, adorned with radiant jeweled bracelets,
she dwells in a magnificent palace of diamonds situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest.
The auspicious goddess Śivā, dwelling in a palace of blue lotuses, was pleased; her hand held a bright kīra-vīra gem playfully tossed about, while the śārikā bird sang clear songs.
Her head is filled with the illusion of a brilliantly illuminated, great dark-blue braid;
she is enriched with excellent ornaments and wears tinkling sandals.
Intent on gazing at the many fruits contained within her jewel bowl,
she wore a great necklace of flower clusters and held in her hand a fragrant chaplet.
In one place, the auspicious goddess Śivā held a jeweled vessel filled with the fragrance of nectar-sweetened incense;
her forehead-locks were like the radiant rays of the moon from her majestic crown.
Her mass of hair flows with a stream of jewel-ornaments, and she is captivating;
she gazes into many jeweled mirrors shown by the Yoginīs. (31)
Dwelling within a palace made of a multitude of moonstone slabs,
she appeared like a streak of shimmering gems fashioned from collyrium for the eyes.
Her splendor issues forth from her hand-gestures; her nails are adorned with rings, her palms shine with diamonds, and her feet are radiant with a crimson luster.
Her dark braid was like a row of many jewel-sevantika flowers upon a funeral pyre;
her garment’s hem, inlaid with precious gold, was adorned with pearls.
The goddess puts on a silken garment within the palace,
which is uniquely beautiful due to the binding fragrance of incense smoke and various ornaments.
Within a palace of jewels, upon a seat radiant with clusters of flowers, the horizons were illuminated by the intense splendor of lamps made from the rays of gems. || 36 ||
She stood there, appearing as if she were many Rudrāṇīs within the lotus-face of [the Lord],
her bodily luster marked by the finest application of liquid sandalwood paste.
Her crest was resplendent with *suramaṇḍāra*, *punnāga*, and *ketaka* flowers, and adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *damana*, *uśīra*, *kaṇṭa*, and beautiful *pāṭala* blossoms.
Adorned with a heavy mass of hair braided with jasmine, Arabian jasmine, and jasmine flowers,
she is uniquely beautiful with the fragrance of musk and camphor and the scent of fine incense.
Her radiant breasts, fragrant with musk, are partially concealed;
she is resplendent with the prominent lines of her arms visible from the loosened knot of her bodice.
The parting line of her hair was marked by sindhūra from the hand of Rudrāṇī;
her face, radiant with a tilaka of excellent jewels, resembled the splendor of the moon. 41.
Her slender body is adorned with the shimmering luster of rings upon her fingers;
standing within a palace of lapis lazuli, she watches the dance of Rudrāṇī.
In some places, there were women devoted to the music of the lute, whose great strings were bound at the top with blue gems, gourd-sounds, jewels, pearls, and diamonds.
In some places, she sang the beautiful name of Śiva, which is sweet and sublime,
while being fanned by whisks as bright as the rays of the autumnal moon.
The auspicious lady was fanned with peacock-feather fans possessing jeweled handles,
while streams of jewels eclipsed the lord of the night who had arisen on the mountain.
With her face covered by a shining parasol, refreshed by the flavor of betel,
and holding a betel-roll in her hand, she stood gazing at a painted canvas.
That form of Sadāśiva, the Lord of Scribes, was thus depicted;
it was beautifully adorned with the luster of coral and the red hue of the bimba fruit.
Resplendent with the radiance of the rays of jewels from her necklaces, thought-fulfilling gems, and pearl strings,
she was adorned with shimmering jewel-handled whisks and the sound of tinkling bells.
She shines like a rising poetess, wearing a pair of earrings resplendent with the sun and moon, and her face is adorned with a nose-ornament of pure pearls.
She rests upon a magnificent pavilion consisting of a great stream of the essence of the Jewel-Ganges;
she is resplendent with a jeweled girdle of shimmering gems fastened around her hips.
Resplendent with the brilliant jewels in her anklets that shine like the intense light of the sun-lotus,
she is uniquely beautiful with the sweet, tinkling sounds of her jingling anklets, which are like the cries of swans.
With the gait of a king of swans, her limbs adorned with divine necklaces,
she shone with vine-like arms raised in the *vaṅkikā* and *nāgabandha* gestures.
Her skin was covered by clusters of pearls dangling from the tips of her elbows,
and she was adorned with a series of beautiful jewel-ornaments hanging from her forehead.
Adorned with a magnificent head-ornament marked by the sun and moon,
the Supreme Goddess is there served by millions of Yoginīs.
The joyful Śivā remained seated in a great palace made of emeralds,
upon a jeweled couch prepared with divine pillows and spread with a fine covering.
In the circle of the quarters perfumed by incense, enchanting with jeweled lamps,
and with the sky covered by clusters of flowers suspended from a canopy;
Śivā dwelt comfortably upon well-spread cushions for her feet and arms;
accompanied by the resonance of lutes, she was followed by the streams of Rudrāṇī’s songs.
She remained in her house made of vaidruma wood, listening to the names of Śiva,
amidst trees resembling golden plantain clusters and emeralds.
In the midst of that [city], she took refuge in an excellent palace made of crystal,
situated within the palace of Garuḍa which was surrounded by Tamāla, Sāla, and Nīpa trees.
Seated upon a great throne fashioned of jewels,
she of enchanting appearance [surrounded] by the captivating calls of quails, peacocks, and cocks.
The delightful shore of the jewel-lotus pond, its banks adorned with large, emerging arrows [or reeds] from the horns of rams and antelopes, was encircled on all sides by magnificent great gems.
In a pavilion beautiful with jewels arranged along its banks,
Śivā [beheld] parrots with variegated plumage perched within jeweled cages.
Beholding a pomegranate seed upon a beautiful cluster of grapevines entwined around a betel-nut tree, she places it within the beak of a parrot.
It was beautified by the moonlight flowers, as crimson as the blossoms of the twilight creeper,
and possessed the milky water of nectar from the smooth jeweled banks of the surrounding canals.
Delighted by the fragrance of blossoming *hallaka* flowers opening at the touch of the sun, beautified by great machines that shower down torrents of rain, and perfumed with sweet scents; || 65 ||
Seated upon a grand couch within a jeweled pavilion shaded by the crown of a betel-nut tree,
the auspicious goddess Śivā gazes upon the dance performed by a sporting peacock.
(Verse 67) [The city] was adorned with palaces constructed from great lordly jewels,
and it took delight in houses draped with garments made of various multicolored cloths.
O Goddess, in this enchanting place where curtains are arranged on all four sides,
which is illuminated by jeweled vases and adorned with pillars of precious gems!
In one place she stood engaged in conversation with her friends,
amidst great palatial mansions shaped like chariots, as well as circles of jewels and horses.
As if reaching its limit, that palace was adorned with lions and swans;
right there, within the inner apartments, was the pleasure-chamber of the Goddess, the Sovereign.
It was of incomparable form, shaped like the Śrīcakra, enchanting with its finest jewels,
extending for a thousand yojanas, and adorned with windows variegated with gems.
It was variegated with wonderful rows of swans, lotuses, and great vines;
its floors were colored by the flow of the great essence from jeweled pillars.
Adorned with canopies and garlands, with clusters of pearls hanging down,
and with great jeweled pedestals suspended even below;
Upon them were spread great beds, provided with pillows and enchanting,
resembling the orb of the moon and possessing the luster of foam and cow’s milk.
Rich with the fragrance of intense joy, strewn with jasmine flowers,
and adorned with various jewels shining from houses filled with wandering lamps.
The vast courtyards of the God and the Goddess, variegated with the essence of their play and other pastimes,
were adorned by thousands of incense trees, lamp trees, and those fashioned from jewels.
And with betel-leaf boxes, auspicious jeweled water-pitchers,
incense burners, lamp vessels, and containers for flowers and betel.
It was unsurpassed, resplendent with bowls of fruit filled with jewels, water-pots of precious gems containing nectar,
and the radiant glow of jewels fragrant with incense.
With the graceful fanning of chowries fashioned from jeweled figurines, and accompanied by figurines holding fans, mirrors, and betel; (79)

O Sage, the Lord was devoid of his attendants, and Śivā was separated from her companions; yet those two, Śiva and Śivā, sported within that palace of the Śrīcakra (or, according to another reading, in its center).

Skanda: On Mount Kailāsa, upon a pedestal shimmering with the jewels of the nine Śaktis, born from the speech of the Great Principle (Mahātattva), and extending for many tens of millions of leagues— situated in the center of the Śrīcakra;
In the Bindu, which consists of a pair of ten million moons and suns, upon its pedestal—the Mañca composed of the five Brahmans—we, together with Girijā, inhale [the breath] from the heart. || 81 ||

On Mount Kailāsa, upon a couch shimmering within a palace made of the nine gems, in the midst of the ocean of nectar—[according to another reading: "in a garden belonging to the Kalpa-tree"]—surrounded by golden jeweled doors and radiant with the *cintāmaṇi* gem;
there he dwells together with the Mother of the World, as a single solar form within his body of nectar.
Day and night, he constantly casts up the ball of form with that very same [mind]. || 82 ||

On page 112): You, who exist eternally upon the manifold throne of the monasteries (maṭha) comprising the four quarters, manifesting as the eight deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the King of the Gods—as well as the four aims of human life, the four ages, the collection of Vedas, and the divine multitude of fruits; you who act thus...
Playing together with the entire collection of fortunes, he made his home highly esteemed.
Having fashioned here a gaming board made of the entire multitude of living beings as its squares,
Śiva sits playing dice together with his Mother, using Time, Karma, and the Noose as his pieces.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Introduction," in the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*, within the description of Kailāsa.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Kailāsa and the Narration of the Worship and Praise of the Goddess," begins with Skanda saying:
"In that very place, there is yet another beautiful abode of the Goddess."
It was a hundred yojanas in extent, radiant with the brilliance of emeralds.
It was adorned with numerous windows set in its gabled roof, featuring projecting cornices;
its pillars were radiant with jeweled pedestals, and it was decorated with coral figurines.
It was enchanting with clusters of excellent jewel-like coconuts, excellent jewel-like plantain fruits,
and excellent jewel-like areca nuts.
Its ground was covered with canopies hanging from fruits like precious jewel-vines, and it was teeming with bees wandering about to taste the flavor of flower garlands. || 4 ||
Upon that divine great couch, resplendent with a bed of flowers,
its canopy was covered by a cloth woven with sandalwood and ushira grass.
Upon that lofty mosaic floor, which was like a mirror and was forever unfading, beautifully adorned with garlands of radiant lotuses made of precious gems.
The Great Goddess always dwells surrounded by the wives of the Rudras— women with hair-braids adorned with beautiful, stainless flowers and faces like the lord of the stars.
Young women, endowed with beauty, their breasts resembling the frontal globes of elephants,
enriched with necklaces and jeweled neck-ornaments, and adorned with armlets of pearls and gems.
All were liberated and unobstructed, wearing crowns fashioned from moonlight,
beautiful with divine unguents, and their feet adorned with tinkling anklets.
There, in those excellent palaces, those goddesses with uplifted hips move about like streaks of lightning and constantly serve the Goddess.
Clad in costly garments, their faces adorned with tilaka marks,
they were enchanting with lower lips as red as ripe bimba fruit, stained by the color of betel.
Some held yak-tail whisks in their hands, some carried sandalwood paste,
some held black ointments in their palms, and others likewise bore parasols.
Some held betel-boxes and jewel-caskets, while others carried ointments in their hands; some held combs in their hands, and others likewise carried boxes of ornaments.
(113) One has turmeric and saffron in her hands and holds lac-dye;
another bears vermilion and has her hand firmly grasping a sandal.
Some bore jewels, gold, garments, and the like, along with jeweled screens shining with gems; some held jeweled lutes in their hands, while others likewise held playful parrots.
One [goddess] bore a magnificent peacock-feather crown adorned with emeralds;
another held a jeweled mirror in her hand and carried a full-blown flower.
With great hands like campaka flowers and the like, holding jeweled ewers in their hands,
they carry swords, shields, scimitars, arrows, and bows in their palms.
With one hand resting upon her quiver, she holds a playful ball;
her other beautiful hand is adorned with a staff decorated with jewels for the hallīśa dance.
Some carried boxes of cosmetics, others offered the fragrance of musk;
they perfumed the very horizons with the boundless scent of fragrances contained within jeweled vessels.
Some had their hands raised with vessels filled with fine fragrant powders, necklaces, clusters of flowers, and crests; likewise, others held jeweled tridents.
Intent on awakening the Śārikā, they respectfully recited the names of the goddesses;
one held a vessel of excellent incense, while another held a lamp.
Likewise, some held water-jars filled with fragrant oil from which gems were emerging;
others held out trays of betel-leaf, while others held fruits in their hands.
Some held lotuses and water-lilies in their hands, while others likewise held ointments for the body; others had hands shining with vessels of gold, filled with fruits and jewels. || 23 ||
Some charming Rudrāṇīs, holding jeweled jars filled with nectar in their hands, thus serve the goddess Ambikā from all sides.
Skilled in the delights of serving her in various ways and following the will of the Goddess,
they [waited] upon her in palaces, on couches, and upon jeweled lion-thrones.
Likewise, some prepare flower beds covered with fine rugs;
others are skilled in various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as in drinks and excellent flavors.
There, the Rudrāṇīs in the bloom of their youth serve the Goddess;
there, in the great palace of the Goddess, [the floor] is variegated with the nine jewels.
The inner sanctum of Maheśa and Devīśvara was delightful, provided with enclosures and gate-towers, and adorned with jeweled archways. || 28 ||
It was joined by the majestic Rudra-play-bulls from the ruby mirror,
and its crest shone with beautiful jewel-pitchers and banners.
There, the linga whitens the quarters of the sky with its flood of nectar;
its summit is adorned with a bilva fruit shining upon the hoods of a serpent.
Adorned with a sphere of jewels set within a section of a palace of nectar,
that very Liṅga of Devīśvara is always worshipped by Ambikā.

With pitchers born of the nine gems filled with the waters of the ocean of nectar, and with fragrant, delightful waters consisting of great streams of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [he bathed the Lord]. || 32 ||
Beautifully adorned with garments wrapped around her body and anointed with an ointment of yakṣakardama,
she wore garlands of bilva, campaka, dhuttūra, and jeweled lotuses.
Then Śivā [honored] the Lord, who was enchanting with his crest-ornament beautified by a row of jasmine flowers, with the smoke of incense arising from *takola* and *agaru*.
Its interior was illuminated by lamps with the luster of kuruvinda gems,
and adorned with garlands of exquisite white lotuses and wreaths of fresh blue water-lilies.
One should worship Śivā with thousands of bilva fruits resembling emeralds;
one should worship the Daughter of the Mountain with heaps of various excellent foods, both solid and soft.
With betel leaves produced from the essence of khadira wood, gold, and pieces of camphor;
with lustration rites accompanied by the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and maddala drums.
(Verse 38) With the beautiful sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, kettledrums, and other instruments;
with the dances of Rudrāṇī and the playing of the hosts of Yoginīs.
Thus she worships at the three times of day, her locks of hair adorned with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra),
her form radiant with the supreme pearl-jewels fixed as Rudrākṣa beads.
Wearing two pure, stainless garments,
the auspicious goddess, unwearied, praised the great Liṅga, the Lord of the Goddesses.
The goddess, with her palms joined in reverence, [beheld] that most excellent form consisting of eight bodies.
Goddess:
Hara, Hara! Protect me, O friend of the distressed! O Destroyer of Cities, O God, O treasure-house of compassion, O steadfast one!
O Great Hero, whose lotus feet are worshipped by the Slayer of Mura, and who bears the manifest moon as your crest-ornament! 42.
O Śambhu, clad in the hide of the noble elephant and the donkey; O destroyer of Māra, who wears the finest of excellent serpents as a necklace!
Protect me, O Bharga, treasure-house of compassion, three-eyed one, whose body is devoid of the fraction of Time (Kāla). 43.
O Śambhu, whose excellent horse is the Veda, whose throat is dark blue like the *tamāla* flower, and who wears a crown of blossoms;
O remover of the fear of worldly existence, O destroyer of the cause beyond [the world], O you whose hand is marked by the bow of Hari and Giriśa! 44.
Protect us, O All-pervading Lord, wielder of the trident, clad in human skin and tiger-skin, protector of the young!

O Śambhu, whose hand shines like a swan upon the neck of Brahmā (or, according to another reading: "the hand that slays [the enemy]"), you who have consumed the body of Kāma with the fire from your lotus-eye! 45.
To this Śaṅkara, who is the vessel for the offering of the hymn revealed by the divine sage Durvāsas, who is saluted by Sanandana and Sanātana,
and who possesses the highest blameless qualities, [I bow] along with the hosts of excellent sages and the gods.
With great devotion, the hosts of the best of Gaṇas danced, some with protruding bellies and others with distended abdomens. || 46 ||
"Skanda," thus the goddess praised the Supreme Lord, the Master of the Goddesses,
while she was surrounded by the host of Rudrāṇīs and served by the assembly of Yoginīs. (47)
Residing in the midst of Mahākailāsa and reclining upon the divine lap of the God,
that auspicious Śivā, the Mother of the World, also worships the Lord incessantly.
To the God of gods, Mahādeva, who moves with the gait of a preeminent bull, whose crest is adorned by the moon—the abode of nectar—and who is praised by the Vedas; (49)
Maheśvara, whose matted locks are adorned with a crown, whose forehead is marked by the fire-eye,
who is blue-throated, who has deformed eyes, and whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
He who delights the deer, the death of Death, the treasure-house of compassion,
smeared with ashes, marked with the triple-tilaka, and wearing a beautiful necklace of rudrākṣa beads.
His neck was adorned with a jeweled necklace from the hoods of great serpents,
and his body was as white as camphor, resembling the rising rays of the moon.
Seated upon a divine lion-throne in the palace of Great Kailāsa,
he is served by the Gaṇas Skanda, Mahānandi, Bhṛṅgi, and Caṇḍīśa.
His head is adorned by the splendor of the Ganges flowing unrestrained from his crown;
he has eyes like the lotus, Mitra, and Agni, and his locks of hair shine with the crescent moon.
The god, whose neck was graced by a garland of blooming white lotuses,
was adorned with a magnificent wreath of *nandana* and *mandāra* flowers.
He whose forehead is surrounded by the burnt gate-towers of the demon Tripura,
who is the destroyer of Andhaka, who is worthy of being sought as refuge, and who is affectionate toward his own devotees.
I bow to Vāmadeva, whose radiant sandals are honored by the crowns of all the gods and others,
who is praised by the great Sāman hymns of the Stoma chants, and who transcends the reach of the senses.

He who is pleased by the sound of the *rathantara* chant, who is gratified by the prostrations of shining kings, and who possesses the splendor of the great Vairāja king and the arts of the king of kings. (58)
Meditating upon the Lord, who is as if the unified essence of all the Upaniṣads, that Great Goddess beheld him dwelling within the lotus-abode of her own mind.
Her lotus-face drenched by the streams of the essence of that meditation,
the Goddess thought of nothing else— not even the origin and duration of the world.

Thus meditating upon the feet of the Moon-crested Lord, seated within her blossoming heart-lotus, the Goddess Girijā was so utterly overwhelmed by internal passion that she perceived nothing else at all;
indeed, she thought, "This entire world in the three realms is devoid of essence. (Note: An alternative reading is *nānyat kiṃcid amanyata*.)
Having rendered [other things] insignificant, she whose supreme mind is greatly pure [placed] her own self as the Lord within her heart. || 61 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship and Praise of the Goddess," in the first part of the *Śrī Śivarahasya*, concerning the description of Kailāsa.
The twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Palace.
Skanda said:
And within that [palace] was a rampart variegated with the nine jewels.
It was fashioned with a height of eighty-eight thousand yojanas.
He was fashioned by the mind alone of the Fourteenth Great Lord;
his crown reaches the summit of the cosmic egg, and he possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns.
Neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor yakṣas, uragas,
or rākṣasas can easily behold that wall fashioned of jewels, even by the lords of the gaṇas.
There, the mountains were established by Śiva himself in the eight directions:
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, Vindhya, Malaya, and Dardura.
Mandara, Himavat, and Nīla were likewise manifested right here;
at that time, Śambhu was exceedingly pleased by their ascetic penance.
Out of compassion, Śiva granted them a permanent residence even in his own abode, the great mountain Kailāsa.
Elsewhere, those rocky mountains on Kailāsa resemble jewels;
they were fashioned by the wielder of the trident at the eight corners of its ramparts.
To the east shines Niṣadha, and in the southeast Hemakūṭa;
that Vindhya shines in the south, and Malaya is situated in the southwest. (8)
Dardura shines in the western quarter; Mandara shines in the northwestern quarter;
Himavat shines in the northern quarter; and the Nīla mountain shines in the northeastern quarter.
Situated in the eight directions upon the great Mount Kailāsa,
these best of mountains illuminate the expanse of the quarters with their own crests.
With the pinnacles of its palace towers, which surpass the sun and moon in brilliance,
it possesses the luster of rubies and the radiance of Indra’s bow in the sky.
Resembling an indragopa insect, it shines, illuminating the quarters of space;
with its own peaks scraping the clouds, it seems to lick the very sky.
Resplendent with the light of boundless jeweled gate-towers situated upon its summits,
it is further adorned by various incarnations of Rudra and by sacred bulls.
It shines, illuminating the circle of the quarters and stealing away the eyes with its splendors—
that mountain-peak, which possesses the lofty frontal globes of a great elephant’s head.
It has a lofty throne-like base as vast as a thousand oceans, possesses immeasurable luster,
and is a great palace with a vast foundation, adorned with a thousand pillars.
Resembling the seeds of a pomegranate, with a vast expanse of clear luster,
it was provided with staircases and platforms and adorned with a thousand floors.
It was adorned with pillars and finials made of ruby gems,
and its interior was embellished with great garlands of various jewels.
And by the luster of those jewels, the orb of the sun shines with the colors of the gems of the eastern quarter, as does the circle of Indra’s direction through the reddish glow of those palaces.
O brahmins, the sky shines a reddish hue due to the splendor of those mountains,
which is further intensified by the thick, highly fragrant smoke of burning agaru incense.
There, seated upon his lion throne together with the Goddess, Maheśvara was attended by breezes bound by the fragrance of blossoming forest-born flowers.
Exceedingly joyful and attended by throngs of his retinue, he sports there,
[beholding] those great, unbroken pillars fashioned from rubies.
Possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, Śambhu himself illuminates the interior; gazing toward the eastern direction, he beholds Amarāvatī right there.
There, he saw the gods of Indra’s abode— the immortals headed by Indra—
as well as the wind from the Nandana grove of the gods, fragrant with the scent of blossoming flowers.
The Lord smelled his own body, which was a great feast for the stomachs of the Kāka-serpents,
and which possessed rows of waves struck by the movement of the seven oceans.
Delighted by the joy of Śiva’s son, he [the ocean] was adorned with networks of foam-bubbles and,
with its wave-hands, seemed to be perpetually bowing to the other oceans.
The various oceans, great continents, and mandalas; the rivers, mountains, and forests; the path of the gods, and likewise the destinations of the celestial beings.
Seeing the enjoyments of those who perform penance, he rejoiced with his mother;
there was the abode of the Lord of Niṣadha, enchanting with its jeweled water-pots.
Then Niṣadha, manifest in bodily form, worshipped that liṅga there,
endowed with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and with divine five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, bowing down, he honored him with perfumes, garments, bilva, mandāra, and campaka flowers, as well as incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel leaves.
(Verse 30) He stood there constantly praising the Lord of Niṣadha with circumambulations.
Niṣadha said:

I perpetually bow down in this very manner to the Lord of Niṣadha, the medicine for the disease of worldly existence, who is perfectly seated amidst the entire multitude of beings, whose eyes are uneven [three], and whose body is free from all impurities.
Skanda— Thus Niṣadha, situated in the eastern direction, praises Mahādeva;
likewise Hemakūṭa, possessing great splendor, [praises him] on his crown in the south-eastern direction.
With his lofty head resplendent with the great gem gomedaka, this sovereign stands facing the south-eastern direction, illuminating it with his own radiance.
With its gate-towers reaching beyond the sky, its peaks resting upon the slopes of the celestial crown,
and its summits surpassing Maharloka and adorned with the finest great jewels;
With the life-stories of the incarnations of Rudra, with the heads of the most excellent bulls, and with expansive jeweled jars hung with strings of gems; (35)
There stands a great palace, lofty and beautiful with *gomedaka* gems;
O exalted one, it possesses thousands of great balconies made of the finest *gomedaka* jewels. (36)
Seated upon a pedestal of Sahasrapālī, with coral figurines on its pillars,
he protected a thousand excellent seats made of lapis lazuli there.
Endowed with a thousand slabs and possessing a rim clear as a stream of jewels,
it stands situated within the great southeastern corner and the gate-towers.
It was provided with railings and plinths, adorned with divine cow-pens,
featuring a magnificent bull as its crest, and encircled by a valabhī roof.
He remained seated upon that jeweled couch, which cast a shadow like the rising sun and produced the luster of a pure inner pillar, while he himself hung suspended there.
The Lord dwells together with Ambā upon a couch that is encircled by a canopy shining with jeweled chains, and is well-spread with cushions and rugs.
The wind blew, beautiful with the forest fragrances rich in the scent of aguru,
and lovely with the joyful aroma of incense.

The Tamālasundara forest, an ornament for the world of Agniloka, situated in the palace of the southern quarter—[according to another reading: "frequented by palaces of fire"]—is there, most enchanting, and well-served. (43)
For the Vahnis indeed worship the Liṅga named Agnīśvara there,
along with the Āgneya Gaṇapas and the inhabitants of that world.
In the past, having worshipped that liṅga while consuming all things, Agni was then liberated; beholding him, Śaṅkara was together with Ambā.
Accompanied by Ambā, he beholds the multitude of worlds there, surrounded by the seven oceans, along with the continents, forests, and rivers.
The great mountain Hemakūṭa, being embodied as the Liṅga of Īśvara,
was installed there under the name Hemakūṭeśvara through meditative contemplations.
Hemakūṭa, who observes auspicious vows, praises the god Mahādeva. (Note: There is an alternative reading: "the mountain Hemakūṭa, wearing ashes and rudrākṣas.")

Hemakūṭa—O Hemakūṭa, supreme thunderbolt against the peaks of the mountain of sin; O Hemakūṭa, who has made the entire Mount Sumeru a mere trifle; O Hemakūṭa, whose crest-jewel is as radiant as the broad slopes of the rising moon’s mass; O Hemakūṭa, who has brought the scriptures through the horse [Ucchaiḥśravas]; protect me! 49.
Thus, on Hemakūṭa, he always praises Maheśvara there.
On the peak of the mountain-palace of Parameśī, he whose crown is marked by a beautiful crescent moon sports on all sides with Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Gaṇapati, and the pure words of the crest of the Vedas.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Palace," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Palace.
Skanda said:
That Vindhya mountain, with its beautiful caves, which in former times vied with Mount Meru;
This very mountain peak is where the Goddess resides upon its crown.
There, to the south, shines a mountain made of sapphire;
exceedingly beautiful, it sits as if licking the worlds with its tongue.
Having abandoned his own extreme suffering born of birth, there, by the power of the one born from a jar (Agastya),
the horizons were marked with peaks whose movement surpassed even the sun.
The Vindhya mountain, rejoicing in the intoxication born of its refuge in Maheśa,
surpassed even the bulls with the lofty peaks of the gate-towers upon its crest.
The quarters of the sky were turned dark blue by the great blue hosts of attendants emerging [from him],
while his crown was adorned with thousands of magnificent white lotuses serving as its forehead marks.
Supported by deformed beings with terrifying fangs,
that most excellent palace was adorned with a thousand pillars and provided with altars and friezes.
There, with great incense of agaru wood and lamps blazing with flames,
there was a blue water-pot joined with a thousand surfaces, its crest radiant.
It was adorned with blue-sapphire bulls whose eyes were like jewels,
and its paved floor was marked by lattices of crystal and great sapphires.
Adorned with beautiful garlands made of blue lotuses floating upon the water,
the lovely sky there appears as if it were latticed with windows.
In that most excellent palace, upon a couch with broad feet of sapphire,
the Lord Īśvara shone atop that couch, his body blue and red.
Accompanied by the Goddess and constantly attended by the hosts of his attendants (gaṇas), Śambhu remains ever gazing toward the southern direction, where Yama, the lord of Saṃyaminī, resides.
And there, Śaṅkara beheld the various states of the hells,
where those of great sin were being tormented, burned, and cooked.
Furthermore, those who are non-Śaivas, the most wicked, those devoid of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
those who neglect the worship of the liṅga, and likewise those who have abandoned the name of Śiva— [these one should avoid].
There, Śaṅkara [beheld] those who were devoid of the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya, bereft of the five-syllabled mantra, deprived of the food offerings to Śiva, and consumers of impurity.
Maheśvara [beheld] the regions of the earth bounded by the seven oceans,
as well as mountains, sacred rivers, forests, and groves.
The Lord Maheśvara, exceedingly joyful,
sports with his consort in the great palace upon the crown of the Vindhya mountains, fashioned from sapphire-blue jewels.
There, Vindhya, having worshipped the Vindhyeśvara Liṅga with devotion using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the juices of fruits, sandalwood paste, incense, and lamps;
With *bilva*, *campaka*, *mandāra*, *karavīra*, and excellent lotuses, as well as with circumambulations, prostrations, and the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) with jewels. (18)
Having worshipped him, he praised Śiva as Vindhyeśvara with devotion.
Vindhya:
O Lord of Vindhya, may my days never be barren today through the worship of your feet, the offering of hymns, and praises;
even one who is barren shall become a consumer of food offered at your feet, and indeed, he shall obtain a son more steadfast than the Vindhya mountain itself.
Skanda:
Thus does Vindhya, the king of mountains, ever praise Vindhyeśa there;
and to the southwest shines Malaya, resplendent with its beautiful peaks. (21)
Resembling a topaz gem, it possessed various waterfalls and caves;
it was radiant with rows of gateways shimmering upon its beautiful mountain peaks.
Accompanied by Rudra’s play and other [manifestations], adorned with a preeminent bull,
the Mountain shines with its own radiance, illuminating all worlds and transcending them.
There shines a great mountain, adorned with magnificent palaces,
supported by the lofty peaks of a thousand cranes.
Adorned with a thousand pillars fashioned from emerald gems,
it was provided with excellent jeweled pitchers and graced with a thousand floors.
He rests upon an excellent lion-throne inlaid with the most precious jewels;
his seat is adorned with large clusters of jewel-like flowers hanging down from its surface.
Adorned with ornaments, Śaṅkara sports there with the Goddess amidst breezes fragrant with sandalwood paste produced from great Malaya sandal trees.
His limbs were anointed with moon-like sandalwood paste, he bore the flowers of the great eon,
and the horizons were made fragrant by the pervasive smoke of the lovely incense of guggulu.
Śambhu beheld those hosts born of Nirṛti in the southwestern direction—
black, terrifying, and hideous, bearing swords as their excellent weapons.
Maheśvara [created] the corners of the seven oceans, as well as the land situated within them, the islands, the rivers, the mountains, and the forests.
There, Malayaja indeed worshipped the Linga named Malayeśvara,
which consists of the abode of jewels and grants all desires.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), sandalwood, bilva, mandāra, and campaka flowers;
with incense, lamps, food offerings, prostrations, and other such rites.
He praised him with supreme devotion, together with Mount Malaya.
Malaya:
O Lord of Malaya, Great Lord Śaṅkara, Sovereign of the Pramathas, you whose crest is the beautiful moon!
O Śambhu, this world indeed arises from you, and at the time of dissolution, it returns to dissolution within your own belly. (34)
Skanda:
Thus does Malaya, the best of mountains, ever praise the God;
and to the west shines Dardura, the refuge of various excellent peaks.
Then, it was exceedingly radiant with the boundless peaks of its towers, which possessed the beautiful luster of a sapphire-essence thread.
Crowded with great bulls and hosts of attendants through the deeds of Rudra’s incarnations, it was beautified by rows of banners fluttering from the tips of his uplifted horns. || 37 ||
Supported by a thousand great tigers, it was endowed with the luster of their jewels,
possessed a thousand pillars, and was provided with altars and plinths.
Its interior was covered by a canopy spread with clusters of pearls,
and its surrounding quarters were gladdened by the abundant fragrance of incense smoke.
Adorned with a beautiful interior made of the essence of vaidūrya,
there stood a divine lion-throne measuring five yojanas.
Upon that couch provided with a most excellent covering, Maheśvara sports with the Goddess amidst his inner attendants, just as Varuṇa resorts to Vāruṇī.
Then, the Lord of the Oceans,
whose crest was bound by the crescent moon upon the slope of his crown of lapis lazuli gems, protected that quarter inhabited by aquatic creatures.
His limbs were whitened by the radiance rising from his jeweled earrings,
and his hands were adorned with hoods that shone like the lord of serpents encircled by its coils.
He was colored by streams of smoke arising from the fine incense of black agallochum;
he was clad in most precious garments and fanned with waving yak-tail whisks. || 44 ||
With the interior of his knowledge illuminated by the stream of that great Vaiḍūrya thread,
he beheld Varuṇa, the lord of the western quarter, as well as his attendants.
There, one sees those with nooses in their hands, green in color, and possessing formidable, reddish fangs;
as well as the circle of the seven oceans, and the rivers, streams, and forests (or, according to another reading, the mouths of the rivers).
And there, the Great Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow, enjoys himself together with Ambā in that palace, along with the divine portions and the sacred fields located therein.
By him, the one named Dardureśa was worshipped, whereby he attained a divine abode;
[he worshipped] with libations of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), perfumes, bilva leaves, and campaka flowers.
With incense, lamps, food offerings, prostrations, and hymns of praise,
Dardura extolled the Lord Maheśvara, known as Dardureśa.
Dardura:

O Śaṅkara, you who remove the frontal globes of the elephant of endless sin; you are the formidable Dardura, with the radiance rising from the nails of your hand which shines upon the excellent bracelet of the Lord of Serpents.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Palace," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirtieth chapter, titled "The Praise Composed by Śaila.
Skanda said:
"To the northwest of that place is Mandara, with its caves as beautiful as jewels."
He is eternally beloved by Maheśa and is gladdened by all the Mandāra flowers.
The directions were illuminated by mandāra trees standing upon his crown,
while the intermediate spaces between the quarters were adorned by the mass of light from emerald gems.
It is ten thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and height;
it is incomparable, the singular beauty of the entire multitude of mountain peaks.
His face was gladdened by sandalwood, his fragrance was most excellent, and his crest was radiant;
he shone with a crown of jewel-like sāla and tamāla trees and a surrounding border of bees.
Right there, those peaks, dark-green like emerald and resembling lush meadows, shine with their crests towering above Mount Mandara and possessing immeasurable luster.
The face of that region shines, endowed with various birds and deer;
its sky is illuminated by the finials atop the gate-towers of its crest.
Adorned with the auspicious deeds of the incarnations of Rudra, and with herds of cows and young calves,
he shone like a row of celestial palaces atop a thousand-peaked mountain.
It was provided with altars and staircases, adorned with a thousand pillars, and embellished with terraces,
encircling railings, and variegated gables.
Within that [palace], from the jeweled pedestal, there arose an excellent, pure, and transparent lion-throne,
which was the refuge for the wind carrying the thick fragrance of sovereign incense.
It was adorned with a lattice-work of jewel-nets and great sala-tree nets; there blew a most beautiful breeze arising from Mount Mandara that brought great joy. || 10 ||
His chest was covered with garlands blooming with the fragrance of divine mandāra flowers,
and his interior was filled with streams of essence from great emerald lamps.
There, Śiva is seated upon a magnificent green footstool, attended by the Goddess, who possesses a green luster and stands on his left side.
He saw the wind, the lights that speak the truth, the guardians of the hosts dwelling there,
the islands born within the oceans, the forests, the rivers, and the mountains.
Thus the god, along with the goddess, awaited the worlds;
meanwhile, on Mount Mandara, the beautiful Liṅga was worshipped in that lovely temple.
By name alone [he is] Mandareśāna, possessing a luster like that of the moon or the kunda flower;
[one should worship him] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as with water, sandalwood, and bilva sprouts.
And with the nectar of lotuses, with flowers from the mandāra trees, with incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise with prostrations; || 16 ||
He praises with devotion through hymns that are beautiful, noble, and full of joy.
Mandara:
O Śrī Mandareśa, whose lotus feet are the bees delighted by the massed crowns of various scriptural traditions;
O you who are adorned with the crescent moon, I pray that I may serve your lotus feet, which are worshipped by the assembly of Vṛndārakas. 18.
Skanda:
Thus does Mandara, with its beautiful caves, ever praise the God;
the quarters of the sky are tormented by the towering crests of my maternal grandfather.
The Himalaya, transcending the sky, shines as if composed of the essence of diamonds,
consisting of great torrents of the essence of snow and moonstones.
The world was radiant with the splendor of his beauty; it shone with great gate-towers and was resplendent with the sacrificial rites of the bull, through the deeds of the incarnations of Rudra.
Extending for a million yojanas, it is situated on the northern part of Kailāsa;
it is brilliantly white, shimmering with the flanks of the manes of thousands of lions.
It rested upon the peaks rising from the palaces of the great serpents who wore it as an ornament;
it was provided with a thousand pillars and possessed beautiful staircases and altars.
It possessed a pedestal of moon-crystal that had become thick with great snow,
and its breezes were fragrant with the scent of blossoming, joyful forests.
It was a great forest of trees intoxicated by the fragrance of resinous exudations,
with the heady scent of *takola*, agallochum, musk, and sandalwood crowning it.
He possesses the unrestrained fragrance of kuraṇṭaka, aśoka, bakula, and campaka flowers;
he has the great face of a karṇikāra flower, and his head is marked with a tilaka.
Wearing a crown of abundant *kuṭaja* flowers and bearing matted locks as long as banyan roots,
he is beautiful with the *takka* and *kola* fruits that serve as the markings for his triple-ash tilaka.
He has the form of a great sea-monster and is the mountain upon which the great, excellent serpent rests;
he shines with the brilliant luster of the snowy abode, gleaming amidst the matted locks on the head of Hara.
His neck was enveloped by the cascades of the overflowing waters of the divine Gaṅgā,
and he possessed a radiant luster resembling a lotus situated upon the palace of his own crown.
Then the Lord of the Mountain, whose heart’s darkness was dispelled by meditating upon the lotus feet of Gaurī-Śaṅkara,
joyfully experienced the bliss of having a daughter-in-law and a granddaughter.
He stood as if shedding incessant showers of tears of joy,
his cavernous mouth radiant with the boundless hues of blue, yellow, and crimson.
There, upon that mountain peak, on a couch made of great emeralds, covered with a network of diamonds and having legs as clear as diamond thrones; || 32 ||
It was spread with the most excellent coverings, perfumed intensely with tagara,
and its masses of darkness dispelled by the moonlight-like luster of diamonds and gems.
His body was adorned with a multitude of great serpent-king jewels as if they were ornaments,
while the Goddess’s form was exceedingly beautiful with her body fashioned from emeralds.
Seated in the very center of the couch, Maheśvara shines intensely with splendors;
on the summit of his father, the Goddess, adorned with a most pleasing attire, shines all the more.
Just as a maiden delights the Lord of the Gods in her father’s abode,
she does not delight her husband as much in her father-in-law’s house.
Accompanied by the Goddess, Īśāna was wandering while gazing toward the direction of the Lord of Wealth,
where the host of Yakṣas dwells, as well as the city of Elāpura.
The great golden ground, as well as the Northern Kurus,
the sacred celestial gardens, and the encircling of the seven oceans.
There, the ground is fragrant with the scent of golden palm fruits;
likewise, there is a land with a copper-colored surface extending for a thousand yojanas.
Situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar is a jewel-island dear to Śiva;
it is a vast forest of *nīpa* trees, surrounded by jewel-like *nīpa* blossoms. (40)
In that palace with the appearance of a pure snow mountain, Maheśvara sports at will with the Goddess, fanned by waving chowries. (41)
There, Śaṅkara was adorned with garlands of precious Campaka flowers,
surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, who shone with tridents raised aloft in their hands.
The Himācaleśvara Liṅga, which has the brilliance of moonstone,
was worshipped by the Himālaya mountain with boundless services.
With the five nectars, fruit juices, fragrant substances, and yakṣakardama paste; with bilva, lotus, kahlāra, campaka, and bakasambhava flowers. || 44 ||
With offerings of incense, lamps, and oblations, and through prostrations and other such acts,
Himavān, with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord of the Snowy Mountains.
O Himavat, whose splendor is like the mature light of snow, adorned by the Ganges shining with matted locks—

behold quickly with those eyes resembling the sun, moon, and fire, which possess the luster of lotuses and blue water-lilies, as beautiful as your own lotus-face! (In some readings, the phrase "behold quickly the radiant one" is added.)
Skanda:
Thus Himācala praises Maheśvara, whose crown is snow;
and Nīla shines in the northeast on the pure mountain Kailāsa.
To the left is the mountain Nīla, resplendent with coral-like gems, endowed with hundreds of beautiful ridges and surrounded by a thousand peaks.
With its sky-licking peaks, most noble and profound, it shines in the northeast with its gate-towers, surrounded by the sports of Rudra. (49)
It was exceedingly brilliant with jars resembling the rising sun,
and it was surrounded by beautiful, radiant mountains that served as a refuge for the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas).
Yoked with great oxen, he was the color of coral with broad, reddish-brown flanks; his head was adorned with exceedingly high crests fashioned from coral, set with jewels.
Supported by thousands of great śarabha beasts, that most excellent palace stood there— delightful, radiant with the luster of gods, and the destroyer of the darkness within the heart.
There, it shone forth, adorned with various altars and staircases,
joined by a thousand pillars, and fashioned from coral and jewels.
Seated upon the crest of the king of palaces, he shines with the brilliance of the rising sun,
bearing a jeweled pitcher of coral upon his thousand-hooded crown.
Adorned with a single cluster of mālatī blossoms, as clear and round as coral,
right there, bees were intoxicated by the fragrance of the flowers.
In that place, which was spread with a carpet and where the fragments of darkness were dispelled by the moonlight from the coral-jewels,
she lay down upon a bed of coral.
The moon-crested Maheśvara dwells in joy with the Goddess,
even amidst the continents and the boundless lands surrounded by the seven oceans.
Maheśvara [beheld] forests, rivers, mountains, and even fields;
and right there, the world of Īśāna, surrounded by various hosts of Rudras.
It is joined by those dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth, who bear weapons and nooses;
and by those who move among trees, herbs, food, on paths, and upon mountains. (59)

[He was surrounded] by the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the serpents, who bore crests of matted hair from which moons and suns shone like forehead-marks, and whose eyes were reddened with wrath.
Accompanied by Ambā, he beholds Īśāna, who is joined by those who shatter the cosmic egg and who have drunk the roar of the oceans.
Skanda said:
On the lofty peaks of those various excellent mountains, there are temples of Śiva; and all around them, there are also supreme liṅgas bearing their names.
Listen, O Jaigīṣavya, for the sole purpose of destroying all evil:
Hemakeśa, lord of Niṣadha; Vindhyeśa, lord of Malaya.
Dardureśa, Mandareśa, Hara the lord of the Himālaya mountains,
and Nīleśvara— these are situated on all sides, taking refuge in excellent great palaces.
There, mountains endowed with beautiful gate-towers and possessing embodied forms worship the lingas there with charming bilva leaves.
Nīla also, having worshipped Nīleśa there with many flowers,
incenses, lamps, and food offerings, praised Śiva as Nīleśvara.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he [beheld] that which had reached the supreme light born from the jewel upon his own crest.
Nīla:
O Blue-and-Red One, whose great neck is like an emerald, adorned with skulls and serpents;
O Blessed One, the Death of Death, ocean of compassion, quickly deliver me from the net of the cycle of worldly existence! 67.
In this manner, those mountains then praised Giriśa, the Lord of the Mountains.
The Mountains:

Hara, Hara, Supreme Lord, God of gods, destroyer of the fear born of Tripura and Andhaka! O Consort of the Daughter of the Mountain, O Lord, protect us, O Sovereign, Universal Monarch of the Gods! 69.
While you, the remover of worldly existence, dwell upon the crowning palaces of the peaks of heaven,
we too remain stainless— though we are but mountains, consisting of rocks, forest creepers, grass, birds, and shrubs.
O Śambhu, whose crest is the moon, even the deer are exceedingly blessed by having attained refuge in you;
O Blessed Lord Rudra, you are celebrated in the Vedas as Mīḍhuṣṭama, Śaṅkara, Babhru, Śambhu, the one who produces unbroken sound, Ugra, and Bhīma.
"You are our sovereign; protect us with compassion, for you are renowned as one who is without a superior lord. (71)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Praise Offered by the Mountain," in the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
(Chapter 125) In the description of the rampart, the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Worship of the Rudra-Gaṇas," Skanda said:
"Therefore, O Brahmins, the Gaṇas and the gods such as Viṣṇu and others are most excellent."
On the crown of Kailāsa, that [palace] of Śambhu was adorned with nine jewels.
The rampart, measuring one hundred thousand [cubits] in length, is approved for its height and breadth;
it consists of great slabs of excellent sudhā-maṇi stone, resembling indragopaka insects.
O best of the twice-born, Maheśa himself conceived that supreme abode of Kailāsa in his mind alone, and Viśvakarman then constructed it.
What can be fashioned by the mind, even with all the various arts,
that is as radiant as a multitude of diverse jewels and gems and as beautiful as the moon?
This supreme one is the essence of the luster of pure jewels licked by the touchstone;
this lofty one is beautiful, having a form like that of a city of the Gandharvas.
Adorned with excellent, towering jewels and bulls upon its ramparts,
the hosts of Rudras in the sky were the protectors of that glorious enclosure wall.
Indeed, eleven thousand [demons] followed, with bows and arrows in their hands,
leading great quivers, and wearing moon-shaped ornaments upon their matted hair.
All were young men with lion-like physiques, adorned with polished earrings; their thighs and staff-like arms were rounded like the tusks of elephants, and they bore excellent weapons.
It possessed gateways with a shower of wish-fulfilling gems, was adorned with golden pitchers,
beautified by the deeds of the incarnations of Rudra, and was exceedingly enchanting.
O Śambhu, the leaders of the Gaṇas always protect that eastern gateway of yours, which stands upon the crown [of your head], bringing great joy and delighting the entire expanse of the quarters.
And all of them, with tridents raised in their hands, [guarded] the rampart;
there, the linga that grants all desires was worshipped by the attendants of Śambhu.
Known by the name Maṇirudreśvara, he is the abode of a single, rising pitcher at the exhaustion of the multitude of wish-fulfilling gems, and he is worshipped by the lords of the Gaṇas.
At that time, he was praised with supreme devotion by the hosts in the intermediate space.
O Lord Maheśvara, quickly destroy with Your beautiful glance the great disease born of the torments of saṃsāra; You are Rudra,
whose fame is sung by the pure crest-edges of the Vedas— protect us, O Lord, for You are the sovereign physician according to the words of the Vedas.
Skanda said:
Thus do the Gaṇas praise that god Maṇibhadreśvara;
and to his south is a rampart constructed of pearls and gems.
In its center was an excellent gateway constructed of jewels and rubies,
adorned with a crest and secured by a pinnacle-stake of great gems.
Accompanied by the exploits of the incarnations of Rudra and by the bulls,
there were indeed eleven thousand [soldiers] armed with javelins and excellent swords.
There, the auspicious divine hosts possess great strength and great enthusiasm;
they are enriched by the beauty of their matted locks and crowns, and they bear a digit of the Lord of the Stars.
All of them, carrying out the command of Śiva, their bodies intoxicated with youth,
indeed worship the divine Rudreśvara there.
Having worshipped the great Liṅga in the abode of Maṇi and praised the Lord, they remained there. || 20 ||
The Rudra-gaṇas:
O Divyeśvara, destroyer of the multitude of cities and the mass of suffering and torment born of the three classes of gods;
O Lord of Gods, O Īśa, you who are the vessel for the essence of the grace of granting boons; O Sadāśiva, protect us always. (21)
Thus those Rudras then praised the divine Rudreśvara;
and the Gaṇas constantly guarded that gateway and the rampart.
After that, there was a city with ramparts fashioned from jewels and gate-towers of gems,
adorned by the life-stories of the incarnations of Rudra, who have the bull as their crest-ornament.
And there, the leaders of the Gaṇas, bearing excellent weapons such as missiles and tridents, guard the place with their towering humps and crowns of supreme jewels.
They bore three lines of sectarian marks on their foreheads, wore large matted locks as excellent crowns,
and possessed crescent moons that shone brilliantly, resembling the rising sun.
Indeed, eleven thousand Gaṇapas,
who emerged from the limbs of Maheśa for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice, always protect [him].
There, the excellent Gaṇas known as the Raumyas, possessing the prowess of elephants in rut,
worship the Lord of the Raumyas, who resides in a palace of jewels.
The hosts of the Raumyas worship and indeed praise Śiva.
O Lord, the hosts of Śiva and Viṣṇu, who are born from the pores of Your hair, protect the worlds even during their dissolution;
bearing the dust of Your lotus feet upon our heads, O Lord, protect us today with compassion and a glance moist with grace.
Thus do the inhabitants of Raukmi praise Maheśa, permeated by devotion;
they are the hosts of the high-souled Śambhu known as the Bhaumakas in the north.
Eleven thousand [demons] had their weapons unsheathed;
their faces were terrifying with bared fangs, and they bore fragments of the moon bound within their matted locks.
Possessing bodies with the brilliance of water-laden, unrestrained clouds, they were endowed with incomparable luster;
smeared with ashes, marked with the triple-tilaka, and radiant with rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.
Resounding with the noise of clattering hooves like the roar of a mass of lightning,
they possessed a fury exceeding that of the lord of serpents and a speed surpassing the lord of serpents.
Those who carry out the commands of Śiva, endowed with strength, heroism, and prowess,
[reside] thereupon within the northern enclosure, which possesses the brilliant luster of a jeweled wall.
And in the middle of that, within the city gate, was a great jar of jewels, adorned with Rudras, sporting bulls, colored and possessing a brilliance equal to the sun.
They remain there and guard that rampart and that gate-tower;
and by them, the Lord of the Earth (Bhaumeśvara), situated within a temple of jewels, has been worshipped.
Maheśvara, established within the Liṅga, was praised with supreme devotion. || 37 ||
O Lord of the Earth, who rejoiced in the gift of formidable chariots and great chariot-wheels by Hari, Hara, and the lotus-eyed one;
O You who transcend the earth and whose movement is all-pervading; O You whose head is the supreme abode of the moon; O You whose beautiful body is honored by celestial damsels—protect me! 38.
Skanda—
thus do those inhabitants of the earth praise Mahādeva, the treasury of compassion,
who is surrounded by twenty thousand jeweled gate-towers forming a rampart.
It was adorned with variegated bulls, uniquely beautiful through various artistic crafts,
so captivating that they could not be compared even by mental inference.
In all four directions, those Rudras were the slayers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
they all held weapons and tridents in their hands, with bodies white as ashes.
They were graced by a pair of thighs whose rounded form was comparable to the trunk of a plantain tree,
and they were covered in golden armor that resembled the broad surface of a chest-door.
Some with turbans and crowns, their great heads adorned with lordly serpents, were running;
some stood still, while others lay down to sleep.
Equipped with quivers and wearing armor, with arrows and bows in their hands,
they rained down showers of shafts, driving back the inauspicious ones with their discharged missiles.

On the road, at the tree, and in the water; situated on the ocean and upon the earth; likewise in the forest, in the village, in the city, in the hamlet (*kharva*), and likewise in the wolf-den (*vṛka*).
All of them were executors of Śiva’s commands, blazing like fire and possessed of great majesty.
Sūta:
Thus, together with the excellent gate-towers, the Rudras [established] a rampart on all four sides, filled with the finest jewels and precious stones, and presided over by the royal bull. || 47 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Worship of the Rudra-Gaṇas," in the description of the ramparts within the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
The thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Assembly Hall."
Skanda said:
Within that space, they were then fashioned by Śiva himself with his own mind,
measuring twenty thousand [yojanas] in both length and height.
In the east, south, west, and north, they are accompanied by the wielder of the trident (Śiva),
whose crown rests upon Mount Kailāsa, and who possesses a splendor exceeding the light of jewels.
Adorning the lofty peak of the mountain of refined gold like a forehead mark, they shine like the four aims of human life, resembling the crests of the four Vedas. || 3 ||
The performance hall of Maheśa, of Śambhu who is the dancer at twilight,
was adorned with a thousand great pitchers of gold.
Fashioned from refined gold, they resembled the caves of Mount Meru,
adorned with thousands of great pillars in the form of various jars.
With steps made of well-set jewels, radiant with friezes and plinths,
and with beaks pecked by pearls rising from the rows of royal swans;
Adorned with networks of gems and pearls from blue and yellow *utkoca* stones, their interiors were filled with clusters of pearls and lattices of endless garlands.
(Verse 8) The pillars were fashioned from coral creepers, and the coral figurines were set within them;
the surrounding railings were made of emeralds, with lotus-hand motifs adorning their borders.
They were pinned down by circles of hair-like rays from great topazes and emeralds;
their massive heads, like the frontal globes of elephants, were dark blue and as thick as elephant trunks.
Adorned with the beauty of naga-bonds rising from threads of lapis lazuli,
they are as lovely as a flock of young pigeons and swans upon a row of crests.
Their broad jeweled crowns were encircled by clear eaves inlaid with gems,
while their interiors were covered by networks of garlands of large, blossoming kuruvinda flowers.
They were secured by staircases consisting of streams of pure water within the finest crystal,
and they possessed great sapphires covered by various lattices and screens.
They were adorned with playful embankments made of ruby-like lotuses with the luster of Bimbas,
and they shone with rows of *rambhā* and betel-nut trees fashioned from gold.
They were covered with seven-leaved trees whose interiors were as brilliant as emeralds,
and they were secured by stakes of ivory and bulls upon which rows of swans rested.
Seated upon pedestals on the parapets, they possess noses like precious tigers;
they are radiant with clusters of golden ketakī flowers and rows of their fruits.
They were hung with fruits such as *maṇipāna* and *jāmbū*,
and their interiors were covered by garlands strung together with *mātuliṅga* and *likuca* fruits.

Adorned with jars bearing streams of jewels and filled with beautiful sprouts and flowers, their surfaces were covered by vast canopies of *damanaka* flowers, while the sky above was shrouded by white cloths.
Resplendent with clusters of uśīra cloth hanging and swaying,
they were made beautiful by gentle breezes arising from the binding of fragrances.
Enveloped by great, lofty, and unrestrained columns of incense smoke,
they were graced by excellent houses filled with revolving rows of jewel-lamps.
They were hung with vessels for a thousand lamps and incense trees,
and their expansive floors were fashioned from various colors using the finest jewels.
All the floors were paved with crystal, hung with beautiful mirrors,
and variegated with the brilliance of gold lines and diverse gems.
At that time, there was the dancing of the Goddess, who had manifested as various forms of Rudra and others;
she was surrounded by the preeminent lords of Śambhu’s Gaṇas, who were adorned with diverse and wonderful ornaments.
They were joined with very beautiful jeweled altars, perfumed with incense,
extensive in width and length, and adorned with a thousand pillars.
Their inner selves are surrounded by the vast net of the great principles of the six systems of philosophy;
they are preeminent bulls, shining with excellence and adorned with jeweled jars.
Adorned with ten thousand parasols and chowries featuring jeweled handles,
their top banners were fluttering, and their interiors were hung with jeweled bells.
They were showered with excellent flowers fragrant with musk, camphor, and sandalwood paste;
their spotless lattices were reflected in the lofty jeweled mirrors.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the unrestrained and deep roar of the *mandala* drums— [an alternative reading is *maddala*]—
along with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, *niḥsāṇas*, small drums, *ānakas*, and *gomukhas*.
They were filled with the sounds of trumpets, drums, flutes, and lutes,
and were adorned with jewels and Mandāra, Vakula, Pāṭala, Aśoka, and Campaka flowers.
Those [trees] were adorned with long, clear garlands, beautiful at the base like tamāla leaves, and their canopies were covered by great clusters of blossoms from the kṛtamāla trees. || 29 ||
Their interiors were draped with garlands of jasmine buds and blossoms;
from their clusters, which bore the weight of trickling streams of honey, swarms of bees hummed. (Alternatively, there is a variant reading: *gacchadalivrajāḥ*. || 30 ||
They were beautiful with clusters of kadamba flowers, intensely fragrant with damana blossoms, and delighted by the sweet scents of kurava, uśīra, and maruva.
(Verse 32) Beautiful with swaying garlands made of *uśīra* root, their grounds were covered by nets of pearls released from the sky as they were tossed upward by the stars.

Resounding with the sounds of hand-drums, great cymbals, and jhallarī drums, and filled with the "huṃ" cries of the host, they were beautiful within, imbued with the "huṃ" sounds from jeweled madduka drums. || 33 ||
The quarters of the sky were filled with the deep, far-reaching sounds of trumpets,
while the tinkling of their jingling anklets produced a resonant *naṭ-jhaṇajhaṇa* noise.
They bore the forms of cow-faced, elephant-faced, and fierce jackal-faced beings;
they roared with the sounds of *dhūtkāra* and thunder, produced by rows of conch shells.
He was praised by the mouths of Brahmā, unrestrained and exalted by the four Vedas;
he was filled with the sounds of the Vāmadeva, Mahāsāman, and Rathantara chants.
The horizons of all directions were filled with the whistling sounds arising from the *rathantara* chant;
they were beautifully adorned by the preeminent *vairāja* melody and the resplendent *rājan* and *hiṅkāra* syllables. || 37 ||
Resounding with the cries of eight-faced vultures and the sounds of eight tusks,
they were filled with the thundering noise arising from the temples clinging to the tips of Mahāgaṇeśa’s trunk.
They were made beautiful by the unrestrained, loud shouts of the six-faced god (Kārttikeya),
and by the great, rhythmic clapping produced by Nandin and Bhṛṅgin through their many hand-claps.

Fie, fie upon those who, with their minds averse to Śiva, block out every sound with their cries of "Tāṇḍi, Tāṇḍi!"—those whose quarters of the sky are made beautiful by the resonance arising from the beat of the *taṇḍu-ḍiṇḍima* drums. (40)

Their speech was their great lute, with the melodies of the garland of Śiva’s names; they were uniquely beautiful with the sounds of celestial music produced by the instrument of their vocal cords. || 41 ||
The best of sages, headed by Nārada, praised him with unrestrained singing; [the reading *tumburu-uddāma* is found in some texts.
They were instructed in the various musical notes (*mūrchanās*) by Hāhā and Hūhū, [with *bharata-akṣara-śikṣitāḥ* as an alternative reading. || 42 ||
The waves of their limbs rose high through the skillful practice of the Yakṣas,
while the melodies (*mūrchanās*) dwelling in the three registers were rendered beautiful by passionate women.
There was the supreme sound of "Tandhi" from the intense beating of cymbals and drums;
the walls were made of excellent crystal, beautiful with the luster of peacock feathers. (44)
The excellent cuckoos were awakened by the humming sound of the gems being struck,
and they were delighted by the resonant warbling of the cuckoos' sweet, melodious notes.
Situated within a jeweled cage, parrots, mynas,
and jārava birds performed a frantic dance to the deep resonance of the mṛdaṅga drums.
The deer there were intent on gazing at the faces of the throngs of singing Gandharvas;
the elephants, bearing jewels, were magnificently trumpeting with their uplifted trunks.
The assembly halls were surrounded by beautiful pillars and plantain trees entwined with sugarcane,
and were further adorned with jeweled creepers and archways that hung down and swayed.
Their tresses were stirred by canopies moved by the gentle breeze,
and they held streams of nectar filled in great golden jars.
There, Śambhu’s great assemblies were beautiful with beakers shining from mouths of excellent foliage, and possessed the supreme essence of vast betel-nut trees.
Indeed, Śiva himself fashioned them there through his mind and contemplation;
therein, in the eastern direction, stands an assembly hall made of gold.
The assembly hall of great jewels was fashioned for Śambhu to the south;
then, on the silver mountain, the silver assembly hall was established behind Śambhu.
And to the north of Śambhu is the Citsabhā, made of silver and situated on a moving base;
likewise, there are the Sabhās of Sannāha and Ānanda situated in the other four directions.
The description of its nature was given by the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
likewise, the Lord is the breath of the Vedas, manifest in embodied form along with their auxiliary limbs.
Furthermore, the Ṛgveda, through twenty-one branches,
praises Maheśvara, the God of gods, within that assembly.
Likewise, the Yajurveda with its hundred branches, within the Jewel Assembly Hall,
joyfully praises the god Virūpākṣa with palms joined in reverence.
In the assembly hall made of refined gold, the Sāmaveda, with its thousand excellent branches,
then praises Mahādeva there with Sāman hymns.
Likewise, in the assembly of consciousness, he praises the Lord with his own heads in the form of the twenty branches of the Atharvaveda— Atharvan hymns that grant satisfaction to the Lord.
Skanda:

And may he shine in assemblies that possess the sun, the manifest light of the Lord of Heaven, and the moon; and in that which possesses shimmering luster, born from the interior of jewels renowned for their brilliance like the flame of fire.
In the abode fashioned by light, he who is a master of dance performs his dance. || 59 ||
The Lord of the Assembly, who transcends the senses, though surrounded by the hosts of the Lord of the Pramathas,
possesses infinite majesty and is the essence of aesthetic flavor; he has reached the pure crest-ridge of the Vedas and bears the luster of the jewels set upon the crowns of the lords of the gods.
He whose continuous nails are radiant was praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the gods. || 60 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Assembly," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Dance in the Assembly Halls.
Śrī Skanda said: Maheśvara, together with Sanātana and Sananda, was filled with joy.
And where those assemblies were, the God who is the joy of Pārvatī’s heart was present.
The Lord of the assembly, the Sovereign, served by hosts of attendants,
together with me, the elephant-faced one, and with Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, and the Lord Ṛṣiṭa;
With Taṇḍu, Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, and others— those fierce arrows, Rāvaṇas, and Caṇḍikas—
he prepared to perform a grand and majestic dance before the Goddess.
In all those assemblies, the Lord of Umā was the presiding master;
every evening at the onset of twilight, he was the expert in the great Tāṇḍava dance.
He is radiant with the lotus-feet shining above the one afflicted by epilepsy;
he is clothed in the skin of a lordly elephant, and his splendor blazes from the slopes of his matted locks and topknot.
He bears the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā situated within the hollows of his matted locks;
right there, his head is covered by the friends of the full-blown white lotuses.

His great throat was deep blue like a mountain; he wore earrings that were the lords of all ear-rings; his face was equal in splendor to the abode of the moon; and his teeth and nose were like the Campaka flower.
Beautiful with three eyes like blossoming lotuses,
his forehead adorned with the excellent triple-line mark (tripuṇḍra), his body smeared with sacred ashes.
With his left hand, he holds a garland whose radiant jewel is suspended from a foot adorned with red lac on the tips of his nails;
it is a garland shimmering with the sound *dhagaddhagi*. (9)
He wears garlands of great precious gems, pearls, and rudrākṣa beads;
his neck is adorned with a necklace of jewels from the hoods of hooded serpents.
Adorned with a jeweled necklace, his beautiful hands were set with bracelets;
he was graced by a network of tinkling bells and small bells that produced a jingling sound.
With one hand he holds a *ḍamaru* drum, and with another, [he holds] that which possesses brilliant radiance;
his excellent hands are illuminated by the upward-pointing crest of the seven-tongued [fire].
He is the manifest bestower of devotion and fearlessness, with fingers adorned by excellent jewels;
he shines with a silken cloth draped over his hips and is radiant with a tiger skin.
The radiance of his swaying tail-cluster, beautiful as it hangs down, is shimmering;
his neck is graced by a garland of a great multitude of Brahma’s severed heads.
With his jeweled anklets producing a tinkling sound as he danced,
and with his dancing feet slightly contracted, he nourished the three worlds.
Beholding Maheśvarī seated upon a throne adorned with great jewels,
her pure eyes resembling the petals of a lotus.
The lotus-face of the Goddess surpasses the abode of nectar (the moon),
with its playful curls, rising tilaka-mark, and adorned with jeweled earrings.
It shines like a rising poet, beautiful with a nose-ornament of clear pearls and resplendent with a jeweled necklace deepened by the three folds of the neck.
The Lord gazed upon her auspicious throat, beautiful with its playful thoughts,
and her lovely breasts which resembled the high frontal globes of an elephant and were like golden jars.
Her belly is beautiful and noble with three folds, containing within it the three worlds as its interior;
her waist resembles that of the king of beasts, and she wears a jeweled girdle.
