Her garments were like molten gold, and she surpassed the sky with the downpour of streams of liquid vermilion;
her tresses were made fragrant by *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṇnāga*, and *saugandhika* flowers.
She is beautiful with a jeweled parting situated in the center of her braided hair,
and she possesses a line of vermilion shining upon her forehead that reaches down to her eyebrows.
With her wrists bound by bracelets of many tinkling jewels and her hands adorned with moving rings upon which rested jeweled water-pots.
Her thumb was encircled by a finger-ring glittering with gems and a bracelet,
while her thumb-wrap was fashioned from a single slab of great diamond.
Her sandals were colored by the dye from her slightly reddened lotus-feet, and the bees [of her toenails] produced an endless *jhana-jhana* sound upon her toes. || 25 ||
The ground resounded with the jingling of anklets made of jewels,
and it was thick with the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and camphor.
She delighted all the quarters of the sky with the great fragrance of her fine garments;
she was the very embodiment of the essence of the stream of beauty, and her face was like the lord of the stars (the moon).

One should meditate upon Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī, who is easily grasped by the crocodile [of the world], while another [serpent] hangs down from her; she holds a noose, a goad, and displays the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. (28)
Beholding the Goddess in the assemblies as she gazes upon the face of the Lord with sprouts of sidelong glances, Śaṅkara always dances.
Surrounded by Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Skanda, and Heramba, Śaṅkara arrived in the evening amidst the sounds of delightful musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas.
In various assembly halls, he dances accompanied by Ambā;
listen to that, O best of sages, lords of the Gaṇas, and most excellent of gods.

I bow to Him whose mass of matted hair is adorned by the dust of the kings and king-like deities, who removes the dust of the world, whose left side is eternally graced by Rāmā (Pārvatī), and who is constantly worshipped by Śrī Rājarāja;
He who dances with His chest flashing with a garland of skulls formed from human heads.
I meditate upon the illustrious Dhūrjaṭi as he dances in the golden assembly hall of the silver mountain.
The surging waves of the Gaṅgā in his matted locks were filled by the downpour of rain flowing from millions of cosmic eggs as they fell, struck by the dancing skull-cups of Brahmā;
it was a sight where Viṣṇu and the other gods, having arrived for the sake of service, offered prayers with palms joined in reverence.
I meditate upon the illustrious Dhūrjaṭi dancing in the golden assembly hall of the silver mountain. || 33 ||
While the eloquent Tāṇḍava beats the ḍiṇḍima, maṇḍala, and ḍamaruka drums like Indra himself, while the lotus-eyed Brahmā bows with his hands to the illustrious Lord Caṇḍikeśa,
and while he is intent on swinging the bells during the divine-praised Śrītāṇḍava dance— O Paṇḍita! [Salutations to you.]
I meditate upon the illustrious Dhūrjaṭi dancing in the golden hall of the silver mountain. || 34 ||

I bow to Śiva, who dances for the delight of his beloved, whose stainless garland of skulls is bound to his head, whose circle of matted locks performs a dance, and whose hot rays of light issue from the streams of nectar mingled with poison and fire that serve as his ornaments; he who has ascended to the summit of the Vedas.
I meditate upon the illustrious Dhūrjaṭi dancing in the golden hall of the silver mountain. || 35 ||

Before the Goddess, whose face shines with a gentle smile and who is adorned with many arms, Śiva dances, causing all mobile beings beginning with Brahmā to become motionless by the flood of jingling sounds from the golden bracelets bound upon his feet.
I behold the illustrious Śambhu in the golden assembly hall of Mount Kailāsa.
Thus does Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods, dance with the Goddess in the golden assembly hall of Kailāsa, surrounded on the eastern side by the foremost of his Gaṇas.
To the south of that, in the midst of an assembly hall fashioned of jewels, the god Maheśvara dances for the delight of Ambā; listen to this, O Lord of Sages. (38)
Skanda—
[I salute him] who, during the Tandava dance, displays great splendor with earrings swinging from his cheeks,
and who manifests his mastery in the Tandava through his hosts of attendants such as Candesvara and others, who have faces like those of birds.

I worship the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, who dances in the jewel-adorned assembly hall of the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa), being praised by Śiva with the unfailing torrents of words that are the essence of the Upaniṣads.

(Page 133) Victorious are the unrestrained words of Taṇḍu as he stands near the illustrious Slayer of Kaiṭabha: "O Brahmā, abandon your Vedic chants! O Hari, withdraw [your lute] and cast it far away!
Such were the cries from the vicinity of the sovereign dancer as she was about to begin her dance.
I always behold Śambhu dancing in the jeweled assembly hall of the Silver Mountain.
In that [form] where there is a dense mass of crescent moons dripping with nectar from crests moving in the swaying dance;
where a host of gods shines, reddened by the glowing orb of the rising sun;
and which is rendered motionless by the weight of the fresh, curved coils of the multitude of serpents upon his crest—
I always behold Śambhu dancing in the jeweled assembly hall of the Silver Mountain.

The Goddess beholds Śaṅkara dancing with a gentle smile, his two feet causing the earth, the remaining mountains, the sun, the moon, and the quarters to tremble as they leap like moving golden mountains, while he looks toward Nandin with great joy and delight.
I always behold Śambhu dancing in the jewel-adorned assembly hall of the Silver Mountain.
In that Lord, the abode of a mass of overflowing bliss, where they perform their dance,

he places his foot slowly, his heart apprehensive lest his ornaments should tremble or fall; and he extends his hands so that his garment may not become loose— [this is the Lord] whose [garment] flows down...
By contracting his eyebrows, the Blessed One makes the two excellent wheels appear. || 43 ||
With a joyful heart, Śiva did not dance impetuously in the assembly hall during the night. || 44 ||
Thus, on the Silver Mountain, within the Hall of Jewels,
the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, performs a dance before the Goddess this evening.
Afterwards, in the assembly hall fashioned of silver, Maheśvara,
accompanied by the host of his attendants, dances while gazing at Ambā’s face.
Śrī Skanda said:

[I bow to] Him whose feet resound with the tinkling of armlets, joined by a noble lady whose left side is adorned with a mass of bees from the garlands on the heads of the creators of the universe, as He dances, wearing Hari as His ornament.

Upon her hip is draped a garment of black antelope skin; she dances with unrestrained energy, while we, with half our bodies bound to her, have our shoulders adorned with flower-garlands held by children.
I meditate upon Him as He dances, intent on His dance, in an assembly hall made of refined gold.

O Govinda, O worshipful Hari! While you, whose mind is submerged in the ocean of bliss, speak various unartificial clusters of words within this assembly of lotuses, and while the entire courtyard of the gods drinks in those words slowly, as if drinking honey; (pṛ0 134) [the world rejoices].
I meditate upon Him, intent on dancing, as He dances in an assembly of golden swans.
In whom this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, dances; from whom nothing whatsoever can be said by the wise to be distinct;
such [is He], whose splendor is made manifest through the dramatic performance of His dance, and who is radiant with the serpent Śeṣa as His ornament.
I meditate upon the feet of Śambhu as he dances in an assembly of golden swans.

O mind, devote yourself to Him, having gone to whom a human being shall not undergo rebirth; to that Three-eyed One, the ocean of compassion, blazing with the glorious Kālakūṭa poison, who performs such a most wondrous and supreme *tāṇḍava* dance.
I meditate upon the foot of Śambhu as it dances in an assembly of golden swans.
In whom the entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, revolves; from whom the cosmic egg, bursting forth, leaps up in its entirety;
and by whose light the sun, the moon, and other luminaries shine continuously—[to that Brahman, I bow].
I meditate upon the foot of Śambhu as he dances in an assembly of golden swans.
When this [treatise] has appeared, even a tortoise— whose bones are shattered,
whose large eyes and ears protrude from the exertion of dancing, and who emits hissing breaths—
finds no peace; for that Veda, along with its limbs, exists, and those like Upendra live by taking refuge in it.
I worship Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha, whose sweat-water is the great ocean, and from whose rising multitude of jewels on the Silver Mountain (Rājata-giri) there arises a hall of refined gold.
Thus did the moon-crested Īśāna dance at will before Ambā in the assembly hall made of silver from Kailāsa.
In the northern assembly hall,
Mahādeva Maheśvara, whose feet are served by the lords of the Gaṇas, gazes upon his Mother as she dances.
Śrī Skanda said:

[I bow to] Him who, through His form as Śivā (Hrīḥ), is composed of the Virāṭ; who always resides within the heart-lotus of those who are ashamed of worldly things; who brings benefit to those who take pride in proclaiming the glory of Śiva; and who is the ocean of playful grace for the arrogant.

I worship Naṭeśa, who is charming with garments fragrant with hrī, berā, and other perfumes; whose bow and arrows are made of gold from the mountain; whose stainless footstool is marked with the syllable hrīṃ; and who is delightful to the heart. || 56 ||
I bow to Śrīdhara, who possesses a resplendent form of five colors within the illustrious Jñānasabhā;
whose pair of lotus feet are praised by the goddess Vāṇī and worshipped by Śrīvallabha;
who delights in the Śrīvidyā mantra and bestows prosperity upon those who have heard it.
I worship Śrīman Naṭeśa, the auspicious one who dwells within the Śrīcakra. || 57 ||
I bow to Him whose face is like a fresh lotus, who is worshipped by Nārāyaṇa during his ritual ablutions,
who sports upon the river of the city that is the abode of the serpents (the Ganges), who is adorned with a serpent-skin,
who is skilled in various forms of dance and the like, and who is encircled by a multitude of lotuses.
I worship Naṭeśa, whose essence is sound, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain King. || 58 ||

I bow to the Lord who stands as the mediator, whose feet were sought by the enemy of Madhu, the sovereign of my lineage, the foe of Māra, possessing an exceedingly beautiful form with a radiance white as the Mandāra flower;
he who has transcended illusion, is a treasury of all auspiciousness, and is realized through my own devotion.
I worship Naṭeśa, the venerable one who dwells within the cave-palace of the sky, the center of all. || 59 ||
I bow to the Lord, whose sandals are honored by the learned, who bestows auspiciousness, who bears the crescent moon,
who is the very art of protecting his devotees, who has weakened the flood of sins, who is dear to Pārvatī,
who is the protector through his teachings, and whose nature is the destruction of even the head of the Lotus-seated Brahmā.
I worship the auspicious Śrī Naṭeśa, whose eyes have cool outer corners. || 60 ||

I bow to him whose majesty is praised by Vāṇīvallabha, who is a wish-fulfilling gem for those who seek refuge, who is adorned by the Lord of the Wind, who is a vast ocean of supreme compassion for yogis,
who fulfills all desires, who is extolled by Balaripu, and who has made the Vedas his vehicle.
I worship Naṭeśa, whose beautiful woman is on his left side, who dwells within my heart. || 61 ||
I bow to the one who is the friend of the Lord of Yakṣas, the crusher of Yama, whose face is the Lord of Night,
the destroyer of the sacrifice, praised by the foremost of ascetics, the sovereign of sacrificial rites, the one to be worshipped,
appearing in the form of a sacrificer, and whose feet are difficult to reach even with the wealth of Yama through great effort.
I worship Naṭeśa, who has become a bull for the vehicle [of Dharma], who is praised by the lords of ascetics, and who is worthy of being worshipped through sacrifice.
Those who daily recite these seven verses named *Cintāmaṇi*, which are marked with the five great syllables (*mahāpañcākṣara*) of the radiant *Cidambaram*— the glory of Māyā—
attain manifold fortune, long life, excellent learning, and virtuous sons.
The Lord of the assembly of Śrī-Cit bestows all that is desired instantly. || 63 ||
Śrī Sūta said:
Worship Dhūrjaṭi, whose matted locks are as fierce as lightning, who is praised by the eloquent speech of the goddess of learning, and who wears the crescent moon upon his forehead;
we worship him.

May Śiva be auspicious— he whose excellent spear is struck by the slapping of the cheeks of his fierce-faced young attendants shouting at the edges of his hips, and whose garment is adorned with the skin of an elephant.

I worship Śiva, who forcibly subdued the wicked Asura, who brings about the destruction of suffering, who wields the bow that pierces the elephants of the quarters, whose feet rest upon the back of the tortoise,
and who has arisen from the primordial pedestal of the three worlds held within his belly.
The hymn of praise to Janārdana, which is firmly established in the hearts of yogins, [is effective]. || 65 ||
Worship always the blue-throated Lord, who holds the excellent axe, who has the lord of night-lotuses as his crest-jewel, and who is adorned with the finest deer.

I worship the one whose lotus-feet are the source of destruction for the pride of the lords of the Rakshasas, who are afflicted by the epilepsy of delusions such as "gone" and "not gone," produced by the memory of [their own] demons; he who is dark like a great Śiva-rāta flower blooming from its sheath, and whose thighs, head, neck, and shoulders are as pure as the clearest crystal.

The gods bowed from afar to the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign who dwells upon the Silver Mountain, who is borne by the hosts of Kekeya, Mūṣaka, and Gaṇapati; he who is the great, preeminent ḍamaru-drum arising from the resonance of *nāda*, and who is the Lord of the supreme fire within the full-blown lotus.

Nandīśa, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Suranandika, Somanandi, Caṇḍīśa, Tuṇḍavara, Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, and Bhadra; the illustrious Bāṇa, Rāvaṇa, and the hosts of Gaṇas with their millions of fierce faces; Brahmā, Hari, Īśvara, and the other leaders of the assembly of the immortals. || 69 ||

On the stage composed of the great cosmic illusion (*māyā*), which is elevated by pillars fashioned from clusters of coral maidens, by golden great mother-figures (*mahāmātṛkā*), and by radiant enclosures and *śaktis*,
the entire casket of the whole world unfolds at his mere glance. (pṛ0 137)
By whose very glance this [world] is protected, into him alone it dissolves in an instant.
He too, Śiva, having entered such a theater pavilion, surrounded by all beings, accompanied by Rudrāṇī, joined by Gaṇeśa and Guha at his sides, and attended by the lords of the gods,
by Brahmā, by Viṣṇu, and by Śiva himself—
With his feet served by the wives of Rudra and the lords of the Gaṇas, he rejoices while present upon the stage.

O Great Tortoise, may your repeated praise bring me joy— praise that causes even the great tortoise to break from his inability to endure the slight impact of the soles of [your] feet upon the earth, as his skin cracks and shatters;
and which makes his own abode unstable when tossed by the wind falling from the tips of [your] fingers.
The entire universe, a wondrous spectacle, triumphs as the dance of the Supreme Lord.
Bending his multitude of hands for the sake of the quarters, bowing even his matted locks at the edge of the sky, and again bowing his feet— the foremost of which are directed toward the netherworld—
downward, he stands without support, having transcended the worlds known as the Lokas.
The Lord performs dance solely for himself, and solely before the Goddess.
Sūta:
And in the assemblies, he is the presiding lord of the assembly, together with Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others;
with Sanandana, Sanātana, and others; and with Hara, Sunandin, Nandī, and others.
Standing upon the stage of dance, he dances with the sounds arising from the excellent great jewel on his hand, which are fashioned like the finest cymbals. || 74 ||
O Lord of the Vedas, the Veda itself, being devoted to You, O Blessed One, praises and extols You alone; therefore, it is the Veda that knows the Lord who presides over the assembly.
Yet, how can the Veda know even Your formless form, for You are the one whose very nature is formlessness?
Therefore, O Maheśvara, thus indeed speech is forever withdrawn from you.
(Verse 76) He declared: "Even your form cannot be known by others through speechlessness."
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Dance in the Assemblies," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Pavilion for the Four Aims of Human Life.
Skanda said:
That pavilion, which served as a rampart for the summit of that mountain, was situated amidst various palatial mansions.
Indeed, it was fashioned by Śiva from the essence of moonstones and precious stones. || 1 ||
Indeed, he is truly indivisible, free from the joining of broken or cracked parts;
his essence is the flowing nectar of the digits of the Lord of Night as she rises on the lunar days.
Measuring thirty thousand [yojanas] in length and height,
it is resplendent and adorned with bulls fashioned from pure crystal.
Adorned with eyes as pure as sapphires and with beautiful horns,
they stood upon the unbroken walls of that enclosure and at the gate-towers.
There, the wall and its gate tower rose ten thousand [cubits] high;
it was adorned with excellent jeweled pitchers and recounted the deeds of Rudra’s incarnations.
It was adorned and situated on the eastern part of that excellent enclosure wall;
and likewise on the south, there was one made of great crystal.
It was adorned with the playful manifestations of Rudra and even by bulls;
and in the west, there was a most brilliant gateway made of crystal stone.
Adorned there with bulls and water-pots representing the playful incarnations of Rudra, that [shrine] shines forth, measuring ten thousand [cubits].
To the north of that is an excellent gateway, white as crystal,
adorned with kalaśas representing the incarnations of Rudra and also with bull-figures.
With thousands of stories and banners raised upon their peaks,
they were beautified by clusters of pearls and networks of garlands made of coral and bees.
With divine chambers, corner rooms, pigeon-cotes, and successive cornices;
with great balconies, lofty pillars, and coral figurines.
There, the pavilion was situated facing east, beautiful with its width and height,
and shaped like a lion, a tiger, a śarabha, an elephant, or a horse.
It was adorned with pillars made of jewels, resembling parrots, herons, and swans,
and resplendent with lion-heads, great cornices, and rows of maidens.
It was joined with pillars set with jewels, possessed no inner chamber or gateway,
was expansive with altars, and was great with the luster of red lotuses.
Its walls were as beautiful as jewels with the appearance of the surface of a clear mirror;
its quarters were illuminated by incense and by those jewel-lamps, as if by the rising of magical spells.
The ground was sprinkled with sandalwood essence, camphor, fragrant oils, and the like; it was adorned with jasmine-scented mandāra flowers and garlands of jewels.
There, it was covered with seven-leaved *saptacchada* trees whose gems were as brilliant as pure turmeric; there, it was draped with strings of pearls reaching to the far shore of clear coral.

(Verse 18) Its interior was filled with unfading flowers, and its walls were adorned with many various jewels. [An alternative reading is "its interior was fragrant with flowers. There, he sang upon those walls.
To the east shines the pavilion named Mokṣalakṣmīvilāsa, which possesses excellent forms made of various jewels depicting the sports and incarnations of Rudra. (19)
On the right side as well, it was inlaid with tens of thousands of various gems for the purpose of stabilization;
it extended from the interior of the sanctum up to the gateway in both height and width.
Adorned with jewels, it shines as the bestower of liberation through its own likeness; its interior is surrounded by brave and steadfast men who gleam with the luster of *gomedaka* gems.
Exceedingly beautiful with its stage-like walls shaped like mirrors made of precious gems, its interior was suffused with the radiance of clusters of jewels and rubies found there.
It was well-smeared with fragrant mud scented with musk and tagara,
and its interior was covered by a multitude of garlands made from the boundless flowers of the Nandana grove.
It was adorned with rows of hanging clusters of plantain trees and betel nuts,
and beautified by pillars of agallochum exuding jewels and by rows of swans.
On its walls were fixed the various forms of Rudra’s divine sports and so forth;
in each of their particular ornaments, whatever color was present appeared exactly as it was.
It was filled with many beautiful forms of Śiva fashioned from various precious gems,
and it was perfumed by the smoke of fragrant incense made from excellent guggulu resin.
Extending from the western inner sanctum to the gateway,
its ground shone auspiciously, adorned with millions of pillars.
This pavilion, known as the Bestower of Liberation through Sālokya, possesses ten thousand pillars;
therein, its pillars are fashioned from lapis lazuli, and its ground consists of one unbroken mass of pure essence.
With the boundless streams of its threads, it is a ground of wondrous beauty;
it possesses a magnificent pedestal for the lion’s crest and is as beautiful as a row of pigeons.
It has many excellent rows and sub-rows inlaid with jewels and gems as its foundation,
and is provided with jars filled with water, kesara flowers, and the rising light of deer.
Its floor was sprinkled with fragrant water, it was adorned with garlands of jewels, and it was hung with long necklaces of diamonds, the finest pearls, and precious gems. || 31 ||
There, its upper surface was composed of beautiful slabs of lapis lazuli;

it was exceedingly lovely with the radiance streaming forth from them, and all its variegated patterns were reflected within. (Alternatively, there is the reading "all its variegated paintings were reflected. || 32 ||
It was filled with the smoke of highly delightful incense made of black agallochum;
its walls were fashioned from clear jewels, and it was graced by the sports of Rudra and other such splendors.
It shines exceedingly beautiful, adorned with rows of exquisite jewels and gems,
and with *padmaka* fruits hanging from clusters of precious *ketakī* blossoms.
Adorned with great lion-thrones and pedestals, shining with tier upon tier of railings,
and featuring legs of coral and pearl with sandals of fine silver and gems.
And above me, with canopies of pearl nets suspended from the pavilion, and with flower-beds and charming pillows; (36)
It was covered with cloths spread over surfaces thickly perfumed with fragrant scents,
and it resounded with the sounds of beautiful, resonant lutes and the deep rumbling of kettledrums.
There, within the excellent pavilions, it stands in a uniform form,
extending from the base of the western gateway to the vicinity of the inner sanctum.
To the north of that shines the temple of the Lord, beautiful with jewels;
extending as far as the gateway of Śambhu, it possesses sandals ten thousand cubits high.
It was fashioned with topaz gems and adorned with jewels on its upper and lower surfaces;
it was graced by magnificent coral and pure figurines, which were rendered beautiful by their luster.
It had the forms of a spotted deer, a parrot, an elephant, a deer, and a bird;
its ground was beautified by pillars and fastened with stakes made of the finest gems.
(Verse 42) The quarters of the sky were colored by the light streaming forth from the lattice-work of jewels;
it was adorned with excellent, clear walls strewn with the balconies of pleasure-pavilions.
Therein, his form was fashioned from jewels beginning with the incarnation of Rudra;
its loftiness surpassed the mass of light-rays of the autumn moon.
He possesses clusters of beautiful, stainless, and lovely golden lotuses;
he is the sole source of fragrance for the abundance of liquid sandalwood, camphor, and musk.
Its surface was spread with a canopy, adorned with jeweled plantain trees,
and it was constantly filled with a humming resonance from the incense of *sāmrāṇya* and *agaru*.
It was resplendent with rows of blossoming ratnacāmpeya flowers and gems,
and was surrounded by hanging clusters of blooming blue lotuses from its pedestals.
There, the light from the puṣparāga gems spread across the pillars colored the excellent inner pavilion with the luster of those jewels.
It was perfumed by fragrant scents, spices, and fine incense; it was enveloped in delightful, cool breezes brought forth by the movement of the wind.
In that excellent pavilion, seated upon a divine lion-throne, the Goddess sat surrounded by her attendants; I beheld that spectacle which was a marvel to the sight.
The name of the pavilion there was conceived by Śrī Maheśa;
it is called Sāyujyalakṣmīdāna and was fashioned by Ratnasundara. (50)
Skanda:
There, in the spotless pavilions, the Blessed One dwells joyfully with Ambā, amidst throngs of devotees adorned with ornaments and the like acquired through their boundless merits.

Surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, who are most sweet and noble with the excellent flavors of their respective activities, Śiva bestows upon his devotees the finest ornaments worthy of those various sublime abodes. (Note: An alternative reading is "dayārasaiḥ," meaning "with the flavors of compassion.")
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pavilion of the Fourfold Aims of Human Life," in the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
The thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga," begins with Skanda saying:
Therein, situated within a clear pavilion and beautiful at the gateway, [is the Kailāsa Liṅga].
Divine, resembling Indra’s bow, and resplendent with various jewels.
The wall was ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
in some places it was green, and in some places it resembled collyrium [with a variant reading: "in some places it resembled water"].
Its form was most beautiful, radiant with pure kuruvinda gems;
in some places it resembled a mass of lightning, and in others, a dark blue cloud.
In some places it has the luster of the rays of the rising sun, resembling the moon as it emerges;
and in other places, indeed, it resembles the blossoms of the palāśa and śalmalī trees.
Its stalk resembles the luster of a pure sapphire gem;
it is like a ruby (indragopaka) and similar to the neck of a peacock. (5)
In some places it has the luster of a pigeon's neck, in others the brilliance of the *karṇikāra* flower; elsewhere it resembles a diamond encased by the rays of the shining moon.
In some places it was colored by the luster of gomedaka, puṣyarāga, and emerging vaiḍūrya gems; elsewhere it resembled the pure, streaming radiance of coral, jewels, and pearls.
The sky was filled with various splendors by the networks of light from its ramparts,
and it shone with rows of gate-towers inlaid with jewels and rubies.
It was endowed with the deeds of the incarnations of Rudra as the preeminent jewels,
and it shone in the four directions with crest-ornaments that resembled beautiful jars.
There, within the house of the Lord, was a charming inner chamber,
resplendent with pillars and pedestals fashioned from solid pieces of the nine gems.
That inner sanctum, illuminated by a mass of wish-fulfilling gems,
shines before Śambhu, adorned with a thousand pillars.
The pavilion named Sumuktimanṭapa is praised as the crest-jewel of all the Vedas;
by its radiance, the worlds and the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, are illuminated.
The guardians of the directions, hosts of yakṣas and rakṣasas, nāgas, apsarases, and kinnaras;
serpents, horses, deer, chowries, and sṛmas. || 13 ||
There were lions with manes like nets of rain-clouds, as well as śarabhas, bears, frogs, rhinoceroses, deer, and buffaloes. || 14 ||
It was fashioned with millions of jewel-topped, lofty pillars;
it was covered with networks of jewels and possessed jeweled staircases and pedestals. || 15 ||
It was provided with friezes and archways, endowed with pedestals and eaves, adorned at its summit with jeweled pitchers and beautified by a lattice of gems. || 16 ||
Beautifully adorned with a great garland of jewel-clusters and a network of nets, he possesses the luster of thousands of suns and a radiance equal to ten million moons. || 17 ||
Abounding in the singular fragrance of incense, illuminated by the radiance of jewel-lamps,
beautiful with its spread canopy, it was ever like the color of an emerald.
He was adorned with clusters and bunches of flower garlands that delighted the inhabitants of the Nandana grove;
his radiant complexion was as lovely as a garland of unfading, reddish-pink lotuses and water-lilies.
Golden with the rising fragrance of fresh ketaka flowers,
it perfumed the horizons with the intense scent of garlands of full-blown campaka blossoms.
There, beautiful with the fragrance characteristic of the Kadamba flower, radiant with jewels,
it was adorned with various lion-thrones fashioned from precious gems.
Its wall-mirrors were adorned with pure rubies,
and it was embellished by millions of banners, water-pots, and jeweled bulls.
At the base of the Liṅga, near the presence of Kailāseśvara, a pavilion shines;
within that, O best of men, is the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) of Kailāseśa.
It possessed a pedestal made of the nine precious gems, beautiful with the surface of its altar,
and was resplendent with inner chambers, decorative bands, and divine shrines.
It was made beautiful by flocks of swans moving upon its roof-terraces,
and it was adorned with jeweled lions and bulls situated along the rows of its pigeon-cots.
The splendors of Dakṣiṇāmūrti were spread abroad by the guardians of the directions, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others,
in the south, the west, as well as in the east and the north.
He is the one who brings about the destruction of the Asura Tripura, which arose from the darkness produced by the Linga;
he is the source of Brahma and Vishnu, the Lord of Tandava, and the beautiful one.
Clad in an elephant hide, joined by Heramba upon his shoulder,
wandering for alms, bearing a skeleton, and with a trident held in his hand— such is Hara.
His lotus feet were placed upon sandals whose necks were encircled by a girdle;
his noble head was entwined with matted locks, possessing a brilliance as pure as hundreds of moons and jasmine flowers.

On another occasion, the captivating Lord, adorned with the moon as his crest-ornament, borne by his bull, and surrounded by a multitude of attendants, sat upon a throne with Umā, gazing at Gaurī. (30)
Intent on propitiating Gaurī, he beheld her hand upon her bow;
adorned with half a woman’s form, she possessed the luster of a sapphire.
His face was equal in splendor to the moon shining from a jeweled serpent-earring;
he wore garments of tiger-skin and jewels, and was radiant with the triple-line forehead mark and the tilaka.
Adorned with excellent ornaments shimmering with jewels, bearing various divine fragrances,
his lotus feet were reduced to half a quarter, as the sound of his tinkling anklets remained.
Śiva wears half of the divine jewel-throat of Garuḍa;
he is the supreme refuge for the mass of waters of the Gaṅgā, which rose from the head of the Moon-destroyer.
He is served by Lokeśa and Hari, who stand on his left and right sides;
he protects the twice-born by embracing the Liṅga that was terrified by the son of Caṇḍāṃśu.
His matted hair is adorned with the waves of the Gaṅgā;
his body is marked by beauty; and the lotuses of his feet are worshipped by the great eyes of the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu). || 36 ||
Adorned with a garland of Brahma’s skulls and earrings upon his ears,
he was likewise graced by Rudra-avatars fashioned from unbroken jewels.
And it was surrounded on all sides by the glorious, divine forms of Maheśa, adorned with necklaces of moonstones and pearls, and with gems produced from flowers, go-medas, and sapphires.
The images of the Goddess, as well as those of Indra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the guardians of the quarters, were fashioned from emeralds and rubies. (39)
Fashioned from jewels according to their respective portions, they were conceived as being born from the essence of gems;
they possessed sweet smiles and eyes, and each shone uniquely with its particular limb.
Resplendent with rows of ornaments made of gems, pearls, corals, and the like,
they shine brilliantly with excellent kings and bulls stationed at their respective corners.
The dimensions of the [divine] forms were conceived as ten thousand yojanas;
however, all the local manifestations there are measured at five yojanas.
These delightful [cities] were fashioned by the illustrious Maheśa with his mind alone;
they are fifty yojanas in height, composed of solid diamond and essence.
Its circumference was vast and exceedingly smooth, shining with the brilliance of the sun; its broad expanse rose high, resembling the flower of a plantain tree.
Therein is the inner sanctum of Śambhu, praised by the Vedas and Vedāntas, which shatters the interior of the cosmic egg as vast as the blazing, revolving moon.
It was resplendent with a jewel altar as beautiful as the essence of Kailāsa; right there, within that great seat (mahāpīṭha), it resembled ten million suns.
The web of worlds shines with radiance, brilliant as the pure crystal of the moon;
it has the seats of Hari, Brahmā, and the Great One (Maheśvara), shaped like a long rectangle, a circle, and a cow’s face respectively.
The great Liṅga is of immense form, resplendent like unbroken crystal;
by the streams of its essence, even Mount Kailāsa became exceedingly white.
It illuminated the circle of the quarters, was adorned with palaces and gate-towers,
encircled by a priceless and excellent enclosure, and beautiful with its fragrance.
It was resplendent with nets of garlands of lotuses and water-lilies made of jewels,
and adorned with lakes of blue lotuses made of a thousand sapphire gems.
Its head was adorned with excellent *bilva* fruits made of unbroken, radiant green gems;
it was joined by clear clusters of blossoming *sūtra-vaiḍūrya* and *campaka* flowers.
It was fashioned with topaz gems and surrounded by beautiful, pale-red lotuses;
it was encircled by a pericarp made of refined gold and clear karṇikāra flowers.
It was covered with a lid made of clear crystal, like a great stream of the essence of diamonds;
it was enclosed by a casket fashioned from *gomedaka* gems.
[The chariot] was adorned with mandāra, kunda, bandhūka, baka, droṇa, and arka flowers, as well as jewels;
its excellent crest was firmly fixed with pegs made of crystal stones.
(Verse 55) [The mountain] is adorned with lofty pearls as bright as the radiance of jewels,
and it is illuminated by the gems on the hoods of the great Śeṣa, who has a thousand mouths.
Resplendent with the great passion of rubies and the tilaka-mark of the Tripuṇṭra,
the worlds were illumined by its luster and became oceans from the torrential downpour of its streams.
That stainless, auspicious-bestowing Liṅga named Kailāseśa is worshipped upon the crest of the great mass of the essence of Mount Kailāsa.
It was manifested by a downpour of glances from the eyes of Maṅgalāpati,
proclaiming the greatness of that Liṅga through its support upon boundless peaks.
He cannot be known even slightly by the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, nor by the Rudras or the sages; he is like the Vedic utterances of the mute.
In the jeweled abode of Mount Kailāsa, there is a divine liṅga named Kailāsa, a wonder of the three worlds;
here, the mountain shines with its vast peaks drenched by the streams of light from the beautiful crescent moon upon the crest of that liṅga.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ritual for Worshipping the Lord of Kailāsa.
Skanda said:
All those born from that *liṅga* [pervade] the fourteen worlds.
The gods and others, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, are born from that Liṅga.
The worlds, including the seven continents, forests, and mines, are established within that Liṅga;
even at the time of dissolution, all the worlds, together with the gods, go to their dissolution therein.
It is called a *liṅga* because it is that into which the world quickly dissolves (*līna*);
therefore, O Sage, it is declared to be a *liṅga*, known by the name Kailāseśvara.
From which words turn back, along with the mind, unable to reach it—that Bhūman is indeed that Great Liṅga; let one establish it as the very tail-end of the Vedas.
O Brahmins, that single Brahman alone is both with signs and signless;
it is the light of lights, and it is indeed the consciousness of consciousness.
That Liṅga is eternally truth, bliss, and the single indivisible essence;
even upon seeing that Liṅga, my mind does not turn away from it.
And by the Vedāntas, its characteristic is established through the formula "not this, not this.
Know that very thing to be Brahman; there is no diversity whatsoever here.
The Supreme Brahman is the cosmic order (ṛta) and the truth; it transcends the self and the mind.
It is indeed devoid of senses, stainless, unattached, and undecaying.
The Lord is devoid of all phenomena arising from all beings;
he is space and yet not space, possessing form and yet formless.
Brahman is indeed the cause of all causes;
it possesses that very mark, transcending name and form, peaceful, beyond the qualities (guṇas), yet the locus of the qualities.
The form of Śiva is devoid of hands and feet, impenetrably pure, a mass of bliss, non-dual, free from qualities, and invisible to those who have not disciplined themselves.
That alone shines as the all-pervading, that sign which is beyond darkness;
it is not [fully grasped] even by the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the gurus, or the sacred scriptures at all times. (12)
That very wonderful, qualityless form of the God of gods is impossible for anyone at any time to perceive or even to take refuge in. (13)
And although it is devoid of qualities, that Liṅga remains within the range of vision for the worlds; Śambhu himself always worships it together with the Goddess.
The Supreme Lord, the three-eyed one with a blue throat, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, is worshipped with both external and internal offerings. || 15 ||

Devoid of the sense of "I" and the like, and free from both existence and non-existence—him whom men and gods call "I am indeed Brahman," [the reading being "he who is beyond the fourth state, ageless and immortal"]. || 16 ||
Having transcended both meditation and its object, and remaining beyond even his own greatness,
he was thus perceived as being solely Śiva, together with the Goddess.
Beyond darkness is Mahādeva, who, with the Goddess, is both with attributes and without attributes;
he, who is beyond the reach of mind and speech, accepts worship through external offerings and other such means.
Śaṅkara, the moon-crested Lord, indeed imagines [his consort] with his mind at all times,
especially during the evening hours on Mount Kailāsa.
Listen attentively with a concentrated mind to that worship;
having become one who transcends the four bodies and is devoid of all sense organs.
Having abandoned the sense of "I," I am Śiva alone, non-dual;
I am the pervader within all that is pervaded, and I am established beyond the qualities (guṇas).
I have no end and no beginning; I am eternally the entire universe. Yet I transcend the universe, am undecaying, unattached, and free from all attachment.
I am all-pervasive, eternally full, and devoid of the net of qualities;
I am formless, the self of all beings, and free from the attributes of the body.
Space is all-pervading and indestructible; I abide within that which is destroyed.
I am truth, consciousness, and bliss, devoid of both the known and the knower.
Everything has arisen in me alone; everything is established in me;
everything goes to dissolution in me; therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman.
Meditating thus, the wise man should worship the external linga,
marked with the triple-crested lines of sacred ash and adorned with the finest ornaments of rudrākṣa beads.
Devoted to the fivefold meditation and dedicated to the five syllables,
he should remain facing either east or north, seated upon a cloth or a kusha-grass mat.
Having meditated [on him] seated upon a lotus in one's own heart, resembling pure crystal,
with a serene face, three eyes, and adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
One should invoke the god who has the crescent moon as his crown, whose neck is blue, and who is the lord of Umā, upon an external liṅga made of crystal or of the material used by Bāṇa.
One should worship Śiva even in a clay liṅga, in sand, and in a stationary image,
using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), streams of water, and so forth.
Having diligently consecrated Maheśvara with the five Brahmans, the Pāvamāna hymns, the Rudras originating from the Vedas, and the Sāman chants; || 31 ||
Having wrapped that linga with cloths, one should smear it with an application of fragrant paste;
likewise, one should adorn Śiva with unbroken grains of rice and jeweled globes.
With bilva leaves, kahlāra lilies, campaka flowers, and karavīra blossoms,
as well as with wild flowers and other fragrant ones.
With incenses, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and jewel-lamps;
with lustration rites (nīrājana), excellent umbrellas, chowries, and even fans. || 34 ||

By reciting hymns of praise and prostrations, by performing circumambulations and beautiful dances, and again by further circumambulations as well as by the chanting of the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), [one attains the goal]. || 35 ||
Having established the Lord within the heart-lotus, one should begin the worship and the ritual dismissal;
thus, by means of this procedure of worship, one should worship the Supreme Lord. (36)
The person who worships once, twice, or thrice a day attains knowledge through these supreme internal modes of worship.
This stainless Liṅga of the Lord of Kailāsa bestows both heaven and liberation; it cannot be known even by those who are the crest-jewels of the entire web of Vedas,
nor by Īśa, nor by Gajānana, nor by me, nor by the Goddess, nor even by the lords of the Gaṇas.
By Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, and the immortals, as well as by the hosts of sages, the Tantras, and likewise the Āgamas.

O twice-born one, I believe that in the three worlds there is no one capable of describing, hearing, or even perceiving a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of a mere fraction of its greatness. (39)
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of the Lord of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dwelling on Kailāsa.
Skanda said:
Thus was this Kailāsa mountain ordained by the wielder of the trident.
O Brahmin, there were also walls and palaces made of jewels, as well as gate-towers.
There, mountains of jewels served as the construction for the dwellings of the hosts,
while assembly halls and pavilions were fashioned for the various incarnations of Rudra.

Likewise, Śaṅkara does not find delight anywhere else even while dwelling in all abodes; he is beloved by the Goddess as well as by Skanda, Heramba, Nandikeśa, and the others. [Note: there is an alternative reading, "nandikeśādapīti. || 3 ||
This is indeed the abode of Maheśa, the Lord of the Mountain;
for Giriśa does not delight even in Avimukta as much as he does here on the snowy mountain.
The Lord of the Pināka bow felt no pleasure on Mount Mandara, nor on Niṣadha, nor likewise on Gandhamādana, nor indeed on any other of the lords of mountains.
This abode of the Liṅga is Kailāsa, radiant with its beautiful peaks and trees; it possesses the most lovely summits of jeweled peaks and charming, beautiful caves.
The mountain dispels the mass of darkness from all directions with the luster of refined gold;
it is a mountain consisting of all sacred fords and a mountain consisting of all lingas.
This Kailāsa is the lord of the Gaṇas, the eternal abode of Śiva;
it is a mountain composed of all sacred fields (kṣetra), for it is always the refuge of the lords of those fields.
And this [mountain] consists of all medicinal herbs by virtue of its being the refuge of the Lord of Herbs;
this Kailāsa is a forest-dweller by virtue of its being the refuge of the Lord of Forests.
For Mṛgāvāsa is always and eternally dear to Paśupati;
his true form cannot even be known through the Vedas.
All the worlds are exceedingly purified by the boundless peaks of Kailāsa;
the winds that touch the surface of its summit are the purifiers of purifiers.
O Lord of Sages, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as the sages, while remaining in their own respective worlds, then pray to Anila. (12)
"When will Vāyu, having arrived at the peak of Kailāsa, purify us?
For we have not performed any penance for the sake of beholding Kailāsa. (13)
Even the movement of those born from eggs has been forbidden by the Moon-crested Lord;
indeed, there is no radiance or illumination from the sun, the moon, or fire.
The directions were illuminated by the unrestrained splendors of its very peaks;
the bliss that comes from staying upon the crest of Kailāsa lasts for even a mere moment.
For that supreme happiness is not found even at the end of a kalpa in the realm of Viṣṇu or Brahmā,
nor in the domain of Indra, on the peak of Meru, or in the Nandana grove of heaven.
Whether in the multitude of cities of the world-protectors, or in the solar or lunar realms—
even throughout the fourteen worlds— there is not even a ten-millionth part of a fraction of that happiness.
Without the grace of Śambhu, it is difficult to go there,
neither by ritual action, nor by austerity, nor even by various religious duties.
Even news of Mount Kailāsa cannot be conveyed; how then could one go there?
Formerly, the gods such as Viṣṇu and others, as well as Brahmā and the attendants of the Lord [could not do so].
Even today, those sages, the best of gods, remain intent on performing penance for the sake of beholding Mount Kailāsa,
holding fast to their desire to go to that mountain.
For the sake of attaining the grace of Śiva, some perform supreme austerities,
remaining devoted to the practice of the five fires and subsisting on air alone.
Some, with their leaves loosened from the stalks, remained suspended in the waters;
others, drinking the crest of the smoke from the straw-fires, stood with their arms raised upward.
Some were covered in ashes and established in ashes, chanting the Śrī Rudra;
others, marked with ashes, were devoted to the five-syllabled mantra at the roots of bilva trees.
Some, devoted solely to the name of Śiva, carry heaps of millions of excellent rudrākṣa beads;
others are intent on worshipping the liṅga three times a day with bilva leaves.
In this way, O lords of sages, the gods and sages perform most severe austerities;
for the grace of Sadāśiva will surely be theirs.
O Sage, those who travel to all the worlds and are devoted to all dharmas do not all return again; however, those who have gone to Kailāsa do not return at all.
Even ascetics whose impurities have been washed away by knowledge turn back;
for this Kailāsa, attainable only through the grace of Śiva, is indeed exceedingly difficult to reach.
On the peaks of Meru and Kailāsa, the excellent devotees of Śambhu attained the state of the Lord Īśāna through worship performed with faith.
Those who are happy rejoice in a state exceeding ten million times the qualities of heaven;
what then need be said of our arrival at Great Kailāsa for the sake of human beings?
Indeed, those devoid of Śiva’s grace cannot hear His stories;
He is attained only through penance performed over many millions of kalpas.

Not by the gift of jewels, gold, and other riches resembling Mount Meru and Mandara; nor by the performance of sacrificial sessions such as the Atirātra; nor by tens of millions of recitations of the Vedas. || 31 ||
Neither by the gift of ten million cows, nor by knowledge, nor even by austerity,
nor by religious merits such as sacrifices and works of public utility, is there any failure to attain Kailāsa.
This grace, which is difficult for men to attain, is obtainable through the favor of Śiva;
it cannot be attained even by the Goddess, by me, by Gaṇeśa, or by Nandin and the other leaders of the Gaṇas.
On the outer wall of Kailāsa, she requested a place to stay through her asceticism;
Śiva was gratified by her penance, which had been performed for many eons.
By the grace of Śiva, we who take refuge on that outer peak are counted like grains of sand upon the earth, and like the stars in the sky.
Indeed, there is no counting the liṅgas situated on the boundless peaks of Kailāsa;
even there, I have heard of ten million supreme liṅgas.
(On page 147: Even more than that, a hundred thousand *liṅgas* of the highest class were indeed described by Śrī Śiva to the Goddess.
By whom can the count of the illusory power of the Lord who wields the glorious trident— the one whose nature is inexpressible illusion— be calculated, even in hundreds of millions of aeons?
Who indeed knows the greatness of that Liṅga situated upon his crest? Only he knows it—the omniscient moon-crested Lord, who is the breath of the Vedas.
The very presence of Śiva is true presence; it is an ocean of jewels for the lotus-feet of the Lord of the Gods.
It is the bridge across the faults arising from birth and destruction, and a deep reservoir of satisfaction through the specific practice of bathing and chanting.
Yugādhi alone is the treasury of all prosperity, whose pure mind is devoted to Bhava, and who has torn asunder all mental afflictions.
Thus, having seen the multitude of great liṅgas situated there in the boundless abode of Śiva— supported by the single clusters of water-pots atop the finest, stainless peaks of Mount Kailāsa,
and produced by the playful movements of the minds of infinite lords— Maheśvara himself [appeared].
He has the form of a child half-grown, wears the moon upon his crest, and has fire as an ornament on his forehead and eyes in his brow.
The enemy of Time (Death) fashioned a mountain peak of gold, filled with rows of lingas.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Dwelling on Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga.
Jaigīṣavya said:
O Blessed One, O Slayer of Tāraka, O stainless one, foremost among the devotees of Śiva!
I bow to your lotus feet; what was that spoken by Śiva to the Goddess?
"Whether it be a secret or something public, you ought to explain that to me.
Having carefully considered what was thus spoken, Skanda, his lips curved with a gentle smile, [replied].
To that one devoted to existence and possessed of great wisdom, while the gods were listening at that time.
The Sūta said:
Having meditated upon Śrī Mahādeva within the pure lotus of his heart, he spoke in the presence of the sages, the gods, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Skanda:
While wandering alone upon the lofty peak of Mount Kailāsa at the excellent gate, the Goddess was watched by me with eyes wide with wonder.
Gladdened by Śiva, the Goddess spoke to the Lord with her palms joined in reverence.
The Goddess said:

O God of gods, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara [also read as "abode of compassion" (karuṇāvaruṇālaya)], abode of compassion! O you who have the moon as your crest-jewel, omniscient one, wearer of the Ganges water and matted locks! (7)
O Bhava! O Bharga! O Lord of the gods of gods! O you adorned by the jewels on the hoods [of Śeṣa]!
O Lord whose banner is the bull! O enemy of Kāma! O destroyer of the cities [of the demons]! O destroyer of Yama! || 8 ||
O Lord of Beings, whose skull-topped staff, hand-drum, and noose resound throughout the world; O Trident-bearer, Sky-haired One, you who are clothed in the directions!
O Lord, O Śaṅkara, who performs the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the net of the three worlds, there is no wonder at all for you; this is merely your divine play.
The worlds, the objects of perception, and the supreme gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the other deities— are all subject to arising, persistence, and destruction by the Lord.
Through the mere contact of Your side-glance, there is the dissolution and emergence of all things;
O Supreme Lord, tell me, what cause for wonder is there in that? (12)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, daughter of the best of mountains;
there is nothing in the three worlds that I must conceal from you.
"O Goddess, this secret residing in my heart must not be revealed by you;
nevertheless, O Śivā, I shall speak this chapter on the Liṅga to you."
O Ambikā, the circle of Liṅgas situated upon the crest of Mount Kailāsa cannot indeed be known even by me, for my mind is already fully occupied by that [task].
I am the form of ten million liṅgas, and I am also the one who ordains their worship;
O Umā, those [liṅgas] have not been worshipped by gods, sages, or gandharvas.
O Goddess, the best of the lords of the Nāgas have heard [your name—*namadgaṇaiḥ* being an alternative reading]; how much more so have they seen you?
O Goddess, what need is there to speak of worship? This mountain is inaccessible even to me.
I behold this with a serene mind and with wonder:
by my very glance, the worship of all the *liṅgas* shall be accomplished.
O Śivā, O Great Goddess, behold as far as the range of your vision extends.
O Daughter of the Mountain, this Liṅga-maṇḍala has its supreme head graced by a crescent moon;
it is adorned with the excellent hoods of Kuṇḍalīśa and is the shatterer of the great mountain that is the web of sins.
Behold, behold, O Girijā, upon the crown of the mountain [Śiva], my beloved who bestows supreme satisfaction—a garland of skulls adorned with lotuses and a paste of bilva and sandalwood. (21)
O Śivā, this Kailāsa is surrounded on all sides by tens of millions of abodes of exceedingly beautiful great liṅgas, as well as by jeweled mansions containing similar liṅgas;
and its summit is crowned by the finest bilva tree, with its clear flowers and fruits—
The wind, bound by their fragrance, was laden with the weight of pollen and sprouts from the forest trees. || 22 ||
My temple of the Liṅga is always being swept by the loads of peacock feathers from the crests of the crested birds;
it is always perfumed with the fragrance of agallochum by the smoke rising from the forest fires ignited within the bamboo thickets. (p. 149) 23.
Behold the multitude of lingas, perpetually illuminated by jewel-lamps arising from chambers filled with gems,
and well-honored by the scents of forest bilva leaves and flowers brought forth by the wind.

With clusters of trumpet-flowers (pāṭala), with karṇikāras, with sarasotphulla flowers shining intensely with seven colors, with aravinda lotuses having the hue of a multitude of rubies (kuruvinda), and with fully blossomed navanīlotpala hallakas; || 25 ||

[The trees were] white, red, and pure-colored, with fallen stalks, exceedingly fragrant, and sporting with masses of nectar. [There is an alternative reading: *śīrṇavṛntaiḥ* (with withered stalks). || 26 ||
O Śivā, my [forests] are always covered with most beautiful Mandāra trees whose crests are adorned with bees upon their lingas;
with blossoming Mallīs, excellent Puṇḍarīkas, Kumudas, and Karṇikāras, O Śivā;
and with Dhana-phalas that are ever-shrouded and which distill a rising flood of nectar.
O Śivā, [I offer] that which is always well-prepared among the food offerings and presented in the temples of the Liṅga. || 27 ||

Behold, O Queen, how these [mountains] upon their peaks have been sprinkled with the essence arising from the spray of the trunks of elephants, and have been made fragrant by the rubbing of the musk from the bodies of musk-deer, using the essence of the moon from their own crests as the unguent. 28.

Fanned by swarms of blossoming yak-tails, with the dance performed by peacocks and the melody of cuckoos and swans, having worshipped this assembly of my lingas—which removes sin, grants a happy rebirth, and is supreme—[I bow]. (29)
Skanda:

Thus, as he beheld the Goddess with the mountain Kailāsa engaged in excellent conversation comparable to the celestial river, and as he observed the formidable lingas of Śiva’s boon granted to the multitude of mountains;
Kālāri, whose body was exerting itself as the crest-jewel for the excellent Śiva— the one whose crown is the moon of Niyati—
shook his own great head and gazed intently at the serpent with a most compassionate look.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kailāsa Liṅga," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Chapter Thirty-nine: The Majesty of the Kailāsa Mountain Liṅga.
Īśvara said:
"Behold, O Goddess Umā, my liṅgas situated within the abode of jewels."
O Śaṅkarī, they are pervaded by the streams from the great jars upon the crests of the palaces.
O Śaṅkarī, they are anointed with moon-like sandalwood paste, radiant with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
and wear upon their heads beautiful jewels and mandāra flowers.
O Pārvatī, they possess within them the essence of the beauty of the finest Bilva fruits,
and are adorned with hoods bound by excellent hooded serpents.
O Mother Ambikā, though adorned with sandalwood and garlands of Nandana-forest blossoms that bring joy, these [forests] are constantly perfumed by the smoke of agallochum burnt in forest fires.
"Behold these, O Goddess of the gods, which are illuminated by the beautiful radiance of a lattice of jewel-flames; see how my mind is intent upon the worship of the Liṅga."
O Mother, my mind is not thus intent upon creating the net of the world;
my mind is not fixed on its preservation, nor on its destruction, nor on any other duties.
This mountain Kailāsa is mine, an ocean of all bliss;
pleased by his penance, I granted him an excellent boon.
I shall dwell upon your crown, taking refuge in various forms;
by the power of my presence, there shall be no destruction for you through the dissolution of the universe.
Thus addressed, this king of mountains, who always bestows bliss upon me— [the reading is "Śiva, the bestower"]—
is surrounded by hundreds of oceans at the time of universal dissolution.
O Goddess, even the mountains will come to rest at the soles of your feet,
amidst the surging waves of the Mahāvīci hell that extend as far as the Maharloka.
O Daughter of the Mountain, even when shaken by the seven winds, those [mountains] remained as they were;
likewise, on Himācala and Mandara, there is the one known as Kedāreśvara.
O lady of beautiful eyes, I shall dwell there forever, for that [Liṅga] is my refuge;
O Great Goddess, even on Meru, my peak is beautiful.
North of that, on Mount Kailāsa, there is a peak resplendent with various lingas;
there I dwell, worshipped by the gods.
O Daughter of the Mountain, I am here alone, non-dual and formless;
pleased with you on the peak of Kailāsa, I have chosen to dwell there.
O Goddess, although I am the abode of all, I dwell upon Kailāsa;
on my mountain Kailāsa, there are infinite billions of liṅgas.
The radiance rising from the crest of the jewels on its palace,
surpassing the sun, moon, and Indra, is indeed impossible to describe.
Even there, O beautiful one, it is said that the number of liṅgas reaches ten million;
O Great Goddess Pārvatī, they are unsurpassed even among the most excellent.
There too, a thousand lingas of mine alone bestow delight;
through seeing them, touching them, and worshipping them, they grant liberation.
O Śivā, O Maheśvarī, [liberation] is not attained without knowledge, austerity, action, and faith; nor by those ignorant of the path, nor by vows, conduct, yoga, or Sāṅkhya.
O Śivā, just as that goal cannot be attained even through the worship of other liṅgas,
so too is the sight of the liṅgas situated upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa [rare].
O Śaṅkarī, these are difficult to attain even for all the gods, let alone for humans;
the Liṅgas, headed by Kailāseśvara, are truly most wonderful.
I have also always worshipped those [images] which are situated upon other elephants with uplifted frontal globes and banners, resting on a base within a palace of jewel-essence.
O Maheśvarī, O auspicious one, listen as I respectfully describe to you the series of Liṅgas at those times—forenoon, midday, afternoon, and dusk. (Page 151)
O Śaṅkarī, even by hearing the kīrtanas, these [names] shatter sins;
they swiftly bestow heaven and liberation upon men, even when merely chanted.
Formerly, O fair-faced one, [I dwelt] on my Kailāsa among various families of Liṅgas,
as well as to the south and to the west of that mountain.
Even further beyond that, O Goddess of gods, there are various regions consisting of light;
it is impossible, O Goddess, to describe them even by the gods and Śeṣa, O beautiful lady.
O Śivā, even in ten thousand aeons, how could the greatness of that Liṅga be described in detail?
It is impossible to speak of it fully; therefore, O beloved, hear its names.
O Goddess, there are two hundred and fifty [tīrthas] in that direction;
O Great Goddess, they are indeed renowned with reverence even among the boundless regions.
It rested upon the broad summit of the far shore of Kailāsa, its lofty head reaching toward the sky as if licking the circle of the celestial jars.
It was fashioned from pure, transparent slabs of jewels, rising a yojana in height,
and adorned with a halo of radiance as white and clear as the autumnal moon.
Situated within a chamber of jewels, it possessed a most beautiful jeweled altar;
it was divine, spread with the luster of gems, and radiant with blue, yellow, and crimson light.
O Umā, the pedestal is also made of pure crystal, beautiful with a radiant luster from coral, rubies, and other gems such as agate and lapis lazuli.
Anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents, worshipped with bilva sprouts,
and adorned with garlands of mandāra and kunda flowers, he is uniquely decorated with a crescent moon.
It was covered with serpent-gems, radiant with the light of jewel-lamps,
perfumed by the great incense of divine agaru, and filled with the fragrance of scents.
His body was marked with three lines of diamond-dust and adorned with a tilaka of musk,
appearing as magnificent as the pinnacle of a palace atop the peak of the great Mount Kailāsa.
O auspicious lady, behold the multitude of lingas, their garments covered with shimmering luster rising from jeweled pitchers; they bestow prosperity even by the mere sight of them.

O Goddess, even by merely beholding the tip of the stream from the pinnacle of its white-domed cupola, gods and men who listen with devotion attain liberation. [Note: "mātrataḥ" is an alternative reading.]
Offer salutation, O Goddess of gods; listen attentively, O Daughter of the Mountain, to the names of the Liṅgas derived from the Vedānta.
O blessed lady, the lineage of Liṅga shines like a sprout of liberation rising upward;
it bestows merit upon hearing it, and by seeing it, one is indeed liberated.
Such lingas do not exist on earth, nor in Pātāla, nor in Svarga, nor even in Satyaloka; how much less, then, on the land of Bhārata?
The linga situated in the netherworld (pātāla) is superior to the linga on the earth;
from the netherworld, it is surpassed by that located in the heavenly world (svarga), and from that, by the one residing with Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra.
O Goddess, the first [form] is known by the name Kailāseśvara; it bestows auspiciousness and is not known even by the Vedas or by all the Vedāntas.
In this very place, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara go to dissolution (laya).
Because it is the place where all worlds dissolve, it is called a *liṅga* by the wise.
O Maheśvarī, this very form of mine is directly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
by its light alone, all the fourteen worlds shine.
O Dear One, by the consciousness of this very [Self] alone, the entire world perceives;
O Dear One, by a mere fragment of its bliss, everything becomes composed of bliss.
This Linga, O Goddess of gods, possesses a splendor exceeding that of the abode of fire and the abode of the moon;
it is indeed Brahman itself, and it is most dear to me. 46.
From which words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it—
pure as clear crystal, of the nature of space, and supreme.
O Daughter of the Mountain, that from which all beings are born, in which they always abide,
and into which they finally go to their dissolution— that is this Liṅga.
O Daughter of the Mountain, since Brahmā, Īśvara, Viṣṇu, and Indra were born from you,
this eternal Brahman alone is truth, consciousness, and bliss.
More subtle than the subtlest, directly perceived, neither gross nor atomic,
it is entirely free from all sense organs and devoid of all phenomenal attributes.
It is without smell, taste, or touch, and it is not the locus of smell or taste;
this very eye is the eye of eyes, eternally composed of all vital breaths.
It transcends the qualities of all the senses and is ever-pervasive among all beings;
for it is eternally undecaying amidst the decaying, and herein there is no diversity whatsoever.

O Daughter of the Mountain, when this is worshipped, known, and meditated upon within one's own self, the bearer of the *liṅga* shines as one who has transcended the *liṅga*; this indeed is the supreme *liṅga*.
Transcending name and form, it shines forth, known by the name Kailāseśvara.
O noble lady, lotus-faced one, listen with reverence to its names.
O Umā, this mountain ridge of mine, its clear slopes covered by a beautiful grove of *bilva* trees and its ground shaded by spreading branches;
where the wind, laden with the massed fragrance of fully blossomed flowers and the scent of *japā* and *celima*, brings forth its fruit—this is my beloved. (55)
Adorned with rows of pollen from full-blown lotuses, engaged in unrestrained play against the cool breeze,
and clinging to the lotus-beds of the lake on Mount Kailāsa, he nourishes his noble body joined with Ambikā.
In the ocean of white plaster that flows through the network of palaces at the base of the jewel-adorned mansion,
the two lovely ones, like a pair of birds, sport amidst the heat of the sun’s rays.

Alone within the lattice of our palace, you are preeminent in beauty; O Daughter of the Mountain, your moon-like face today cannot be compared even slightly to anything else, for neither the moon nor the sun can equal it. (58)
May the lofty lingas adorning the crown of Mount Kailāsa protect me—
lingas that are covered by masses of dust raised from the tails of the female serpents on the heads of the snakes,
and by the thick swarms of bees drawn by the streams of rut-fluid flowing from the temples of the mountain-elephants during their play.
And [the breezes] were filled with swarms of bees hovering over the masses of pollen from the *gandhaphalī*, *kadamba*, and *jara* flowers, which were being crushed by the laboring [wind].
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Kailāsa Mountain Liṅga," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.

Ananteśa, Kardameśa, Mṛḍeśa, Babhrukeśvara,

Uśīnareśvara, Gargeśa, Mantrakeśvara, Tantreśvara, Sāmakeśa, Vyomakeśa, and Digīśvara; || 17 ||
Kapālamocaneśāna, Maṇigarbheśvara, as well as Jātukarṇeśvara, Nṛgeśa, and Pāṭaleśvara. || 18 ||
Karṇikeśa, Chatrakeśa, Piṅgaleśa, Śileśvara, Madhvīśvara, Vāmakeśa, Yauvaneśa, and Sthireśvara. || 19 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain, [the Lord] is Bhrāntīśvara, Ujjahnukeśa, Gomedeśa,
Akhileśvara, Viśāleśa, Siṃhikeśa, and Ghaṇṭākarṇeśvara.
Vyāghreśa, Jambukeśa, Laliteśa, Dhṛtīśvara, Vedeśvara, Diṇḍikeśa, Kaholeśa, and Dhvanīśvara. || 21 ||
Bindukeśa, Gaṇḍakīśa, Narmadeśa, Anileśvara, Picaṇḍileśvara, Atrīśa, Kanakeśa, and Adhvareśvara. || 22 ||

Bhāgakāreśvara, Mugdhakeśa, and likewise Rogeśvara;
Bhallūkeśa, Virāgeśa, Krathaneśa, and Dhaneśvara. || 24 ||
Urageśa, Kaṭhoreśa, Dardureśa, Urvarīśvara, Kṣipreśvara, Dālbhyeśa, Vinateśa, and Śaśīśvara. || 25 ||

Pārijāteśvara, Mandāreśa, Jaṭeśvara, Trijaṭeśa, Śikhaṇḍīśa, Barhīśa, and Panaseśvara; || 19 ||

Arundhatīśa, Vāgīśa, and likewise Padmagarbheśvara.
Lord of the emerald, Lord of food, Lord of welfare, Lord of the boat;
Lord of Uddālaka, Lord of night-wanderers, Lord of Aparṇā. || 21 ||
Śāṇḍilyeśa, Chāgaleśa, Niriccheśa, Kuśeśvara, Dūrveśvara, Anamitreśa, Karkandheśa, and Aguṇeśvara. (22)
Kuruvindeśvara, Paṭṭīśa, Kuṭajeśvara, Śrīśaileśa, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Haridvāreśvara; || 23 ||
Gaṅgādvāreśvara, as well as Kurukṣetreśvara; Surābhāṇḍeśvara, Yayātīśa, and Kutheśvara. || 24 ||

The forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liṅgas at the Western Gate of Kailāsa.
Īśvara said:
"On the mass of peaks on the southern side of Kailāsa, there are abodes of Śiva."
Although there are infinite lingas, those most excellent among them have been declared by me. || 1 ||
O Śivā, listen to the lineage of Liṅgas at the western and westernmost peaks;
O beloved, listen also to those well-known Liṅgas that are dear to me. (2)
Tatpuruṣeśa, Sthāṇvīśa, Paiṅgeśa, Ruḍajeśvara, Sālveśvara, Sthānakeśa, Vainateśa, and Saleśvara. || 3 ||
Musaleśa, Hāṭakeśa, Rudradhanvīśvara, Jvarāpahārakeśa, and likewise Kṣayahareśvara. || 4 ||

Balāśaśīśvara, Ghanaghoṣeśvara, Vedagarbheśvara, Oṃkāreśa, and Śikhīśvara; || 6 ||

Lord of birds, Lord of winged creatures, wielder of the thunderbolt, and lord of the forest;

Barhidhvajeśvara, Kapoteśa, Khaṇīśvara, Śateśvara, Romakeśa, Kāvyeśa, and Varṣakeśvara; || 11 ||
Somanandīśvara, Triphalīśa, Khareśvara, Hanehatīśvara (the reading is *Hanehatīśvara*), Śatarceśa, and Bhaveśvara. || 12 ||
Viḍūratheśvara, Karambhīśa, Sruveśvara, Gaṇeśvara, Vardhikeśa, Saddhrīśa, and Krikakeśvara; || 13 ||
Citravyādheśvara, Raupyeśa, Bandhakeśvara, as well as Paśupatīśa and Bhayahārīśvara; || 14 ||

The Lord of Wind, the Lord of Water, the Lord of Clouds, the Lord of Lightning, the Lord of Delight, the Lord of the Partridge, and likewise the Lord of Heaven and Earth. || 17 ||
And Gajājinadhareśa, as well as Narasiṃheśvara;
Aupāsaneśvara, Havyeśa, and Gaṇakeśvara. || 18 ||
Karṇikeśa, Udadhīceśa, Jhaṅkeśa, Karkaṭīśvara, Jābāleśa, Subāleśa, and likewise Purahāreśvara. (19)
The Lord of the Ṛgveda, the Lord of the Atharvaveda, the Lord of the Purāṇas, the Lord of Urvaśī, the Lord of the Itihāsas, and likewise the Lord of the Essence of Dharma.
Sāṅkhyeśvara, Yogeśa, Maulīśa, Pālikeśvara, Kujambheśa, Jambheśa, and likewise Rājarājeśvara; || 21 ||
Kauthumīśa, Viśākheśa, Skanneśa, Phalikeśvara, Kadalīśa, Pṛṣṭakīśa, Pṛthvīśa, and Kārmukeśvara. || 22 ||
Antarikṣeśvara, Maitreśa, Kumudeśvara, Udāvaseśvara, Malleśa, and Brahmakeśvara; || 23 ||
Taraṅgeśa, Kuraṅgeśa, Makarandeśvara, as well as Sudhādhareśvara and Dhṛtakeśeśvara. || 24 ||
Vyāleśvara, Vitarkeśa, Kānaneśa, Munīśvara [the reading "Timīśvara" also exists], Bhadramāleśvara, and likewise Ketumāleśvara. || 25 ||

Īśvara: [I bow to] the moon upon the head of the Lord of Bilva trees, whose mass of lingas is like the nectar-drops falling from the autumnal moon, and whose splendor is renowned as resembling the hue of an emerald.
His forehead is marked by the sectarian tilaka drawn by the circle of hoods of the lord of serpents;
he dwells in the supreme abode of the lord of jewels, and his garments are perfumed with the fragrance of celestial incense.
On the mountain behind me, she fashioned for me a row of lingas with the luster of the moon.
O Daughter of the Mountain, behold [this form] which is most blessed by the pair of eyes,
which destroys families of great sin, which dispels all sorrow,
which grinds the rays of the sun and moon, and which brings joy to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
She who has the lord of serpents as her supreme ornament, and who burned the body of Madana. || 43 ||
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liṅga at the Western Gate of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liṅgas and Temples at the Northern Gate of Kailāsa.
Īśvara said:
Thus, the number of liṅgas situated in the western part has been declared by me.
Listen as I tell you about that on its northern and western peaks. || 1 ||
Listen to that with devotion, O Ambikā, always keeping your mind focused;
behold, O Pārvatī, the crown of the most meritorious collection of Liṅgas.
O Goddess, there are Vāmadeveśvara, Girikeśa, Sukeśvara, Bṛhaspatīśvara, Vardhaneśa, and Pikeśvara. || 3 ||
Kokileśa, Picaṇḍeśa, Vāmakarṇeśvara, as well as Ānandeśa, Karmareśa, Cāmareśa, and Patīśvara; || 4 ||
Vairāgyeśa, Kalpakeśa, Haribrahmeśvara, as well as Gaṇeśa, Triguṇeśa, Brahmāṇḍeśa, and Śaṭheśvara; || 5 ||
Vilāseśa, Sukeśeśa, Cāmakeśa, Plaveśvara, Annakośeśvara, and likewise Prāṇakośeśvara. || 6 ||
Vijñāneśa, Aghanāśeśa, Catmeśa, Rakṣakeśvara, Āhananyeśvara, Mugdheśa, and Koṭikeśvara. || 7 ||
Nisarpīśa, Nāmaneśa, Āmreśa, Kamaṭheśvara, Śanāśaneśvara, and likewise Corugāyeśvara. || 8 ||
Kapiñjaleśvara, Karkeśa, Ṣaṇḍakeśvara, Asaṅgeśa, Saṅgeśa, Jyotīśa, and Kāraṇeśvara; || 9 ||
Harirudreśvara, Kṛpāṇeśa, Nimīśvara, Kanakāvartakeśa, Harīśa, and Bhāruṇeśvara; || 10 ||
Āmreśvara (an alternative reading is Abhreśvara), Dabhrakeśa, Dandaśūkeśvara, as well as Udāreśa, Indumaulīśa, Makheśa, and Sabheśvara. (Page 160) || 11 ||
Harikeśa, Kiśoreśa, Kuddāleśa, Arbhakeśvara, Yuveśvara, Vṛddheśa, Dardureśa, and Brasīśvara. || 12 ||
He is the lord of the intellect, the lord of the forest-dwellers, the lord of those in the planets, and the lord of enemies;
he is the lord of a thousand, the lord of a hundred, the lord of a lakh, and the lord of ten million.
Cāṣeśvara, Bhānukeśa, Daṇḍirāvartikeśvara, Kastūrīśa, Madantīśa, Manasvīśa, and Arbudeśvara; || 14 ||
Airāvateśvara, Tañjeśa, Lindukeśvara, Ahaṅkāreśvara, and likewise Phālanetreśvara. || 15 ||
Likewise, Ailabileśa, Kṛkeśa, Carakeśvara, Padmāsaneśvara, Vāreśa, and Tarageśvara. (16)
Vaṭamūleśvara, Trasanneśa, Lutīśvara, Nakuleśa, Vaṃśeśa, and likewise Padmanetreśvara; || 17 ||
Upaśāntīśvara, Dameśa, Vratakeśvara, Ulūkeśa, Ruṇḍeśa, Kāleśa, and Kamaleśvara; || 18 ||
Bhagandhareśvara, Bhadreśa, Bharaṇīśvara, Aśvinīśa, Rohiṇīśa, Paṅkajeśa, and Avaṭeśvara; || 19 ||
The Lord of the End, likewise the Lord of the Upper, the Lord of Ashes, and the Lord of the Even;
the Lord of Existence, the Lord of All, the Lord of the Vedas, and the Eternal Lord. || 20 ||
Jvāleśvara, Sālakeśa, Tamāleśa, Puṇyakeśvara, Upadhyeśa, Aṇimāṇḍeśa, and likewise Sarvarakteśvara; || 21 ||
Śunaḥparṇeśvara, Mādaneśa, Pratheśvara, Śipiviṣṭeśvara, Aṃśeśa, and then Mṛgeśvara; || 22 ||
Gajānaneśvara, Bāṇeśa, Vīrakeśvara, Caṇḍeśvara, Muṇḍeśa, Cakreśa, and Phaṇikeśvara. || 23 ||
Anasūyeśvara, Gandhamādeśa-īśvara, Bhaṇḍeśvara, Prajaṅgheśa, and likewise Kālakaṇṭheśvara; || 24 ||

The Lord of the Conqueror of Death, the Lord of the Mountain, the Lord of the Lake, the Lord of the Pathless, the Lord of Dreaming, the Lord of Waking, the Lord of Deep Sleep, and the Lord of Day. || 25 ||
Śitikaṇṭheśvara, Sūryeśa, Kāntikeśvara, Sphaṭikeśa, Rudreśa, Varadeśa, and Anṛṇīśvara; || 26 ||
Lord of the tiger, Lord of impetuosity, Lord of Puṇḍra, Lord of the dance;
Lord of the rudrākṣa beads, Lord of the chief of poets, Lord of the armor, and Lord of the jewel. || 27 ||
Pilippileśvara, Āmardeśa, Druṇeśvara, Pitāmaheśvara, Kuṭileśa, and Jhaṣeśvara; || 28 ||
Bharateśa, Kesarīśa, Cakṣuśśrotreśvara, Daṇḍakeśa, Laṅkeśa, and Maṇibhadreśvara; || 29 ||
Ghaṭotkaceśvara, as well as Pureśa, Naṭeśvara, Karamardeśvara, and likewise Āmrātakeśvara. || 30 ||
Phaṇibhūṣeśvara, Ratnabhūteśvara, Biḍālakeśvara, Aṇīśa, and Mahatīśvara; || 31 ||
Pūruṣeśa, Uparambheśa, Girīśa, Ramaṇīśvara, Kavaṅgeśa, Karīndreśa, Māgheśa, and Vāṣkaleśvara. || 32 ||
Mahānādeśvara, Maṇṭapeśa, Balīśvara, Jariteśa (with *Rajateśa* as an alternative reading), Kūrmakeśa, and likewise Caturbhadreśvara; || 33 ||
Puṣparāgeśvara, Gomedeśa, Laveśvara, Tṛtīśvara, Kṣapeśa, Prasādeśa, and Kuleśvara. || 34 ||
Vajreśvara, Kṣetrakeśa, Karṇikāreśvara, as well as Karavīreśvara and Puṇḍarīkeśvara. (35)
Vīṇāpāṇīśvara, Tantrīśa, Nāgakeśvara, Hāhāhūhūśvara, Payodeśa, and Kratheśvara; || 36 ||
Guḍasāreśvara, Śvetadānapradeśvara, Pradāneśa, Śilādeśa, Kandeśa, and Padadeśvara; || 37 ||
Trilocaneśa, Bhāṅkṣeśa, Sthūlakarṇeśvara, as well as Prakaṭeśa, Dhārakeśa, and Kośātīteśvara; || 38 ||
Yantreśvara, Mantreśa, as well as Kanakhaleśvara, Gargareśa, Pratāpeśa, Ātāryeśa, and Kuṇīśvara; || 39 ||
Bhagīratheśvara, Dilīpeśa, Kṛtīśvara, Anādīśa, Mantravidīśvara, and Guṇahareśvara. || 40 ||
Śaṅkeśvara, Piśaṅgeśa, Pāryeśa, Tāraṇeśvara, Kakāreśa, Mātṛkeśa, and likewise Kuṣṭhahārīśvara. || 41 ||
Hārīteśa, as well as Akṣeśa, Bakadālbhyeśvara, Lopāmudreśvara, and likewise Surābhāṇḍeśvara [an alternative reading is "Kumbhajanmeśvara"]. || 42 ||
Maṇihastīśvara, as well as Citradhvajeśvara, Ratnadhvajeśvara, Kāmeśa, and Rudraṇīśvara; || 43 ||
Avantīśa, Karpaṭīśa, Dhvajeśa, Chatrakeśvara, Devakanyeśvara, and likewise Nāgakanyeśvara. || 44 ||
Satyeśvara, Sunātheśa, Kubereśa, Vaneśvara, Pavitreśa, Valakṣeśa, Mahokṣeśa, and Nageśvara. || 45 ||
Sudheśa, Vibudheśa, Phullaśaulālikeśvara, Śayaneśa, Dhāvateśa, and likewise Samāsīneśvara; || 46 ||

The Lord who fulfills all desires, the Lord of true consciousness, the Lord of bliss, the Lord who removes the distress of those who bow to him, and likewise the Lord of the five products of the cow (or, according to another reading, the Lord of the five Gaṅgās). || 47 ||
Padmanābheśvara, Pañcavaktreśvara, Pañcākṣareśa, Candeśa, Sudeśa, and Kauśikeśvara; || 48 ||
Ādarśeśa, Kālakeśa, and likewise Kālāvarteśvara;
Tāmradhvajeśvara and also Haṃsadhvajeśvara. || 49 ||
Vṛṣadhvajeśvara, as well as Siṃhadhvajeśvara, Piccheśvara, Kumāreśa, Niṣaṅgeśa, and Kulīśvara; || 50 ||
Īśāneśa, Vikarteśa, Surabhīśa, Aṇukeśvara, Sāraṅgeśa, Khaṅgakeśa, Bandhureśa, and Gameśvara. || 51 ||
Śacīśvara, Sādhu, Īśa, and likewise Rudragaṇeśvara.
Īśvara said:
O Umā, these names of the divine liṅgas have been told to you; whoever should worship or recite this upon rising in the morning, [shall attain the fruit]. 52.
One shall obtain the fruit of worshipping all the Liṅgas situated on Kailāsa;
by reciting this meritorious chapter on the Liṅgas, one becomes an attendant of Rudra.
O Śivā, a thousand have been described among those various [liṅgas] as the most excellent;
O lotus-faced one, there are also infinite liṅgas by the millions.
O Mother, O Pārvatī, the essential signs have been described to you by me; they exist upon the peak of Kailāsa, as I have told them.
What more need be said? He dwells within all signs and is free from a womb. || 56 ||
