(Verse 57) O Daughter of the Mountain, this multitude of lingas here— divine, lofty, and fashioned from moonstones from the jeweled abode of Mount Kailāsa—
is indeed that very mass of peaks upon whose crest-line this [Lord Śiva] is drenched by the streams of nectar from the crescent moon.
O Goddess, that crest-jewel of the mountain ranges shines indeed with the pot-like luster of the supreme jewels of Śiva’s liṅga resting upon its crown;
surpassing in splendor hundreds of thousands of millions of suns and moons, that best of mountains resplends with its own radiance.
O maiden of the mountain ranges, O you with bee-like eyes,
by taking refuge in your lotus feet which possess the splendor of a thousand suns,
I shine with exceeding luster through the fragrant breezes arising from the groves of trees crowned with beautiful flowers.
The King of Mountains was adorned with eyes formed from his own limbs and ears that reached to the farthest limits.
The mountain of the playful artistry of refined gold, with its peaks bearing the great luster of the crescent moon resting upon my head,
and the lord of mountains whose joy is kindled by the mass of my matted locks shining like blazing fire, stands there like the pinnacle-finial of my most excellent palace.

The preeminent city shines, its great vault of the sky kissed by the water-jars which possess the luster of the sun gleaming upon the temple of Śrīliṅga; all its turrets are set in motion by the wind from the red cloth-bags of its fluttering banners.
With the water-pots placed upon the peaks of Mount Kailāsa— resembling the rising young sun and moon,
and adorned with rubies and pure diamonds— and with the hosts of Śiva’s attendants residing in those various worlds who have become filled with wonder at the sight of the temple of Śiva;
This mountain surpasses in its great splendor the combined light of various suns and moons. || 62 ||

This abode on the mountain of silver can be attained even by those whose multitudes of sins have been shaken off through worship of the *liṅga* adorned with a crown resplendent with the king of stars (the moon);
yet it cannot be attained even through the yogas of self-restraint, breath-control, fasting, asceticism, and the like.
Even by the hosts of Maruts, beginning with Brahmā and Indra, my darkness is always to be attained.
For those whose minds are embraced by devotion, [the goal] is easily attained; indeed, there is no other path.
Blessed is that Mount Kailāsa, the crest-jewel of the mountain ranges, the sole crown of the multitude of Liṅgas.
Having gratified the Sun (the friend of the lotus), the one with variegated arrows (Kārttikeya), and the eye-devouring Rāhu, [he is] the devourer of the eyes of Svarbhānu (Rāhu).
Through pure austerity arising from the pair of my eyes, I obtained a boon from Śaṅkara. || 64 ||

On that very mountain, the abode of the Lord, O Lord of the Mountain King, you formerly made a request for the sake of the liberation of all beings, seeking it as the object of your love while performing acts pleasing to Śiva. (65)
Skanda:
Having heard these words of Śiva, Gaurī bowed at the feet of the one who bears a digit of the moon.
Surveying the multitude of lingas all around, the goddess, her body covered in horripilation, spoke: (66)
Pārvatī said:

O Śambhu, O Bhīma, O destroyer of Bhava, Andhaka, and the Asuras; O three-eyed one, O lord of Aṣṭaroman, my protector, O sovereign of the Pramathas, O wielder of the crescent moon, speak to me out of compassion!
Or rather, what austerity was performed by this Kailāsa that produced such favor in you, since by its own countless merits it has made you dwell right here? (67)
Or what supreme austerity has been well-performed by him for so long, O Lord, that he has practiced only the worship of the Liṅga? Oh, how he has become an object of Your love, O Lord!
What was done by this ornament of the blessed lords of mountains, and how were You worshipped by him?
This [place] is now the abode of the infinite crest-peak of the Liṅga; there is nothing other than the Lord of Mountains.

Blessed is this crest-jewel of the kings of mountains, whose crown is adorned with a multitude of lingas; for your family of sins, whether it remains constant or exists but for a moment, this Linga indeed destroys it—
wherein resides the lineage of the most excellent Lingas, reaching unto the supreme palace of the Great Lord.
By following the path of speech associated with this [teaching], people become liberated from all [suffering]. (69)
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Linga and Temple at the Northern Gate of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Austerities at Kailāsa.
Īśvara said:
Listen, Aparṇā, to the reason for the mountain's performance of penance.
Of me, Kailāsavarya, and of the abode of all liṅgas.
And this king of mountains is the tilaka-mark of the earth, possessing various waterfalls and caves;
it is endowed with hundreds of various trees and resplendent with various birds. || 2 ||

O Goddess, filled with flocks of various birds and teeming with diverse herds of animals, it stands as if desiring to gladden me with the songs of its avian throngs, endowed as it is with various trees and creepers.
O Śivā, this mountain, whose crests and peaks shine with various minerals, was formerly fashioned by me alone in my mind. (4)
He became exceedingly delighted with my mere creation,
and for the sake of my grace, he performed penance for two yugas.
O Queen of the Gods, listen to all that I say, O Lord of the Mountains:
with all my limbs tormented by the heat of blazing coals, [I am consumed]. || 6 ||
Scorched from above by the rays of the sun, he who was devoted to the recitation of the Śatarudriya remained on the mountain for a thousand years,
subsisting only on leaves and then on air.
For a thousand [years] he subsisted on smoke, for a thousand [years] he subsisted on water,
and for a thousand [years] he remained without food, always indeed covered in ashes.
Then, for one yuga, he dwelt there, devoted to the worship of my Liṅga;
he worshipped that Liṅga named Śaileśvara with Bilva sprouts.
Worshipping with devotion at the three times of day and meditating on me within his own heart,
the mountain [saw] me as three-eyed, blue-throated, and bearing the shining crescent moon.
Adorned with a garland of lotuses shimmering like the waves of the Gaṅgā,
his entire body was smeared with ashes, and he was graced by a crown of matted locks.
He wears a sacred thread made of serpents and is resplendent with ornaments of snakes;
his entire body is smeared with ashes and beautifully adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The god was accompanied by Umā, his limbs radiant with unguents,
and his chest adorned with a rising garland of Mandāra and Kunda flowers upon his neck.
He was resplendent with the hip-region adorned by a shining garment made of elephant hide,
and his beautiful earrings were set with the multitude of great jewels from the crests of serpents.
Her two lotus-feet shone with great red silk cloths, while her beautiful bracelets were made of diamonds,
sapphires, and excellent rubies of great essence.
The god Sadāśiva, clad in costly garments, with a serene countenance,
was resplendent with rows of nails resembling the moon on the eighth day.
His face has eyes like full-blown white lotuses and is as beautiful as the god of love;
it is adorned with a row of teeth resembling the seeds of a pomegranate.
Adorned with lips as beautiful as ripe bimba fruits, resembling a blue lotus, and possessing eyes that are dark blue and reddish; (18)
I behold the Lord himself, whose face is gracious with favor, the witness of the worlds;
and I behold you as well, seated upon my lap, your form resembling a sapphire.
The ornament of the lords of mountains meditated upon her, who was beautified by a wreath of flowers and adorned with a divine nose that shone with a blooming campaka bud.
She shines with a prominent nose like a clear pearl,
and is beautifully adorned by a parting line marked with vermilion upon her forehead.
Her pair of eyebrows was radiant like a great bow with a jeweled staff;
she was enchanting, with the region of her forehead shining with a musk tilaka.
She was endowed with eyes as red as the petals of a blossoming, dark-blue lotus,
and she shone with a row of teeth as pure as the finest diamonds.
I bow to the auspicious Umā, whose lower lip has the luster of a pomegranate flower and the taste of its juice,
whose mouth is filled with betel, and who is gracious and smiling.
Adorned with ear-ornaments shining like the sun and the moon,
her cheeks were resplendent, beautified by a multitude of radiant jewels set in her ear-leaf ornaments.
The horizons were made to shimmer by the mirrors of its cheek-like ramparts,
adorned with Campaka, Uddāma, Kahlāra, Vakula, Aśoka, and Nāgaka trees.
It was surrounded by a multitude of *mallī* flowers shining like the *maruddamanaka* plant,
and its crest was adorned with a crescent moon marked by the jewel of a circle of bamboo.
Her neck shone with a string of pearls attached to the gems of her necklace, and the continuous line of her silver foot-ornaments sparkled like a shower of pearl-motes from the waves of her anxiety.
(Verse 29) Her broad chest was adorned with a firm necklace of nine-jeweled gems,
and her long braided hair was held fast by a cluster of flowers made of exquisite jewels.
She was joined by *ketakī* flowers whose stalks rose from the opposite shore and were yellowed by being drunk [by bees],
while her limbs were fanned by cool breezes made fragrant by the scent of the *ketakī*.
She is graced by a form made beautiful by the three bends [of her body],
and she shines with a large, round pearl necklace as pure as the stars.
The horizons were adorned by the clear luster of the jewel-like hands of the shimmering feet,
and she was graced by the brilliance of jeweled necklaces and rows of fresh gems.
Her breasts, radiant with the golden hue of the frontal globes of a mad elephant,
were smeared with the essence of sandalwood, musk, camphor, and sandal-paste.
Resplendent with the singular fragrance of cloth-perfume, aloe-wood, and sandalwood oil;
her breasts shining with nets of pearls that extend to the borders of her jeweled bodices.
Adorned with a beautiful navel and a noble belly graced by three folds,
she was embellished by two arms lovely with jewel-like lotus stalks.
Adorned with many arm-ornaments set with various jewels [an alternative reading is "studded with gems"],
and with pearls dangling from the jewel-adorned hoods of the serpents bound as bracelets.
Adorned with shining jewel-lotuses in the form of curved stalks and buds,
and beautified by bracelets on her hands inlaid with gems and rubies.
Her rows of nails were resplendent, shining with jeweled rings,
and her big toes were encircled by bands of pure, great diamonds.
With the tips of her big toes raised high, she illuminated the horizons;
she was radiant with the intense luster of fresh gems set in her jeweled girdle.
Below that, she was beautiful with the tinkling of small bells dangling there,
and her lower garment was colored by the luster of blossoming pomegranate flowers.
Her breasts were drenched by clear streams of liquid whose essence was as pure as jewels;
her two lotus-feet were in constant contact with the tinkling sound of jeweled anklets.
Her lotus-feet were like flower-clusters arising from the tips of her big toes as they encircled them;
her two feet were marked with red lac by the ornaments upon her toes.
Meditating upon you— who are the mother of Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and who are like a thick flash of lightning upon my lap—
that king of the city remained steady-minded.
Thus meditating with constant joy upon me, Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā and who is like the sun that causes the full-blown lotus of his own heart to blossom, he remains.
O Goddess, for many groups of years, the Lord of Mount Kailāsa remained amidst five fires during the summer heat, and took refuge in the open sky during the rainy season.
During the winter, he slept in the water and subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits;
for more than two yugas he lived on leaves, and for another yuga he subsisted on bulbs.
For two ages he shall subsist on air alone, remaining like one who feeds on wind;
devoted to the worship of my *liṅga*, his head adorned with *rudrākṣa* beads (or, according to another reading, his body adorned with ashes and *rudrākṣas*).
Devoted to the recitation of the five-syllable mantra preceded by meditation on the Five-Faced One (Śiva),
he is intent on the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya with his mind fixed upon Rudra.
Thus, for ten yugas, the Lord of Mountains performed intense and unrestrained penance, devoted to fierce worship while undergoing his austerities.
O Goddess, this mountain, with its formidable appearance, brings wonder to the gods, the sages, and the lords of the hosts; it is this very mountain that has gratified me.
Having restrained the collection of his senses, with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose,
endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he destroyed his impurities through breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Constantly intent on the *praṇava*, ever engaged in yoga, taking refuge in Me, devoted to the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*), and taking shelter at the feet of the Eight-formed Lord (*aṣṭamūrti*). (52)
Having his sole abode in a hut of leaves, the mountain remained steadfast and shone with majesty;
he made his heart the temple of love for Dhūrjaṭi.
His body was covered by an anthill, though he was a mountain-like sage exceedingly emaciated;
he was a mass of asceticism, like the ocean [drying up] the lotus of the mind.
Constantly recollecting me as dwelling in the center of a great lotus blossoming within his heart,
he never once allowed the stream of his meditation to be interrupted.
The tree sustained its own livelihood by means of fruits, leaves, filaments, and pericarps that had fallen from the tips of branches due to being severed at their stalks by the movement of the wind;
it performed ten thousand years of constant and intensely austere penance.
While performing the tearing apart of the vital organs of wild oxen, he subsisted on the foam from their chewing of the cud.
But my devotee, devoted to Śiva, looks upon the lord of rivers as a mere mouthful of water, the sun as a firefly, Mount Meru as a clod of earth, the wish-fulfilling tree as a piece of wood,
the philosopher’s stone as a fragment of rock, and the lord of the earth as a servant.
Furthermore, one regards saṃsāra as a heap of straw and one's own body as a burden. (56)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Penance at Kailāsa," in the first part of the glorious Śivarahasya.
The forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of the Boon upon Kailāsa.
Īśvara said: Having observed his disposition, I was then impelled by you.
After a long time, O Goddess, I went into his presence. || 1 ||
Upon a bull fashioned with the form of dense autumnal clouds, [he sits] on a jeweled lion-throne adorned with a radiant circle of light. || 2 ||
Adorned with a pearl nose-strap shimmering with a jeweled saddle-cloth,
and graced by a beautiful horn-shaped crown with chowries hanging from its ears.
Resembling the rising sun, radiant with the beauty of his eyes, and joined by a neck adorned with the tinkling sound of jeweled bells; (4)
O Goddess Śivā, I am mounted upon you, O auspicious one, who are white, whose banner-top is rubbed by the luster of the Lord of Night (the Moon), and who are a bull that moves at will.
He arrived in the very presence of that [Lord], attended by a multitude of Gaṇas;
the gods were driven away by Nandin, while he was highly praised by a host of sages [or, according to another reading, by sages and Gandharvas]. || 6 ||
He was most brilliantly radiant, covered by a great umbrella made of pure jewels held by Tuhuṇḍa and Dhṛtaratna,
and served by Somanandin and Tuhuṇḍu with fly-whisks having jeweled handles.
Then he was fanned by Caṇḍī with a handheld fan emitting radiant light, and he was graced and served by winds that were exceedingly fragrant and cool. (Page 167, Verse 8)
The Lord of the Gaṇas has arms whose appearance is radiant with banners;
Bāṇa, bearing arrows and a bow, possesses a thousand arms.
O Goddess, he was adorned on all sides by the shaven-headed bearer of the quiver;
his inner being was gladdened by the sight of the battle-arrays and the *bhṛṅgi*-dancing.
With the sound of the *taṇḍu* and *ḍiṇḍima* drums, the quarters of the sky were filled with grandeur;
the horizons were rent asunder by the joyful, white resonance of conch shells.
The earth and the sky resounded with the unrestrained sound of Caṇḍīśa’s maddala drum,
while the vast beauty of the scene was enhanced by the deep, thundering roar of Heramba’s large kettle-drum.
Filling the quarters of the sky with the boundless sound of his six faces and his kāhala drum,
he was cheered by Bhairava, who stood upon his jeweled sandals and crown.
The ground beneath his feet is graced by the auspicious crests of moving bulls;
he is made beautiful by the resonant, noble, and sweet sounding of Nārada’s lute. 14.

Beautiful with hymns of praise from those bowing at the feet of the gods, he was accompanied by drums struck by the great hands of Maṇibhadra, which were split open by his mighty weapons. (Alternatively, the reading is "split open by the blows of the great drums in his hands. 15.
O Mother, I was served there by you through the mouths of the best of scribes,
and by Keśin with the joyous sound of his excellent, loud jhallarī drum.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the sound of horns blown by the breath from the mouths of Sukeśa, while Subhadra produced a roar like that of a drum’s loud peal.
O Goddess, I beheld him— praised by Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the lords of the gods, and lauded by those of meritorious deeds— his body emaciated by veins.
This world of Malla beheld the excellent mountain Kailāsa standing like a sage;
it was white by its very nature and rendered even more pale-white by the ashes.
O Umā, I am like a head covered by its own shadow even when scorched by the rays of the sun,
or like a lake filled with water yet shrouded by a mass of lotuses.
Seeing that best of mountains subsisting on sapless, withered leaves,
compassion arose within me, even though he had been granted a boon.
He was touched by me with my hand, which was as pure and blossoming as a lotus; at the mere touch of my hand, that king of mountains then rose up.
Seeing me, he bowed down, prostrated himself with palms joined in reverence, and sang this, his hands making the rhythm of the dance while tears flowed from his eyes. (23)
With his body covered in horripilation arising from his beautiful limbs, he spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Kailāsa:
O Bhava, O Śiva, O Blessed One, wielder of the Pināka bow, whose feet are adorned by the crowns of the best of gods and Kinnaras;
O ocean of boundless compassion, O moon-dweller, I bow down at your lotus feet. (25)
O Śambhu, whose name and form are delighted by a multitude of virtues, who are devoid of [material] nature, beyond the three qualities (guṇas), and free from old age;
O All-pervading One, sovereign of Hari, Rudra, and the Lotus-born, whose crown is adorned by the host of gods arisen from the praised Vedas! 26.

O Śambhu, whose forehead is beautified by the eyes of the moon, the sun, and fire; O bearer of the great digit of the moon that quivers upon it; O you who wear matted locks from which the excellent waters of the Gaṅgā flow—be gracious! Bestow upon me quickly your favoring glance. (p. 168) 27.

O Moon-crested Lord, who causes the lilies that are the sages to bloom, O remover of sins, O steadfast one who carries us across the shoreless ocean, protect me with your glance—the eye fashioned by the moon—with the essence of your compassionate side-long looks. (28)

O Śambhu, praised by the hosts of gods, known through the Vedas, whose pure necklace is the king of serpents, O blue-throated Śiva, protect me with compassion! May your residence be upon my very head, and may the status of Lord of the Gaṇas be mine today. (29)
Thus, O Maheśvarī, I was pleased by the words of the Lord of Mountains;
O Goddess, I granted him the unsurpassed status of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
In his sovereignty over the lords of mountains, the Lord of Mountains was consecrated;
Himavat, Niṣadha, Vindhya, Mandara, and Meru [were present]. (31)
Nīla, Mahendra, Ṛṣabha, Trikūṭa, Citrakūṭaka, Kaṅkata, Raivata, Pāriyātra, and Kesara, O Goddess. (32)
Airāvata, Bhadra, Maināka, Gandhamādana, Irāvān, Hastiśaila, Malaya, and likewise Dardara. (33)
Sahya, Govardhana, and likewise Udaya and Astamaya—these are remembered as the principal lords of mountains there, by their mere mention. (34)
Having arrived before me, those mountains bowed to me and offered hymns of praise. || 35 ||
The Mountains said: O Blessed One, Bhava, Lord of Beings, Śambhu, wearer of the pure serpent-king as a necklace, Lord of Pārvatī!
Behold us with your stainless eyes—us whose crowns are raised by the dust arising from the lotus-feet of your grace.
Your very presence removes sorrow; we have come here by the mere thought of you.
Speak, O God of gods, what shall we do? Grant us your command for those who are rendered helpless by your gaze. (Note: An alternative reading is *vitatāṃ vidhehi cājñām*. Grant us your command. 37.
O beloved, having heard these words of Śaila,
I indeed greeted them as they stood bowed low with palms joined in reverence, and spoke to them.
Īśvara:

Kailāsa has been well-arranged as my dwelling place; the leadership of the Gaṇas has been granted to you, and even the status of Lord of Mountains has been bestowed by my grace. By good fortune, I have been pleased with you.
Therefore, I am pleased with your practice of unremitting austerity which dispels all suffering;
having worshipped and joyfully bowed to this best of mountains, my very abode, [you shall attain your goal]. (39)

"Go, O Mountain, and having consecrated him with well-fashioned golden waters,"— having spoken thus, the mountains then bowed to the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) and brought [the waters], as some readings add "with excellent jars.
They also brought the supreme lion-throne, the moon-like parasol, and the beautiful fly-whisks.
Then, together with Candra, Upendra, and the hosts of Maruts, [he approached] the Lord of Mount Kailāsa.
Having consecrated Śaileśa at the word of Śaṅkara, the gods and the mountains said:
"Blessed are you today! You are indeed a devotee of Viśveśa, the king of mountains among the lords of gods and men.
May this Lord, dwelling upon your crown, bestow only auspicious things upon you."
You are always purified by the masses of moonbeams resting upon his crest. || 41 ||
Abounding with various waterfalls and filled with excellent deer, may you prosper for our well-being. 42.
Thus, through these words, Śiva—whose mind was entirely absorbed in Śivā—increased like a mass of clouds with an exceedingly great collection of flames;
as if being nourished by streams of molten gold, he spoke these words impetuously out of joy.
Kailāsa—
[I bow] to Him whose left half is ever resplendent with the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Pārvatī),
whose forehead is marked by a triple-crested line glowing like a mass of flames, and who is adorned with the tilaka-mark of fire.

I meditate upon the Destroyer of Time, who, seated at the foot of the Kalpa tree, has playfully gazed upon and consumed the body of Kāma, and who incessantly causes the entire web of worlds to tremble with his sport.
With one hand brandishing a trident and with the other holding a young deer,
his neck resembling a dark and luxuriant tamāla tree, adorned with the jewel that is the moon,
and bathed by the waters of the Gaṅgā—
He whose crest is always adorned with the crescent moon shining from his hut-like mass of broad, matted locks; || 45 ||
I bow to Him who is seated upon the summit of Kailāsa and is expert in the beautiful tāṇḍava dance and other arts.
Touching his head in salutation, the Mountain said: "O Śambhu, obeisance, obeisance to you, O Lord of the Mountain!
May you, filled with affection, dwell upon my own head and within the rows of great lingas on Mount Pāra. (47)

(Verse 170) Even the Veda itself, O Lord, declares its own primordial nature through words ending in "salutations to Rudra," proclaiming Your state as the Self of all; moreover, it always praises You, the Supreme, with supreme devotion.
By the power of Your presence, O All-pervading One, I too shall praise and bow down to You again and again.
And again: "Where you sit with the mantras," for who indeed is more blessed than I? 48.
O Ambikā, having thus heard the words of Mount Kailāsa,
I spoke to that great mountain, Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
Śiva:
I dwell at will upon the rows of Lingas atop the excellent palatial towers on the slopes of Mount Kailāsa;
I utterly destroy the sins and the worldly suffering of the people, and I bestow both liberation and worldly enjoyment.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise Offered by Rāvaṇa upon the Shaking of Kailāsa.
Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, having received a boon from me, Kailāsa, the upholder of the earth,"
And I was somewhat filled with pride, thinking, "I am dear to the Lord of Pārvatī. || 1 ||
Salutations! The Lord, who always resides within all lingas upon the mountain peaks, dwells eternally within me, crowned by the jewel-palace.
Where is Meru, Pāriyātra, Maināka, or even Mandara; where is Vindhya, Niṣadha, Gaurī, Himavat, or Naga-adhi? (3)
Is it Nīla, Asta, or Udaya; or Bhava, or Śataśṛṅgaka? Or is it Raivata, Vamana, Śrīka, Kumuda, or Gandhamādana? || 4 ||
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Dardura, and Citrakūṭa—whom among these principal mountain ranges are all most dear to Śambhu? (5)
O Ambika, I alone am always dear to Śambhu and indeed his very abode;
along with Kailāsa, I have been transferred to the mountain of pride, O Mother of the Cities.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having observed that state of mind of his— the best of mountains— which possessed a hardness like the core of a rock, even the gods [were moved].
Through my own wrath against Dakṣa, all the hosts of deities,
including Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others, were indeed disciplined by Bhadraka.
O Goddess, because of their censure of the burnt [sages] who were accompanied by Dakṣa and headed by Brahmā,
those Daityas were repeatedly afflicted by floods of misery in age after age, O Goddess.
O Great Goddess, I cast those devoid of devotion into the ocean of worldly existence in battle with the gods; those who are bereft of devotion to me I cast into the ocean of suffering.
All those who are devoid of devotion to me always fall into birth, death, and old age; indeed, those who are not Śaivas fall into both heavens and hells within the state of Sadāśiva. (11)

Those who are revilers of me, of the sacred ash, of the rudrākṣa, or of Śiva; or those who revile the liṅga of Śiva, the sacred field of Śiva, the triple-tilaka, or the path of the Vedas—[may they be destroyed].
Whoever should revile my devotee— be they a god,
a king, or even an ascetic— I cast that person into suffering.
Or, O Maheśvarī, out of delusion, one may neglect the Vedānta, or the Guru,
or the five-syllabled mantra that grants liberation, or even my Rudrādhyāya.
O Goddess, in the worship of Śrī Mahādeva, one should recite the mantra consisting of a hundred branches, which wards off the multitude of evils and is praised by all the Vedas.
Indeed, the Śruti declares that Mahārudra alone is to be worshipped;
for whoever speaks of Rudra—who is beyond the universe—as being equal to another, [is a fool].
Abandoning everything else, I, the Lord of Pārvatī, am to be meditated upon;
for is anyone seen or even heard of who is equal to me or superior?
I am the atom among the subtlest, and the greatest among the great;
by the words of Indra, Mitra, and others, I alone am the inner self of all.
All the Vedas and Upanishads proclaim me alone;
I am the Fourth State (Turiya), the non-dual Śiva, the Truth, Knowledge, and the Beloved.
Deluded by words contrary to the Vedas, people lead me astray;
I cast those evil-minded ones into hell and into sinful wombs.
For you alone are my supreme power, the auspicious one who creates the universe;
from your glance, the web of the world comes into being age after age.
For you indeed reside within all; yet, failing to recognize this, the lowest of gods, whether they be men or Brahmins, [neglect] the worship of my linga.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, those wicked ones shall have no wisdom;
consequently, both gods and demons shall be submerged in an ocean of suffering.
Those Brahmins who are devoid of devotion to me become outcasts and great sinners; for them, there is suffering at every step.
For those wicked-souled Śaivas who do not honor Maheśāna,
calamities arise immediately, as well as terrible hells.
For those evil-minded people who are not devotees of Śiva and have not recited the Śatarudrīya,
calamities arise immediately, as do most terrible hells.
For those evil-minded ones who have not recited the five Brahmans and are not devotees of Śiva, there arise... terrible [consequences]. || 27 ||
For those evil-minded ones who are not Śaivas and who do not recite the Liṅga-sūktas, there arise... terrible [consequences]. (28)
For those whose inner selves are devoid of meditation, though they possess the five external signs of self-restraint, there arise... terrible [consequences]. (29)
For those who have not recited the five syllables arising from the five colors, there arise... terrible [consequences]. || 30 ||
For those evil-minded non-Śaivas whose bodies are not smeared with ashes, there arise... terrible [consequences]. || 31 ||
For those whose limbs—namely the forehead, throat, thighs, and arms—are devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), there arise...
terrible [consequences]. || 32 ||
And for those wicked-souled ones who are not Śaivas and who do not maintain the path of the rosary, there arise... terrible [consequences]. || 33 ||
The fierce [consequences] of those wicked-souled non-Śaivas who have not seen my liṅgas come to pass... 34.
For those wicked-souled non-Śaivas who are devoid of worship during the evening twilight, there arise...
terrible [consequences]. (35)
For those evil-minded ones who are not Śaivas and are devoid of the worship of the elements (bhūtas), there arise... terrible [consequences]. 36.
For those wicked-souled non-Śaivas who are devoid of the Monday [observance], there arise... terrible [consequences]. (37)
For those evil-minded non-Śaivas who are devoid of the worship on the eighth day, there arise... terrible [consequences]. (38)
And for those who have abandoned my field, the non-Śaivas of evil soul, there arise... terrible [consequences]. (39)
And for those evil-minded non-Śaivas residing in other fields, there arise... terrible [consequences]. (40)
For those evil-minded ones who lack my name and are not devotees of Śiva, there arise... terrible [consequences]. 41.
For those evil-minded non-Śaivas who are deprived of my food offering, there arise... terrible [consequences]. 42.
O Goddess, those great sinners who perform the worship of Viṣṇu and others as equal to my Liṅga shall experience unrestrained suffering. (43)
For those evil-minded non-Śaivas who have discarded the bilva leaf, there arise misfortunes and most terrible hells.
O Goddess, those who look upon me as equal to Viṣṇu and the other gods shall experience calamities and the most terrible hells.
O Goddess, for those fools who look upon my devotees and the devotees of others as equal, the hells are not far away; they are even closer than the bow.
O Goddess, even the hells are not far for them;
likewise, O Śivā, even gods are like men whose minds are devoid of dharma.
Those very same ones have been born as donkeys— learned men of great renown who,
being non-Śaivas of dull intellect, apply a clay sectarian mark on their foreheads.
O Mother, those who feel shame at wearing the triple-ash mark (tripuṇḍra), the rudrākṣa beads, or in the worship of Śiva, are indeed hell-beings; they are sinners who become the guests of Yama.
O Goddess, those are indeed donkeys; O Mother, they are guests of Yama.
O Umā, the worship of the Liṅga is eternally proclaimed by all the Vedas as my [duty].
O Goddess, O Ambikā, those who have abandoned the worship of other deities, yet are devoted to the lips of a donkey while remaining householders— though they are ascetics, they become guests of Yama.
Those Brahmins who bear the marks of a burnt wheel on their foreheads with ashes, yet are devoid of Vedic knowledge—
even if they shine with proper conduct— they are Asuras in the guise of gods of the earth.
Those who, regarding me as equal to other gods, remain even for a moment, O Śivā, they are all indeed outcastes; they are truly unworthy of performing sacred rites.
Those base individuals who worship the Liṅga of Maheśvara with the emblems of other deities have their limbs scorched by that Liṅga and are born into the womb of a sow.
Therefore, the worship and meditation upon me must not be abandoned by Vedic twice-born ones;
for it is only through devotion to the worship of my *liṅga* that they attain self-knowledge.
Those who are constantly devoted to the ash-observance and are the best among those who know the meaning of the Rudrādhyāya, they are... devoted [to them]. 56.
But for those who are devoted to the five-syllabled mantra and always wear rudrākṣa beads, they [are]... devoted. || 57 ||
But those who are devoted to my field, following the very path declared in the Śruti—for them... [they are] devoted. (58)
Therefore, let him be devoted to me as his supreme goal; I am the liberator of them, O Maheśvarī, the one who delivers them from the ocean of suffering that is the cycle of existence born of sin.
The son of Viśravas was created for the purpose of destroying the pride of the gods;
and Viṣṇu, due to the curse of Bhṛgu, shall take birth among human beings.
(Verse 173) Because of his abduction of my wife and his harassment of the sages,
Rāvaṇa once came to Kailāsa out of sheer arrogance.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having transferred his unabated pride and having stripped even Kailāsa of its arrogance,
he lifted up Mount Kailāsa with his two arms.
By him, Kailāsa—the abode of various Liṅgas—was shaken;
then, by my great wrath, he was cast down.
O Goddess, I, who am to be known through the Vedas, was praised by him with the Vedas; for a thousand years, he propitiated me, the eightfold-formed Himavat, with Sāman chants.
O Goddess, my chest was crushed by the ten-faced one with his arms, which pressed down upon the base of Mount Meru so that its foundation sank beneath the tips of my thumbs.
Then, having been released through compassion while praising me with a hymn,
he departed after offering praise and bowing down, looking toward the direction of Śammanā.
Even Kailāsa, O Great Goddess, became divested of its pride.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, tell me now how you were praised by him;
O Lord, I desire to hear what kind of austerity he performed."
Īśvara said: O Pārvatī, listen attentively as I speak this hymn of praise to you;
O Goddess, Rāvaṇa, stationed at the base of my excellent mountain, cried out in lamentation.
With a wretched voice, extremely distorted, and with eyes clouded by tears—[the reading "sāsrāvilavilocanaḥ" is also found]. || 70 ||
Rāvaṇa:

[He whose] crown is resplendent with the king of stars (the moon), who is adorned by serpents, and who shows reverence for the ashes on the limbs of Māra (Kāmadeva) shimmering from the luster of his body which resembles camphor;
He was pressed by the tip of his toe in anger due to his lifting of Mount Kailāsa.

I worship the god Śaṅkara, the destroyer of cities, from whom all sounds of Rāvaṇa were released when he shattered the aged bones of the son of Viraja with the blow of a mountain and his own arms. 71.

I bow to the God who is exceedingly delighted by the *hiṃ* sound of King Vairāja, whose head is gracefully adorned, who is white as the moon-king, who has formed a friendship with the lord of the Yakṣas, who is accompanied by Umā, and to whom the king of the gods offers salutation. (72)
I bow to the beloved of Ilādharasuta, the beloved of the excellent Sunandi, the most dear to the Lord of the Gods, and the one who cherishes the garland of kunda flowers;
to him who is worshipped by the eyes of Mukunda, the destroyer of worldly existence, and who dwells upon Mount Sumeru.
Śaṅkara, who was worshipped by the pair of beautiful eyes of Ramā’s lover.

O ocean of compassion, storehouse of mercy, friend to all, source of power! O granter of desires, enemy of Kāma! [I bow to] that which is sweet with the humming of bees, bound by fragrance, possessing the beautiful conduct of Rudra’s eyes, and boundless. (74)
O Supreme Lord, O Friend, I praise you with excellent words and Sāman hymns; deliver me, who have fallen into distress, quickly! 75.

With a face possessing the luster of the lovely moon, like the lover of the night (Śiva) who delights in the mountain (Kailāsa), and with his own beloved’s face occupying half of his body— his eyes and head likewise graced—
the Lord of Gods is ever adorned by her, who is endowed with all her arts and bears the mark of a young crescent moon.
I worship that Guru of the worlds, the remover of the sins of the three worlds, who is of such a nature. || 76 ||
Thus, at that time, the distressed Rāvaṇa praised me, the Lord of eightfold form, the sole sheath illuminating all bodies, the Master who destroys the suffering of the world, and Umā; then,
releasing his arm-hold from Mount Kailāsa and bowing down, he went to his own abode.
O Śaṅkara, the worshiper of the Liṅga shall always have his primary residence in Laṅkā.

O Daughter of the Mountain, he whose chest was marked by calluses formed from being struck by the tusks of the gods' elephants, whose hosts of deities were made to cry out on the battlefield, and who staked his very life against Rāvaṇa—[that Lord of the Gods (Śiva) has been won]. (78) *Note: There are variant readings for this verse: "paridhṛtakiṇataḥ" is read as "paridhṛṣṭapraṇataḥ kiṇatsu vakṣāḥ," and "paṇitaprāṇagaṇassarāvaṇeśaḥ" is read as "paṇitaprāṇagaṇeśarāvaṇo'drikanye."*
O Mother, this son of Pulastya, born in the Nandana grove of the Alakā city,
attained the status of Lord of the Gaṇas by propitiating me; indeed, he became unslayable by the gods,
for he performed such penance that he cut his own flesh and offered it into the fire.
Long ago, while wearing his own lotus-garland upon his head as a mark of his status as a wrestler,
he offered it to his two brothers as a trophy of fame for having conquered the vast earth bounded by the great oceans through their own prowess.
With the Vairūpa, Vairāja, Bṛhat, Rathantara, Śrī, Vāmadevya, Vara, Rudra, Śāṅkara, Śrī, Raivata, Ilādharaka, Mahendra, Mahāṣṭadaṃṣṭra, Vara, Vaiśva, and Mitra [sāmans]. || 81 ||

O Mother, he then praised the Moon-crested Lord with Sāman chants, while Rāvaṇa caused all the worlds to resound with his roars; the Lord, who was pleased by those well-sung Sāmans, [remained unmoved].

(Verse 83) [This foot remains incomplete: ...pleased by the extensive worship of the lotus performed by the Lord of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), who is noble-minded (*dhīrodāra*), and further praised by the Creator with excellent words;
[he who is] served by those whose noses are attached to the fragrance of the hundred-petaled lotuses.
May the multitude of eyes of Śiva protect this Mitra today with his very first glance; by that [glance], may Śiva deliver her from the great calamity of the mountain of immeasurable sin. 84.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise Offered by Rāvaṇa during the Shaking of Kailāsa," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Secret of the Vedas. The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O ocean of the essence of compassion!"
O All-pervading One, whose commands surpass all things, O bestower of bliss upon those who bow before You! || 1 ||

O Moon-crested Lord of Beings, bestower of bliss upon those who bow before you [the reading "triṇetra-madānandaka" is also found], I desire to make a certain request; please speak it to me out of compassion.
O Lord of Gods, knowing that I am a vessel for your compassion, speak even that which is most secret, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods— even though it is a mystery.
Skanda: Then, having heard the words of the Goddess, he remained on the peak of Kailāsa,
seated upon a great throne-couch situated within a jeweled palace.
With a face radiant from hundreds of moon-dwelling [teeth] and possessing a digit of the moon,
he has eyes of the moon, sun, and fire, the form of whose splendor rises up through the three worlds.
His neck was adorned with a circle [of hoods] like water-laden, unrestrained clouds;
he was embellished by large, hissing hoods and shining jewel-earrings.
He is resplendent with many garlands and nets of jewels set in nine precious gems;
his broad forehead shines brilliantly, adorned with a triple-tilaka mark [the reading *sukuṇḍalataṭojvalaḥ* is also found].
His supreme body mocks the whiteness of jasmine, the moon, and snow;
it bears the fragrance of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and the essence of sārāguru.
The Lord of Śiva is attended by winds that are profound and intensely fragrant, made beautiful by the dense clusters of divine mandāra garlands.
Upon a circle of jeweled couches spread with costly Kāśi cloth, adorned with excellent gems and garments, and beautifully graced with hundreds of pillows. (10)
Adorned with jeweled floors shining with various mirrors,
illuminated by a jewel-lamp, its interior was filled with the light of radiant knowledge.
Through the lattices of those windows, he observed the activities of the world,
his eyes being the moon, the sun, and fire under the pretext of closing and opening [his own eyes].
There is the place of torment for enmity between the gods who dwell in heaven and the Daityas;
and their various beautiful portions in the Nandana groves and other such places.
On this earth, for kings who desire victory over one another and who have war as their companion,
the practice of dharma is supreme.
He also saw the practice of emaciating the body by ascetics and those in the stages of life,
as well as their departure to heaven and other realms, and the succession of enjoyments therein.
The fall at the end of enjoyments, the succession of rebirths,
the downfall of sinners, and the hells with their extreme torments.
Beholding with his own eyes the coming and going of the worlds, as well as their birth, destruction, and duration, he likewise effects the transitions of time.
The leader of all beings [is he who] brings about the rising and setting, as well as the night and day in succession,
and the destruction and growth of all living creatures.
Thus the Lord, the Great God, the time of time, free from the limitations of time, dwells within the palace of the Goddess.
Of those who are bound by the limitation of time—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara;
of Indra and the others, the sages, the planets, and likewise the seers.
He is the eternal one of the seven seers, the perfected beings, and the ancestors;
he is Śaṅkara of all beings—those of the past, those of the future, and those of the present.
He performs the creation, destruction, and maintenance of time and its conceptualization for those—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara— who are deluded by his illusory powers.
Having entered the bodies, he indeed creates this world of the moving and the non-moving;
and he alone rises up, taking away the vital breaths of all beings.
He alone, having taken away the vital breaths of all beings, sets at rest,
always through the enjoyment of women, food, and drink within their respective bodies.
The conscious Lord Śaṅkara spreads supreme delight even among the insentient;
for he alone is present even in the states of waking and the rest.
Devoid of states yet abiding within all,
that very one, the Great Lord, alone sleeps among beings while they are awake.
For he alone, whose very form is bliss, by means of a single fraction of that bliss,
makes this web of the world— which is essentially dear to him— appear as a giver of suffering.
And this insentient world, though unreal, appears as if real by virtue of its own reality;
likewise, the conscious one makes everything insentient appear sentient through his own consciousness.

Though eternally unattached, Śaṅkara shines within these worlds; though impartial, the Lord of the Universe appears as if possessed of attachment—he is Śiva, the Lord of All, who dwells within the innermost core of everyone.
He is the awakener of the intellect and the thinker of the mind; he is the coming and going of the mind.
Being without breath, yet appearing in the form of breath, he is indeed beyond even space.
Brahmā, consisting of Brahman, shines as the eternal Śiva himself;
in the ultimate sense, he has neither instrument nor effect, nor any action.
While the networks of bodies decay, he remains forever undecaying;
while the world undergoes transformation, he remains established in changelessness.
His form is not visible; he is indeed Śiva alone. Even while perishing or decaying, he is indeed Śiva alone, for he is hidden in the cave of the heart, desireless, and eternally free from duality.
He is the cause of causes, for he is not great; he is beyond darkness, from whom Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and all others—the Rudras and the hosts of Maruts—proceed.
(Verse on page 177) Born from Mahādeva, there is no one else superior to him;
the Vedas, adorned with their various branches, are his very breath.
O twice-born ones, he by whose knowledge the liberation of all is attained from every side crosses over this essence-less and fear-inducing cycle of existence.
This is the Essence (Saras), by whose essence the world becomes composed of rasa;
He alone is the light of lights, the eye, and the great austerity.
That plenitude is absolute bliss; its awakening is absolute auspiciousness. That alone is neither gross nor subtle—Rudra, the destroyer of the world's suffering.
He is devoid of sense faculties, yet he is the movement of the senses; he is the Teacher, the Great Lord.
He is without appearance and without attachment, yet he is the initiator of the manifestation of the universe.
O lords of sages, the entire world—from Brahmā down to a tiny ant—dissolves into that Great God, Brahman; yet it shines forth directly within that knowledge through the power of Māyā.
Through the grace of the Great Lord, everything shines as Śiva;
that Puruṣa consists of sixteen aspects, and here there is not the slightest diversity.
For all this is indeed a modification within that which is unchanging;
O twice-born one, it has become modified through His very austerity, meditation, and worship of His own signs.
One certainly crosses over all sorrow; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
All knots are severed for one who perceives through oneness.
That very Self, Mahādeva, who exists in the form of the universe—
fire, wind, water, earth, and space (according to the reading *vidyate viyat etat*)— is Maheśvara.
The emanations of these [principles] occur in both direct and reverse order;
they are born here and dissolve back into that very Maheśvara.
Therefore, all beings are born from Him, and they also live within Him;
even the entire world of moving and non-moving things goes to dissolution in Him alone, who abides as the Lord.
"All this is pervaded by the Lord"—in Him everything proceeds;
he who knows thus through the Vedas and Vedāntas, by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Through faith in the Guru and by the Guru’s word, he is omniscient and of the nature of Śambhu;
he is both a sage and Śiva himself, the most excellent knower of the knowledge of Śiva.
Skanda said: You are without hands and feet; you are devoid of sense organs; you are form, touch, sound, smell, taste, and so forth.
You are the knower of all, yet no one knows you; no one at all knows you, the seer of seeing. 49.
"You are old, you are a child, you are a man, and you are young; you are a woman, a eunuch, yet you are nothing at all.
You are a pillar, and you appear as the world of past and future beings joined with bodies; therefore, I bow to you. (50)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Secret of the Vedas," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
Chapter Forty-Eight, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī":
Skanda said—
Such is Mahādeva, formless yet existing in embodied form.
Then the Goddess, bowing with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Mahādeva.
The Goddess said:
O ocean of compassion, O moon of boundless nectar, O you whose head is adorned with a crest of matted locks, O you whose neck is encircled by a great garland of Brahma’s severed heads!

O supportless Mahādeva, support of the universe, O Dhūrjaṭi, whose form is beautiful bliss, for whom the Mandāra tree was won through effort [the reading "support of those who have sought refuge" is also found]. 3.
O Śiva, how did the emergence of the liṅgas on the peak of Kailāsa come about?
O Śambhu, omniscient one, my beloved, I have a great curiosity to hear this; please tell me.
O Mahādeva, the origin of the liṅgas here on the summit of the mountain has indeed occurred; O Śambhu, tell me that in detail.
Skanda—
Thus questioned by Gaurī at that time, the Great Lord Mahādeva, who is supremely compassionate,
the Soul of the Universe, Maheśvara, spoke to her with a joyful heart.
Īśvara said: Listen, O young daughter of the mountain, O girl with eyes as pure as lotuses;
this secret must be kept hidden and should not be told to just anyone.
It should be given only to my devotee; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
He who is devoted to being adorned with sacred ash and who shines solely with the *tripuṇḍra* mark—[to him it should be given].
He whose hands are marked with rudrākṣas, whose pure ornaments are rudrākṣas, who is well-pleased by the chanting of the Rudra-mantras, and who is devoted to the worship of my liṅga. || 9 ||
He who constantly lies upon ashes and is devoted to the recitation of the five-syllable mantra;
he who is well-pleased by the worship of the *bilva* tree and who is fond of worshipping the *bilva*.
He who is intent on hearing the supreme nectar-like stories of my devotion, who eats my food offerings (naivedya), and who avoids the food offerings of others;
He who is constantly absorbed in meditation on me, forever free from other meditations;
he who is devoted solely to my name and entirely devoid of other names.
He who dwells in my field, avoiding other fields;
he who is fond of my devotees, yet turns his back on the devotees of others.
O Śivā, he who constantly nourishes my devotees with wealth— or food, according to another reading—
and who is always a worshiper of Śiva, endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), [attains the highest state].
O Śivā, O Goddess of the Gods, this secret is to be revealed by me today only to those who have mastered the essence of the Vedānta; it is not for others, for it must indeed be kept hidden.
Having imparted the essence of the teaching to one who possesses knowledge, one shall attain liberation;
O fortunate one, it takes root like the seed of a banyan tree in fertile soil.
O Śaṅkarī, having bestowed this secret of Śambhu upon one who is deluded and possessed of little wisdom,
it becomes as futile as water poured into a broken jar.
O Śaṅkarī, it is the same among fools who follow the ways of beasts;
he incurs a great sin for which there is no atonement in this world. || 18 ||
Just as a donkey adorned with fragrant camphor and sandalwood might smear its own body with the dust, ashes, and dried dung of a street.
O beautiful lady, O Śaṅkarī, that which is given to one who is not established in Śambhu does not lead to benefit;
however, that which is given to one who is preeminent in Śambhu attains expansion.
Just as oil poured upon water spreads out, so too, O Goddess, this [teaching] should be shown only to the virtuous; it is most secret.
This mountain Kailāsa, covered with various groves of trees and a refuge for all the best of birds, was created by my own mind alone. || 22 ||
Endowed with excellent jewel-palaces and possessed of delightful lotus-ponds,
that mountain extends for ten million yojanas and is utterly empty.
"Though this king of mountains is delightful, adorned with ranges of forests,
and a constant refuge for deer, it appears to me utterly desolate."
Therefore, O Great Goddess, this has been well-determined by me in my mind:
all that which possesses an auspicious form indeed takes refuge in the Śiva-liṅga.
For that which is devoid of gender, O Goddess, is considered inauspicious;
whether in a village, O Goddess, or in a city, or even in a forest.
O Śivā, a place devoid of my liṅga is like a cremation ground;
however, wherever a Śiva-liṅga may be situated within a lofty temple, it is auspicious.
Whether in a village or even in a forest, that sacred field is Avimukta;
those residing in that village, even while seeing the abode of Śiva in the morning, [attain liberation].
Their connection with sin is liberated from that very day;
O Goddess, wherever there is a temple of the Liṅga—[the reading "Liṅgakula" also exists]—that land alone is indeed blessed.
Wherever there are Brahmins devoted to Śambhu, who delight in the worship of the Liṅga,
their bodies adorned with sacred ash, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and rosaries of rudrākṣa beads.

O auspicious Śivā, that place where people are devoted to the chanting of the Rudra-hymns, where they are fond of the five-syllabled mantra, and where there is a grove of Bilva trees— that is supremely blessed.
Even upon seeing him, the destruction of sins occurs in an instant;
by the mere sight of the Three-Eyed One’s emblem, sin perishes in a moment.
Fie upon the ploughshare devoid of ashes! Fie upon the village, an abode of inauspiciousness!
Fie upon a life that does not worship the Lord! Fie upon knowledge that takes refuge in the inauspicious!
O auspicious one, O daughter of the mountain, I remained established in meditative absorption for a hundred years within the Śivaliṅga family, situated in a palace of jewels.
Clad in a tiger skin, smeared with ashes and taking refuge in ashes,
his forehead was adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and he was beautified by matted locks like the Ganges and the moon.
With his body, head, and neck held erect, his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose,
meditating upon the Self by means of the self within the self alone— that state cannot be described in words.
He who is all, yet transcends all; peaceful, woven like warp and woof, eternal, unborn, undecaying, the object of aspiration, abiding in the heart, and pervading the three worlds and the universe.

Inaction, which cannot be expressed by mind, speech, or the Vedas; which transcends the treasury [of the senses], yet shines as that very treasury; and which is devoid of space, time, and other such categories.

Neither gross nor subtle, devoid of parts, unattached, tasteless, all-pervading, a mass of indivisible splendors [the reading "tejasām" is noted as "agandham tejasām"], yet itself devoid of splendor, transcending all qualities.
It is devoid of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader; it is great and expansive.
It is bliss, the nectar of immortality, the object of enjoyment, yet free from the enjoyer, the act of enjoying, and so forth.
Free from sorrow, stainless, subtle, ungraspable, transcending the qualities (guṇas),
possessing true desires and true resolve, and devoid of the web of conceptual constructions.
I do not know anything else whatsoever that is devoid of truth, knowledge, and the rest;
I am of the nature of bliss, motionless—that I am the absolute Brahman.
(180) While I was situated in this state, a thrill of horripilation arose from my body,
born from the realization of the identity between the embodied self and the Supreme Self arising from the destruction of the notion of "I" and "mine."
O Pārvatī, from the surging ocean of my bliss, certain waves have arisen; they are the drops of sweat upon my body, which serve as the lingas established on Kailāsa.
Then, O Goddess, after some time had passed, when I had ceased from my meditative absorption,
I beheld all those things in the form of lingas, O Daughter of the Mountain.
O Śaṅkarī, upon those whose crests are wreathed in flames white as the rising moon,
there are three principal [shrines] headed by Kailāseśvara, along with more than ten million others.

Adorned with crowns, necks, and thighs as beautiful as the essence of the finest jewels, and provided with palaces featuring massive domes and great gate-towers, they were further graced by the weight of divine offerings.
Having seen that family of liṅgas— which bestows auspiciousness— with their crowns of bilva and mandāra flowers and their hoods serving as crowns, he was filled with wonder.
That liṅga on Mount Kailāsa is worthy of worship; you too should worship them.
This task is dear to me, performed for the sake of worldly sport and diversion.
This has been told to you, O Goddess; it must not be disclosed to just anyone.
If this primordial teaching offered to those who are not of Śambhu’s lineage should prove futile, then it is like an oblation poured onto ashes by one devoid of the Vedas;
it does not grow, just as a tree born in a salty desert cannot flourish.
Nevertheless, it becomes like a blade of grass for a man devoid of fortune.
The ocean of suffering consisting of the various hells, which is not a refuge for those who do not seek Śambhu, becomes a refuge for that very person once they have cast off their heap of ashes—
provided their inner self is not swollen with the lack of hearing the nectar of my worship and sacred narratives.
How does one become turbid with the water of impurity like a pig, yet fierce like a lion? 52.
A person of poor intellect, who eats both the desirable and the detestable, does not cross the unfathomable ocean of birth, destruction, origin, prosperity, and suffering—
unless he is intent on death as his own misfortune and has abandoned the name of Śiva Maheśa.
One born in the Karaṇṭaka family is devoid of fortune and base. || 53 ||
May this nectar of the sweet names of Śiva be explained for me by those with eloquent tongues; may those who worship with auspicious bilva leaves with their two hands,
and those devoted to my stories concerning Śaṅkara, become vessels of fame through their attentive ears.
Through their well-performed deeds, they attain a supreme state that is entirely unique.

O Umā, for those who possess devotion to me as their essential core, liberation alone is attained; they possess the singular essence of happiness through the multitude of heroic, noble, youthful, and beautiful wives, and for them,
the suffering born of the fluctuations of saṃsāra between this shore and the next is certainly not found.
Those whose mental distress, passion, and other afflictions have been completely destroyed by the pollen of my lotus feet. || 55 ||
For they are indeed treasure-vases, ever resting in the surging play of the ocean of bliss and the ocean of nectar; theirs is constant happiness upon this earth,
and even at the dissolution of the body, they remain celebrated as worshippers of the Moon-crested Lord.
O Śivā, having established this Nageśvara here, let my householders dwell in my abode.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī," in the first part of the glorious Śivarahasya.
The forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Words of the God.
The Lord said: "In former times, while I was sitting comfortably in a beautiful cave on Mount Mandara,"
In the variegated cave, beautified by the boundless splendor of various excellent trees.
On the auspicious bank of a lotus pond, expansive with beautiful lotuses,
in a charming celestial garden shaded by a forest of deodar trees.
It was crowded with various perfected beings (siddhas), graced by sages and gandharvas,
and filled with clusters of flowers from the mountain peaks that had broken off in dense bunches.
In that place, which was densely covered by clusters of *muditā* bees, strewn with *śalmalī* blossoms, and filled with the exceedingly cool breeze arising from the *punnāga* trees; (4)
It was adorned with excellent peacocks, spotted deer, intoxicated monkeys, and elephants,
and beautified by the sweet warbling of male cuckoos, parrots, and cranes.
It was beautiful with the sounds of the cries of swans and cranes from the Kalahaṃsa groves,
and it was graced by gentle breezes arising from the Mandāra flowers.
What is this sound of clay drums produced by men on the horizon, [heard] by the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and the Marīci sages? (7)
With uplifted arms like clusters of rising fierce suns,
the ascetics were adorned with the splendor of matted locks shimmering upon their crests.
And by the lords of sages, whose nests were made of matted hair, who rested amidst the breezes arising from the wings of birds, and whose bodies were warmed by the rays of the sun; (9)
It was filled with hundreds of beautiful peaks, resplendent with emerging mountain ridges,
and perfumed by the excellent incense arising from forest fires produced by *tagara* and *agaru* resin.
Seated comfortably with you in an excellent palace smeared with fragrant pastes,
he wears a crest-jewel fashioned from a crescent moon white as the rising rays of the moon.
Adorned with bracelets that bowed before the jewels on the hoods of the royal serpents,
wearing a great necklace of serpent-kings, blue-throated, and three-eyed.
Maheśvara, who has a tiger skin as his upper garment, who bears matted locks as yellow as the Gaṅgā, whose arms are adorned with a trident, and who holds a deer in his hand. (13)
Deluded by my very own māyā are the gods—Rudra, Indra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Mitra, Soma, Bhaga, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Gandhavaha (Vāyu), as well as Anala, the Vasus, and the Maruts. (14)

Then all those best of gods, having bowed with palms joined in reverence, spoke: "We have been overwhelmed by your splendor and are terrified by my great majesty. (Note: There is a variant reading, *mām āhu rojasā*, meaning "they said to me with vigor.")
The gods said: Who are you? What is your form, O sole source of manifold wonders?
You are naked, O Lord of the lords of gods, with the head of Brahmā as a beautiful garland around your neck. (16)
Three-eyed, the consumer of poison, blue-throated, and the benefactor Śaṅkara, whose neck shines with the luster of a jewel-garland set within his great serpent-bracelet. || 17 ||
You always wear the ashes produced from the cremation ground;
O Mahādeva, you have matted hair and a great bull for your vehicle.
You are fond of the skins of the fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, and bull;
you eternally wear the elephant hide, and you are the eternal one with the moon upon your head. 19.
O Maheśvara, you are the bearer of the great trident with the young deer;
you are the enjoyer of the universe, whose left side is graced by a single, radiant beloved.
You shall always be fond of the mountains and you will move about unattached;
O Lord, the multitude of your hosts cannot be calculated.
O Lord of Gods, O ocean of compassion, tell me: what is your ultimate state?
You possess a physical body, and thus your true nature cannot be fully known.
Deluded by the nooses consisting of your māyā, we— the gods and the Brahmins—
behold you as a corporeal being and worship you accordingly.
O elephant-faced one, O six-faced one, you are filled with affection for your two sons;
we recognize you as the God of gods, free from the six waves of worldly existence.

And we all— the guardians of the world, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, the Rudras and others, the protectors of the quarters, the planets, the lunar mansions, the constellations, and the gods— [are present].
Brahmā creates the worlds, Viṣṇu protects the universe, and Rudra destroys it at the end, along with Candra, Indra, and the leaders of the gods. [The reading "Indro 'yaṃ suranāyakaḥ" is also found.]
In battle, the Lord of the World, the consumer of oblations, slays all the Daityas;
and the Viśvedevas and the Ṛbhus also drink the Soma at the sacrifice.
O Śambhu, by Your command, the Aśvins drink the Soma, as do the Vasus;
thereafter, O Śambhu, the Sun protects [the world] with his rays.
The Lord of Night is always the Moon, as well as the stars and other planets;
Indra, Agni, the Son of the Sun (Yama), Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Marut,
Yakṣendra who is the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and this Īśāna— such is Maheśvara.
The Manus and the sages likewise attend to their respective duties.
This entire assembly of stars and even these fourteen worlds—you are beyond them all; who are you, O Lord? Tell me now.
O Lord, manifest also those deeds of yours that transcend the universe;
for you are not merely beyond the world, O God, you are indeed superior to the universe.
O Lord, how is it that you, though formless, appear as if possessing form?
Though you are not attached to the qualities (guṇas), you appear as if possessed of qualities. || 33 ||
O Lord of beings, you transcend the universe, yet you appear as if you possess the universe;
O Lord of gods, though devoid of qualities, you appear as if you possess qualities.
Dwelling upon the summit of Mount Kailāsa with this Goddess,
you are yet always destitute of possessions, even as the source of the nectar of all good fortune.
Indeed, those who are fixed upon the edge of vision become lords;
for even the gods, asuras, gandharvas, humans, and even animals [are so].
Wherever you take delight with all the Pramatha lords, accompanied by Skanda and Heramba, through your supreme compassion for everyone; [there you are most excellent].
O Maheśvara, today your boundless deeds have become an object of knowledge;
O Blessed One, you are praised by the Vedas, yet you do nothing at all.
Your liṅga is worshipped with bilva leaves by all the gods, asuras, and eminent sages; indeed, you are their liberator.
O Maheśvara, what use have you for snares consisting of the web of worldly existence?
O Blessed One, you are fond of ashes; your compassion is indeed directed toward those who abide in ashes.
Those who wear rudrākṣa beads are indeed the best among your devotees;
and for those devoted to the five-syllabled mantra, you are always the granter of liberation.
O Śaṅkara, you destroy the nets of sin for those whose minds are intent upon explaining the meaning of the Rudrādhyāya and devoted to its recitation.
O Blessed One, you are fond of devotion; we have been deluded by your māyā, and with our hearts filled with doubt, O Maheśvara, we question you.
O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, please tell us by what grace you possess such a form;
for in the worlds you appear as if you were truly endowed with beauty, just like us.
O Maheśvara, you dwell amidst the enjoyments of women, food, drink, and so forth, yet you are subject to old age and death; for you are always equal toward both enemies and friends.
O Lord, you who have taken away the hearts of the demon lord Tripura, Yama, Andhaka, Gaja, and others—you are supreme;
how then could we ever be so?
The conduct of Śambhu is seen; tell that by the power of his compassion.
Skanda said:
Thus questioned by the gods who were deluded in this manner, Maheśvara spoke to them;
O Sage, listen to that which originates from the Vedas and Vedāntas.
The Lord Viśvākṣa is indeed possessed of arrows and is renowned as the soul of all; he is the thousand-faced one among the hosts of Rudras, the omnipresent possessor of power who,
though alone, sports within the various forms created by the world as the soul of all.
In that same way, he remained there on that excellent mountain with Śiva, overflowing with the essence of playful delights. || 49 ||
In one place the Blessed One sports with his retinue in a lofty palace; in another, he sports with his entire entourage amidst special marks of honor;
and in another, he sports in a blue palace, stationed at a window.
In some places he sports upon a couch of flowers, [partaking] in the delicious essence of conversation.
Sometimes standing still, sometimes running after a deer with bow and arrow in hand;
sometimes he plucks flowers from the clusters of flowering trees for the Goddess;
and sometimes he sits talking while the Goddess plunges into the lake.
In some places with flowers and fragrances, and in others with dwellings made of networks of jewels.
In one place he watches a dance, and in another he listens to the sounds of the lute; in one place he eats food and sports on swings with Śivā;
in one place he plays at dice, and in another he is joined by the hallīsaka dance.
It was a dwelling with excellent windows fashioned from great jewels. || 52 ||
Constantly tossing his play-ball upward, as if contemplating the world’s reverence for the Goddess as being one with his own self— even though he is truly one, appearing in manifold forms—
thus does the Lord dwell perpetually upon the Kailāsa mountains.
What deed of such a Bhavānī shall I praise here today? || 53 ||
Therefore, I shall somehow speak a little—or perhaps only of the deeds of Hara—impelled suddenly by the very devotion of worshipping the lotus feet of Śambhu. (54)
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Words of the Deity," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The fiftieth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Sura.
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of the gods, Śiva—stainless and pure—[responded].
Overcome by the essence of compassion, he [addressed] the gods who were trembling and struck with awe.
O Śivā, having heard these words of the hosts of gods, "O Lord!", I,
O Goddess, with a gentle smile upon my lips, was filled within with wonder and bliss.
O Mother, perceiving that they were deluded by my māyā, I then spoke to them:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others—Indra, Agni, Anila, and Mitra."
O Vasus, headed by the Aśvins, all you Bhagas and Ādityas, Maruts, and entire host of Ṛṣis—
listen to my universal selfhood, through ignorance of which gods and demons [have come to conflict].
(Verse 185) Deluded by my māyā, you are high-born and most excellent;
yet all of you, including everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, are but bound souls (paśus).
Binding the gods and asuras with the snares of my illusory power and my desires,
I sport together with the Goddess in this world of the moving and the unmoving.
I alone, permeated by devotion, am the liberator of all the gods;
yet you, failing to recognize my true form, perceive me as a mere physical body.

Having seen my various activities governed by the qualities (guṇas), and knowing me to be deeply attached to sense objects, those who have transcended the qualities have fallen into the utmost delusion.
I shall remove that very thing this very day; listen to my supreme knowledge, which is more secret than the secret, as it resides in the Atharvaśiras.
Born from the crest of all the Vedas, the direct destroyer of ignorance,
I alone exist without support, forever like space.
O gods, my mind is never at all tainted by the organs of action,
nor by the aggregates of the great elements, nor by time, nor by the directions.
In reality, I am the unconditioned, unattached, and disease-free Supreme Self; I am the unmanifest who dwells within all.
I am the beginning, I am the middle, and I am the eternal end;
yet, through my activities, I am not the Lord who causes the birth, destruction, and other states of the world.
O gods, from me alone the entire universe arises; in me alone this world remains.
Indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Indra, and yourselves exist only through me.
"O gods, you have indeed emerged from this web of the world;
O gods, I am Soma, the progenitor of all of you."
That entire world of moving and non-moving beings exists within me alone along with you;
there is nothing whatsoever separate from me, nor is there any diversity here at all.
Having realized me, they know this entire universe as the one eternal reality;
O gods, what delusion can there be here once my oneness is fully understood?
Indeed, for those who know me, there is always supreme peace;
such gods are never overcome by the knots consisting of actions performed out of desire.
"O gods, you are indeed bound here helplessly by my *māyā* through words consisting of the *guṇas*; that fruit is obtained in heaven."
In whatever way the gods approach me through various modes of worship,
even so do I fulfill them today, according to their respective dispositions.
In that very same way, I impel him today; he becomes devoted to egoism, and not recognizing me as the impeller, he thinks, "I am the doer. (21)
O gods, take refuge in Him who manifests the qualities of all the senses yet is devoid of all senses; the Lord and Master of all, the cause of all. (22)
Without hands or feet, I am devoid of speed; yet, unwearied, I see.
I am without eyes or ears, and I transcend both mind and vital breath.
All this is to be pervaded by me; having known me, one is liberated.
Indeed, it is I alone who cognizes within all bodies.
No god whatsoever knows me, even one who is disciplined in yoga—[the reading is "for the sake of liberation"]. For I am eternally the refuge of all and the support of all, O best of beings.
I am devoid of the five sheaths and have transcended the five elements;
I have transcended the five vital breaths—O gods, where then is this body and these senses?
(Verse 27) Always impartial toward all beings, [the yogi remains] undisturbed by the worldly joys and sorrows as well as by the six waves [of mental fluctuation].
I am not at all smeared by bodies, for I abide without a head;
just as the sun sets all the world in motion through its activities.
And just as that [world] is devoid of activity, so do I abide as the witness, free from the body, vital breaths, mind, and the various phenomena arising from the ego-sense. (29)
O gods, there is no stain upon me from either dharmas or the snares of sin;
I am the ultimate wood, I am the supreme, and I am the illuminator even among the insentient. (30)
Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises;
out of fear indeed do the moon and Yama exist; out of fear this entire world stands still.
I am the light of lights here; I transcend both the manifest form and the formless. Neither unity, nor duality, nor multiplicity exists for me at all.
O gods, there is neither liberation nor bondage in me, the Lord of all;
O deities, I am the plenitude of all things, devoid of both witness and the witnessed.
Neither the atom nor the great, neither devoid of qualities nor possessed of qualities; neither illusion nor the magician, nor anything at all, nor even I myself as the Lord.
I am this supreme bliss; I am the essence pervading all things.
O gods, I alone am always all this, beginning with Brahmā.
All of you together are indeed the boundary-ground; for I alone am it—not by Vedic doctrines or Vedānta, nor by the words of a guru, nor by sacrifice, but by my own will.
"O gods, not even a single person attains this through ritual action or austerity;
rather, O deities, choose only my devotee, for it is solely by my grace."
Does anyone truly know the culmination of the Self through every aspect of being, or not?
Yet, the evil-minded person leads the meaning of the Vedāntas in a contrary direction.
Without knowing me, one will certainly not be liberated from the floods of suffering.
O gods, listen as I describe my supreme majesty,
by the attainment of which no other gain can be obtained through my grace.
One should reveal this only to those who are constantly devoted to the embers.
This is revealed for those whose foreheads shine with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
this is revealed for those whose great bodies are adorned with rudrākṣa beads. || 41 ||
This is revealed for those who are devoted to the Rudrādhyāya;
this is revealed for those who desire the worship of my liṅga [with means such as bilva leaves, according to the variant reading].
For those whose minds are solely intent on the recitation and meditation of the excellent five-syllable mantra,
knowledge born from the crest of the Vedas arises within them as brahmins.
This is revealed to those who are devoted to the field of Śiva,
who possess exclusive devotion toward me, their teacher, and who are constantly intent upon the Vedānta.
This is revealed to those gods who are single-minded, who are always free from crookedness, and who are truly devoted to my name.
For those who consider this to be the most excellent among all the hosts of gods,
and who are indeed devoted to the intermediate state— for them this is revealed.
At midday, one should contemplate the essential meaning and purport of the Vedas and Vedānta;
for those who are unable to do so, contemplation of my own form awakens that [realization]. (47)
One should meditate upon me, Nīlakaṇṭha, the three-eyed one with the moon as my crest-jewel,
whose form has Umā as half of his body, and who resides within the temple of the lotus of one's own heart.
O gods, by constantly cultivating that [knowledge] with disciplined application, one shall attain it;
indeed, his knowledge will certainly become direct perception.
O gods, in this way, knowledge is difficult to attain for those devoid of the means of accomplishment;
it is heard through the states of the guru’s mouth, by means of the intellect, and through the comprehension of words and their meanings.
Devoid of my grace, whether he be a householder, an ascetic, or a forest-dweller, he shall not attain that knowledge even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Therefore, he would certainly not attain that knowledge which directly liberates one from saṃsāra. || 52 ||
In whatever village or city there are those who are constantly familiar with the boundless conduct of the Śaivas,
who are devoted to the chanting of the Rudrādhyāya, who respectfully apply the cool and shining sacred ash as the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
and who are indeed ardent worshippers of the liṅga of Śambhu— they are by no means afflicted by disease.
From whom they experience fear, or [fear] arising from the destruction of birth, old age, and disease. || 53 ||
O gods, this knowledge is exceedingly difficult to obtain; through devotion to me, it generates both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It is the primordial, stainless [truth], eternally contained within the ocean of nectar consisting of the well-reasoned words of the Guru. (54)

It is said that this [teaching], which pierces the heart of the bondage of those whose merits have ripened, is obtained by someone through the power of my compassion; for it cannot be attained by gods, nor by any other path, nor by ritual action. (55)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Instruction to the Gods," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya. || 50 ||
The fifty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of the Śruti.
The Lord said: "O best of sages, listen as I shall describe my divine manifestations (vibhūti)."
O best of gods, having known which, there remains nothing further to be known.
I alone am the support of all, and I am the impeller of the universe;
I am this entire universe, and into me alone does it finally dissolve.
I am the creator and the ordainer; there is no one else whatsoever other than me.
