We worship Him who wears the king of serpents as a necklace, who bears the fire of great poison, who is the excellent deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence, and who is terrifying to the great forces of evil;
we worship the destroyer of Death himself, the bestower of the state of Maheśvara, the leader of the lords of gods and demons, whose body is half-formed by his matted-hair consort. (p. 216) 19.

I always worship with my heart Śiva, who is accompanied by the Maruts, whose great splendor fills the space between his arms, who is the friend of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), whose face is beautiful like that of a well-bred horse, who is ever intent upon the three worlds, who is averse to those with outward-turned faces, whose face is smiling, and who is the destroyer of all misery and evil countenances. 20.
One should meditate in the heart upon Him who is the friend of the friend of the peacock (the wind), who is the friend of the waters, and whose face dances toward all beings.
The Rudras [praise Him]:
Whose limbs are smeared with the ashes of the God of Love, which were reduced to ash by the mere spark of the corner of His eye;
whose inner heart is like the sun; who dwells in the luster of the moon; and who is worshipped by Him whose vehicle is a bird (Garuḍa). 22.
I worship Śiva, who has entered the eyes [of Śivā] and whose body is Śivā’s; whose head is joined with the feet of the one worshipped by Brahmā (Viṣṇu);
who is the teacher of Dakṣa, the most skillful; who rests upon the back of the great bull; who loves the bird-vehicle (Garuḍa); and who is worshipped by Viṣṇu (Adhokṣaja). 23.
I worship Him who is devoid of heart and eyes yet remains unimpaired, who is free from decay and the like, and who is utterly devoid of indifference toward the multitude of His devotees.

I eternally worship within my heart the Lord Virūpākṣa, who bears the moon upon his crest, whose forest-like eyes have made the sun their friend, whose form is invisible even to a hundred thousand unimpaired eyes, and who possesses three eyes.
O Ādityas,

[we praise] Him whose divine lotus-feet serve as sandals for the quarters, who are honored by the songs of those dwelling in all the worlds under the leadership of the Lord of Gaṇas, and who have become the guests of the quarters.
I ever worship the Lord who resides upon the head of the Night-Lord (Śiva), which is like the sun, and from whose crest the river of celestial collyrium flows forth.
Gaṇeśa—He who has completely dried up the entire multitude of manifested worlds, leaving only a residue; who nourishes the desires of the sages; who is adorned by the great serpent Śeṣa;
who dries up the waters of the ocean; whose eyes are exceedingly pleasing; who draws forth the great masses of clouds; and whose roar is like that of lightning. (26)
I worship the speaker of the Vedas, the cause of the creation of the Creator.

Skanda: [I bow to Him] whose chest bears a pair of firm breasts like stars, whose beautiful eyes are filled with compassion for those afflicted by the heat of the summer season, who has cast out the multitude of evils, who is endowed with mercy toward His own devotees, who is exceedingly fond of the ashes of the sacred axle (the *akṣa* tree), and whose neck is encircled by a dark cloud-like hue.

I worship Sadāśiva, the dense mass of inner consciousness, who always dwells within my heart; he whose circle of skulls, from which the seed-syllables of the ritual emerge, resounds upon the tips of his nails.
(p. 217) Nandīśvara:
[He is] the one who causes the moving and the unmoving to tremble, the sustainer of the source of the earth, the destroyer of night-stalkers, the four-faced...

I worship Śiva, who is praised by the multitude of lotus-faces of Brahmā, whose domain is pure discernment, who is the object of the five faces [of Śiva], who is perfectly immovable, who is fanned within the heart by a multitude of beautiful whisks, and who rides upon the great bull. 30.

And Caṇḍī [worships] Śiva, who is exceedingly fierce, who wears the elephant-hide from the slopes of Hari’s matted locks (or, according to another reading, who wears the hides of the multitude of male and female dancers), whose heart-slope is the haughty swan, and who dwells at the root of the great banyan tree. 31.

Bhṛṅgī [praises him who is] Mṛḍa, the firm one, the most powerful, firmly seated deep within the heart; whose face is beautifully arrayed even for the utterly deluded; who is gratified by a multitude of ritual acts;
who is the friend of the unmarriageable Daughter of the Mountain; and who has fully grasped what lies hidden within the heart.
The sounding of the ḍhakkā drum arising from the light produced by the great hand-lotus. || 32 ||
Ishvara: O Shive, it is said that when the gods, their purpose unfulfilled, were performing the rite of churning the ocean of milk with Vāsuki as the rope and Mount Mandara as the churning-stick;
From that lotus as well arose a multitude of great jewels and a herd of cows;
and from the lord of herbs (the moon) were born the celestial tree and the deer-marked one (the moon).

Seeing that [poison] spread abroad, its flames variegated by the smoke of uprooted *kālakūṭa* and surpassing all [other fires], and seeing the multitudes of gods and demons rendered utterly terrified and fleeing in all directions, I alone felt compassion.
Having swallowed it, I became one whose throat was dark-blue, praised by the entire assembly of gods. (34)

With the arrangement of his crest being the collection of clever words free from deceit, he steals away the passion for the multitude of rivers; having manifested the pride of the earth through the skin of the elephant’s temples, he displays the pride of dancing upon the lotus-hearts of the far-reaching hypocrites. 35.
In the fierce whirling dance of Bharga, who is addicted to the grand display of his twilight *tāṇḍava*, there arise merely the gale-winds from the regions of his dancing, fiercely circling arms;
by the sudden force of these winds as they surge upward, the mountain ranges within the battle arrays are instantly [shattered]. (p. 218)
Then, while the clouds were being struck by Indra, that thunderbolt was beheld once more.

All the gods said: "O Maheśa, by worshipping your linga may we live for a hundred autumns; O Śambhu, O All-pervading Lord, may we always utter your names, and through you, may we delight your devotees."
May we, being meritorious and free from sin, behold daily the Linga whose head is adorned with the finest Bilva leaves, hear its sacred stories, and remain so every day. (37)

I bow to the primordial God, the sustainer of the earth-supporter (the mountain), the Great Lord (Maheśa), who dwells as the friend of the friend of the lord of the flow of wealth (Kubera), whose pair of eyes is like the moon and snow-medicine (camphor), and who is accompanied by the daughter of the snowy mountain (Pārvatī). 38.
Īśvara:

This is my *liṅga*, whose crest has ascended far beyond the shell of the cosmic egg, having passed through the netherworld which was split open by the digging of the earth, and where the world-dance of the people—shaped like tortoises clinging to the lips of their backs—is performed; it remains unseen by the eyes of the world-protectors. (39)
O Umā, the worship of that Liṅga must be performed through an extensive path of words pregnant with the established conclusions of the Upanishadic scriptures.
Only a rare few do so, and not even they without my grace; for some gods are indeed already filled with the essence of devotion.

O Śivā, when the quarters of the sky— whose singular boundary is the mass of darkness illuminated by the fierce-rayed sun— become as if lit by the glow of fireflies through the entire net of your divine manifestations,
how could even the Nimba tree become equal to the celestial tree? Therefore, may I be blessed.
How can ignorance be equal to knowledge? And how could Viṣṇu and the others be his equals? || 41 ||

May this abode of my desire, which has its crest in the form of a linga transcending the sky, its base rooted in the depths of the excellent netherworld (Pātāla), and all directions whitened by its splendor, be equal to your face. 42.

The hosts of gods, their heads bowed toward the surface of the earth and filled with an abundance of joy, beheld the Lord in the sky, blazing with boundless splendor, with their hands joined in reverent salutation.
Sūta:
[I bow to] Him who has the celestial water-lily as His moon-like head, whose crown is the abode of the Moon, who is the limit of the quality of sweetness, who is sung by Bhūman, Sāman, and others;

who possesses a body as soft as a flower, who is both the Terrible One (Bhīma) and the Lord (Īśa), the Moon (Soma), who is far removed from the path of the wicked-minded, the granter of desires, and the destroyer of desire. (44)
I bow to him whose venerable feet are worshipped by those with eyes as pure as lotuses; who is the great ornament upon the slopes of the matted locks of the enemy of Kamalā;
who possesses the lofty grace of the Ganges flowing through his tresses; and whose feet are worshipped by the sage born from a water-jar (Agastya).
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Praise of All the Gods," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
The fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of My Own Characteristics.
Jaigīṣavya said: "Oh, by means of immersing oneself in the nectar of the stream of the great bliss of knowledge..."
Their hearts were immersed in bliss, and their misfortunes were destroyed by the knowledge of Śiva. || 1 ||
We are blessed, there is no doubt, for we are uniquely abundant in the bliss of the aggregates;
however, tell me now, what is that *liṅga* which was spoken of by Maheśa?
What is that linga, who is the possessor of the linga (lingin), and who is the worshiper of that linga?
What is attained through the worship of the linga? Tell me this now in detail.
By the streams of the nectar of your speech, the forest fire of my sins has been extinguished,
and my mind has become perfectly tranquil, moving upon the waves of the great ocean of bliss.
Sūta said:
His inner heart overflowing with the waves of Jaigīṣavya’s words,
Skanda, for whom the Mandāra tree was made to rejoice, [revealed] that supreme secret of the Lord.
What was told to the Goddess by the God, he then related to Śambhu.
Skanda said: O Sage, just as you have asked this question which is difficult for all to cross,
so too was the Blessed One questioned after seeing him upon the summit of Kailāsa.
And having bowed to the Kailāseśvara Liṅga with devotion worthy of praise. || 8 ||
The Goddess said:

The Linga on the crest of Kailāsa, which alone brings an end to the boundless torment produced by worldly existence, which is the sole bee upon the lotus of my heart, and whose head is more beautiful than the sun, the moon, and the fire; [that Linga...]

Tell me of that union with meditation which is the destroyer of worldly existence—the union with the Śārṅga [Viṣṇu], which is solely attached to the bliss of dhyāna, which is unattached even to the destruction of the various births and old ages [of transmigratory life], and which is peaceful, being solely attached to the inner self. (9)

Indeed, O Blessed One, this Liṅga of yours has certainly not been seen by the various lords of men, nor by Viṣṇus and Rudras, nor by the hosts of the best of immortals, nor by the multitudes of Daityas and Gandharvas, nor by the throngs of the assembly of excellent sages, nor even by Skanda, Heramba, and the others. || 10 ||

How is it that one endowed with love beholds this face of the Fireless One (Analākṣa) through self-restraint, observances, austerity, supreme generosity, or sacrifices; or by the penance of a hundred births? O Maheśa, is there anyone at all in the abode of the three worlds who is able to see You, the Lord?
"O Śambhu, tell me in private: what indeed is this wonder? For even I, O Blessed One, did not recognize your linga."
Skanda—

having heard these words of his mother, the moon-crested Lord, whose heart was exceedingly beautiful, then gazed upon his mother with deep reverence, his lotus-face adorned by a swarm of bees that were his most languid eyes.
Hara, the sun to the lotus of the Vedānta and the foundational support of the three worlds, Śaṅkara, whose face was like a blossoming and enchanting lotus, spoke joyfully to the Goddess.
Bowing down once more, that goddess spoke to the Lord, the enemy of Kama.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, supreme among the most compassionate!
What is that *liṅga*, who is the *liṅgin*, and what is called a *liṅga* in the world? (15)
O Śaṅkara, what is the linga and who is it that worships the linga?
Please explain that to me in due order, if you have favor toward me. (16)
Skanda:
Thus, in the past, the Goddess questioned Maheśa, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
and Śipiviṣṭa related that meritorious narrative to her.
With his heart fixed upon the Goddess, the eight-formed Lord, being highly pleased, spoke to the Goddess with delight; listen to that, O best of the Gaṇas. (18)
This eternal secret must be kept hidden by the followers of Śambhu from the lords of the gods, the lords of the sages, and indeed from anyone else who is devoid of knowledge. (19)
Īśvara said:
O Queen of the Gods, O Aparṇā, listen attentively to the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the Liṅga as it is spoken by me out of affection; hold it in your heart. (20)
This secret of mine must never be told to anyone under any circumstances. O Śivā, it is called a *liṅga* because of its being the place of dissolution for all the worlds.
It makes the hidden meaning understood; therefore it is called a *liṅga*.
And because it goes (*gacchati*) to the play (*lāma*) of the world, it is so called. || 22 ||
Therefore, O Dear One, the wise know that the *liṅga* is devoid of the *bindu*;
and I shall now describe its worship, as well as the worshipper in particular. (23)

The *liṅga* is devoid of the three qualities (*guṇas*), free from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, and is without a pedestal (*pīṭha*) or a deity seated upon it (*pīṭhya*), being entirely devoid of both the object of worship and the act of worship.
Devoid of meditation, objects of meditation, and the like, it is without qualities and beyond darkness;
it is free from the arising, abiding, and destruction that cause the birth of the world.
Beginning with the syllable Oṃ and accompanied by the Praṇava, yet devoid of the three morae;
free from existence and non-existence, and transcending both existence and non-existence.
It is devoid of awakening, the object of awakening, and so forth; it is free from the pervaded and the pervader;
it is bereft of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower; and it is free from both the fragmented and the whole.
It is devoid of origination, destruction, concealment, and so forth;
it is free from meditation, the object of meditation, and the like; it is far removed from great meditation. (Note: There is a reading "mamādhyānavidūragam" [far removed from my meditation].)
Devoid of the characteristics of the unperceivable and free from the cowherds and cowherdesses;
it is neither being nor non-being, nor both being and non-being, nor even that which is not non-being.
It is the vision of one's own Self alone, devoid of mere existence and the like;
it is free from both manifestation and non-manifestation, and everything is illumined by its own radiance.

It is devoid of a master or a servant, free from the perishable and the imperishable, devoid of the moving and the unmoving, and free from means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth. || 31 ||
This is directly the witness, devoid of the witness and the witnessed, and so forth;
it transcends the *bindu* and the *nāda*, and it transcends the reflected image (*bimba*), being devoid of appearance and the like.
It is neither visible nor invisible, devoid of the grasped and the grasper;
it is beyond the ninefold speech, inaccessible to words, and incomparable.
It is neither mind nor that which is attainable by the mind; it is neither breath nor that which awakens the breath;
it is neither the eye nor that which is devoid of form, being entirely free from the knowledge of the visible.
The ear is not devoid of hearing, for it is space, incomparable;
nor is the nose devoid of smell, for it is inseparable from earth.
Indeed, O Śivā, that [consciousness] is devoid of taste, free from the location of the tongue and so forth, and it is indeed devoid of the hands, feet, anus, and the vital airs.
It is devoid of form, taste, smell, and so forth, as well as sound and touch;
it is neither space nor non-space, yet it is the cognizer even of space.
It is not earth, yet it is devoid of derivative elements and free from solid density;
it is not fire, yet it is devoid of heat and is the activator of all light.
Nor is air dependent on motion, for that [motion] merely awakens the air;
nor is this water directly capable of causing the liquefaction of water.
Devoid of the primary elements, yet the source of the primary elements, the beginning of all beings, and eternal;
it is without hands, feet, or face, and is devoid of eyes and ears.
Transcending the qualities of all the senses, devoid of all the senses,
the Lord and Master of all, the refuge and friend of all.
Charming with the qualities of all the senses, eternally beautiful and ever-arisen,
it is established upon a divine throne within the house of the nine gates.

That which is without support, yet worthy of trust; whose hands and feet extend everywhere; whose head is the universe and whose seat is the universe; that which is beyond even the highest of universal seats.
Nothing whatsoever appears there as a form, for beyond that there is nothing else;
it is that which is to be known through the Vedānta, devoid of qualities, that which transcends speech, and from which this manifold world has indeed arisen. (44)
In which Liṅga this [consciousness] resides, and in which Śiva the universe is dissolved;
that upon which this entire world, consisting of the three qualities, revolves as its support.
Indeed, by whom can the dimensions of that Liṅga be described?
It is devoid of all measurement and transcends the three divisions of qualities.
O Maheśvarī, that Liṅga, which exists above the undivided, single-mass Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa),
has neither a foundation nor a location.
O Great Goddess, it does not reside in the *ālaya*; O Mother, it is all-pervading, great, the great treasury of all beings, and situated within the inner sanctum.
Subtler than the subtle, yet greater than the great;
the support of all, yet itself unsupported; the universal form, the illuminator.
One should realize the Self as pure consciousness, self-luminous, devoid of the distinctions of individual soul (jīva) and Lord (īśa),
the inward-facing awareness, a mass of bliss, and non-dual.
That Liṅga, which is free from the network of pedestals arising from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others,
is to be known solely by one's own self and is established within oneself alone.
In that state is supreme bliss; therein there is nothing whatsoever.
When that sign (liṅga) has been seen, the seer assumes the form of the sign.
Even one who possesses signs becomes signless through the constant cultivation of those very signs;
others do not see that sign, and no others at all understand it.
That Liṅga is supreme bliss, devoid of flavor yet transcending all flavor;
it is to be worshipped always by all, for nothing whatsoever surpasses it.
There is no greatness whatsoever for him who is established in his own majesty;
the Linga, which resides in the hearts of all, is eternal and the illuminator of all.
Free from distinctions of states, it is the interior of the chamber within Māyā;
it is eternally worshipful and devoid of the six, the three times, and so forth.
It has entered the mass of its own veiling darkness, illuminating itself with its own light.
Therein, speech or mind never exists, nor is there any contact with the senses, vital breaths, or elements.
It is incapable of illuminating itself, for that which is of the nature of pure vision is solitary and devoid of cognition.

Once, Brahmā and Viṣṇu—the individual soul and the Lord—having lost sight of that very Liṅga within their own hearts, were deluded by the conceit of being "the slightly knowing" and "the all-knowing," their inner selves rendered helpless by egoism and Māyā. || 59 ||

Speaking these words that act as a *japa* for becoming a *haṃsī*, the individual soul (*jīva*), submerged in the snares of delusion, has been struck down by the multitude of weapons of the practice of ego-grasping (*ahaṅgraha*) against the Omniscient One Himself who stands face-to-face—[where the reading is either *abhimukhe* or *bodha*]. (60)

Then Viṣṇu, who was wise regarding the Lord yet ignorant of his true nature, and he whose inner self was under the sway of egoism, said, "I am the Lord of all," and having thus spoken, he whose characteristic signs were visible addressed what was known. (61)
And so they fought with false weapons; behold those two, blinded by delusion!
O Bhavānī, when they occasionally cast off their delusion, Vidhi and Viṣṇu beheld the perishable and the imperishable.
"O Mother, let us two be free from delusion; having seen this, they both said:
'Having beheld this Liṅga, let us again behold its crown and its base with the nooses produced by Māyā. (63)

When they beheld that the Liṅga had no end, no base, and no summit, and had come to rest within Śiva, those two—bearing bodies in the form of a boar and a swan—praised the Liṅga and then desisted. (p. 223) 64.
The individual soul and the Lord— those two,
the perishable and the imperishable, Hari and Brahmā— having meditated upon the God as Śiva by means of the mantra called Haṃsa,
they then perceive the Lord who is both the knower and the ignorant, the ruler of the earth, whose form is beyond all forms, and whose nature is like that of space. || 65 ||
Then, freed from delusion and devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), those two became non-existent; for here there is nothing at all.
That very state is my *liṅga*, O Goddess; it is not a *liṅga* for men who are weary with the toil of ritual worship, O Śivā.

O Bhavānī, for the sake of crossing the ocean of worldly existence, people should worship with bilva leaves the stone, metal, or clay liṅga, as well as the Bāṇaliṅga, whether it be mobile or fixed, and even the distinguished liṅgas. 67.

O Śivā, the worship of the talliṅga can never be performed by such men, nor by gods, nor by the foremost of the Gaṇas and brahmins, even through various means such as gifts, austerities, fasting, and the like.
O Bhavānī, I shall now describe that secret worship, which is always accessible only to the most wise;
that worship is attainable only by meritorious men and is unattainable by others who possess the nature of kings and sons. (69)

He was praised and worshipped by those whose faces were like lotuses born from the merit of living beings—those who, in the form of Hari as the All-Knowing One, tore asunder the mountains that served as the abode of the elements, appearing in the guise of a boar; while others, in the form of a dwarf, [praised Him] with faces like the lotuses of the merit of living beings who were but partially wise, resembling swans.
O Umā, behold with your mind the heart-linga as being of the nature of the Self; by seeing it as being of that very nature, you will become as if wonderful.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Self-Liṅga," in the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī, the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liṅgas of the Upaniṣads," the Lord said:
"I am the Lord and I am the individual soul"— thus do we both conceive of ourselves through egoism.
O Śivā, those two, Hari and Brahmā, are merely reflectors of His [Śiva's] form.
And that which is the root of their crown is proclaimed as Ahaṅkāra (the ego);
for those overcome by the pride of "I," there is no worship of Śivā.
Those who toil in the great dharma of the castes and stages of life do not worship him;
for those devoid of his worship, there is never liberation.
One may be liberated through its worship, and not otherwise even by ten million ritual acts;
the worship of my *liṅga* is superior to the worship of the forms of the gods.
O Maheśvarī, my worship of the physical liṅga with bilva leaves is indeed the worship of that liṅga through the realization of oneness with the Self, according to the traditional lineage.
O Maheśvarī, one should engage in the direct auxiliaries (*sannipatyopakāra*) and so forth; furthermore, the wearing of the *vibhūtis* is declared to be an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñāna*). (6)
The wearing of rudrākṣa beads is also declared to be an auxiliary to knowledge;
likewise, the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra is also declared to be an auxiliary to knowledge.
Furthermore, the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya is declared to be an auxiliary to knowledge;
[one should meditate on] the three-eyed Maheśvara, accompanied by Ambikā and blue-throated, O Great Goddess. (8)
The consumption of the food offering (naivedya) for the purification of the mind is ordained by the Śruti;
this is done with the mantra "tadaśyāma" and the mantra "triguṇasāta."
This sequence of ritual procedure is established by the verse beginning with "antarikṣe" and by the Jābāla Ārṣeya mantras that originate from the Kaivalya-śikhā.
Regarding the worship of the ash, the rudrākṣa, and the liṅga, and concerning the five-syllabled Rudra mantra, [the following] has been declared for Śiva:
"One should meditate upon the Lord" and "Śiva is one. (11)
Indeed, through mantras beginning with "Umāsahāyam" and the conceptualization of the limbs of meditation,
these are directly contributory acts for the worship of the Heart-Linga.
Furthermore, sacrifices, gifts, and vows bound by the rules of caste and stage of life provide assistance only indirectly;
they do not contribute directly to the worship of the Liṅga.

And this worship is not attained when it is devoid of both the object of worship and the worshiper; nor is it attained when it is lacking incense, lamps, and the like, or when it is devoid of perfumes and flowers. (14)
She who is devoid of offerings such as the sprinkling of the five nectars and food oblations, yet easily attained through mere meditation, is difficult to reach even for yogins. (15)
Seated upon the great Gaṅgā of the ford of wisdom, entirely silent,
and having bathed in the reservoir of my own self with the thought "I am eternally pure," I remain.
His form is white, smeared with the great ashes of self-knowledge;
he shines with the series of triple-crests formed by the rising light of wisdom and dispassion.
He who possesses the rosary of rudrākṣa beads through the practice of yoga consisting of peace, self-restraint, and restraint;
he who is purified by the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) of the five elements and the great principles (mahātattva). || 18 ||
He is intent on the five syllables that strive to pierce the five sheaths;
he is devoid of the five vital breaths, the mind, the qualities, and all the sense organs. || 19 ||
"I am the Lord, the supreme Brahman, devoid of the signified and the signifier;
meditating thus, my intellect is submerged in the waters of the great bliss of the realization of identity with my own Self."
He is uniquely established in the abode of the womb of great illusion from which delusion has departed;
he is devoid of the boundless, stainless knowledge residing within his own self-liṅga.
He sprinkles the five flavors of the five organs of action with the five products of the cow;
he sprinkles the five nectars that reach the further shore of the five organs of cognition. || 22 ||
The consecrator, through the repeated practice of contemplating the indivisible unity,
reveals the great fragrance of the dissolution of the mind and other such [spiritual] ointments.
One should worship the Linga of one's own Self with the unbroken grains of the realization "I am That," wrapped in the garment of the manifesting state of universal selfhood.
One should worship with bilva fruits that are the investigation of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya),
and with ornaments consisting of the Great Sayings arising from the essence of the four Vedāntas.
Having offered presentations of various foods and edibles arising from the multitude of his adorned limbs, he announced,
"I am here," with offerings of betel leaves and other services.
With bilva fruits, flowers, and lotuses born of meditative absorption from one's own self,
and through prostrations and other rites performed while free from the network of the physical body and so forth.
With songs of great joy and great torrents [of melody], with the clapping of hands, and with songs proclaiming "I have become the universe," there were dances and performances.
Having worshipped with the parasol, fly-whisks, and mirror of the renunciation of all attachments,
through the sequence of dissolution of the worshipful object, the act of worship, and the worshipper.
I am indeed nothing at all, nor is this world manifold in nature;
O daughter of the mountain king, by worshipping oneself, one truly worships that [Supreme Self].
O Śivā, for this [practice], there is no end to the worship, nor is there any conception of its dismissal;
there is no restriction of time or place, nor any requirement for the adoption of specific means of accomplishment.
At all times and with one's whole being, one should worship the mark of the Self;
this visible world of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas is the food offering presented to it. 32.
Having eaten, one obtains happiness by partaking of that food which has been offered;
thereafter, one should drink water from three conch shells, [the food] being devoid of the three qualities (guṇas) and other such attributes.
"I am Sadāśiva"— drinking this as one would a draught that leaves no residue—
thus has the worship of the Great Liṅga of the Self been described to you, O Śivā.
Thus worshipping constantly, while remaining free from the distinction between the worshipper and the object of worship,
the worshipper attains the state of being worshipped and becomes eternally identical with the Liṅga.

Indeed, this [state] is not attained through the marks of worship, nor through ritual service and the like, nor by tasting the essence of the stream of Vedānta, nor by the singular mass of merit arising from the practice of the Vedas; rather, O Śivā, it is said to be obtainable solely through my grace. (36)

It is neither the sheath of vital breath, nor the sheath of bliss, nor the sheath of consciousness, nor the sheath of food; it is neither minute nor long, neither bound nor liberated, and neither dual nor non-dual, neither the powerless nor the supreme, and neither with a location nor the Great Lord (Maheśa). (Note: "sadeśam" and "maheśam" are alternative readings. 37.
Nor is that which is pervasive—devoid of space, time, and so forth, and devoid of states and so forth—a mark (liṅga), such as taste and the like [the reading "guṇādi" is preferred].
It is beyond the qualities (guṇātīta), one, consisting of consciousness and bliss, dense, and also indivisible among those things that are always divided. 38.

Beyond mind and speech, beginningless, subtle, ever-pure and enlightened, unattached, and of great dimension; always associated with the mark yet itself signless, most exalted, the inner space within the sky, it is without contact for living beings. (39)
There is neither merit nor sin, neither birth nor death; there is no anxiety, no affliction, and neither greed nor delusion.
There is no teacher, nor indeed any disciple; thus, that which is eternally attained is not difficult to reach through the doctrines of Vedānta.
That which formerly had a thousand faces and hands, and a thousand thighs and feet, now lacks hands, feet, and faces;
likewise, that which was singular in fragrance and endowed with tastes, now lacks touch and is devoid of the nose, tongue, and other senses.
The fourth state, however, is unbroken within bodies, eternal, all-pervading, and devoid of the attributes of all bodies and the like;
likewise, it is accepted as the Self, neither inferior nor superior, beloved, and in reality endowed with all aspects. 42.
That very same [reality], devoid of all nets of enjoyments, is the singular limit of the abode of the mass of great bliss;
that alone am I, the Linga; that alone am I, the past; and this very thing is the future and the present within Śiva. (43)
That alone is the tail that is the support of all, that alone is the foundation; that alone is the primordial Brahman, and that alone, O Goddess, is You, the Sovereign.
"I am that Reality," "I am always That Reality," "I am Brahman"—by such words, [the realization] is difficult to attain. (44)
"This very [Self] is the Self; it is Brahman; I am indeed always become Brahman, and thus I shall surely be Brahman. (p.
226) "For that which is above and that which is below, O Goddess, is that very same; O Mistress, that very same is behind and that very same is in front. (45)

That very [Brahman] today has entered the worlds, as well as the intermediate spaces, the directions, the host of beings, and the network of the Vedas; it has entered the gods, the asuras, and the brahmins, pervading all things as the most excellent and the ultimate foundation.
The youngest [son], who is difficult even for the distinguished and the learned to attain, has entered Śiva and Śivā, the eyes of the world;
by His grace, the wind, the earth, as well as the sun, the moon, and the fires [exist]. (47)
By its light alone, this entire world shines, though it is eternally inert due to ignorance of it;
by its awakening alone everything shines, and upon beholding it, one indeed perceives all this.
O Gaurī, this is not the seer, nor are these two eyes; that is not form, nor is it the visible object, nor even the act of seeing.
It is neither knowledge nor ignorance; it is manifold, yet neither subtle nor gross, and devoid of atoms and the like.
It is not perceived by anyone as anything whatsoever; it is neither seen nor smelled, and it is devoid of touch, scent, sound, and the like.
This very reality resides in the hearts of the gods, situated in the cave of the heart; indeed, it is far beyond the reach of the vital breaths, speech, and even the mind.
It is neither female nor male, nor indeed neuter; for by what characteristic could it be joined?
It is neither child, nor youth, nor old man; neither long, nor short, nor both short and long; neither black nor yellow.
It is neither circular nor indeed quadrangular; it is neither above nor below, nor is it extensive.
It is that very primordial indivisible whole, devoid of parts and the like, pervading all cosmic eggs and even extending beyond them.
O Goddess, I do not see any linga here that is dry, nor moist, nor even solid;
from which Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra were born, and from which, O Goddess, the collections of the great elements arose.
By this alone do these multitudes of great worlds perpetually live, and it always remains;
likewise, at the end, they go to dissolution into that which is both with and without marks—desire to know that very Brahmanhood.
By that very [means] through which the conceptualization of all the sense-faculties is extended, one perceives form and the eye;
having seen that very stainless sign, it is not perceived as manifold, for it does not exist as something visible.
When one perceives speech and all tastes as transcending mere taste, then one beholds that very supreme, divine Linga;
and with that same excellent, divine ear, one hears this very Linga as something to be heard even today.
O Goddess, behold this very sign when one smells a fragrance;
O Goddess, behold that very sign of mine where one experiences the touch of the skin. (57)

That very thing by which the class of living beings breathes, and that sign (liṅga) which today awakens the intellect and so forth, as well as the dharma characterized by emission, bliss, and movement within the hands, feet, anus, genitals, and other organs; (pṛ0 227) [The reading is "yadeva" and "yenaiva" as well. ... 58.
People indeed recognize this as the talliṅga; for whatever is the mind, that very thing is the liṅga.
Just as rivers, flowing toward the ocean, cast off their names and forms upon reaching the shoreless sea, so too does the mind merge into that.
By beholding that Liṅga, a person transcends names and transcends forms and qualities;
for that very Liṅga transcends sound, point, and phoneme, and transcends the qualities of measures and digits.
When one repeatedly utters "Oṃ Oṃ" within the group of vital breaths and within the assembly of Vedānta,
that indeed is the Liṅga of Īśāna— the full, more than full, and perfectly full.

When there was neither darkness nor light, neither night nor day, neither being nor non-being, but that which transcends all signs—that is the Imperishable (akṣara), that is the most excellent glory of Savitṛ; from it, the ancient wisdom issued forth.
That indeed is the nest of the fire that is grasped through meditative states; it is that which brings about both existence and non-existence.
Those who know the *liṅga* situated within the creation of the *kalās*, they offer their bodies as a sacrifice.
Some, being utterly deluded, declare that the nature of things (svabhāva), Īśa, or Time is the Liṅga; others say it is the greatness of this Liṅga.
But having known the Liṅga as it truly is, one who is free from sorrow attains ultimate peace.

In which Liṅga the All-pervading ones have settled, in which this entire universe moves together and apart, from which Prajāpati—the guardian of this world and the sole creator of the multitude of beings—came into existence. (65)
This universe is indeed but a quarter of that Linga which pervaded the entire abode;
subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, that very Linga is hidden within the cave of the heart.
He, freed from sorrow, beholds that very Liṅga—the Lord, the majesty—through the clarity of his constituent elements.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and one's karmas are destroyed when the Linga, both supreme and inferior, is beheld.
That is the Great Liṅga, the light of lights and the consciousness of conscious beings;
for one who perceives that Liṅga, what delusion can there be, and what sorrow?
For those devoid of the vision of Him, there shall be calamities in birth after birth;
for they are perpetually overwhelmed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age.
Knowing the bliss of that *liṅga*, one should never be afraid;
indeed, all beings live solely by means of the bliss derived from the sight of that *liṅga*.
That Liṅga is without hands or feet, for it possesses a power that transcends the mind;
it transcends both space and time, and He alone is the primordial Lord.
One who knows that talliṅga crosses over this eternal sorrow;
know that very one as the sole liṅga established within the mind. 73.
That which is to be meditated upon is devoid of meditation, free from the object of meditation and the act of meditating,
devoid of knowledge and the object of knowledge, and free from name and form.
A certain wise person perceives that Liṅga, which is the support of infinite majesty, whose glory is unestablished [in any other], and which is unborn. (75)
When men will roll up the sky like a piece of leather, then there will be that Liṅga, facing in all directions, with its entire mass wreathed in flames.
Then, by not knowing that sign, there will be an end to suffering;
for that sign is neither "consciousness within" nor "consciousness in both."
O Goddess, that sign is neither wisdom alone nor is it devoid of wisdom;
for that sign is indeed invisible and forever ungraspable.
That sign (liṅga) is indeed the cessation of the phenomenal world and the means of realizing the one Self;
these worlds know that sign, and everything dissolves into that sign.
O Goddess, because it dissolves into that Liṅga, they call it *tajjalāni*;
that Liṅga is the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas and is established at the end of the Vedas.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are merged into that primordial nature which is the Great Liṅga;
He is that Brahman, He is Śiva himself, He is Viṣṇu, and He is the Virāṭ, the self-sovereign ruler.
O Sovereign, Mistress of the Universe, that Liṅga is visible only to those who perceive the subtle;
the wise behold that Liṅga within the heart by means of the mind alone.
O Śivā, that Liṅga has not been found even for the hearing by many;
and though they hear of the Liṅga in Śiva, many do not truly know it.
Someone beholds this as a marvel; someone hears that moving Liṅga as a marvel;
others likewise perceive that which it awakens as a marvel, and they behold that moving Liṅga as a marvel. (84)
One who is devoid of the subtle body (liṅga) does not live by means of either the inhaled breath (prāṇa) or the exhaled breath (apāna). || 85 ||
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
the unborn male, possessing the marks, rejoices in her and lies by her, yet that Self, established in its true nature, abandons her.
That Liṅga, which rests in the city and is established within all beings, should be beheld and heard by those who have mastered the Vedas. || 87 ||
O Maheśvarī, who indeed could breathe if deprived of the Liṅga?
O Ambikā, this essence (rasa) is indeed the Great Liṅga; it is always within this essence.
For this is supreme bliss; this is the self-luminous Liṅga. || 89 ||
Since there is nothing else beyond it, and nothing smaller or greater than it;
since it stands firm like a tree in heaven as the one Linga, therefore this entire universe is filled by the manifestation of that single Linga.
For words, together with the mind, turn back without reaching that Liṅga;
O Goddess, it extends beyond the cosmic egg by the measure of one finger-breadth.
In that [liṅga] the self-manifested liṅga shines; indeed, the moon, sun, and fire do not shine there.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, shines pervaded by its splendor.
Just as those moving above do not find the great golden Linga established on the earth and hidden within the cave by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), even so, O Ambikā, do you behold this Linga.
Having realized that which is the pervasive Liṅga within the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— that is "I"— the possessor of the Liṅga (liṅgin) becomes one who has transcended the Liṅga.
Just as a spider emits a web of threads and withdraws them into its mouth, so does it consume everything;
for in this same way, this web of the universe arises from the *liṅga* and consequently undergoes dissolution at the end. (95)
This eternal Liṅga is Brahman itself; through its own knowledge, it undergoes transmigratory existence and is liberated.
This very Liṅga is to be known through austerity (tapas), and not by other religious duties; and that Liṅga is, in truth, the non-Liṅga (aliṅga).
That very same Liṅga, which transcends all beings and is named Viśvanātha, is established in Avimukta;
those who perceive it as situated between the two eyebrows in Vārāṇasī by means of yoga, they depart from there [to liberation]. || 97 ||
In that very state, their liberating instruction is the Praṇava, the mantra of Brahman beginning with Oṃ.
O Goddess, his vital breath does not depart; rather, it becomes merged with that Liṅga, thus becoming "without a liṅga" (aliṅga).
There, in Avimukta, that Liṅga which transcends all greatness is to be worshipped;
O Goddess of Devas, for one who is unable to do so there, the material [Liṅga] bestows liberation on earth.
Visible to mortals by the eye, that [Liṅga] bestows liberation gradually;
yet within that extended Liṅga, there may be fear for some.
From the statement, "Therefore, from that [Brahman], this Liṅga exists as Brahman," it follows that this very supreme Brahman is the eternal Liṅga of the Self. || 101 ||
Wherein the Vedas, along with the Vedāntas, come to rest—
that stainless Liṅga in the lotus of the heart shines eternally.
That very *liṅga* is *kañca* and *khañca*, all-pervading and free from affliction;
it is a mass of bliss, non-dual, the fourth state, and beyond the mind (or, according to another reading, beyond darkness).
That [space] extends from the small [center] outward, adorned with a solar disc;
it possesses the luster of ten million moons and is visible in every way, O Śivā. (104)
Always free from delusion and fear through yoga and the contemplation of the Self.

By those ascetics of purified intellect who possess the firm conviction in the meaning of the Vedāntic wisdom through the yoga of renunciation—for them alone is this stainless abode of the Liṅga attained today in Śiva, which is not far from the attainment of the goal. || 106 ||
This wisdom is not to be attained through logic; for this mark is truly like a razor’s edge.
It has entered into that supreme, imperishable syllable of the *ṛc* verses; it is this Great Mark, devoid of beginning, creation, and the like. || 107 ||

That which is difficult to attain through liquor and the like, as well as through the rituals of non-yogins, is inevitably attained by abandoning those signs in every way; one becomes free from delusion—this is a secret revealed in the Vedas. 108.
For one who has not desisted from evil conduct, who is not tranquil, and who is not concentrated—
this all-pervading mark is difficult for such an attached person to attain.
In those whose hearts are never crooked or false, the tranquil *liṅga* shines forth within. (p.
230) Therefore, one who desires the Self—and not one who desires sense-objects—is qualified for the worship of the *liṅga*; such a person should worship the *liṅga*. || 110 ||
For this reason, O Great Goddess, it is most secret; for those established in knowledge do not perceive others at all.
There is never a teacher nor a disciple, no worship, no one to be worshipped, nor even the state of being a worshipper.
Even due to one's own fault, there is no defect in the Linga; O Bhavani, the entire world remains as it is without exception.
Even the extraordinary ornamentation of the Great Serpent (Mahashesa) is not flawed here, nor indeed is the crown of his head, which is a mine of jewels.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Upaniṣad-liṅgas," in the dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī within the first part of the *Śrīśivarahasya*.
The Sixtieth Chapter, titled "The Praise of Skanda.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess Śivā; I shall declare to you that which is for your ultimate benefit.
O Goddess, that worship which has been prescribed for the gods and for men at all times— || 1 ||
That worship bestows infinite fruit and destroys the karma of births;
it is supreme consciousness itself, and that worship consists in the dissolution of the mind within it.

O Goddess of the gods, that worship which is common to all is indeed exceedingly difficult to accomplish for one who has not manifested [divine power], except through my grace and by the ripened fruits of one's penance.
Through yogas, sacrifices, and ascetic penances consisting of multitudes of great bliss,
he was constantly devoted to the ash-rite and habitually engaged in the recitation of the Rudra-mantra.
For one who is always marked with the triple ash-tilaka, who constantly wears rudrākṣa beads, who is devoted to the five-syllable mantra, and who is always a worshiper of the liṅga; || 5 ||
O Great Goddess, for one who worships me with bilva leaves at twilight, while eating only at night and performing worship and meditation on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days; (6)
O Goddess, for one who is disciplined and engaged in the practice of the Monday vow, who dwells in my sacred field, and who delights in Avimukta; || 7 ||
O Maheśvarī, for this worshiper of Viśveśvara, whether he be a god or a man,
it is likewise so at the meritorious Mahālaya and at Rudrakoṭi.
At Kālañjara, at Prabhāsa, at Puṣkara, at Amarakaṇṭaka, at Piṇḍāraka, at Kurukṣetra, at Mahākāla, and at Maheśvara; || 9 ||
In the holy Devadāru forest, in Naimiṣa, in Citrakūṭaka,
in the sacred Kedāra, in Kāmada, and in Vaidyanātha, O Maheśvarī.
And likewise at Śrīśaila, at Oṃkāra, and at the auspicious Veṇuvana;
at Āvaṭaṅka, Somanātha, Gokarṇa, and on the Tryambaka mountain.
Likewise, in the glorious Southern Kailāsa, in my Ekāmravana, on Vṛddhādri and Aruṇādri, and on the auspicious Goparvata; 12.
In the hidden lotus of the heart, in Japyeśa, in the white forest, in Gajāraṇya, on Ratnagiri, at Śrīkaṇṭha, and on Mātṛparvata; || 13 ||
At Koṭikā, at Maṅgala, and also at Puṇyadrutivana;
likewise at Kumbhaghoṇa, at Arjuna, and at Śrīsundaragiri. || 14 ||
Mādhavī, Tejinī, Devī, Kṣīriṇī, and likewise Kānanā;
[these are located] in the Śamī forest, the Bilva forest, at Ghaṭeśa, and in the Brahma forest.
On page 231: And in Chāyāvana, in Śrīvāñchya, likewise in the auspicious Vedavana, in Valmīka, in Vātapurī, on the Setu, and indeed on Gandhamādana.
While he, of virtuous character and devoted to eating only at night, was dwelling at Hālāsya, Śālikavana, Gajaśaila, and Mahendraka; || 17 ||
"However, after dwelling together for twelve years with one who is smeared with ashes, that knowledge of mine is obtained through the abundance of someone's good fortune. (18)
O Goddess, through many births, for one who possesses my grace,
is endowed with dispassion and devotion, and has the mind fixed upon the worship of the Self-liṅga;
Through the ripening of merit and in accordance with the purification of the mind,
that which is extremely difficult for humans to attain arises for the sake of destroying rebirth.
O Goddess, for those who follow various modes of conduct and dwellings, and whose minds are attached to sense objects, no desire whatsoever arises in anyone at all.
And for that man who, throughout many thousands of births as animals, immobile beings, and mobile creatures, has been endowed with accumulations of merit; || 22 ||
O Śivā, through my grace spiritual knowledge arises, and not otherwise,
for one who is devoted to and absorbed in the flow of the central channel, the fragrance, and so forth.
Especially for one who has mastered the Ātharvaśiras Upaniṣad along with its chapters and the Śikhā-mantra, who is devoted to the Jābāla-śruti, and who is established in the Śāmbhava path.
And for me, a Brāhmaṇa who constantly chants the Kaivalya-kālarudra and other mantras, who is habituated to the recitation of the Rudra-hymns, and who is ever devoted to the sacred ash.
O Gaurī, knowledge arises in some Śiva-yogi;
even among those striving as Śaivas, only a rare few know me in truth.
O Goddess, the means for attaining supreme knowledge is extremely difficult for men to obtain;
one should meditate upon me, four-armed, seated within the lotus of the chamber of the heart.
He holds a deer and an axe, is gentle, and is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
his radiance is as white as pure camphor, the essence of jasmine, and the moon.
His crown was illuminated by the crescent moon; his matted locks were as pure as the Gaṅgā;
he wore bracelets of serpent-kings and ornaments of precious gems. || 29 ||
Seated upon a lion-throne composed of many divine jewels,
he has three eyes, a blue throat, and a face equal in splendor to the light of the moon.
One should meditate for a moment, or even half a moment, upon [the Lord] together with Umā:
"I am He, the Lord Śiva; I am directly Rudra, Hari, and Brahmā."
I am Indra, Anala, Vāyu, Yama; I am Varuṇa and Aryaman;
I am Candra, Kubera, the Maruts, the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Suns.
Skanda, Vighneśvara, Nandikeśa, and the other Gaṇas—
all of these were born from me, and they have emerged this very day from me alone.
All the eternal Vedas were given by me alone for the sake of Brahmā;
the thousand-spoked Sudarśana was given by me alone to Viṣṇu.
Realizing "I am indeed [He]," one should meditate upon my sovereign form;
for by meditating thus, O Goddess, knowledge of me arises in men.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon me, the god Īśāna, within the solar orb—
the Lord with golden arms, golden beard, and golden hair, who is to be sought after.
O Goddess of gods, for the sake of liberation from all knots, that knowledge of the golden-hued Lord, the Master and Consort of Ambikā, arises within men.
Or else, by means of yoga, for one who is established in the practice of postures (āsana),
one should expel the air through exhalation (recaka) and then fill it with inhalation (pūraka).
During the *kumbhaka* [retention], the wise one should hold [the breath] for three *ghaṭikās*, like a water-jar;
for one whose mind is stainless because the impurities of the body have been burnt away by the fire of yoga.
O Goddess, like frost, smoke, a mirage, lightning, crystal, or a blazing lamp,
the light shines within the heart when it is filled with breaths.
By constant practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), indeed by that which is like the crest of wild rice (nīvāra-śikha),
I am that Great Self of Light, the unattached, auspicious Puruṣa.
He who, through yoga, knows me— the Great Lord who delights in the Self— as abiding within all beings, pervading the body from head to foot.
O Maheśvarī, for him the eight siddhis will certainly be accomplished;
upon his head resides the Great Self within a thousand-petaled lotus.
Indeed, the stream, shaped like a cow’s udder, flows with the single flavor of nectar;
having cleared away that skull, it flows continuously into the iḍā.
Piṅgalā, falling from the center of Kuṇḍalinī onto the tip of the flame—
this Vaiśvānara, my own form, resides within all embodied beings.
There, O Maheśvarī, by means of the moon’s nectar-rays in Piṅgalā,
that Maheśvara is the bliss of self-luminosity, eternally liberated.
Always sporting in the midst of the sky, ever moving within the space of the heart, I am conscious of the group of senses together with speech and the mind.
I am the essence of the *praṇava* and other sounds within the *parā*, *paśyantī*, and *vaikharī* stages of speech;
I am that Self which transcends the three abodes, the Puruṣa who dwells within the city of the body.
I am the Self, devoid of marks, possessing divine delight among gods, animals, and humans;
I am directly beyond name and form, and entirely free from egoism.
O Goddess, I indeed know in every way the tastes, the actions performed therein, the objects of the senses, the pleasure derived from them, and the sixteenth digit known as Kalā.
O Goddess, all those arts shine within me eternally;
I am the thinker, the perceiver, the enjoyer, the knower, and the Lord of higher knowledge.
I alone am the hearer of what is heard, likewise the smeller, and the seer through sight and so forth; for I am indeed the seer of seeing.
Just as the great neck of a tortoise, O Śivā, may become short or long.
Just as flowing rivers, transcending their names, forms, and qualities,
go to their end in the ocean, so do those rays of the sun enter the Lord.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, just as rays of light spread forth when the sun has risen, so does the world expand in my presence.
Just as the lotus family blooms through the rays of the sun, and just as iron needles move by the proximity of a magnet; so too does this [intellect] function.
O Goddess, through the ripening of time and karma, the world thus acts intensely in my presence throughout its maintenance, destruction, and birth.
Thus, having created and entered that very [universe] by way of its names, qualities, and forms—known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara—as before, age after age. (57)
O beloved, I first create myself alone, and from that, the manifold world comes into being,
just as tiny sparks arise from a fire.
I am indeed Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, and Soma;
I am the Manus, the Pitṛs, the wise sages, the stars, the constellations, and likewise the planets.
I alone am this eternal one, both the stationary and the moving;
I am all, transcending all sense-organs and qualities within all bodies.
I alone am the enjoyer of all, the locus of the performer of all actions;
I am not attached to birth, death, or the states of existence.
I am unattached and indeed untainted; I am both external and internal to all.
Likewise, O Śaṅkarī, I am the one who dwells within and am free from all suffering.
He who knows me thus—he is mine, and I am within his heart;
I do not perish for him, and he does not perish because of truth.

O Great Goddess, Yoga and Sāṅkhya have been thus described by me to you—[this is the reading "O Goddess, they have been told by me to you"]. These two are the essence of my heart. O Goddess, I shall now also describe the mode of worship which is common to all.
(Page 233) "I am the Lord without marks; I always abide within the mark.
Just as milk that has entered a cow is not seen in her horns and other parts [of her body]."
O Śivā, just as [milk] is seen in the udder, so am I present within all;
yet for those unable to meditate upon me in the heart through the yoga of knowledge, [I appear thus].
The supreme worship performed at the Liṅga by those who wear the ashes of Śambhu,
who are adorned with my Puṇḍra marks, and who possess excellent Rudrākṣa bracelets;
By the study of the Rudrādhyāya, by the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra,
and by those who have placed even a single bilva leaf upon my head;
O Goddess, I accept that [offering] from my devotees, and I bestow knowledge upon him;
O Śaṅkarī, it is my vow that I shall make him a vessel of knowledge.
O Auspicious One, neither by the various duties of other castes and stages of life, nor even by tens of millions of ritual acts, does my supreme satisfaction arise. (70)
Not by sixteen great gifts, nor by single-day or multi-day sacrificial sessions, nor by the giving of water-stalls and step-wells, nor by the bestowing of maidens, food, and so forth. (71)
O Goddess, somehow or other, devotion to my worship may arise among the Brahmins in Puṇḍravardhana and among the hosts of wandering mendicants.
O Great Goddess, there is no joy at all equal to that which I feel toward those who wear my mark;
one who constantly wears the sacred ash is indeed a vessel for my very knowledge.
Through the worship and meditation upon the Śivaliṅga, the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya,
and the chanting of the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), one becomes a resident of my sacred field.
It is said that only one who wears the triple mark of ashes (tripuṇḍra) should be accepted, and no other;
a twice-born man should not wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), even by mistake or out of delusion.
On the contrary, everything performed by him leads only to hell;
if he should act out of negligence, he shall fall downward along with his ancestors.
Seeing one marked with an upright *puṇḍra*, I close my eyes today;
for by beholding me through my grace, O Śivā, that knowledge arises.
"O Goddess, when my eyes are closed—[and there is also a reading: 'by the closing of which']—how will knowledge arise?
My linga on the summit of Kailāsa is known by the name Kailāseśvara."
Though invisible even to gods, animals, humans, and others, it grants all desires;
by mere remembrance, it bestows spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) wherever one may be.
O Śaṅkarī, the majesty of this Liṅga is indeed not known even by the Vedas, nor by the gods, the asuras, the Manus, or even the lords of the Gaṇas.
The Liṅga known as Kailāseśvara bestows liberation;
O Goddess, this king of Liṅgas is indeed the eternal Brahman.
It is the giver of joy to my very heart, the bestower of heaven and liberation, the raft for crossing the shoreless ocean of worldly existence, and the medicine for the disease of birth.
O Śivā, this supreme Liṅga, which is the very essence of the entirety of Vedānta,
has not been told by me to anyone, nor should it be told to just anyone.
By the power of this Liṅga,
all the creators (Brahmās) expand the creation of the universe in every Kalpa, together with their own sons.
O Goddess of the Gods, the earth, the rivers, the forests, the gods, animals, and humans,
as well as the worlds and those who perceive them— He, the Creator, extends all these from their beginning until their end.
Indeed, in every kalpa, by the power of this liṅga, the Viṣṇus,
through their great and pure discus, shall be the slayers of the lords of the Daityas.
O Śivā, all those who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha are to be known as the husbands of Lakṣmī; likewise, O Ambikā, in every kalpa, they are the Rudras who are the husbands of Gaurī.
By the power of this liṅga, even at the time of universal dissolution,
they withdraw the entire web of the world, including the asuras and humans, likewise mangled by tridents.
O Śivā, at every kalpa, the Manus along with Indra, as well as the gods and asuras, together with the ṛṣis and the ancestors, attain dissolution into this liṅga.
O Śivā, at the time of the great dissolution, O Auspicious One, contract this divine form of mine— the support of all— which consists of the networks of the worlds and the cosmic egg.
O Goddess, together with you and the foremost of my attendants, headed by Skanda and Heramba,
I always dwell within the Liṅga known as Kailāseśvara.
O Goddess, though established as both without and with attributes, I create and I withdraw this entire web of the universe, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
I withdraw [the universe] in the same way at the end; O Śaṅkarī, this is my play. I am one who sports in the Self, delights in the Self, and am the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
I am the cause of causes, the Lord of lords,
the conscious one among the conscious, and eternal, O Supreme Goddess.
I am possessed of a cause, yet I am the overlord of the lords of causes; O Goddess, I have no progenitor at all.

As the Lord endowed with the nature of Time, I preside over others; I am the Sovereign who meditates (or, according to another reading, "I am the Lord who is to be meditated upon"), possessed of attributes, omniscient, and the abode of all beings.
This has been told to you, O Goddess, which reveals the meaning of the secret;
this must not be given even to those who are secret [initiates], but impart it to the devotees. 96.
O Supreme Goddess, this is the primordial secret portion of Śiva;
O fair-browed one, it is this secret knowledge, a compendium of esoteric wisdom.
O auspicious Mother, this must not be disclosed to anyone in jest;
it is the eternal secret of the infinite Vedas.
O Goddess of the gods, out of my affection for you, this secret has been declared by me, revealed to the hosts of deities and sages.
O Goddess, this most excellent secret, more hidden than the hidden, should always be held in the heart;
it is the first and supreme portion of the Secret Ocean of the Jewels of Śiva.
"Your earring-jewel has been described today as something most secret;
truth, truth, and again truth—it is said while raising one's arm."
Having spoken thus to Girijā, the Lord Maheśvara embraced her and sported with Śivā on the summit of Kailāsa as he pleased.
The Goddess said:
"In the rite of washing garments, you possess the nature of the thousand-rayed sun; in the offering of flowers, the nature of Viṣṇu;
in fragrance, the nature of the wind (or, according to another reading, the nature of the bearer of fragrance); and in the cooking of great food, the lordship of Agni."
O Blessed One, O ocean of the waters of compassion, O Paśupati, O Lord, O teacher of the three worlds, there is a golden pit within this vessel; may I perform service for you. 103.
The Ganges became the water for your rinsing of the mouth;
the moon, the abode of nectar, was held by you as an ornament for your crest;
and even the remnants of the flesh of the three worlds, once devoured, served for the satisfaction of you who fill the belly of the triple universe. (p. 235)
Except for you, the Lord of Knowledge, this praise of mine, though my speech be most feeble, [is offered]. 104.
The Sūta said:
Having heard that the great Kailāsa, the abode of the Liṅga of Maheśa-Sundara,
is like a mountain of cotton consumed by fire for the mass of the great ocean of worldly existence;
The mountain of evil comes to rest, and the heap of merit increases further; these stories of the boundless qualities of Śiva’s devotee are sprouts for the joy of Śambhu. 105.
Even in heaven, there is no distinction for men who possess nets of merit containing countless virtues, who are like the nectar-yielding celestial trees, and who are as playful as flocks of swans.
For listeners, this alone is the beautiful, singular essence of the great Śaiva nectar; would it not yield fruit through the narration of the burden of the various duties of worldly existence?
What wonder is there if one shows devotion for even a moment to the lotus feet of the Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain?
May he never again encounter the burden of saṃsāra, which is like a great, devouring crocodile. || 107 ||
Skanda:

Upon the crest of glorious Kailāsa, [there dwells] the one renowned as the Father of the Three Worlds, whose boundless fortitude serves as the bolt for the door of the feet of those who desire liberation from the people trapped in the prison of this worthless cycle of existence.

For the sake of the Goddess’s liberation, through her own skillful means, she alone is the boat for crossing the river of the abode of sins—a boat bound to her feet by love constantly cultivated, the sole limit of the bliss of the Vedas (or, according to another reading, the sole limit of the bliss of knowledge). As for those wretched thieves, they are nothing at all. 108.
For men who are the sole leaders among the noble and who are travelers on the path of the narrated stories of Śiva,

that nectar which was extracted from the heart of Maheśa by Jaigīṣavya for the sake of the Great Assembly has been told to me by the Goddess out of her compassionate regard; that very thing has now been spoken by me.
The Śaiva divine secret, most wonderful, abides as the essence of Vedānta.
Having drunk [this], let those whose minds are full [of joy] always meditate upon the state of Śiva for the sake of liberation.
Jaigīṣavya:
My mind has turned away from all objects, whether desired or undesired; I consider the supreme realm to be one that produces neither the misery nor the joy characteristic of this world.

However, my mind is satisfied and serene, wishing to hear the wonderful stories of the eightfold-formed Lord (Aṣṭamūrti), which remove the suffering of Śipiviṣṭa and destroy millions of evil glances. (110)
Nothing has been gained by me from the worship of the Lord— who is like a great lion that tears apart intoxicated elephants— since he has shaken off all sins;
for him who acts according to his own will and is unrestrained, even the system of castes and stages of life is merely a stage.
Or rather, what need have I for your beautiful stories concerning the great Śambhu, who has emerged from your lotus-like mouth? || 111 ||
Drinking again and again, I rejoice and dance, being free from rebirth and misfortune. || 112 ||

O you who, by your devotion to Śambhu, alone conquered the wicked Krauñca demon who had begun his assault upon the sinless; for us, the sight of you is a blessed day and a glorious dawn. O wielder of the spear, you are indeed a hero whose very stories bring prosperity.
Due to serving the feet of the Lord, sense objects appear to me like poison;

even these sages have become like householders, for they have been freed from the continuous stream of worldly suffering by you. (Alternatively: "Even these householders have achieved their purpose.")
Sprinkled by showers of joy arising from the manifestation of the Śiva-tattva, the sages, gods, and Gaṇas [exclaim]:
"O, you are our Guru! What else could be given to you by those of us who possess such fortune other than prostration? (115)

The sages said: O Śambhu, may your purifying stories— born from the assembly of the pure lotus-like faces of your six sons— immerse us, who are weary from the burden of saṃsāra, in the abundance of the essence of compassion.
O Blessed One, by virtue of meeting this sage who wields the Śārṅga bow, we have obtained the fruit of liberation;
what wonder is there in this? We have been purified by the essence of the stories concerning the Three-eyed Lord. 116.
The Gaṇas:

O Śambhu, it is said that those who worship by meditating on the feet of the Moon-crested Lord, having heard from your mouth the purifying stories of Śambhu— which are infused with the aesthetic flavor of the emotion of intense devotion— [are filled with joy].
O Lord, the preeminence of the bliss of dwelling on Kailāsa is not to be counted as anything at all;
we are simply exceedingly satisfied by the sight of your pure face. (117)
O Skanda, we lords of sages have been drenched by the pure streams of honey from your lotus-face;
we have been sustained by the stories of Śambhu— whose activities are boundless and whose supreme bark-garment is the king of mountains—
and who, for the sake of liberating men from their state of bondage, assumed a form that dispels the vast mass of impurities of the primordial multitude of beings.
For the pacification of the forest fire arising from the delusion of darkness, and for the removal of unfathomable suffering. || 118 ||

Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Īśvara— engrossed in the tasks of creation, preservation, and destruction— are perpetually immersed in boundless suffering; their minds are scorched by the heat of sins born of karma, and they remain mired in the abode of sufferings such as birth and so forth.
Having attained the path arising from the lotus feet of Your Lordship, O Peaceful One, what else indeed remains for us to seek for liberation? 119.
Those hosts, the lords of the gods and sages, praised the Kumāra;
having bowed down, they were all delighted. O twice-born ones, listen now to that hymn of praise.
O incomparable refuge, maternal uncle of the gods and others, Lord of the Earth, source of compassion, granter of desires, destroyer of desire!
O you of beautiful luster born from the Śara forest, O slayer of Tāraka, protect us! 121.
O you whose lovely body is caressed by the sprout-like hands of Haimavatī, born from the essence of fire;
O destroyer of Tāraka, protect us, O ocean of the heart of Mukunda, the enemy of Pura! 122.

O slayer of Tāraka, protect us with your eye that resembles the autumnal moon, with six faces, and with eyes like boundless lotuses— by your own innate childhood which is free from all adventitious conditions.
O son of Girijā, you whose mountain was pierced by arrows; O son of the celestial river, possessing the luster of gold;
O you born from fire, mounted upon a peacock; O slayer of Tāraka, protect us!
Victory to you, beloved of the brahmins, conqueror of the minds of heroes, devoted to your devotees; O auspicious one, salutations!
Victory to you, Śākha, Viśākha, and Kumāra; salutations, protect us, O slayer of Tāraka! 125.
Be before me, be all around me; O Blessed One, protect my burden on the path!
O Victorious One among those free from passion, O Slayer of Māra, protect us, your followers.

(Verse 127) Thus, for those who recollect the Kukkuṭaketa mountain and chant this "Sixfold Hymn to the Six-faced One," there is no exhaustion anywhere for embodied beings who bow before the Moon-bearer (Śiva), who is the source of all joy.
Sūta:
This world, with its blossoming lotuses resembling bamboo stalks, is as minute as an atom;
yet here stands this great sun, the benefactor, like the snowy king of mountains.
Indeed, for the delight of the blessed people, Svarbhānu [eclipsed] Himāṃśu (the Moon), yet this [moon] remains as a single, beautiful dwelling spread across the sky in its proper form. 128.
When the blow of his feet has fallen, the great earth trembles in distress; the lord of serpents shrieks, the herd of elephants wallows, and the host of mountains reels;
while the ocean, awakened by the roar, surges upward, and the daughter of the mountain’s lover remains wide awake.
Behold now my *tāṇḍava* dance, which brings both wonder and terror to the three worlds.

May he protect you— he whose lotus-stalk is the mass of rays from the moon upon his crown, which is unceasingly weary; who gladdens the *cakravāka* birds of the celestial river with the illusory splendor of the setting sun, a radiance effortlessly emerging from the jewels on the hoods of serpents agitated by the fatigue of their exertion.
May the Tandava dance of Dhurjati, in which the bird of Brahma’s chariot flees from the fragrance of severed [limbs], be for my [protection]. 130.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Praise of Skanda," in the first part of the glorious Śivarahasya.
Thus ends the first part of the Śrī Śivarahasya. || 1 ||
